title: ‘Nostradamus of AI’ Leopold Aschenbrenner didn’t have the crystal ball seeing hedge fund portfolio dip 67%
text: ‘Nostradamus of AI’ Leopold Aschenbrenner didn’t have the crystal ball seeing hedge fund portfolio dip 67%. The celebrated crystal ball of the “Nostradamus of AI” hasn’t merely gone cloudy — it has rolled off the table and shattered on the parlor floor. Wall Street breathed a huge sigh of relief last week as an AI-focused hedge fund called Situational Awareness reportedly sold most of its portfolio — reportedly down 67% last month on the backfiring of debt-fueled bets on chipmakers and assorted artificial-intelligence firms — to billionaire Ken Griffin’s Citadel. While the rescue quelled fears of a forced liquidation of the $20 billion fund that could tank the markets, it nevertheless left trading desks across town asking the same question: Is this the canary in the coal mine? Are we finally seeing the start of the dot-com bubble of AI? The prevailing sentiment was best summed up by a veteran Wall Street sage who has seen a lot of flameouts in his day. Let’s just say he wasn’t impressed by Leopold Aschenbrenner, the 25-year-old German-born “Nostradamus” figure who is the founder of Situational Awareness. (Great name for an organization in dire need of a wake-up call, by the way.) “Just your typical leveraged idiot who was right until he was wrong,” the source said, adding that the implosion is a “one-off.” Another source waxed slightly more poetic: “Ah, yes — a 25-year-old kid who’s a billionaire on paper because of a bubble. Everybody thinks they can raise a fund but they forget about how hard it is to be a good fiduciary.” Still, a third trusted source felt there was room for conversation: “A significant issue. Not viewed as systemic right now. I wonder if that changes as more problems arise.” Indeed, the fact is that most of Wall Street is closely monitoring the Situational Awareness situation because they were holding many of the same positions as Aschenbrenner. Another top hedge fund manager I won’t name tells me he has been getting crushed on similar investments in chipmakers essential to the AI supply chain, as well as other companies feeding off this technology. Irrational exuberance Many of them, like the erstwhile wunderkind, had been killing it for the past year, powered by exuberance — or maybe irrational exuberance — that AI is not just game-changing technology for mankind, but also something that will throw off tons of profits. But unlike Aschenbrenner, my source isn’t a novice investor who attracted a cult following that included a few big players with his AI pixie dust. Aschenbrenner graduated from Columbia at age 19, so he must be smart, the thinking goes. He worked at OpenAI, so surely he is a visionary like Sam Altman. He wrote a viral treatise that predicted AI’s dominance across business and culture, so he must be the next Satoshi Nakamoto, right? Well, if you also noticed, there’s not much investment experience on this résumé. Unlike my guy who took some losses in the AI selloff, Aschenbrenner hasn’t been through enough market swings to survive this one easily. Maybe more to the point, unlike Mr. Situational Awareness, my source isn’t 400% leveraged. Surviving market upheavals like the granddaddy of them all in 2008 will teach you that, or in his words, “Sam Altman is a smart guy, but you wouldn’t want him managing a portfolio.” Griffin, of course, is one of the world’s great investors. He doesn’t take risks out of the goodness of his heart. He must see some value in what Aschenbrenner stitched together. After buying it at depressed prices that markets often create when they’re in panic mode, he’s going to make some money when things level out. And yet, I’ve seen this act before, a rumbling before the dot-com crash of 2000 that the excitement over something new and possibly transformational means every company in its ecosystem will change the world and make boatloads of money. In fact, just a few did. Ditto for the 2008 financial crisis. The heart of that problem was securitization. Banks can keep selling mortgages and various loans to anyone even without a job because you eliminate risk by mixing the good loans with the bad ones. But who’s to say what’s a good or bad loan when everyone “thinks” housing prices will keep rising — until, of course, they didn’t. In the bowels of the AI ecosystem I’m hearing similar stories. One big investor at a major pension fund tells me that the “amortized” cash returns with any near-term visibility on most AI companies he’s seeing are negligible. He loves using AI tools, but many of them are free or priced cheap to gain a following. They can’t stay that way forever if they’re going to pay for an infrastructure build that demands hundreds of billions in borrowing. Capital is becoming increasingly scarce for anyone but the largest players, meaning VC shops in this space will face difficulties getting funding and withstanding margin calls on businesses that need more time. A shakeout is coming, my source told me. Situational Awareness is the coal mine’s canary.

title: The Signal Every Global Trader Watches: Inside the Power of the Relative Strength Index
text: The Signal Every Global Trader Watches: Inside the Power of the Relative Strength Index. In trading floors from New York to Tokyo, one technical indicator continues to cut through the noise of volatile markets with remarkable consistency. The relative strength index, commonly known as RSI, has evolved from a niche analytical tool into a cornerstone of global market strategy. Whether analysts are dissecting movements in the S&P 500, evaluating emerging market equities, or tracking cryptocurrency swings, the relative strength index sits at the center of the conversation. And its influence is only growing. Originally developed by J. Welles Wilder Jr. in 1978 and introduced in his book New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems, the relative strength index measures the speed and magnitude of price movements on a scale of 0 to 100. Traditionally, a reading above 70 signals that an asset may be overbought, while a reading below 30 suggests oversold conditions. These thresholds have guided countless buy and sell decisions over the decades. But what makes the RSI uniquely powerful today is how traders are layering it with modern data infrastructure, algorithmic systems, and cross-asset analysis to create far more nuanced signals than Wilder ever imagined. Global equity markets have become increasingly sensitive to momentum indicators, and the relative strength index plays a leading role in this shift. In periods of elevated market volatility, institutional investors rely on RSI readings to identify potential reversal points and manage downside risk. When major indices approach overbought territory — as they have during several high-momentum rallies in recent years — fund managers and algorithmic traders often reduce exposure proactively. This collective behavior, driven partly by RSI signals, can itself move markets, creating a self-reinforcing dynamic that amplifies the indicator’s relevance. What is particularly noteworthy is how the relative strength index has crossed over into asset classes that didn’t exist when it was first developed. In cryptocurrency markets, RSI has become one of the most-referenced indicators among retail and professional traders alike. Bitcoin and altcoins are known for extreme price swings, and RSI helps participants identify when a rally may be running out of steam or when a sharp selloff might be approaching exhaustion. During major crypto bull runs, sustained RSI readings above 80 have historically preceded significant corrections, offering a valuable heads-up even amid euphoric sentiment. Beyond equities and crypto, the relative strength index is reshaping how analysts approach commodity markets and foreign exchange. Oil traders watch RSI closely when geopolitical tensions drive rapid price spikes, using the indicator to distinguish between momentum-backed breakouts and short-lived volatility. In forex markets, where currency pairs can shift sharply on central bank commentary or economic data releases, RSI readings help traders assess whether a move has technical backing or is likely to reverse. The indicator’s versatility across such diverse asset classes is a primary reason it has maintained its relevance for nearly five decades. One of the more sophisticated evolutions in RSI application involves divergence analysis. Bullish divergence — where an asset’s price makes a new low but the relative strength index forms a higher low — can signal underlying buying pressure building beneath the surface. Bearish divergence, the inverse scenario, can warn of weakening momentum even when prices appear to be climbing. Professional traders who combine divergence signals with support and resistance levels and broader macroeconomic context have found this approach delivers more actionable insights than relying on RSI thresholds alone. It is this layered thinking that separates profitable application from mechanical rule-following. Algorithmic and quantitative trading firms have integrated the relative strength index into complex multi-factor models that execute trades across global markets in milliseconds. When a critical mass of these systems simultaneously react to similar RSI thresholds, the result can be sharp, coordinated price movements that appear sudden to casual observers. This is one reason why market watchers increasingly argue that understanding RSI is not optional — ignoring it means ignoring a force that is actively shaping price action at scale. Retail investors have also embraced the relative strength index at an unprecedented rate, aided by trading platforms that display RSI charts in real time with no technical setup required. This democratization of access has created a broader base of market participants using the same tool, which paradoxically can increase its predictive power as more traders act on similar signals. The indicator has become something of a shared language in global financial markets, spoken fluently by hedge fund quants and individual investors alike. What the enduring dominance of the relative strength index ultimately reveals is that markets, for all their complexity and modernity, are still driven by human psychology — by greed, fear, momentum, and exhaustion. RSI quantifies these emotional cycles in mathematical form and makes them visible on a chart. In a world flooded with data and competing analytical frameworks, that clarity is invaluable. As long as markets continue to move and traders continue to seek edge over uncertainty, the relative strength index will remain one of the most powerful lenses through which global market behavior can be understood.

title: Trump’s Polls Hit New Low—With One Notable Exception
text: Trump’s Polls Hit New Low—With One Notable Exception. President Donald Trump’s latest poll numbers have sunk to the lowest levels of his presidency—and are nearing historic lows for any second-term president. There’s one exception, however: a lone past president who ranked even lower. Trump has responded by repeatedly making false claims about his approval ratings. “The highest they’ve ever been,” he preened on Truth Social in June. Late last year, he boasted that his poll numbers were the highest of his entire political career when, in fact, they were the lowest of his second term. He has also claimed he won “all 50 states” in 2020. He didn’t. He lost the election. “He’s always going to project strength regardless of what the numbers are, and he’ll say they’re fake anyway,” Republican strategist Douglas Heye told The New York Times. The latest abysmal polls have found that only roughly a third of Americans—33 percent—support Trump amid his increasingly unpopular Iran war and climbing gas and grocery prices. The findings across a number of surveys are the lowest of his presidency and nearly as low as those of any second-term president since the 1940s, when polling began, the Times noted. Richard Nixon scored lower than Trump—with only 24 percent support—but that was just days before his resignation in the wake of the Watergate scandal. Trump previously scored nearly as low as he has in the current findings following the violent storming of the Capitol by Trump supporters on Jan. 6, 2021. Despite Trump’s inflated claims, while he has won a plurality of votes, he has never been elected by a majority of voters in the elections he has won—though he frequently insists he won in a landslide. He also has never been supported by a majority of respondents in Gallup polling. So many Democratic voters “strongly disapprove” of Trump that they’re more likely to vote this year, handing Republicans yet another headache. One sliver of support, however, is hanging on: Trump himself. He’s apparently convinced that Republicans have the midterms in the bag, thanks to him. He protects himself from the bad news by dismissing any and all damning surveys. “Polls are very dishonest, just like a lot of reporters,” he told journalists during the Group of 7 summit in France in June. Days later, he cited his own survey putting his approval rating at 50 percent. Then he arbitrarily boosted that figure by an additional 15 points. “Other Polls have my Approval Rating at 65%, and more!” he boasted.

title: Breaking Down the Equity Premium and What It Really Signals for Investors
text: Breaking Down the Equity Premium and What It Really Signals for Investors. Few concepts in finance carry as much weight — or generate as much debate — as the equity premium. At its core, the equity premium represents the excess return that investing in the stock market provides over a risk-free rate, typically measured against government bonds. It sounds straightforward, but the forces that drive it, the methods used to estimate it, and the implications it holds for investors are anything but simple. For anyone serious about understanding market dynamics, the equity premium isn’t just an academic curiosity — it’s a foundational signal that shapes capital allocation decisions at every level. The historical equity premium in the United States has averaged roughly 4% to 6% annually over long time horizons, depending on the methodology and time period selected. This means that equity investors have historically been compensated at a meaningful premium for taking on the additional risk associated with stocks versus holding a safe, government-backed asset. But averages can be misleading. The premium fluctuates considerably across different market cycles, economic environments, and geopolitical periods, which is precisely why analysts and portfolio managers continue to monitor it so closely. There are two distinct lenses through which the equity premium is examined: the realized premium and the expected premium. The realized equity premium is backward-looking — it describes what investors actually earned above the risk-free rate over a given historical period. The expected equity premium, by contrast, is forward-looking and inherently more uncertain. It attempts to estimate what the market will deliver in excess returns going forward, incorporating current valuations, earnings growth expectations, and prevailing interest rates. In a world where equity markets are richly valued by historical standards and where interest rates have spent years at elevated levels, estimating the expected equity premium has become one of the most contested exercises in institutional finance. One reason the equity premium matters so much is its direct connection to the cost of capital. When companies or analysts build discounted cash flow models, the equity premium feeds directly into the discount rate used to value future earnings. A higher assumed equity premium pushes discount rates up and valuations down. A lower assumed premium does the opposite. This feedback loop means that subtle changes in how the equity premium is estimated can ripple through corporate valuations, infrastructure project financing, and public pension fund assumptions in ways that are far from trivial. The so-called equity premium puzzle, first articulated by economists Rajnish Mehra and Edward Prescott in the 1980s, remains one of the most celebrated unresolved problems in financial economics. Their research found that the historical equity premium was far too large to be explained by standard models of investor risk aversion. If investors were as mildly risk-averse as traditional utility theory assumed, they should not have demanded — or received — such a substantial premium for holding equities. Decades of subsequent research have offered competing explanations, ranging from catastrophe risk and rare disaster theory to behavioral finance frameworks that emphasize loss aversion, investor myopia, and the psychological cost of watching portfolio values decline. More recently, researchers have explored how demographic shifts, technological disruption, and changes in corporate ownership structures may be altering the equity premium’s trajectory. As passive investing has become dominant and institutional capital has grown more sophisticated, some theorists argue that traditional risk premia may compress over time. Others counter that geopolitical uncertainty, inflationary regimes, and the concentration of market returns in a narrow band of mega-cap technology companies have introduced new forms of risk that may actually sustain or expand the premium over time. The debate is genuinely unresolved and actively evolving. For practical investors, the equity premium serves as a reality check. During periods of extreme market optimism, when forward price-to-earnings ratios stretch well above historical norms, the implied equity premium often compresses to uncomfortably thin levels — signaling that the market may be pricing in too little additional return for the risk being assumed. Conversely, during market dislocations or sharp selloffs, the implied equity premium can spike, which has historically coincided with attractive long-term entry points. Monitoring this metric, alongside yield spreads, earnings growth forecasts, and macro conditions, gives investors a more complete picture than stock prices alone ever could. The equity premium is ultimately a measure of collective market psychology as much as it is a financial ratio. It captures how much compensation investors demand for uncertainty, volatility, and the possibility of loss. Understanding it — not just as a historical average but as a living, dynamic reflection of market conditions — is one of the clearest ways to cut through the noise and engage with markets on an informed, intellectually honest basis. For anyone navigating financial markets with long-term goals in mind, the equity premium deserves a permanent place at the center of their analytical framework.

title: The Signal Traders Watch Before Everything Else: Risk-On Sentiment
text: The Signal Traders Watch Before Everything Else: Risk-On Sentiment. Before the headlines hit, before the earnings reports land, and before the central bank statements drop, seasoned traders are already watching something else entirely. They are watching the mood. Specifically, they are watching whether the market is in a risk-on or risk-off posture — because that single read on collective investor psychology can telegraph where prices are heading long before the broader public catches on. Understanding risk-on sentiment is not a luxury for professional traders alone. It is an essential lens for anyone who wants to make sense of market direction in real time. Risk-on sentiment refers to the collective appetite investors have for higher-yielding, higher-volatility assets. When this sentiment is present, money flows away from safe-haven instruments like government bonds, gold, and defensive currencies, and floods into equities, commodities, high-yield debt, and growth-oriented sectors. The shift is not subtle. It shows up in asset prices simultaneously, in currency pairs, in equity index futures, in credit spreads, and in the behavior of individual sectors. What makes it so powerful as a market signal is precisely this breadth — it moves markets in multiple asset classes at once, confirming or undermining price action across the board. The mechanics behind risk-on sentiment are deeply tied to macroeconomic conditions. When investors feel confident about economic growth, corporate earnings expansion, and accommodative monetary policy, they willingly take on more risk in exchange for higher returns. Interest rate expectations play a massive role here. Lower or declining rates reduce the opportunity cost of holding riskier assets, which fans the flames of risk appetite. Conversely, tightening cycles, geopolitical shocks, or unexpected economic weakness tend to extinguish that appetite quickly, triggering risk-off rotations that can be swift and unforgiving. One of the most reliable ways to track risk-on sentiment in practice is through cross-asset correlations. Traders often monitor the relationship between the U.S. dollar and commodity-linked currencies like the Australian or Canadian dollar. When the Aussie and Loonie are strengthening against the greenback, that frequently signals a risk-on environment. Similarly, the VIX — Wall Street’s volatility index — is a closely watched gauge. A falling VIX alongside rising equity prices is a textbook risk-on signature. High-yield credit spreads narrowing against investment-grade bonds is another confirming data point that institutional investors watch closely. What makes risk-on sentiment particularly valuable for market direction is its tendency to create self-reinforcing momentum. When enough participants believe the environment is favorable for risk assets, they buy, prices rise, sentiment improves further, and more buyers enter. This feedback loop can sustain trends for weeks or even months. Momentum strategies are essentially built on this dynamic — capturing the extended drift that risk-on periods create. Of course, the same logic applies in reverse, which is why risk-off episodes can feel so disorderly and sharp when they arrive. The unwind of crowded risk-on positions happens quickly as confidence evaporates. Sector rotation within equity markets offers another window into risk-on behavior. During genuine risk-on periods, cyclical sectors like technology, consumer discretionary, industrials, and materials tend to outperform. Defensive sectors — utilities, healthcare staples, and consumer staples — lag. Growth stocks with elevated valuations attract buyers willing to pay premium prices for future earnings potential. This rotation pattern is not just descriptive; it is predictive. Identifying early sector rotation signals can alert attentive investors to a shifting risk environment before it is fully priced into major indices. It is also worth noting that risk-on sentiment does not exist in a vacuum. It is shaped by narrative as much as by data. Central bank communication, geopolitical developments, and even social media-driven investor enthusiasm can ignite or dampen risk appetite rapidly. The rise of algorithmic trading has amplified these dynamics, with sentiment-reading models scanning news flows and social signals to position ahead of slower-moving participants. This means that today’s market participants need to be not only data-aware but also narrative-aware — understanding not just what the numbers say, but what story investors are collectively telling themselves about the future. Ultimately, risk-on sentiment is one of the most honest readings available in financial markets. It reflects the aggregate judgment of millions of participants about whether the future looks worth betting on. When that sentiment is strong and broadening, markets tend to climb with conviction. When it falters, even fundamentally sound assets can face selling pressure simply because the mood has turned. Tracking this signal carefully — through cross-asset behavior, volatility measures, sector leadership, and credit market dynamics — gives investors a meaningful edge in anticipating where market direction is headed next, rather than simply reacting after the fact.

title: Mamdani’s city-owned supermarkets will fight the one force no city has ever beaten: the market
text: Mamdani’s city-owned supermarkets will fight the one force no city has ever beaten: the market. Zohran Mamdani stormed into office brandishing the banner of “affordability,” and almost singlehandedly pushed the issue to the center of today’s political debate. Of all the charismatic, 34-year-old Mayor’s initiatives aimed at lowering living costs, the one that’s garnered the most coverage is his proposal to get Gotham into the grocery business. The city-owned food store initiative looks so radical, even for this avowed democratic socialist, because it puts a city in direct competition versus an immense, entrenched private industry. On his other big “affordability” initiatives, providing free bus service and freezing rent on one million apartments, Mamdani’s simply using his regulatory and budget powers in the Democratic mayors’ traditional vein of tightening price controls on housing and delivering more freebees This one’s different: It’s extraordinarily rare for a municipality to challenge local businesses by starting its own enterprises that aim to do the same thing. The only major example: city-backed companies that battle the Verizons and Comcasts to supply broadband. They’re all either struggling, or already flopped. Mamdani’s predecessor Eric Adams shuttered the $2 billion fiber-optic buildout started a few years earlier under Mayor Bill de Blasio. As for supermarkets, Chicago last year killed plans for a city-owned emporium as impractical. Kansas City, apparently the only major metro ever to open a taxpayer-funded supermarket, ended the failed foray in early 2025. Hence, Mamdani’s plan would probably reign as the biggest push any city’s ever made to launch its own business amid a galaxy of private players. The Mayor’s identified a big problem. New Yorkers indeed suffer from extremely high prices for everything from chicken to eggs to milk. The city’s riddled with “food desert” neighborhoods where residents often can’t find much other than processed items nearby, and must travel 20 minutes or more to reach outlets that offer wide choices of fresh foods at low cost. But that problem’s almost totally self-inflicted. Contrary to Mamdani’s claim that “the private market alone has not delivered affordable, full-service grocery options,” here’s the real rub: A web of antiquated regulations—and one in particular that effectively bans big stores where they’re needed most—is blocking major chains from deploying billions of their own capital to open far more of the kinds of giant extravaganzas featuring baseball-field length stretches of checkout lanes that bring far lower stickers to the suburbs just beyond Gotham’s borders. In fact, the Mamdani “solution” would make things much worse by providing rich subsidies enabling his stores to underprice private markets in the same area, potentially forcing them to close. That outcome would extend the deserts as stalwarts exit and the ones that remain raise prices. What New York needs isn’t city stores that threaten the often already struggling purveyors already here, but sweeping deregulation that encourages the entry of what consumer crave, far more supersized supermarkets that offer the widest choices and best prices.. As Mitchell Korbey, chair of the zoning group at Herrick, Feinstein, LLP, who’s represented many large chains in their efforts to establish stores in New York, told Fortune , “Many new, large supermarkets would open if the city would lift the rules that have long outlived their usefulness.” Adds E.J. Antoni, an economist at the Heritage Foundation, “New York is really unaffordable by design, not as a natural outcome of the free market. Its zoning regulations create artificial monopolies that reduce competition and limit what would without those rules be far more and better places for people shop.” Mamdani plans five city-owned stores offering super-cheap prices for family essentials The mayor’s rationale: Grocery prices have jumped 30% since the onset of the pandemic, so the City will reverse that hit by allowing residents to purchase a basic shopping cart of goods 30% cheaper. The blueprint calls for five city-owned supermarkets, one in each borough that will cost $70 million in total to construct, and all operate under the single brand “NYC Groceries.” The first two are already planned, one covering 15,000 square feet in notorious food desert, the Hunts Point neighborhood of the Bronx set to open in 2027 in a former juvenile detention center, and a second in the La Marqueta district of East Harlem, another low-income area, at 9,000 square feet slated for 2029. The stores would offer all the items you’d normally find in a supermarket, but not the cigarettes, beer and lottery tickets that are big money makers at the city’s more than 10,000 bodegas and delis. The big differentiator: The NYC Groceries sites would all offer a standardized, “core basket” of around 20 healthy products, including meat, seafood, milk, eggs and butter. The prices for that roster of produce would average 30% below prevailing retail prices for the same goods throughout New York. The City government wouldn’t run the stores. Instead, the bureau in charge, the Economic Development Corp. (EDC) has issued a 44-page request for proposals to collect bids from private operators. Those purveyors would handle all sourcing, hiring, and merchandising, and most of all, be responsible, in collaboration with the EDC, for establishing the 30% discounts. Pricing for the core basket would remain unchanged for a month, then get adjusted for the following month, a policy that the administration says will protect shoppers from the weekly fluctuations in private stores, empowering them, in the Mayor’s words, “to predict your monthly expenses.” Companies running the stores would receive annual “affordability payments” fully compensating them for the “loss” through selling staples far below market. The operators will pay no rent or property taxes. It’s unclear if that edge would enable them to book outsized profits or even stay in business, since these would probably be smaller operators that at least will lack the big chains’ ability to secure the lowest prices buy purchasing in huge bulk from retailers. Mamdani claims NYC Groceries will render getting fresh goods at reasonable prices “no longer an unsolvable equation,” and “a blow for economic justice.” He’s talking big savings of around $90 a month or $1,000 a year for denizens of his new markets. New York has attracted big supermarkets in recent years, but needs far more It’s important to note that New York has already gone a long way towards breaking from its long history of domination by relatively small, high-cost grocery stores to embracing the national and international chains that offer the widest choices and best prices. Until 1995, the city had virtually no big box supermarkets. Instead, the folks and families shopped almost exclusively at local bodegas, or at “independents” run by individual owners that operated under brand names such as Food Town, Food Emporium, Urban Market, Gristedes and D’Agostino that belong to cooperatives, and Key Food that operates its own coop, that enable them to pool their purchases from wholesalers. Obviously, the bodegas are small at 1,000 to 4,000 square feet, but the independents are also undersized at typically 5,000 to 15,000. Because of their limited scale, the bodegas and the likes of Gristedes and Food Town offered a dearth of inexpensive generic products; they mostly had room for the pricey top brands. And that scenario caused a major turning point. Shoppers in Harlem groused about the lack of low-priced options, and in the early 1990s, lobbied hard for a giant Fairway. Over tough resistance from local merchants, the project got approved and in 1995, a Fairway at roughly 40,000 square feet debuted on 125 th Street and the Hudson River. This writer vividly recalls that many of his preppy, option-starved friends from the Upper East and West sides flocked to this unfamiliar venue in search of suburban-style vast shopping aisles and great bargains. The Fairway (it closed in 2020) helped open the way for a number of never-before-seen, big box supermarkets from national chains. Today, Amazon’s Whole Foods boasts 16 locations in New York, including two behemoths at around 60,000 square feet, one at Columbus Circle, while Trader Joe’s offers around 18 stores, among them an Lower East Side venue at 30,000 sq. ft. The Stop & Shop array numbers two-dozen; its outpost in Rockaway Beach, Queens, occupies 30,000 square feet. International players are coming, too. Wegman’s is also present in two locations. International brands are arriving as well. Aldi of Germany (its parent Aldi Nord also owns Trader Joe’s) operates 26 low-cost supermarkets catering to budget-conscious residents and its compatriot Lidi (owned non-affiliated Aldi Süd) has around 8 locations, also concentrated in lower-income areas. These mega-stores usually offer better pricing and more variety than the independents. While the coop membership helps the single-owner supermarkets buy in bulk, they can’t match the purchasing cloud of a Whole Foods or Stop & Shop that respectively operate 537 and 656 stores across the U.S. What’s missing despite the influx of these big national names is that with the exception of Aldi and Lidi, they tend to cluster in such high-income neighborhoods such as Manhattan’s West Chelsea, Midtown and Upper East and West Sides, and trendier parts of Queens and Brooklyn. That leaves sundry food deserts in such places as Central Harlem, the South Bronx, Central Brooklyn including Bed Stuy and Brownsville, and the North Shore of Staten Island. Dominating these areas are bodegas that sell mainly high quality, processed food. Fresh chicken and fish could be a half-hour away on foot. Even some plushier addresses are wanting, among them Manhattan’s Soho and Long Island City. Clearly, the best remedy to Gotham’s penury is bringing a lot more of the big chain stores the offer the widest assortments at the lowest prices, and they want to come, but in many of the places they’re most needed, the City, including apparently its Mayor, don’t want them. Ever wonder why New York has so many drug store chains, such as Walgreens and CVS where an enormous amount of space is dedicated to food, for more than elsewhere in the country? It’s because these often super-sized venues fill the void caused by the severe shortage of big, full service supermarkets. Shoppers can get soda, chips, snacks and lots of other package good at these pharmacy-branded outlets, but not fresh food. The reason big supermarkets, operated by national and regional operators, are so often excluded is an old zoning law that’s a competition and affordability-killer, and that affordability-king Mamdani is doing nothing about. Here’s the little-discussed zoning rule that’s a big reason for New York’s food deserts In the 1970s, New York City enacted a zoning regulation targeted at protecting the fast-eroding industrial base. The new rule’s purported goal: Keeping big retail stores out of spaces used for manufacturing. The law got strong support, and continues to be championed, by local merchants. “It did nothing to prevent the fall of manufacturing,” says Korbey. “It’s outdated but it remains on the books.” It seems clear that the City Council is reluctant to remove it. Specifically, the regulation requires that any enterprise looking to build or open a retail store over 10,000 square feet in the extensive areas zoned “M” for “manufacturing” must obtain both a special permit from the City Planning Commission and a yes vote from the 51-member City Council. That’s all retail, including food stores. The M zones cover such areas as Bedford Avenue in Brooklyn, Gowanus and the Red Hook waterfront in Brooklyn, sections of East New York, and such unexpected sections as large swaths of Long Island City and most of Soho. Many of the M areas have precisely the kind of big spaces, available land and ample parking needed for big box grocery stores. Yet it’s highly unusual for the authorities to approve them and just to get to the point where the City renders a decision is wildly expensive, a barrier that stops most candidates from even trying. As urban policy analyst Stephen Smith noted in an excellent article published in non-profit think tank Vital City, Wegman’s won approval for its store in the Brooklyn Navy Yard only after pledging to build retail and office space that remains unoccupied, and Whole Foods had to cover a parking lot with wind turbines and solar panels to win its spot in Gowanus. To make matters worse, getting permission for a grocery superstore can also be difficult and costly, if not impossible, in the commercial and residential districts, the other two main zoning designations. Walmart avoided the M areas when tried to land in East New York, the blue-collar Brooklyn area parched for grocery shopping. But in 2012, opposition from small business and labor groups nixed its plan, and Walmart hasn’t returned. In fact, many big stores go underground, where the 10,000-foot ban doesn’t apply. Example: the Whole Foods store on Bedford Avenue that occupies 40,000 square feet of subterranean space. The Mamdani plan not only leaves the monopolistic rules in place, it also suffers from bad economics It’s not just that Mamdani’s doing zilch to foster what’s really needed, letting freedom ring so New York welcomes instead of shuns private stores yearning to provide better deals than most of the ones offer now. The whole NYC Groceries structure is a primer in fighting market forces when it’s the market forces that are bound to win. The most obvious drawback is that the program doesn’t save money for New Yorkers overall. It simply transfers the 30% food savings to all residents in extra taxes. As the Heritage Foundation’s Antoni points out, food retailers garner just about the lowest margins of any industry, about 2 cents for every dollar in sales. The five NYC Groceries mission to sell a large part of their products at 30% less would pull customers from nearby rivals, potentially forcing them to shut their doors. Supermarkets making an average 2% markup on the same items included in the “core basket” would suffer a 28% loss on these important products matching the NYC Groceries prices. Since big grocers in those areas are already scarce, the food deserts would expand, not shrink. And what’s to prevent customers from buying loads of heavily discounted meat and fish, and reselling the stuff at a profit? Mamdani hasn’t proposed any way of monitoring who buys what to prevent such an abuse that appears such an obvious threat. Look for a thriving black market where the big buyers are middlemen who boomerang the produce to new buyers at a fat profit. We’re looking at a classic case where price controls create big rewards for cheaters who game the system. That could actually happen. The story of super-subsidized goods is what we’ve seen in places like Cuba—they sell out fast, leaving the late comers nothing to buy. The NYC Groceries members will be severely pressed to keep shelves well stocked for items tagged almost a third lower than most other places. More likely, the milk, eggs and seafood aisles will go empty in a hurry. New York City’s full of Cuban immigrants who’ve seen stores like this one back home. You’re supposed to get a great deal on chickens and fish, then you stand in line to get them or rush to the store and they’re sold out. Around the globe, government stores all make the same grandiose promises of bounty at a bargain, and customers will find mainly empty shelves. We’ll soon see if this daring experiment can defy all past experience, and defy what’s law rather than theory, that the market always wins. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: The deepening chip rout downwards as stocks take a dive
text: The deepening chip rout downwards as stocks take a dive. Who would be an investor in South Korea right now? “Despair and frustration” spread again on Wednesday as the chip-heavy Kospi index “cratered” during another “hectic session” that triggered a second successive official circuit-breaker, reported Bloomberg. The catalyst was disappointing earnings from local semiconductor giant SK Hynix but, given “already jittery sentiment” around the AI boom, it could almost have been anything. The oncebooming Kospi has now lost more than 33% of its value in a month. ‘Demand destruction’ “The chips are down,” said Bryce Elder in the FT – especially in the red-hot memory sector. Some have pinned the “chip dip”, which has also hit Wall Street with force, on the IPO of Chinese challenger CXMT; others on reports that a stateowned Chinese company is beginning mass production of “immersion deep-ultra lithography machines” – advanced chip manufacturing tools over which the West (especially the Dutch giant ASML) currently enjoys a monopoly. Still, the more obvious concern is “demand destruction”, in what has always been a volatile and highly cyclical sector. Voracious demand from America’s big AI hyperscalers has sent chip prices sky-high. “All that’s needed to wreck 2027 sales expectations is for this cycle to turn from virtuous to vicious. Plus ça change...” Could China do for chips what it has already done for cars? That’s the fear on the Nasdaq, said Eliot Brown in The Wall Street Journal. As Elon Musk recently told The Economist, Chinese manufacturers are “closer than most people realise to solving the lithography problem”. Chinese companies have been restricted from buying the cutting-edge machines – which is why they are “a step behind the US in advanced chipmaking”. ‘Nvidia - the central bank of the AI economy’ Yet what’s particularly concerning about the plummeting shares of chipmakers, said DealBook in The New York Times, is that the rout coincides with a broader crisis of confidence on Wall Street about AI-related corporate debt and “circular” financial arrangements. That was rammed home when it emerged that chip giant Nvidia – increasingly “the central bank of the AI economy” – is brokering a $250bn guarantee for OpenAI’s immense Ohio campus. “Throughout history, almost every generational infrastructure leap has relied on hardware titans to co-sign their buyers’ credit.” But this has also led to devastating “debt crashes”. The chief winner of the current turmoil is Apple, said the FT. It has reclaimed its crown as the world’s most valuable company, with a $5trn valuation, because it is seen as a relative “haven”. The same is true of the FTSE 100, which has hit an all-time high as an “anti-tech” index. Swings and roundabouts. title: Donald Kimball: To make electricity affordable, don't ban data centers. Reform energy regulations. - Sun, 02 Aug 2026 PST
text: Donald Kimball: To make electricity affordable, don't ban data centers. Reform energy regulations. - Sun, 02 Aug 2026 PST. By Donald Kimball Data centers use a lot of energy. So, it isn’t surprising that people believe they are resource hogs that drive up energy costs and create a blight on local communities. This sentiment has driven communities, such as Spokane, Seattle and Tacoma, to enact data center moratoriums, either temporarily or permanently. But for all the furor over electricity cost increases, the numbers tell a different story. Both nationally and in Washington state, data center development has correlated with slower electricity-price growth, not spiking prices. This is counterintuitive. But a national study found that between 2015 and 2024, areas that doubled data center capacity saw residential customers’ electricity costs fall by 3.5%. This same study found no evidence that costs were being shifted from commercial or industrial users onto residential customers. This pattern also appears in Washington state. Grant County, which accounts for one of the largest data center aggregations in our state, saw energy prices increase by an average of 19.5% from 2015 to 2024 while the rest of the state saw an average increase of 30.9% in the same period. Grant County’s prices increased notably less than the rest of the state. Similarly, Douglas County experienced an increase of only 6.6% in energy costs over that time while increasing their industrial and commercial electricity sales by 185%, also driven partially by data center development. One reason this can occur is that large users, like data centers, help reduce fixed costs to maintain the electrical grid. Building and maintaining energy generation and grid infrastructure entails massive costs that must be paid for, which utilities recover in residential and commercial energy rates. Most energy producers don’t operate constantly at full output. When large consumers, such as data centers, are built and start adding demand, it allows local power plants to achieve higher utilization. This means that what needs to be charged for the fixed costs of construction and maintenance gets spread across more kilowatt-hours sold, lowering the costs for other customers. To be clear, data centers will continue to increase electricity demand in the future. This increase highlights the growing need to update energy infrastructure and increase overall energy output. Data center development can help achieve those goals. While some data center developers prefer to stay out of direct energy grid development, Grant PUD requires them to pay increased prices for any upfront capital costs needed for updated infrastructure. Others, like Microsoft, help build clean energy storage compliant with laws and their own commitments necessitating the use of wind, solar and batteries. While data centers are an easy bogeyman for energy cost increases, the major cost drivers in Washington state include energy regulations that artificially increase costs. Puget Sound Energy’s rate adjustments earlier this year added about 12% to an average monthly electric bill due to additional costs from rules such as the Climate Commitment Act , the Clean Energy Transformation Act and others. Similar reasons have been cited by Avista. Other cost drivers include things like electric vehicle sales and home electrification. In the future, energy demands will keep growing, both from data center development and growing electrification. Washington should be forward thinking, taking advantage of private developers who can help future proof our electrical grid. It is also critical to keep our energy options open. Washington should reject the notion of tearing down the lower Snake River dams, the current largest source of clean energy in our state. It should also embrace modern nuclear technology as a safe, clean option to meet growing energy demands. It’s easy to see the large costs associated with building data centers and their energy demands and assume this increases utilities bills, but that doesn’t match reality. Thanks to infrastructure investment and higher energy utilization, data centers can help spread out the fixed cost rates, providing cost relief to nearby residential customers. Data center moratoriums may feel good to support, but if Washingtonians want real cost relief, we should focus our efforts on reforming costly and ineffective government regulations instead. Donald Kimball is the communications manager and tech exchange editor for Washington Policy Center and a contributor with Young Voices.

title: Third places are out, as prices rise. Hosting dinners, craft nights, and book clubs are in.
text: Third places are out, as prices rise. Hosting dinners, craft nights, and book clubs are in.. Emily O'Brien and her friends have been meeting up for book club every month for roughly a year. Rachel Wisniewski for BI Emily O'Brien, 26, said in mid-July that she had about 200 pages to go in "Just for the Summer" by Abby Jimenez, before attending book club at a friend's place the following week. She loves attending the monthly meet-up, which friends take turns hosting at their homes in Philadelphia, a tradition they started roughly a year ago. She finished what she needed to read before gathering with her friends on a rooftop. Talking about the book is less important than making sure the friends meet every month to catch up without breaking the bank, she said. "It's paying off more so than just an occasional dinner would, in my opinion, because you're also sitting there and you just need to talk to one another," O'Brien said. O'Brien said people take turns hosting the book club. Rachel Wisniewski for BI She said that going out to dinner or happy hour every month can be expensive and hard to plan. "Do I really want to end up paying 80 bucks for a dinner and drinks with friends? Or I could just stay in and then not spend that," she said. "80 bucks now, I feel like, is different even than what 80 bucks was a year ago, where I'm like I need that for my groceries." Prices have skyrocketed since 2021, with food away from home rising about 32%, higher than food at home's 27% increase, based on the Bureau of Labor Statistics' consumer price index. The people who spoke to Business Insider find that hosting at home can mean more bang for their buck, since they're sharing food and drinks among many instead of a pricey meal for one or two at a night out, and have leftovers to enjoy. O'Brien is among the people in metros with a higher cost of living than the national average, bringing the " third place ," or the gathering space outside home and work, such as a coffee shop, into their "first place," or where someone lives. Whether for cost-related reasons or easier than gathering in public, people who spoke to Business Insider were looking to make a real effort to bring people together by hosting. "You either go to a third space to search out , or you can take responsibility and step up and volunteer to be the person in your community to make that happen," said Kristin Greene, who is in her 50s, and hosts a craft club on the third Tuesday of the month at her San Francisco home. Here's what some people are doing to intentionally foster community without going to a public space. Taking turns hosting a book club O'Brien hosted the book club twice, one of which she picked up brunch items from Trader Joe's , made floral arrangements, and set up a coffee bar with her Nespresso machine. She estimates she spent about $50 on the first session she hosted and about $75 on the other, but that's because she wanted to, and it doesn't have to be the case for everyone who wants to start bringing people together. O'Brien said people sometimes bring wine or an extra snack, yet the group has found it's best for the host to handle the rest, since everyone takes turns. She thinks it can be easy to avoid social situations because she lives alone, often visits her boyfriend, and wants to avoid the cost of going out. The book club keeps O'Brien accountable for staying connected with others, and although she likes to spend money when she hosts, she thinks it's worth it because it's an activity that brings her a lot of joy. O'Brien said the book club is more about connecting with friends than talking about the book itself. Rachel Wisniewski for BI Prices for food away from home, including dining out, and food at home, including groceries, have both grown about 36% from June 2019 to June 2026 in Philadelphia's metro area. Building a community at home in one of the most expensive metros Ariel and Cyrus Kashfian, who are in their 30s, have an open invitation for anyone who knows them or their plus ones to come to their Los Angeles apartment for Shabbat on Fridays. They also participate in other forms of hosting: Ariel is part of a monthly book club that rotates hosts, and the couple has hosted a murder mystery night with plans for another, among other gatherings. Cyrus said he likes bringing people together because he wouldn't otherwise see his friends. "If I don't make something happen, they aren't the ones to make plans and host and put things on the calendar," he said. He also thinks that going out to dinner continuously can get monotonous and feel less personal. "We could go out with friends and stuff like that, but it's harder to get close to people and to really spend quality time with them if you're not just together in someone's home or doing something in a very private environment," he said. Ariel, who said she and Cyrus are from family-oriented cultures, likes having people over and the positive effects it could have on their two children. "I want my kids to grow up with people always in and out and laughter and warmth," she said. "That's probably the most important part of growing up, is seeing people in your life that just show up for you and want to be around you and have fun." The children can also go to their rooms to play if they need a break from company, making it easier on the Kashfians than if they were taking care of their kids while out with friends. Plus, the couple lives in one of the most expensive metro areas in the US, based on regional price parities. "The price of going out in LA has become very, very, very high for a one-and-a-half-hour dinner," Ariel said. "You get more bang for your buck having people over at your house." Ariel said she made a pot roast, mashed potatoes, salads, and sides for their murder mystery night. While that added up pretty quickly in cost, she said they had leftovers, and everyone was happy with how the night turned out. "It was a memory that people will have for a very long time," she said. "Money and value are not also the same. You're getting a lot more for your dollar when you're hosting people, and doing an activity that's interesting and fun." Working on projects at craft club Greene, who hosts a craft club in San Francisco, fills her dining room each month with people enjoying each other's company over bowls of soup . Her guests work on various projects, from knitting and embroidery to jewelry making and photo editing. People work on different craft projects at Greene's home. Cayce Clifford for BI The craft club started after an experimental craft night at the book club she attends. She said other attendees wanted to do that again, so Greene, a needlepointer who sees value in crafting in a community setting, took the initiative and has been hosting pretty consistently since February 2025. "I finally was sick of us talking about hosting craft club and just decided to go for it, and I think many of us were also just really feeling like the world is complex and challenging, and so looking for pockets of optimism and hope and community," she said. She had some crafts out in case people didn't have anything, but it has turned into people bringing their own projects while they talk. While it started with some people from the book club, it's a mix of participants from Greene's life, including college friends, a former colleague, and a friend of a friend reconnected with at a Fourth of July picnic. It also includes people who are new to her but one to two degrees connected by other women in the club. At the most recent gathering, she was needlepointing and offered cumin orange black bean soup, as she tries to make a different homemade soup each time. She landed on soup because it's fairly easy, removes decision fatigue, and is affordable. Attendees have brought items over the months, such as sourdough bread and treats. Greene makes homemade soup for craft club attendees. Cayce Clifford for BI "I am a person who is really committed to making community, and I've been in communities and groups where we've created what a lot of people get out of third spaces, but we're hosting them ourselves," Greene said. More space to bring people together O'Brien, the book clubber in Philadelphia, said hosting has inspired a desire to get a larger apartment than her 650-square-foot one, which she uses as her "second place," since she works remotely. "My kitchen, my hosting area, my living room, and my office are in the same four walls," she said, adding that she likes that they take turns hosting so she can get out of her space. Andrea Bryson, 30, moved from a studio for herself to a larger apartment where she's sharing space with her boyfriend in Chicago. That means she has more room to host. She did a soup gathering in the fall, in which people brought their own bowls and spoons, as well as bread and soup to share; a show-and-tell art party featuring meat and cheese snacks brought by guests; a sushi-making night; game nights, and craft nights where people brought their own supplies and hung out. Bryson likes being able to bring people together at home because the costs can add up quickly if going out in Chicago . "I do find that I try to limit how much I'm spending when I'm eating out, and if I were to go out and buy drinks and appetizers every time I wanted to see my friends, I think that would add up pretty quickly," Bryson said. Food away from home in the Chicago metro area has increased more so than in the Philadelphia area, at 40% from June 2019 to June 2026. Other ways to connect Those who might not have the means to host at home and don't want to spend money can seek digital third places. "You can have really rich connections where you are helping each other, answering questions, cheering each other on," Greene, who is part of a weekly virtual meditation group with women around the world and a Discord group about needlepoint, said. "They require almost the same amount of effort to create them." A common theme among the people who spoke to Business Insider about why they enjoy hosting was the ability to foster community. Cayce Clifford for BI Bryson said social media can be beneficial in finding third places and groups, or being in a fitness community like she is can be a good way to find people. Her third places are mainly around an active lifestyle, like swimming at a pool or meeting up at the lakefront in Chicago. Bryson said it takes time to find the right spots. She said third places that are businesses like bars and cafés mean spending money, so a way to find free third places could be public parks and outdoor spaces, such as people doing crafts together at a park meet-up. If people do want to get into hosting, Ariel said it doesn't have to be as elaborate as you may see on social media. She said sometimes it can be themed, while other times it can be chicken, salad, and a bowl of rice from the store to share with others from the comfort of your home.
