title: Inside the Activist Investor Stake That Is Reshaping Global Equity Markets
text: Inside the Activist Investor Stake That Is Reshaping Global Equity Markets. Few forces in modern finance carry the same electric charge as the moment an activist investor stake lands in a company’s shareholder register. In an instant, boardrooms tense, share prices lurch, and analysts scramble to decode the signal. What was once considered a niche corner of Wall Street has evolved into one of the most consequential drivers of global equity performance — and the latest intelligence from equity markets around the world suggests the strategy is accelerating in both scale and sophistication. An activist investor stake is not simply a passive bet on a company’s future. It is a deliberate, often loudly telegraphed declaration of intent. Activists acquire meaningful ownership positions — typically between 5% and 15% of outstanding shares — with the explicit goal of catalyzing change. That change might come in the form of forced divestitures, board overhauls, share buyback programs, or even full-scale mergers. The distinction between activism and ordinary institutional investing lies entirely in the willingness to confront management and demand accountability. And in today’s market environment, that willingness has rarely been more pronounced. Global equity intelligence data reveals a striking pattern: activist campaigns are increasingly crossing borders. Historically concentrated in the United States, activist investor activity has surged across Europe, Japan, and parts of Asia-Pacific over the past several years. European companies in particular have become high-profile targets, as governance reforms and shareholder rights movements have lowered the legal and cultural barriers that once protected legacy management teams from outside pressure. In Japan, where cross-shareholding arrangements historically insulated executives from external accountability, foreign activists have scored landmark victories — compelling companies to unlock dormant balance sheet value that had sat idle for decades. The financial impact of an activist investor stake on a target company’s equity can be dramatic and almost immediate. Academic research consistently shows that share prices of targeted firms spike upon disclosure of an activist position, often by 5% to 10% in the short term. But the longer-term story is more nuanced. Campaigns that successfully push through operational or strategic reforms tend to generate sustained outperformance. Those that devolve into proxy fights or prolonged legal battles frequently destroy value on both sides of the table. The difference, most often, comes down to the quality of the activist’s thesis and the discipline with which it is executed. Today’s most influential activist funds are not the corporate raiders of a previous era. Firms like Elliott Management, Starboard Value, Third Point, and Sachem Head have built reputations as data-intensive, analytically rigorous operators who arrive at the table with detailed operational blueprints. When one of these names discloses an activist investor stake in a major corporation, markets treat it as meaningful intelligence — not just noise. Their filings trigger a cascade of institutional repositioning, sell-side coverage upgrades, and media coverage that amplifies their leverage against company leadership. Retail and institutional investors who monitor activist positions have learned to treat these disclosures as high-conviction signals. Specialized databases and real-time monitoring services now track 13D and 13G filings with the kind of urgency once reserved for central bank announcements. The information asymmetry that once gave activists a structural edge is narrowing, but they continue to find it in sectors where complexity, opacity, or misaligned management incentives create exploitable gaps between a company’s intrinsic value and its market price. Technology conglomerates, diversified industrials, and underperforming consumer staples companies have been fertile hunting grounds in recent quarters. Not everyone views the rise of the activist investor stake with enthusiasm. Critics argue that the short-termism baked into many campaigns comes at the expense of long-range investment, workforce stability, and innovation. There is genuine empirical tension here — some studies do find that post-campaign R&D spending declines, even as short-term returns improve. This debate sits at the heart of broader conversations about corporate governance, stakeholder capitalism, and the fiduciary obligations of institutional money managers. Regulators in multiple jurisdictions are weighing disclosure rule changes that would require earlier and more detailed reporting of activist positions, a shift that could alter campaign dynamics significantly. What the global equity intelligence picture makes clear is that the activist investor stake has become a permanent and structurally important feature of capital markets. For portfolio managers, the ability to anticipate, track, and interpret activist activity is no longer optional — it is a core competency. For executives, understanding the vulnerabilities that attract activist attention is equally essential. Companies that ignore the signals do so at considerable risk. The boardrooms that have learned to engage constructively with activists, incorporating their analytical frameworks without surrendering strategic autonomy, are increasingly emerging as the long-term winners in this high-stakes game. The intelligence is there for those willing to read it carefully.

title: Trump’s approval rating on the economy sinks to just 32%, and even Republicans feel like they need ‘to get a loan before I go grocery shopping’
text: Trump’s approval rating on the economy sinks to just 32%, and even Republicans feel like they need ‘to get a loan before I go grocery shopping’. Immigration remains a stronger issue for President Donald Trump than the economy or Iran, according to a new AP-NORC poll, even after three people were killed in encounters with Immigration and Customs Enforcement in the span of under a week in July. Trump is not getting a glowing endorsement on his immigration approach from Americans overall, the new survey from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found. Only 39% of U.S. adults approve of his performance on immigration, a decline from 49% at the beginning of his second term. Despite that, about 8 in 10 Republicans continue to approve of how Trump is handling immigration. That’s a slight decline from the beginning of Trump’s second term, when about 9 in 10 Republicans approved, but his support on the issue within his base has been mostly stable since last summer despite a chaotic year of immigration enforcement actions. Republicans are also more likely to approve of how Trump is handling immigration than the economy or Iran. In just the past month, Republican approval of Trump’s handling of Iran dropped slightly in AP-NORC polling The poll found that about half of U.S. adults say Trump has “gone too far” on deporting immigrants living in the U.S. illegally. That number has also remained steady for over a year, despite multiple immigration crackdowns that deployed federal law enforcement to large cities and at least 10 deaths involving encounters with immigration officers since the mass deportation campaign began. Republicans, however, are much less likely to say Trump has overstepped in his immigration enforcement actions. Overall, Trump’s popularity has fallen since he took office last year, but the findings highlight the relatively muted impact of the past year’s aggressive immigration enforcement on his public standing. That’s a contrast with views of his handling of Iran, where he’s seen more recent signs of slippage , even among his own supporters. Immigration remains a strong issue for Trump with Republicans Americans remain divided on whether Trump has overstepped on immigration. About half of U.S. adults say Trump has “gone too far” when it comes to restricting legal immigration, in line with the last time the question was asked in February. Roughly half — 47% — say Trump has exceeded his authority when it comes to deporting immigrants living in the U.S. illegally. In each case, about 3 in 10 say Trump’s actions have been “about right,” and closer to 2 in 10 say he hasn’t gone far enough. Few Republicans – about 2 in 10 or fewer – say he’s “gone too far” on deporting immigrants in the country illegally or restricting legal immigration. Most Americans, however, say he’s gone too far when it comes to using traffic stops to find and arrest immigrants living in the U.S. illegally — a practice that was at the center of two recent ICE shootings in Maine — and when it comes to sending federal immigration agents into U.S. cities. Republicans were also less likely to see these as oversteps. James Leatherman, a 68-year-old Republican from San Antonio, is overall supportive of Trump’s handling of the presidency and backs him on immigration in particular. “You cannot come in here illegally — you’re breaking the law,” he said. More Americans disapprove than approve of the way ICE is enforcing immigration laws. About half of Americans “strongly” or “somewhat” disapprove of the agency’s approach, while roughly 3 in 10 “strongly” or “somewhat” approve. There’s a wide partisan split, though: About 6 in 10 Republicans approve of ICE’s approach, compared with about 2 in 10 independents and just 4% of Democrats. Eric Coursen, 76, an independent from Chincoteague, Virginia, agrees with the president that there were issues with the immigration system. He said doesn’t believe in open borders — but he’s deeply opposed to how the administration has been enforcing immigration law. “It’s like taking some bread when you’re hungry and you take it, you’re going to shoot that person rather than just, you know, get them for theft?” he said. “It’s just overkill.” Trump’s approval on the economy remains low About 3 in 10 U.S. adults, 32%, approve of how Trump is handling the economy. That’s down from 40% at the start of his second term, and marks a shift from his first presidential term when the economy was a stronger issue for Trump. During Trump’s first term, his lowest approval on the economy was 40% in December 2017. Now, his rating is well below that. Roughly 7 in 10 Republicans – 69% – approve of how Trump is handling the economy. That’s roughly in line with the share who approve of how he’s handing the presidency, but it’s slightly below the 78% who approved early in Trump’s second term. Leatherman, despite his support for Trump, said he’s feeling the pinch of higher prices in his budget. “I almost have to go to the bank to get a loan before I go grocery shopping,” he said. About 7 in 10 U.S. adults describe the nation’s economy as “very” or “somewhat” poor, in line with April. Republicans are more optimistic, with about 6 in 10 saying that the U.S. economy is doing well, compared with about 2 in 10 independents and roughly 1 in 10 Democrats. More Republicans approve of how Trump is handling healthcare Healthcare has never been a strong issue for Trump. Unlike with immigration and the economy, a clear majority of U.S. adults has disapproved of Trump’s performance on healthcare across both presidential terms. That hasn’t changed in the new poll, which found that only about 3 in 10 Americans approve of how Trump is handling healthcare, in line with when the question was last asked in December. He’s seen a rebound on the issue among his own supporters since late last year, though. Roughly 71% of Republicans now approve, compared with 59% in the December poll. That shift comes as Democrats kicked off 100 days until the midterm elections last week, with leaders saying they’ll focus on healthcare cuts , in addition to the cost of living and the war in Iran. Democrats and independents continue to overwhelmingly disapprove of Trump’s handling of healthcare. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Here are the 2 big things we're watching in the stock market in the week ahead
text: Here are the 2 big things we're watching in the stock market in the week ahead. The jobs market steps into the spotlight this week, while second-quarter earnings season continues apace. Here's a closer look at what to expect in the coming days. We'll start with the Club holdings set to report, before touching on the labor-market updates and their implications for Federal Reserve policy. 1. Earnings : The action kicks off Tuesday morning when we'll see results from Qnity Electronics and DuPont . Qnity was spun out from DuPont last fall. We expect Qnity to show robust demand as the company provides chemicals and other materials needed to manufacture all types of semiconductors — both "logic" chips, such as an Nvidia graphics processing unit GPU), and memory chips made by the likes of Micron , Samsung and SK Hynix . Last week, outgoing Apple CEO Tim Cook said the memory market is experiencing a "100-year flood," as soaring demand pushes up prices. That's bad for memory buyers, but great for memory sellers and those supplying products to the semiconductor fabrication facilities, like Qnity. About 20% of Qnity's semiconductor revenue is exposed to memory, according to last year's investor day presentation . In a recent note, analysts at Deutsche Bank said Qnity stands to benefit from improving utilization rates and leaner customer inventories — in other words, chipmakers are running their fabs more often and are needing to replenish their stocks. Now, one thing to keep in mind is that consumer-oriented sales may be under pressure as high memory prices hamper production volume and lead to price hikes for devices. Memory makers are shifting production capacity toward more profitable HBM — high-bandwidth memory — needed for AI chips. This is crowding out the supply of lower-grade memory found in consumer devices like smartphones and personal computers. Qnity also supplies materials used in the advanced packaging of chips, which is increasingly important in the AI era. Revenue: $1.36 billion Earnings per share: $1.07 Q YTD mountain Qnity Electronics' stock performance in 2026. DuPont's reported results on Tuesday will be important, but its guidance and management's commentary on the operating environment will color how investors think about shares into year-end. In the first quarter, DuPont's Water Technologies business saw a mid-single-digit organic decline due to logistics disruptions in the Middle East, which relies heavily on the company's desalination technology for drinking water. While the missed sales should show up in the second quarter results, we suspect some supply-chain pressure remains because the conflict is ongoing (though we got some hopeful news this weekend around calming tensions).We're interested to see what management is doing to mitigate the issue, and whether large desalination projects slated for the second half of this year remain on track. The other issue for DuPont is the rise in oil prices resulting from the conflict. While prices are down from their wartime highs, they remain volatile, so we wouldn't be surprised to see management take a more cautious tone when it comes to the impact of this input cost for key products like Tyvek. The company said last quarter it can fully offset higher input costs through price actions. Revenue: $1.81 billion Earnings per share: $1.76 DD YTD mountain DuPont's year-to-date stock performance. When Eli Lilly reports on Wednesday morning, one of the main focuses will be on GLP-1 sales in international markets. That has been a consistent source of upside in recent quarters, and analysts are expecting that beat-and-raise dynamic to continue this time around. Of course, the magnitude of the beat will likely determine the stock reaction. In April, the beat was massive , resulting in a 10% pop on earnings day. There are also a couple major questions facing its obesity-drug business in the U.S. The first: What is going on with the launch of Foundayo? Uptake of Lilly's new obesity pill hasn't gotten off to a roaring start since its FDA approval on April 1, so investors will want to understand how CEO David Ricks and other Lilly executives feel about the competitive dynamics versus rival Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill. Is there reason to believe Lilly can close the gap and erase Novo's first-mover advantage, just as it did with injectable GLP-1s? Wall Street expects roughly $103 million in second-quarter Foundayo sales, according to FactSet. That's down from consensus of $196 million in late June, as analysts lowered their expectations. A second big question: How is the start of Medicare coverage for obesity drugs going? That temporary coverage began July 1, with eligible Medicare recipients paying $50 a month for access through 2027. Revenue: $20.73 billion Earnings per share: $6.01 LLY YTD mountain Eli Lilly's year-to-date stock performance. On Wednesday evening, we hear from Honeywell Aerospace . We already got the results when Honeywell Technologies reported in July, as the two were not separated until the end of the second quarter. Aerospace results weren't great — sales of $4.5 billion and segment profiting (operating income) of $1.1 billion — so some of that bad news should already been in the stock. As a result, our focus will be on forward guidance, end market commentary, and any new opportunities the team may have discovered since separation to enhance efficiencies. The other major topic of discussion will be regarding supply chain improvements, which is a key pillar of our investment thesis. In the first quarter of 2026, when Honeywell Aerospace was still part of the Honeywell conglomerate, the company's sales were held back by supply shortages for mechanical products. At its investor day in June, Honeywell Aerospace spent time explaining their strategy to transform their supply chain, including better planning, factory throughput and the embrace of AI tools. Now the focus shifts to executing on this vision. HONA ALL mountain Honeywell Aerospace's stock performance since its debut in late June. 2. Jobs, jobs, jobs: It's jobs week, arriving on the heels of Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh's July meeting press conference in which the labor market took the backseat. The conversation was instead dominated by the inflation side of the central bank's dual mandate. Of course, that is understandable. The U.S. labor market has remained mostly solid, despite June hiring missing expectations. Meanwhile, rekindled tensions in the Middle East — and the resulting rise in oil prices — dashed hopes that a June decline in inflation was the start of a sustained retreat. Inflation remains well above the Fed's 2% target, at 3.7% in June , as measured by the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) prce index. While Warsh vowed that central bankers will "win the battle against high inflation," the Fed left rates unchanged. If Friday's July jobs report comes in stronger than expected, that could increase the likelihood that the Fed increases interest rates at its September meeting — provided there's no break in inflation. If the labor market is softer than anticipated, that could give central bankers more cover to look through price shocks from the Iran war. But then again, the market doesn't have a great grasp yet on how Warsh interprets new data. Economists polled by FactSet expect the U.S. economy added 65,000 jobs in July, while the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.3% (from 4.2% last month). The labor force participation rate, which influences the unemployment, is something to watch after reaching a 50-year low in June (excluding the Covid pandemic era). Revisions to prior month reports are also closely watched. Leading up to the government's official nonfarm payrolls report, Tuesday brings the Jobs Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, often called JOLTS. This release offers insights into labor-market tightness by showing the number of job openings and hires, along with a breakdown of why employees left their jobs (quits, layoffs and discharges, and other separations such as retirement). However, JOLTS is the least consequential of this week's monthly labor updates because the data is a month old (June versus July for the other reports). On Wednesday, we'll get the payroll processor ADP's private payrolls report for July — think of this as the opening act for Friday's nonfarm headliner. Investors look at the ADP numbers for clues into the labor market to help them position for the official government release. Economists polled by FactSet expect the ADP report to show private-sector job additions of 80,000 in July. A couple smaller economic updates on our radar include the Institute for Supply Management's (ISM) monthly look at manufacturing and services activity in the U.S. economy, which are slated for Monday and Wednesday, respectively. These so-called purchasing managers' indexes (PMIs) are built on survey responses from businesses, so they offer timely insights into conditions on the ground across various industries. On Tuesday, we'll also get the Census Bureau's full report on June new orders for manufactured durable goods, following the release of the advanced report July 27 , which showed robust activity . title: Amazon Will Give Tariff Refunds to Some Customers
text: Amazon Will Give Tariff Refunds to Some Customers. Months after the US Supreme Court struck down certain tariff-related import charges, some Amazon customers could soon see money returned to their accounts. The online retail giant announced on Thursday that it will issue refunds to eligible customers who paid tariff-related import charges, although the timing and amounts have not been disclosed. Amazon Chief Financial Officer Brian Olsavsky said on an earnings call that the company had received $600 million from the US government following the Supreme Court’s February decision that President Donald Trump’s sweeping tariffs on imports were illegal. From February to April 2025, the Trump administration imposed tariffs on many countries exporting goods to the US, using the International Emergency Economic Powers Act as justification. As of mid-December, more than 301,000 U.S. importers had paid $175 billion to the US government in tariff penalties. The federal government is now issuing refunds to those importers. Under the tariff system, the US importer — not the international exporter — pays the fees to the US government. Olsavsky said that the $600 million payment from the government was the “majority of refunds we expect to receive.” Which customers will get refunds? Amazon did not disclose details about the refund process for customers — who will get them, how much they will get or when. Olsavsky said there were “a limited set of circumstances” where customers had to pay tariff charges on their items. “When we receive those refunds, we will proactively contact affected customers and automatically issue refunds to them,” he said. Olsavsky said most Amazon customers didn’t have to pay import charges and that the company “largely absorbed” the higher prices of products affected by the tariffs. He said the company was able to avoid many tariff charges by building up its inventory before the charges hit. An Amazon representative said the company had no further comment beyond Olsavsky’s remarks on the earnings call. Other large merchants have also received refunds from the US government. Walmart said it would use the refunds to lower product prices, while Costco said it would compensate customers in some form, perhaps not necessarily with payments. Bernstein analyst Zhihan Ma told Barron’s that consumers should not expect to get big paychecks in the mail from retailers. She said companies will pay some of their refund money to suppliers, and that Walmart and Costco would most likely “pass on value to their customers/members” through lower prices.

title: Putin's War: 'The Largest Self-Inflicted Defeat By a Major Power In the Modern Era'
text: Putin's War: 'The Largest Self-Inflicted Defeat By a Major Power In the Modern Era'. The scale of Putin's miscalculation in choosing to invade Ukraine is becoming clearer by the day. In terms of military might, economic thrust and overall reputation as a nation with global standing as a power and a potential threat, Russia has been exposed as a fraud. It's armies, air force and navy have been embarrassed in their failure to perform against a much smaller, less well equipped enemy. It's weapons - once a key source of export revenues - are less effective than those of the west. It's inability to defend its infrastructure from Ukrainian drones has become a financial disaster. And its corruption, delusional self-worth and dependence on a smaller, backward nation like North Korea, as well as its fealty to China, of which it is now effectively a vassal state, means that Putin, for his own personal reasons, has sacrificed all that he and his predecessors had built and for which their people sacrificed so much. JL Joseph Orefice reports in The Geopolitical Economist : Measured against every one of its own stated objectives, Putin's 'special military operation' has failed, and the scale of that failure is massive. History will report this as the largest strategic miscalculation by a major power since the Second World War. Before 2022, the Russian military was widely feared as a juggernaut. Four years later, that reputation is spent. Putin’s war doubled the length of NATO’s direct land border with Russia, the precise outcome the invasion was meant to prevent created the most significant collateral damage Russia’s invasion produced. And Europe, long dependent on cheap Russian gas, spent the war severing that dependence, and has been rearming at a pace not seen since the Cold War, a larger, better-funded, more unified alliance pointed directly at Putin. It i s the largest self-inflicted strategic defeat by a major power in the modern era. In February 2022, Russian columns rolled toward Kyiv expecting a three-day war — a repeat of the 2014 Annexation. The plan was a decapitation strike, a puppet installed, a nation folded back into Moscow’s orbit before the West finished drafting its first sanctions package. Four years later, the columns are gone, the flagship is on the seabed, and Russians in Moscow are waiting in gasoline lines that stretch for miles. The invasion was sold to the Russian public as a limited “special military operation” to secure a buffer against NATO and reclaim historically Russian land. Measured against every one of its own stated objectives, it has failed, and the scale of that failure is massive. History will report this as the largest strategic miscalculation by a major power since the Second World War. Let me walk the ledger, because the numbers tell a story no amount of Kremlin messaging can paper over. The Body Count is Staggering Start with the human cost, because it is the one Russia works hardest to hide. The Center for Strategic and International Studies estimates Russia suffered roughly 1.2 million casualties, including about 325,000 killed, between February 2022 and December 2025, with combined Russian and Ukrainian casualties projected to approach two million by spring 2026. Independent Russian outlet Mediazona , counting only named and confirmed deaths, documented around 352,000 Russian dead by May 2026, and its own methodology concedes that is a floor, not a ceiling. Press enter or click to view image in full size For context, CSIS found that Russia lost more soldiers in the first year of this war than in all its conflicts combined since 1945, including Afghanistan and Chechnya. The Soviet Union’s entire Afghanistan campaign, a decade-long trauma that helped break the USSR, killed roughly 15,000 Soviet troops. Russia has exceeded that toll many times over in Ukraine, and it has done so in a fraction of the time. Now in 2026, Russia is burning through a Soviet-Afghanistan’s worth of dead every few weeks. Even at the conservative end, Russia has taken casualties exceeding the entire pre-war size of its standing army. And these results point to multiple issues within the Russian military from incompetence, greed and archaic tactics. The Drone Wall in 2026 Changed the Math And in 2026, the killing got dramatically more lopsided, because Ukraine’s drones rewrote the arithmetic of the front. CSIS assesses that the Russia-Ukraine casualty ratio has risen to nearly 8:1 in the first half of 2026 , up from 2:1 to 3:1 for most of the war, driven in large part by Ukraine’s use of drones, including AI-enabled ones, in an aggressive air-interdiction campaign. Russia is now losing men roughly eight times faster than the defenders it is attacking. The daily toll tells the same story. Russian personnel losses exceeded 1,000 per day for a sustained stretch of June 2026, on some days ranging past 1,500, according to Ukrainian General Staff tallies analyzed by independent outlets. Press enter or click to view image in full size CSIS estimates Russia’s monthly casualties of over 30,000 have outpaced its recruitment of roughly 27,000 a month, meaning the army is now shrinking under fire faster than it can be refilled. A “drone wall” built by a smaller country is killing the aggressor faster than the aggressor can replace the dead. The strategic result is the cruelest part. For all that blood, Russia’s advance has stalled to a crawl measured in dozens of meters per day, and in April and May of 2026 it began losing ground, ceding territory it had held. Russia is now paying its highest casualty rate of the war to move backward. The Iron Ledger The equipment losses are easier to verify than the bodies, because steel photographs well. The open-source tracker Oryx , which counts only vehicles it can confirm through photo or video, had documented over 3,200 Russian tanks and more than 6,800 armored vehicles destroyed, damaged, or captured as of early 2026, alongside 28-plus naval vessels and hundreds of aircraft and helicopters. Oryx itself notes these are minimums, with true losses likely 30 to 50 percent higher. Ukraine’s General Staff, whose figures should be read as a combatant’s claims, puts the tank number far higher still, above 11,000 . Press enter or click to view image in full size Take even the confirmed floor. Russia has lost more tanks in Ukraine than the entire current tank inventories of Britain, France, and Germany combined. According to the International Institute for Strategic Studies’ pre-war count, Russia’s documented tank losses alone exceed 100 percent of its operational tank force at the start of the invasion. Moscow now fields refurbished T-62s pulled from Soviet-era storage, 1970s armor sent to fight a 2020s war. That last detail is the whole story. A military that was supposed to showcase two decades of modernization is instead stripping mothballed Cold War hulks to keep moving. 👉 The drone campaign that destroyed much of this armor is the clearest signal yet of where warfare is heading. We wrote about that shift here: Skynet Alert — War Is Already Autonomous The Paper Tiger: A Juggernaut That Wasn’t Before 2022, the Russian military was widely feared as a near-peer juggernaut. Four years of footage have replaced that reputation with a different one. The initial thrust toward Kyiv, the operation meant to end the ‘Special Military Operation’ in days, collapsed into the now-infamous forty-mile stalled convoy, undone by mud, ambush, and logistics that could not feed the advance. Press enter or click to view image in full size The Wagner Group , Russia’s mercenary enforcer that had projected power across Syria and Africa, was thrown into the meat grinder at Bakhmut and later turned on the Kremlin itself in a short-lived 2023 mutiny. The tactics on display, massed infantry against dug-in defenders, artillery duels over yards of ground, are recognizably those of 1917, deployed in a century that has moved on. Then there is the navy. Ukraine, a country with essentially no functioning blue-water fleet, sank the Moskva, the Black Sea Fleet’s flagship, in April 2022 with two domestically produced Neptune missiles. It went on to damage or destroy enough additional vessels that Russia’s surviving warships were pulled back from occupied Crimea and largely kept out of Ukrainian reach. A land power humbled a naval one from the shore. What the world feared as a military juggernaut turned out to be a paper tiger with nuclear weapons. The contrast with a competent modern operation is stark. When the United States and Israel moved against Iran in 2025, Iranian air defenses, leadership, and key military sites were shattered in a matter of hours. Russia, four years in, cannot secure air superiority over a neighbor it outweighs on paper by every conventional measure. The gap between reputation and reality has rarely been laid so bare. The Political Boomerang One of the invasion’s central justifications was to halt NATO’s expansion and secure a buffer. It achieved the exact opposite. Finland, which shares an 830-mile border with Russia, abandoned decades of neutrality and joined NATO in April 2023. Sweden followed in March 2024. Press enter or click to view image in full size In one stroke, Putin’s war doubled the length of NATO’s direct land border with Russia, the precise outcome the invasion was meant to prevent. The Carnegie Endowment called the Nordic accession the most significant collateral damage Russia’s invasion had yet produced. Finland’s own defense minister described it as one of Putin’s biggest miscalculations, and it is hard to argue. The second-order effects run even deeper. Western Europe, long dependent on cheap Russian gas, spent the war severing that dependence, accepting real economic pain to do it, and has been rearming at a pace not seen since the Cold War. A continent that Russia hoped to divide and intimidate instead found a resolve it had lacked for a generation. The buffer Putin sought exists now only in the form of a larger, better-funded, more unified alliance pointed directly at him. 👉 The energy dimension of this war rewired global oil and risk markets. Our analysis of that shift: Oil, War, and the Market’s Risk Premium The Economic Reckoning — Now Ukraine Is Sanctioning Russia For three years the story was Western sanctions and Russian workarounds. Moscow leaned on China, India, and North Korea, sold discounted crude eastward, and kept its budget afloat on energy revenue. In 2026 the story changed, because Ukraine stopped waiting for Western courts and began imposing its own sanctions with drones and missiles. Call it enforcement at the speed of explosives. Creating a shell company to reflag a shadow-fleet tanker is fast and cheap. Replacing a refinery hit by a drone is slow and expensive, and Ukraine has spent 2026 working through the Russian refining system plant by plant. By early July, Ukraine’s General Staff assessed that its strikes had disabled roughly 43 percent of Russia’s oil refining capacity , with industry losses estimated at $13.5 billion since August 2025. Press enter or click to view image in full size Independent analysts at the Kyiv School of Economics and the IEA broadly corroborate that a large share of Russian refining was knocked offline, even where their exact figures differ. The new capabilities of Ukraine to reach far into Russia is the shock. Ukrainian drones and new long-range weapons have struck refineries and terminals more than 2,000 kilometers inside Russia, hit the St. Petersburg oil terminal, forced the Moscow refinery offline into year-end, and set shadow-fleet tankers ablaze in the Sea of Azov by the dozen. Russia has been reduced to selling crude to India at a discount while importing refined fuel to cover its own shortfall. The consequences are now visible on Russian streets. Gasoline rationing has reached Moscow. Blackouts have hit occupied Crimea. Drivers queue for miles in a petrostate that can no longer reliably refine its own fuel. For a country whose entire war economy rests on hydrocarbons, having its refining capacity cut in half is an economic cost that mounts daily. Russia invaded to project strength. It now cannot keep gasoline in its own capital. What Was It All For? Step back and total the ledger against the prize. The objective was to absorb territory that once belonged to the Soviet Union. Whatever slice of the Donbas Russia ultimately holds has been shelled into rubble, depopulated, its cities reduced to the kind of ruin that takes a generation and a fortune to rebuild. Russia is fighting to own wreckage. Press enter or click to view image in full size Set that against what the war has cost: on the order of a million-plus casualties, the majority of a modernized tank force, a flagship, a shattered military reputation, two new NATO members on its border, a rearmed and unified Europe, a permanent rupture with its largest energy customers, and a domestic economy taking daily damage two thousand kilometers behind the front. The NATO buffer is gone. The empire is not returning. The reputation is spent. Ukraine, meanwhile, has proven two things that will outlast this war. Western weapons and Ukrainian ingenuity together have outclassed Russian arms, and the cheap, iterated drone, more Ukrainian-innovated than Russian, is now understood by every serious military as the future of the battlefield. The side that was supposed to be erased in three days has instead rewritten how wars will be fought — and teaching the West. Imagine, for a moment, that Russia had faced the full weight the Western military rather than a smaller neighbor armed with exports and improvisation. Applying the recent context of US operations versus Russian, it no longer looks like a fair fight. This was a war of choice, launched by a former KGB officer chasing the ghost of Soviet glory. Thus far it has failed and what came instead was the largest self-inflicted strategic defeat by a major power in the modern era. The scorecard is not finished, and Russia may yet grind out more ground. But even if they achieve full control of Ukraine, Russia has already lost. The Cornered-Animal Problem Here is the real problem — What does Putin do now? The answers are the dangerous parts. A leader this deep in a losing war has very few exits, and the exits that remain get worse as you go down the list. Consider the off-ramps, in ascending order of peril. The first is simply to keep grinding. Russia is vast and Ukraine is comparatively small, and Moscow can in theory absorb losses indefinitely and trade bodies for territory until it holds the Donbas outright. Getting all of Ukraine seems to be a stretch, but eventually possible. But the costs compound with every mile, the domestic strain deepens, and the prize at the end is still rubble. The second problem is at home. A miscalculation of this scale generates turmoil, and there are only so many opponents a regime can jail or kill before the pressure finds another outlet. A leader who cannot admit defeat abroad and cannot silence dissent forever eventually faces a choice between escalation and domestic exposure. The next Yevgeny Prigozhin is likely already in the making. A cornered autocrat with a shrinking set of good options is the most dangerous variable in this entire equation. The Unthinkable Options Which brings us to the options no one wants to name, and which citizens and investors nonetheless have to price. The first is a false-flag provocation against a NATO member , an engineered incident designed to reframe the war for the Russian public as a defensive struggle against the West, justifying the full mobilization Putin has so far avoided for fear of the political cost. The logic is cynical but coherent: manufacture the existential threat that the “special military operation” was supposed to preempt. The United States has just recently explicitly warned Poland and the Baltic states that such an action is very possible. The second is nuclear use against Ukraine , the threat that has hovered over this war from the start. Its incoherence is its only reassurance. A leader who nukes the territory he invaded to absorb is left holding a poisoned, depopulated ruin, having destroyed the very thing he claimed to be liberating. And at the same time guaranteeing a Western response against a military the world has just watched fail against a smaller foe. Both dark scenarios lead to the same door: direct confrontation with NATO. And the battlefield of the last four years has already shown what happens when Russian conventional forces meet even Western-equipped resistance. Against the full alliance, the mismatch demonstrated in Ukraine would not favor the Kremlin. That reality is precisely what should restrain Putin, and precisely why a leader running out of other options is worth watching closely. For citizens, these are the tail risks that turn a distant war into a personal one. For investors, they are the reason a conflict that looks contained still carries a fat, unpriceable escalation premium. The most likely path remains a grinding, inconclusive continuation. But the low-probability, high-severity branches are the ones that move markets and lives, and they sit on the desk of a man with fewer and fewer ways to save face.

title: Cathie Wood sells $5.5 million of surging tech stock
text: Cathie Wood sells $5.5 million of surging tech stock. Cathie Wood, head of Ark Investment Management, likes to lock in gains when her tech darlings rally. That's exactly what she's doing with Snowflake, trimming her position after the cloud software stock surged nearly 10% over the past five trading days ahead of earnings. In 2025, the flagship Ark Innovation ETF gained 35.49%, far outpacing the S&P 500's return of 17.88% in the same period. But so far this year, Wood's flagship Ark Innovation ETF (ARKK) is down 8.51% as of July 31, while the S&P 500 surged 9.41%, Yahoo Finance data shows. Wood gained a reputation after the Ark Innovation ETF delivered a 153% return in 2020. But her style also brings painful losses in bearish markets, as seen in 2022, when the Ark Innovation ETF tumbled more than 60%. Those swings have weighed on Wood's long-term gains. As of July 31, her Ark Innovation ETF has delivered a five-year annualized return of -9.75%, while the S&P 500 has an annualized return of 11.25% over the same period, according to data from Morningstar. Cathie Wood flags "the deflationary impact" of tech innovation Wood usually focuses on high-tech companies across artificial intelligence, blockchain, biomedical technology, and robotics. She believes these businesses have strong growth potential, though their volatility often causes fluctuations in the Ark's funds. Over the decade ended 2025, the Ark Innovation ETF wiped out nearly $5 billion in investor wealth, according to an analysis by Morningstar's analyst Amy Arnott. That made it the fourth-biggest wealth destroyer among mutual funds and ETFs in the ranking. Wood believes investors have been focusing on the wrong signals as they assess the outlook for inflation, interest rates, and stocks. In a June post on X, Wood said the bond market is increasingly reflecting the deflationary impact of technological innovation, particularly artificial intelligence, rather than the inflation risks many investors still fear. Wood pointed to the continued flattening of the Treasury yield curve despite a sharp rise in oil prices over the past year. In previous cycles, she noted, an energy shock of that magnitude would have pushed long-term yields higher. Wood believes the bond market is "discounting something much more powerful: the deflationary impact of technological innovation, particularly artificial intelligence, which is beginning to increase productivity across broad swaths of the economy. " She also said easing tensions with Iran and a decline in oil prices could push inflation even lower.

title: Chevron CEO warns Iran conflict has created 'very real' threat to global oil supplies as gas prices climb
text: Chevron CEO warns Iran conflict has created 'very real' threat to global oil supplies as gas prices climb Chevron CEO Mike Wirth warned of "very real" dangers for the global oil industry as tensions escalate in Iran and Houthi attacks on Saudi oil facilities fuel concerns over a potential new shipping crisis. His comments come as oil prices climb following President Donald Trump's pause on U.S. strikes against Iran and as Saudi Arabia reportedly builds an international coalition to protect vital shipping routes. "We now see, not only the Strait of Hormuz, but the Red Sea and the Black Sea have risks and uncertainties. So, some of the challenges have expanded, and the risks to supply are very real," Wirth said during an appearance on "Sunday Morning Futures." While oil demand remains strong around the world, Wirth said energy markets are "fragile and uncertain" as the U.S. conflict with Iran festers into a sixth month and as global inventories continue to decline. "The world energy system has been stressed and the need for supplies to markets and customers has never been higher," the Chevron CEO said. The Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most vital trade routes, is one of the most contentious aspects of the United States conflict with Iran. Traffic has sunk to only a handful of vessels passing through the waterway each day. Recent Houthi attacks on another vital Middle East shipping route, the Red Sea, have raised fresh concerns about the reliability of that corridor. "I think the unfortunate thing is that energy assets have been targeted in this conflict. And what that means is it degrades the capacity of the energy system to meet global demand," Wirth said. "And how quickly that comes back will be one of the things that determines when markets actually get back to some sort of a new equilibrium." "We've seen supply constrained, we've seen damage to infrastructure. And we have new risks that I think will be priced into the market on shipping." U.S. crude oil is trading at roughly $84 per barrel, while the national average price for a gallon of gasoline stands at $4.09 – nearly $1 higher than the $3.15 average one year ago, according to AAA. Despite the growing geopolitical uncertainty, Chevron's production is up 20% year-on-year, with a 5% increase from Q1 to Q2 of 2026. The oil giant also set a record for producing more than 2 million barrels of oil equivalent in one day, an all-time high for the U.S., Wirth said.

title: As Trump balks again at escalating war, Iran smells ‘blood in the water’ and looks to exploit its newfound strategic advantage, experts say
text: As Trump balks again at escalating war, Iran smells ‘blood in the water’ and looks to exploit its newfound strategic advantage, experts say. In what has become a familiar pattern in the Iran war, President Donald Trump again threatened a massive attack then pulled back from the brink. But while he attributed his latest reversal to U.S. allies pleading with him to give diplomacy another chance, experts also see signs Iran is gaining the upper hand. That’s as Tehran has used its proxies to expand the war across the region, most notably Houthis rebels threatening ships in the Red Sea that are trying to use the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. At the same time, Iran has warned its Persian Gulf neighbors they will be targets in the event of a renewed bombardment after demonstrating that its long-range weapons can evade U.S. air defenses. “Iran and its clients see blood in the water and see a benefit for all of them in escalating and entering the fray,” Afshon Ostovar, an Iran expert at the Naval Postgraduate School, told the Financial Times . He added that their goal is to prolong the conflict instead of inflicting more severe damage as Iran looks to exploit less political endurance on the other side. “So the longer it continues, the weaker the resolve of their enemies will be,” Ostovar explained. “That is how they see it.” Indeed, Trump’s approval ratings on his handling of the economy have slumped alongside his numbers on the Iran war, with support slipping even among Republicans. And now that midterm elections are just a few months away and gas prices are back up again, Tehran sees leverage in the U.S. political calendar. An Iranian diplomat told the Wall Street Journal that the regime is prepared to take advantage of Trump political vulnerability and would consider preemptive strikes if talks fail. That aggressive stance was on display last week, when Iran launched unprovoked attacks on U.S. bases in what Central Command called an “attempted surprise attack.” By contrast, Trump’s continued restraint comes despite Iran crossing his red line for resuming all-out war after it killed U.S. troops in Jordan last month. To be sure, the U.S. still retains significant military assets in the region and continues to enforce a naval blockade on Iran that’s causing more economic pain. But the U.S. and its allies have also severely depleted stockpiles of interceptors needed to repel Iranian attacks, making critical pieces of their energy infrastructure more at risk. Global energy markets have also sharply drawn down inventories of crude oil and refined products, with analysts warning that “tank bottoms” will be just around the corner unless the Strait of Hormuz reopens soon. The combined effect is that the overall playing field has tilted in favor of the Islamic Republic. “Last night’s events underscore a reality that is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore: for now, Iran appears to hold the strategic advantage in deterrence,” Dennis Citrinowicz, a former Israeli intelligence official who specialized in Iran, posted on X . “It has succeeded in creating a form of mutual deterrence that is shaping Washington’s calculations.” Despite suffering heavy losses at that start of the war, Iran has since shown it can hold the global economy hostage by threatening maritime chokepoints and its Gulf neighbors, he added. In fact, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke directly with Trump on Saturday to express concern over the plans for massive new U.S. strikes on Iran, sources told Axios . The kingdom’s de facto ruler reportedly urged Trump to de-escalate and refrain from launching the attacks, days after the Saudi defense minister conveyed a similar message. “President Trump may still decide to order military action. But the fact that Washington continues to hesitate suggests that it recognizes the risks of escalation and is not convinced that a broader campaign would compel Iran to back down,” Citrinowicz wrote. title: STAT+: Michigan Supreme Court ruling allows probe into Lilly insulin pricing
text: STAT+: Michigan Supreme Court ruling allows probe into Lilly insulin pricing. A divided Michigan Supreme Court ruled on Friday that the state’s attorney general may investigate Eli Lilly over its pricing practices for insulin. In its 4-to-3 decision , the court rejected a lower court decision that prevented Michigan Attorney General Dana Nesel from proceeding with a probe that began four years ago. At the time, Nessel cited state consumer protection laws, alleging the drug maker had artificially increased the price of its insulin medication. Lilly was accused of charging “grossly” excessive prices for three different insulin products — Lispro, Humalog and Basaglar — that forced some patients to ration or forego insulin, restrict their diets or buy less-effective alternatives. title: Redfin shows why the housing market is better than you think
text: Redfin shows why the housing market is better than you think. Higher home prices. Fewer pending housing sales. At first glance, data from Redfin's Weekly Housing Market Tracker looks kind of dismal. Not to mention that the 30-year Freddie Mac mortgage rate has hit 6.66% — its highest point in a year. But the housing market isn't as bad for homebuyers as it may seem. And I'm not saying that to placate anyone. The data backs it up. In a recent Redfin report , the company puts today's real estate market into perspective. In fact, today's homebuyers have a lot of advantages they might not recognize. Specifically, the report notes that many homebuyers look back on the market during the Covid pandemic (think 2020-2022) through rose-colored glasses because mortgage rates were so low. "It’s important for house hunters to remember that while mortgage rates were much lower during the pandemic, every listing was ultra-competitive; buyers often had to pay tens of thousands of dollars over the asking price to win a home," said Bonnie Phillips , a Redfin Premier agent. Mortgage rates have spiked since 2022 I can't deny it — I'm happy that Redfin is helping contextualize today's housing market. Not only did I cover the housing market as a journalist in the early 2020s, but I also bought my first home in the Seattle area in 2022. I can testify from both a professional and personal standpoint that the housing market was the Wild West. None of the usual rules applied. Mortgage rates started to drop in early 2020 when Covid-19 hit the United States. The Federal Reserve began slashing the federal funds rate and buying up more mortgage-backed securities to stabilize the economy, and home loan rates fell in response. Related: Cooler PCE inflation data can't fix today’s mortgage rates National rates stayed below 4% for about two years, until early 2022. The lowest 30-year fixed mortgage rate on record was 2.65% in January 2021, according to Freddie Mac . As of July 30, 2026, the 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 6.66% . People are definitely missing those sub-3% rates. But if you weren't actively buying a home in the early 2020s, you may not realize how volatile and overwhelming the experience was. In reality, low mortgage rates were among the few things the housing market had going for it at the time. At the peak of the Covid pandemic, mortgage rates were low, but sales prices were high. Newsday LLC &sol Getty Images Redfin explains the trade-offs of higher rates The current higher mortgage rates are frustrating, especially when so many people expected lower rates in 2026. But in many ways, the housing market is better for homebuyers than just a few years ago. "Rates are higher now, but bidding wars are unlikely, and buyers are often able to negotiate prices down and get concessions from sellers," Phillips said. In spring 2022, over 53% of homes in the U.S. sold above asking price, according to Redfin data . (Lucky me — this was exactly when I was buying my first home.) Homes selling above the listing price were often the result of brutal bidding wars. That share dropped to 28% by July 2026. More Housing Market: Fewer foreign homebuyers won’t fix U.S. affordability Mortgage rate forecast resets after Fed decision Americans reject homebuilders despite price cuts Homes also sold much more quickly in the early 2020s, which meant you had to rush to make an offer if you found a house you really wanted. Sometimes you were lucky if you had enough time to view the home in person and craft an offer before someone else swooped in and bought it first. The typical home sold within 15 days in June and July 2021, according to Redfin data , with many buyers making offers without seeing the properties in person. The median amount of time a home spends on the market is now 41 days . As I mentioned, I bought in spring 2022. Like everyone else in the greater Seattle area, I wanted to buy a house to lock in a mortgage rate before rates spiked. My real estate agent told me at the time that we'd have way more leverage if a house stayed on the market for an entire week, because that was considered a long time. This kind of pressure led to even greater competition, because buyers in my area were panicked. 'Patience over panic': How homebuyers benefit in the current housing market You will almost undoubtedly get stuck with a higher interest rate in 2026 than you would have in 2020 or 2021. However, the home-buying process will likely be much smoother. America is a buyer's market right now, meaning homebuyers have more power than sellers. You don't have to rush. You don't have to weigh whether you should try to buy before seeing a house. You don't have to scrape together savings to offer tens of thousands of dollars over the asking price. As a result, you have the time to find a home that is actually a strong fit for your family. One you might be happier with in the long term. And remember, when mortgage rates decrease later, you can refinance into a new loan with a lower rate . "Marry the house, date the rate." The saying is a classic for a reason. "Today’s housing market rewards patience over panic: If you can afford to buy, focus on finding a home you love and negotiating a good deal rather than trying to perfectly time mortgage rates," Phillips said. title: Activist Investor Stakes Are Reshaping Corporate Boardrooms Across the Globe
text: Activist Investor Stakes Are Reshaping Corporate Boardrooms Across the Globe. When a prominent hedge fund quietly accumulates a significant position in a major corporation, markets take notice — and for good reason. An activist investor stake is no longer just a Wall Street spectacle. It has evolved into a powerful global signal that can trigger leadership shake-ups, strategic pivots, and billion-dollar restructuring plans. From Tokyo to Toronto, institutional investors are watching these moves with unprecedented intensity, and the ripple effects are being felt across industries that once seemed untouchable. The mechanics are deceptively straightforward: an activist investor acquires a meaningful ownership stake in a publicly traded company, then leverages that position to push for changes they believe will unlock shareholder value. But the outcomes can be anything but simple, often sparking boardroom battles, proxy wars, and public debates about the very purpose of a corporation. Understanding why these stakes attract global attention requires looking at both the strategy behind them and the market forces that make them so consequential today. The Strategic Logic Behind an Activist Investor Stake Activist investing is built on a core thesis: that a company’s current management is leaving significant value on the table. When an activist investor stake crosses certain regulatory thresholds — typically 5% in the United States, triggering a Schedule 13D filing — it signals that the fund has not only taken a position but intends to influence the direction of the business. This disclosure alone can move a stock price by double digits within hours. The demands that follow vary widely. Some activists push for share buybacks or special dividends to return cash to shareholders. Others call for divestitures of underperforming business units, executive leadership changes, or even full-scale mergers. In more aggressive campaigns, activists seek board seats directly, giving them a formal seat at the table during critical strategic decisions. Funds like Elliott Investment Management, Starboard Value, and Third Point have built reputations precisely because their activist investor stakes consistently precede significant corporate transformations. What makes these strategies particularly compelling to global observers is the data supporting their effectiveness. Studies consistently show that companies targeted by activist investors tend to outperform their peers in the 12 to 36 months following an initial engagement, particularly when management responds constructively rather than defensively. This performance track record has legitimized activist investing in the eyes of even traditionally conservative institutional allocators. Why Global Markets Are Increasingly Responsive Activist investing was once considered a predominantly American phenomenon, rooted in the shareholder-primacy culture of U.S. capital markets. That geography has changed dramatically. Europe, Asia-Pacific, and emerging markets are now active theaters for activist campaigns, driven by several converging forces. Corporate governance reforms across developed economies have made it easier for minority shareholders to exercise their rights. Japan’s ongoing push to improve return on equity among its listed companies has opened the door to activist investor stakes that would have been culturally and legally unwelcome a decade ago. In the United Kingdom, regulatory frameworks that protect shareholder engagement have made London a fertile ground for campaigns targeting conglomerates and financial institutions alike. Technology has also accelerated the global spread of activist investing. Real-time disclosure requirements mean that an activist investor stake filed in New York generates immediate analysis in Singapore, Frankfurt, and São Paulo within minutes. Institutional investors managing globally diversified portfolios now treat activist disclosures as leading indicators — not just for the target company, but for entire sectors. When an activist takes aim at a major consumer goods company, competitors and suppliers feel the pressure too, as markets reassess whether similar value-unlocking moves could be replicated across the industry. The Corporate Response and Its Market Implications Companies have not been passive in the face of rising activist pressure. Many have adopted sophisticated early-warning systems designed to identify activist investor stake accumulation before public disclosure thresholds are reached. Investor relations teams now monitor unusual trading volumes, analyze ownership registry data, and maintain open dialogue with large institutional shareholders to detect shifting sentiment early. When a campaign does go public, the corporate response strategy matters enormously. Research shows that companies that engage constructively with activist demands — even partially — tend to fare better in both the proxy contest outcome and subsequent stock performance. Those that dig in defensively, adopting poison pills or launching aggressive public counter-campaigns, often face prolonged uncertainty that erodes value for all shareholders. Boards are also increasingly adding independent directors with financial restructuring expertise as a preemptive measure, signaling to the market that governance is being taken seriously before any activist investor stake appears on the radar. This proactive posture has become a recognized best practice in corporate governance circles, reflecting just how deeply activist investing has influenced how companies think about their own structures and strategies. What This Means for Individual and Institutional Investors For investors seeking to capitalize on activist situations, the opportunities are real but require careful analysis. Buying into a stock simply because an activist investor stake has been disclosed can be a profitable strategy — but timing, campaign credibility, and management receptivity all influence outcomes significantly. Not every activist campaign succeeds, and those that drag on for years can create substantial uncertainty for shareholders who entered at inflated post-disclosure prices. - Monitor 13D and 13G filings for early signals of activist accumulation - Assess the activist’s track record in comparable situations - Evaluate the fundamental valuation gap the activist is targeting - Consider how management has historically responded to external pressure - Watch for secondary effects on sector peers and supply chains The rise of activist investing as a global force reflects something deeper than opportunistic financial maneuvering. It represents a fundamental shift in how capital markets hold corporations accountable. As long as governance gaps and strategic underperformance persist in public markets, the activist investor stake will remain one of the most closely watched signals in global finance — one that no serious investor, board member, or market strategist can afford to ignore.

title: Which company lost your business this year? Reddit users name big brands
text: Which company lost your business this year? Reddit users name big brands. The thread, posted to r/AskReddit by u/FriendlytoNature, attracted more than 4,000 comments as Redditors shared the brands they no longer trust. Some named major corporations, while others called out local businesses. Some celebrated companies they had personally stopped supporting. Reddit users reveal the companies they refuse to support The highest-rated response came from a former smoker who wrote, “I quit smoking so Marlboro lost my business hopefully forever.” Many commenters congratulated the user instead of criticizing the company. “Good for you man,” one reply read. Other responses focused on frustrating customer experiences. One Redditor accused Safelite of filing a lawsuit after one of its technicians suffered an injury while working at their home. The commenter claimed they provided first aid and took the worker to the emergency room before receiving legal papers weeks later. “Safelite was suing me for workers comp,” the user wrote. “Scumbags.” Several replies expressed disbelief. One commenter responded, “That’s heinous. They have insurance for a reason and shouldn’t be going near you.” DoorDash also drew criticism throughout the thread. One user claimed a driver stole their order and said the company refused compensation. Others complained about high delivery fees and higher menu prices. One commenter argued that ordering directly from restaurants often costs much less. Another Redditor criticized Airbnb. “The scourge of hosts expecting guests to do all the household chores and even wash the bedding!” they wrote. “I’m not paying you for the luxury of cleaning your home.” Replies echoed that frustration. One commenter questioned why guests still pay cleaning fees after completing extensive checkout chores. Another former vacation rental cleaner claimed property owners often keep much of those fees instead of paying cleaning crews. Verizon, Panera, Taylor Farms, and Spectrum also appeared repeatedly Several brands appeared multiple times throughout the discussion. One Redditor said Verizon gradually reduced discounts before increasing monthly prices despite earlier promises. Another user claimed their bill changed almost every month despite keeping the same service plan. Panera Bread also drew complaints from longtime customers. One commenter said the restaurant once served “amazing” food but now tastes like “the worst food at a regional airport.” Another joked that Panera changed from “upscale hospital food” into simply “hospital food.” Taylor Farms also surfaced repeatedly. One commenter simply named the company. Another user urged shoppers to avoid several private-label salad brands that the commenter claimed source products from Taylor Farms, including Walmart’s Marketside, Target’s Good & Gather, Aldi’s Little Salad Bar, Whole Foods’ 365, Kroger’s Simple Truth, Publix GreenWise, and Safeway’s O Organics. Spectrum also received criticism. One Redditor called the internet provider “pieces of sh–.” Another replied that the company often operates in areas with few alternative providers. The Reddit thread highlighted how quickly everyday frustrations can turn into permanent brand boycotts. The claims came from individual users and remain unverified by The Daily Dot.
