title: Weekend - Trump cancels Iran strikes as deal 'perimeters' agreed, Tehran denies request
text: Weekend - Trump cancels Iran strikes as deal 'perimeters' agreed, Tehran denies request. A confirmed stand-down from strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure would remove, for now, one of the more acute supply-side risks weighing on oil markets, particularly given the scale of the reported bombing campaign under discussion. Any de-escalation touching the Hormuz Strait carries outsized significance given the volume of global crude that transits the waterway daily, and traders will likely read the prospect of guaranteed passage as a bullish signal for freight and a bearish one for the geopolitical risk premium embedded in prices. However, Iran's official denial of the central premise, that it requested a pause, introduces meaningful uncertainty: markets may be reluctant to fully price out risk until both sides confirm the same version of events. Sentiment is likely to stay choppy, with any further US military signalling or Iranian rhetoric capable of reversing the move quickly. --- In a weekend social media post Trump claims a deal has averted Iran strikes, but Tehran insists no such request was made. Summary: Trump posted on Truth Social saying he had cancelled planned strikes on Iran He said Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked the US to hold off pending a deal The proposed deal would reportedly include full opening of the Hormuz Strait and an end to Iran's nuclear threat Iran's Mehr news agency denied any such request was made, calling the claim "a new lie" Iran's acting Defence Minister Majid Ibn al-Reza said Tehran treats every threat as real and credible US media had reported the US and Israel were planning intense strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure, discussed at Friday's cabinet meeting Donald Trump says he has called off planned strikes against Iran, citing an agreement in principle on the shape of a broader deal, even as Tehran disputes the central claim behind his announcement. In a post on Truth Social, the US president said Washington was "locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II." Despite this, he said, Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked the US to hold off on any attack as the "perimeters" of a deal had been agreed. He said the arrangement would involve the immediate and complete opening of the Hormuz Strait and an end to Iran's nuclear threat, and that he had agreed to cancel the strikes on that basis, subject to a deal being reached rapidly. Israel, he added, had joined the commitment. Iran's semi-official Mehr news agency rejected Trump's account outright, describing it as nothing but a new lie. The country's acting Defence Minister, Majid Ibn al-Reza, said Tehran regarded every threat from its adversaries as real and credible, even those forming part of psychological warfare, adding that Iran would neither be caught off guard nor remain passive. The exchange follows reports in US media that Washington and Israel had been preparing one of the most intense bombing campaigns yet against Iranian energy infrastructure. According to sources cited by CBS News, the BBC's US news partner, the plan was raised during Trump's cabinet meeting on Friday. The US government has also urged Americans in the Middle East to remain alert and ready to leave the region should tensions escalate further. It is not the first time Trump has issued dire warnings toward Iran only to later frame the situation as one where diplomacy is being given room to work. Whether this latest reversal marks genuine progress toward a deal, or another cycle in an already volatile standoff, may depend on how quickly the two sides can reconcile their conflicting accounts of what was actually agreed. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

title: The Signal Every Equity Investor Should Watch: Institutional Accumulation Is Reshaping Market Trends
text: The Signal Every Equity Investor Should Watch: Institutional Accumulation Is Reshaping Market Trends. When large asset managers, pension funds, and hedge funds begin quietly building positions in specific equities, the market rarely announces it with fanfare. Instead, the evidence surfaces in volume patterns, price action, and order flow data — subtle footprints left by some of the most sophisticated participants in global finance. Understanding institutional accumulation is no longer a niche pursuit for technical analysts. It has become one of the most important lenses through which equity market direction can be understood and anticipated. Institutional accumulation occurs when large entities systematically purchase shares of a stock or asset class over an extended period, often without triggering dramatic short-term price spikes. These buyers have both the capital and the patience to build substantial positions gradually, absorbing available supply while minimizing market impact. When this behavior becomes widespread across multiple sectors, it tends to precede broader market advances — making it a powerful leading indicator for individual investors and portfolio managers alike. What the Data Is Telling Us About Current Market Positioning Recent equity market data paints a compelling picture of deepening institutional conviction. On-balance volume metrics across large-cap technology, industrials, and select financial stocks have shown sustained upward trends even during brief periods of surface-level volatility. This divergence — where price dips are met with rising volume rather than selling pressure — is a textbook signature of institutional accumulation in progress. Funds are using weakness as an opportunity, not a warning sign. Sector rotation patterns further reinforce this narrative. Capital has been flowing into cyclical sectors that typically benefit from economic expansion, while defensive plays have seen comparatively muted inflows. Institutional investors don’t rotate into economically sensitive sectors unless they have a constructive view of forward earnings and macroeconomic conditions. The breadth of this accumulation across multiple industries suggests a coordinated bullish outlook, not a speculative bet concentrated in one corner of the market. It is also worth examining 13F filings, which publicly traded institutional investment managers must submit quarterly to the SEC. These disclosures, while lagged by up to 45 days, reveal meaningful shifts in portfolio composition. Recent filings have shown notable increases in equity exposure among some of the world’s largest funds, particularly in sectors tied to infrastructure spending, artificial intelligence infrastructure, and domestic manufacturing. The consistency of these additions across unrelated funds underscores a shared macro thesis — and reinforces the argument that institutional accumulation is not an isolated phenomenon but a broad, structural market dynamic. Implications for Equity Market Outlook When institutional capital commits to equities at scale, the medium-term implications for price action are generally positive. Large funds don’t exit positions quickly — the same logic that governs their entry governs their exit. This creates a kind of gravitational pull that supports prices even when retail sentiment turns cautious. For individual investors, recognizing when institutional accumulation is underway can help frame a more grounded, evidence-based market outlook rather than one driven by headlines or short-term noise. That said, institutional accumulation is not a guarantee of linear price appreciation. Markets can remain range-bound for extended periods even while large players are quietly building positions. External shocks — geopolitical disruptions, unexpected monetary policy shifts, or earnings disappointments — can delay the realization of price targets that institutions have identified. This is precisely why sophisticated investors treat accumulation signals as one input in a broader analytical framework, rather than a standalone buy trigger. Liquidity conditions also deserve attention. When central bank policy remains relatively accommodative or credit spreads stay compressed, institutional capital tends to flow more freely into risk assets, amplifying the effects of accumulation. A tightening backdrop can slow this process considerably, making macro awareness an essential complement to any accumulation-focused strategy. The broader takeaway is this: institutional accumulation represents informed, patient capital making deliberate bets on future value. When the data shows these bets being placed across multiple sectors and asset classes simultaneously, the equity market outlook deserves serious attention. Investors who learn to read these signals — rather than waiting for the move to be obvious — position themselves to act with the kind of conviction that typically drives superior long-term returns.

title: Weekend - OPEC+ agrees 188,000 bpd September hike, completing rollback of 2023 output cuts
text: Weekend - OPEC+ agrees 188,000 bpd September hike, completing rollback of 2023 output cuts. The September increase is largely symbolic given that export flows from the Gulf remain constrained by the Iran conflict, meaning the barrels are unlikely to show up in physical markets in the near term. The more consequential signal is the option value it creates: should Trump's weekend claim of a de-escalation with Iran hold, and Gulf flows normalise, Saudi Arabia and its partners would have room to lift real output and help unwind the supply squeeze that has been pushing up gasoline and diesel costs. That combination, a completed rollback plus a potential ceasefire, points toward downside risk for the geopolitical premium currently embedded in crude, though Iran's denial of Trump's account keeps that risk two-sided. Traders will also be watching for signs of OPEC+ positioning ahead of a fourth-quarter pause, which Rystad's Jorge Leon frames as the base case while the group prepares for 2027 quota negotiations. --- Earlier: Weekend - Trump cancels Iran strikes as deal 'perimeters' agreed, Tehran denies request OPEC+ completes its supply revival just as Trump's claimed Iran de-escalation raises the prospect of normalised Gulf flows. Summary: OPEC+ approved a roughly 188,000 bpd production increase for September, completing the rollback of a 1.65 million bpd voluntary cut agreed in 2023 The core group, Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman, has raised quotas monthly throughout the Iran war despite limited real-world supply impact OPEC+'s statement gave no guidance on fourth-quarter policy, though Rystad's Jorge Leon expects a pause while the group prepares for 2027 quota talks A separate OPEC+ committee reiterated concern that attacks on Iranian energy assets are costly and time-consuming to repair, weighing on supply Trump said over the weekend the US would hold off on new Iran strikes after Tehran and other Middle Eastern nations indicated they were working toward a deal Roughly 2 million bpd of separate 2022-dated cuts remain in place until the end of the year, with capacity reviews underway ahead of 2027 quota-setting OPEC+ has agreed to raise its collective production target by around 188,000 barrels a day from September, completing the phased rollback of a 1.65 million bpd voluntary supply cut first agreed in 2023, the producer group said Sunday. The increase, approved by core members Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman, closes out a restoration campaign that has run largely on paper for much of this year. Export disruptions from the Gulf, along with flows from Russia and Kazakhstan tied to the Iran and Ukraine wars, have meant successive monthly OPEC+ hikes have had little real impact on physical supply. According to Reuters, OPEC+'s statement made no reference to what the group intends for the fourth quarter, despite sources indicating before the meeting that a pause was likely once the rollback was finished. Analysts said OPEC+ now faces the task of managing a surplus that could emerge as export flows normalise, adding that with the restoration campaign complete, the group has little incentive to rush into further supply changes. Cited base case arguments are for a fourth-quarter pause while OPEC+ turns its attention to negotiations over 2027 quotas, a process complicated by members such as Iraq pushing for higher individual allocations to reflect greater production capacity. A separate OPEC+ panel, the Joint Ministerial Monitoring Committee, also met Sunday and repeated concerns about the cost and disruption of repairing energy assets damaged in the US-Israeli war on Iran. Roughly 2 million bpd of a separate, older layer of cuts dating to 2022 remains in place until the end of this year across most members. The output decision landed alongside comments from President Donald Trump , who said over the weekend that the US would hold off on further strikes against Iran after Tehran and other Middle Eastern countries indicated a deal was taking shape. Any genuine easing of the conflict would carry particular weight for OPEC+'s calculus, since a return to normal Gulf export flows would give Saudi Arabia and its partners scope to convert this month's largely symbolic hike into real barrels, helping to rebuild global stockpiles depleted by the supply squeeze. The exit of the United Arab Emirates from the group in May, after years of friction over output limits, continues to fuel speculation that OPEC+ could eventually face a contest over market share once the current restoration phase gives way to the harder question of 2027 baselines. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

title: Costco's changes fix members' biggest problems
text: Costco's changes fix members' biggest problems. Membership sales and retention drive Costco 's business and the chain has succeeded in creating a very loyal membership base. "Who we found is the best at customer loyalty is Costco, which may not be surprising," UBS Analyst Michael Lasser told CNBC . Costco, he noted, excels at value and convenience. Lasser called traffic the best way to judge retail loyalty. That's a metric Costo has done well with. "Over the past two years, Costco has made several moves that risked upsetting its famously loyal customer base – including raising membership fees in September 2024 and restricting food court access to members only. But visit data suggests that, rather than deterring shoppers, these changes have supported rising engagement and a broadening customer base," according to data from Placer.AI . The chain, however, has grown its foot traffic. "Costco entered 2026 with solid visit momentum. Both total and same-store visits posted healthy year-over-year gains through the back half of 2025 and into January," added Placer. AI . It's a level of success that has actually caused another problem for the warehouse club — overloading its stores — which the chain has taken a number of steps to address. Costco makes real changes Costco has taken some key steps to spread out the traffic at its stores to keep the shopping experience positive for members. The first involves making simple changes designed to spread out traffic. That's something CFO Gary Millerchip spoke about during the chain's third-quarter earnings call . "I do think there is a lot of work that we have done over recent quarters to create more opportunity for members to visit more frequently, whether it was the extended hours for our gas stations, before the recent growth in gas that we have seen with higher prices," he said. In addition to extended gas station hours, Costco also has opened its warehouses earlier exclusively for Executive members. Costco has also invested in improving its existing warehouses so they can serve more members. "So far this year, we have also completed two relocations with one more planned in Q4 as we continue to relocate select high-volume warehouses to larger locations with more parking and expanded gas stations to provide a better member experience and drive more volumes in these warehouses," CEO Ron Vachris said during the call. Related: History of Costco: Company timeline and facts Costco keeps adding warehouses As Americans continue to prioritize value amid concerns about household budgets, Costco has become a primary grocery destination for a surprising share of shoppers. “A recent survey found that 15% of Americans ages 18 to 24 and 17% of Americans ages 25 to 34 do most of their grocery shopping at Costco. That share declines among older generations — 9% of those ages 35 to 44 do their grocery shopping at Costco, 3% of those ages 45 to 54 prefer Costco for groceries, and 6% of those 55 and older shop for groceries at Costco,” according to GOBankingRates . Costco, Vachris shared during the Q3 earnings continues to build new warehouses, often to take stress off of existing locations. "We target 30-plus net new openings per year in the coming years. In the quarter, we opened four net new warehouses, including three in the U.S., and one additional Canadian business center. Those openings brought our total warehouse count to 928 worldwide," he said. More Costco: Costco makes silent gas change members will love Big changes could be in store for Costco Costco faces a food safety problem members need to know Former CFO Ron Galanti talked about how the chain picks new locations during its first-quarter 2024 earnings call . “I don’t have the numbers in front of me, but I know, in fiscal ’23, we had something like 25 or so locations that did over 400 million, and another 160 or so that did 300 million to 400 million. Those are huge numbers. And certainly, as we get to 350-plus...when it starts having a three in front of it, certainly at $350 million, we want to start looking to see what we can do to cannibalize it, frankly, and to have more growth in that market,” he shared. You have to be a member to shop at Costco. Shutterstock Costco moves have a big impact Costco typically relocates four-to-six locations each year and the impact of that on sales is meaningful. “When we do these, we normally are moving a building that is underserving the market and goes into a larger facility [with] better parking. [We can see] extreme 50%, 60% increases when you add a gas station and really add a lot of parking to a 20% uplift to a building that had everything [and] just got into a better facility,” Vachris said during the chain’s first-quarter earnings call . Kenneth Schuckman operates Schuckman Realty, a full-service commercial real estate services firm serving New York City, Long Island, and the surrounding tri-state area and New Jersey. He shared some insights on how Costco picks new locations. “CEO Ron Vachris calls the approach strategic cannibalization. The idea is simple: build new warehouses near overburdened locations to redistribute customer volume and improve the shopping experience. These in-fill locations allow customers to spend less time battling for parking spaces or waiting in long lines, which in turn encourages more frequent visits and higher spending,” he shared on his website . Analysts support Costco's moves Gary Sankary, a retail veteran with 50 years of experience, sees little reason to question anything Costco does. “Costco has been incredibly successful, and not by accident. They place their stores in markets where they are likely to succeed. This means the market has the right population density, the right economic and competitive profile, and can be efficiently supported by their supply chain ,” he posted on RetailWire . At the same time, analysts note opportunities for improvement. “Costco can improve in areas like collect from store, checking what’s in stock at the warehouse, and making the ecommerce process easier,” GlobalData Managing Director Neil Saunders posted on RetailWire . In addition to adding warehouses and relocating others, Costco has also made investments in faster checkout, digital membership cards, and other technology that improves the member experience. Dominick Miserandino, CEO of RTMNexus , told TheStreet that Costco has a very simple motive with its tech investments. “Costco isn’t digitizing for buzz. Its digital and in-store tech is translating directly to faster service and stronger member engagement,” he shared. The warehouse club continues to report strong membership gains and renewal rates. "We ended the quarter with 82.9 million total paid members, up 4.1% versus last year, and a 149 million cardholders, up 4% year over year. In terms of renewal rates, at Q3 end, our U.S. and Canada renewal rate was 92.2%," Millerchip said during the Q3 call. Related: Rebel sports league faces Chapter 11 bankruptcy

title: Trump Revives Spotlight on California Offshore Oil Project
text: Trump Revives Spotlight on California Offshore Oil Project. President Donald Trump reignited his administration's ongoing energy dispute with California in a Truth Social post on Sunday, highlighting a previous executive order designed to restart oil operations tied to the Sable Pipeline and significantly expand offshore oil production off the state's coast. When contacted for comment about Trump's post, California Governor Gavin Newsom's office directed Newsweek on Sunday to previous press releases from the governor on the issue. "Donald Trump started a war, admitted it would spike gas prices nationwide, and told Americans it was a small price to pay. Now he’s using this crisis of his own making to attempt what he’s wanted to do for years: open California’s coast for his oil industry friends so they can poison our beaches," Newsom said in March, later adding, "California will not stand by while the Trump administration attempts to sacrifice our coastal communities, our environment, and our $51 billion coastal economy." Newsweek contacted the White House for comment via email on Sunday. Executive Action Targets Sable Pipeline Restart A White House graphic posted to Truth Social on Sunday by the president spotlighted an executive order enabling the Department of Energy (DOE) to use the Defense Production Act to restart the Sable Pipeline. The post noted Energy Secretary Chris Wright was to issue an order resulting in the “immediate production of 50,000 barrels of oil per day,” which the White House said would increase offshore oil production in California by 550 percent. The post also stated that the pipeline would produce “20 million barrels of oil equivalent per year” to meet urgent Department of Defense requirements—referenced as the “Department of War”—to supply 50 military installations on the West Coast. The post asserted that the order would preempt “radical California climate laws,” framing the initiative as an effort to end the Golden State's “coordinated regulatory attacks on American energy dominance.” The DOE announced in March that Wright had directed Sable Offshore Corp. to restore operations at the Santa Ynez Unit and Santa Ynez Pipeline System, citing supply disruption risks and national defense needs. The action was executed under Defense Production Act authorities delegated through an executive order amended by Trump. Wright said in the DOE announcement that the order would “strengthen America’s oil supply” and restore a pipeline system he described as “vital to our national security and defense.” The department said Sable’s facility can produce about 50,000 barrels per day, which it described as a 15 percent increase to California’s in-state oil production, and said the output could replace nearly 1.5 million barrels of foreign crude each month. Trump's decision to reshare the graphic follows months of emphasis by the administration on energy security, alongside concerns regarding disruptions to oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy chokepoint that carries roughly 20 million barrels of oil per day, amid the Iran war. Newsom and West Coast Governors Push Back The Sunday post follows conflict between Trump and California officials over offshore drilling. Newsweek previously reported that Newsom had dismissed reports of a Trump plan to expand drilling off California’s coast as “dead on arrival in California” and said the state would “absolutely” challenge the plan in court if finalized. Newsweek later reported that the Trump administration had unveiled a five-year leasing plan including six offshore lease sales along the California coast between 2027-30, where no new federal leases had been issued since the mid-1980s. That proposal also included drilling in waters at least 100 miles off Florida’s shoreline and more than 20 additional lease sales off Alaska. California has repeatedly opposed new offshore drilling. Newsom said in November that Trump’s offshore drilling proposal was “idiotic” and a “reckless attempt to sell out our coastline to his Big Oil donors.” In January, Newsom joined the governors of Oregon and Washington in formally opposing new oil and gas lease sales off California’s coast, warning of risks to coastal economies, marine ecosystems and communities. California regulators and environmental groups have already mounted legal challenges over the Sable restart and related pipeline approvals. California Attorney General Rob Bonta, joined by the Office of the State Fire Marshal, has challenged federal efforts in January to shift oversight of the Las Flores pipelines from state regulators to the federal Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration, as well as DOE’s Defense Production Act order directing the restart. Environmental groups, including the Environmental Defense Center, the Center for Biological Diversity and Earthjustice, have also sought to intervene in support of California’s challenge, according to the Santa Barbara Independent. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Steve Mollman and Anthony Murray.

title: 'Are you kidding me?' Ex-Trump aide blasts economic 'slap in the face'
text: 'Are you kidding me?' Ex-Trump aide blasts economic 'slap in the face'. The messaging coming out of the Trump administration about the state of the economy lit a fire underneath a former Trump White House official on Sunday. Sarah Matthews, who was Trump's deputy press secretary during the first term, told MS NOW's Nicolle Wallace on "Deadline: White House: Weekend" that the second Trump administration is trying to "gaslight" Americans about the state of the economy. She pointed to a recent appearance by Trump's top economic adviser, Kevin Hassett, where he claimed that the economy is " amazing " despite a wealth of evidence suggesting otherwise. " They're trying to gaslight their voters and tell them everything's fine," Matthews said. "Putting Kevin Hassett out there and having him go on the news and say that the economy is amazing. I mean, are you kidding me?" Trump has consistently boasted about the economy, even as recent data suggests it's " nothing to brag about ," as the Wall Street Journal's conservative editorial board recently surmised. The economy grew at a "tepid" 1.5% during the last quarter, the editorial board noted, and stubborn inflation caused the Federal Reserve to leave its benchmark interest rate in place. Matthews said that messaging is a "slap in the face" to people who helped put Trump in office. " It's just amazing that they clearly have not learned the lessons of the previous administration, and then are trying to tell their voters that everything's fine. And the thing is ... people do feel bamboozled," Matthews said. "They voted for President Trump because he said that he was going to lower prices on day one. He said that he was going to be the peace president. He said he was going to do all these things. And it turns out that he's done the exact opposite. So, it is just a slap in the face to the people who put him into office and have supported him f or them to continue to try to gaslight them."

title: Costco shoppers are saying goodbye to cheap gas after station abruptly shuttered for months
text: Costco shoppers are saying goodbye to cheap gas after station abruptly shuttered for months. A BUSTLING Costco store has shuttered its gas station, and customers will have to go elsewhere for cheaper fuel options. Drivers suffering from rising gas prices are going to feel pain at the pump elsewhere during the month-long station blackout. The Town Center Costco in Kennesaw, Georgia, a northwest Atlanta suburb, closed its gas station on July 13 for an expansion project. Stunned drivers were greeted with a message attached to fuel pumps saying the revitalized station will be “newly expanded and improved,” the Marietta Daily Journal reported. This means more fuel pumps are going to be added, according to a Costco employee who spoke with the outlet. A row of four new pumps is being added to the fueling island, the plan approved by the Cobb Board of Commissioners in 2024 states. read more motors stories The change won’t affect any of the supermarket’s parking spots. The construction project is set to be complete in November. The gas station expansion comes as a disappointment to shoppers who are heading in droves to fill up at the cheaper pumps, Costco execs say. The massive supermarket-branded stations have gotten so popular the chain is opening up standalone ones throughout the US. Last year, Costco CEO Ron Vachris expanded gas station hours to boost convenience for drivers. But shoppers should know they can’t actually access the pumps unless they’re a card-carrying Costco member.

title: Japan to vow coordination with US on weak yen in historic battle
text: Japan to vow coordination with US on weak yen in historic battle. By Makiko Yamazaki and Leika Kihara TOKYO, Aug 3 (Reuters) - Japan is expected to announce on Monday that it took joint action with the U.S. to halt the yen's slide to 40-year lows and express its commitment to rare bilateral coordination that it hopes could mark a turning point for the currency. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama will announce on Monday morning that Tokyo and Washington acted together in the currency market last week to arrest what they consider excessive yen declines, two Japanese government officials told Reuters over the weekend, with one saying the operation was "still ongoing." Her expected remarks to reporters follow what market sources say were rounds of yen purchases by the Japanese and U.S. authorities, the first joint intervention in 15 years, seeking to support the battered currency. Japan has been struggling to curb a relentless drop in the yen that pushes up import prices and stokes broader inflation, hitting households' wallets and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's public approval ratings. Japan may have sold as much as $58.97 billion to buy yen when it intervened in New York markets on Thursday, Bank of Japan data indicated, followed by another suspected foray into the market on Friday. On Friday, the U.S. Treasury told a number of banks it too might intervene in the yen market, a source told Reuters, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent — who had said the yen "seems very undervalued" — had a handwritten "To Do" list at a cabinet meeting that said, "Buy Japanese Yen (JPY) $5-10 bil", a Reuters photo showed. In line with Bessent's repeated calls for higher Japanese interest rates, the Bank of Japan on Friday offered its most explicit signal to date of an early rate hike, even as it kept monetary policy steady. In a sign of broader policy coordination, South Korea stepped in to buy its won currency on Thursday. The dollar ended Friday trading around 157.60 yen, having retreated from near 164 yen, the highest since 1986, which it hit earlier in the week. Japan intervened in April and May, buying yen, causing only a brief rebound. The BOJ's June rate hike to a 31-year high of 1% also gave the struggling currency little lasting boost. (Reporting by Makiko Yamazaki and Leika Kihara in Tokyo; Editing by William Mallard)

title: CXMT’s blockbuster IPO will test whether China’s memory makers are ready for the spotlight: ‘It does not yet mean China is broadly catching up’
text: CXMT’s blockbuster IPO will test whether China’s memory makers are ready for the spotlight: ‘It does not yet mean China is broadly catching up’. Chinese chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, became the country’s most valuable company almost overnight. CXMT’s shares surged over 500% in its Shanghai debut last Monday (July 27) and rallied throughout the week, jumping 8.95% on Friday to close at 57.60 yuan ($8.50). Its market capitalization also hit 3.54 trillion yuan ($523 billion) by the week’s end, toppling reigning chart leader , the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China . Yet experts are split on whether the rise in CXMT’s stock price is a temporary boost fueled by AI-driven memory shortages, or a long-term shift in global AI supply chains where Chinese chipmakers are now coming to the fore. “China is clearly becoming a more important memory chip player, but this is happening in a market distorted by AI demand, supply shortages and state-backed industrial policy,” says Barbora Valockova, a research fellow at Singapore’s Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy. “It does not yet mean China is broadly catching up to the leaders across the full chip stack.” According to Valockova, though shortages are forcing companies to explore Chinese chip supplies, adoption is still likely to be selective and politically contested, especially in the U.S. On July 30, a group of U.S. lawmakers led by Indiana Republican Jim Banks and New York Democrat Chuck Schumer penned a letter to Apple CEO Tim Cook , urging him to abandon any efforts to buy chips from ‘blacklisted’ Chinese semiconductor suppliers like CXMT and Yangtze Memory Technologies Co., or YMTC. “This short-sighted move would be a mistake, and it would ensure the world’s most valuable consumer electronics company grows dependent on critical supplies from a firm the U.S. government has formally designated as a Chinese military company,” the senators wrote, noting that the two Chinese chipmakers were on an updated Pentagon list of Chinese entities believed to be supporting Beijing’s military. Apple had previously been in negotiations to acquire chips from both firms, as it battles a global memory supply shortage which sent product prices skyrocketing. “We’re seeing some very significant constraints currently, with limited flexibility in the supply chain,” Apple CEO Tim Cook said during an earnings call last Thursday (July 30). “We’re in what I would characterize as a 100-year flood on the memory pricing, with exponential increases in memory prices.” Other experts, like Kong Tuan Yuen, a research fellow from the East Asian Institute at the National University of Singapore (NUS), argue that while the memory shortage will boost demand for Chinese chips, most global firms will still look to CXMT only as a secondary source. “While it may be necessary for companies to diversify their supply chains, they will maintain multiple sources of supplies that are located in different geographic locations to mitigate long-term geopolitical risks,” he said. Most firms will likely also opt to use SK Hynix, Micron or Samsung chips as their primary source, since CXMT still incurs higher costs in chip manufacturing, Rolf Bulk, Futurum’s head of semiconductor and infrastructure equity research, told CNBC . “CXMT is still two to three generations behind SK Hynix , Samsung, and Micron when it comes to the performance of their chips. So for every chip they produce, they have to spend 20% to 30% more on a cost per bit basis,” Bulk said. Global chipmaker stocks tumble Though Chinese chipmakers remain a few generations behind other incumbents, the global tech market was rattled by recent advances in China’s AI space, which included CXMT’s blockbuster debut and Moonshot’s Kimi K3 release . AI chip giant Nvidia saw its stocks fall by 5% on Monday, while South Korea’s SK Hynix and Samsung both plunged over 13%. (Semiconductor stocks recovered by Friday, however, with strong earnings from Microsoft and Amazon reigniting optimism over AI spending.) Experts like Chen Gang, the deputy director and senior research fellow at NUS East Asian Institute, are positive that this momentum will lead to long-term gains for Chinese chipmakers. “We should not underestimate the pace at which Chinese companies can catch up to top global manufacturers,” Chen says. “Companies like CXMT and YMTC can leverage China’s massive capital market and governmental support to expand their scales of production and research at much faster speeds than their foreign peers.” Last Monday, The Information reported that an unnamed Chinese company has started manufacturing an immersion deep ultraviolet lithography (DUV) machine. These machines etch circuit patterns onto silicon wafers, a critical part in the process of producing semiconductors, and are primarily made by Dutch manufacturer ASML . China has long tried to make a lithography machine that could be competitive with non-Chinese offerings, as part of a broader effort to build its own semiconductor industry. This drive has taken on greater intensity in recent years in response to U.S. export controls barring the sale of chips and chipmaking equipment to China. “The combination of government-led AI investment, mandates for local tech companies to tap domestic memory suppliers and rising demand from foreign firms like Apple will create a self-reinforcing cycle helping Chinese chip companies to move up the semiconductor value chain,” concludes Kong of NUS, though he admits the negative impact from geopolitics and U.S.-China relations will “always be a drag”. Investors, on the other hand, will get another chance to bet on China’s semiconductor sector. Yangtze Memory Technologies Corporation (YMTC) is now in the pre-IPO process for a listing on Shanghai’s stock exchange. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Behind the Short Interest Spike: What Active Traders Need to Watch Right Now
text: Behind the Short Interest Spike: What Active Traders Need to Watch Right Now. When short interest in a stock suddenly surges, the market is sending a message — and traders who know how to decode it can gain a serious edge. A short interest spike doesn’t always mean a stock is doomed. In fact, for active traders, it can be one of the most actionable signals available, pointing toward potential short squeezes, institutional conviction, or significant volatility just around the corner. Understanding this metric isn’t optional for serious market participants — it’s essential. What a Short Interest Spike Actually Tells You Short interest measures the total number of shares that have been sold short and not yet covered. When that number rises sharply in a short period, you’re looking at a short interest spike — a rapid increase in bearish bets against a stock. This can happen for a number of reasons: a company may have released disappointing earnings guidance, a sector rotation is underway, or institutional investors have identified fundamental weaknesses that haven’t yet been priced in by the broader market. The key data points traders track alongside short interest include the short interest ratio (also called days-to-cover), which measures how many days it would take for all short sellers to exit their positions based on average daily trading volume. A ratio above 10 is often considered high and can amplify price swings in both directions. When short interest spikes and the days-to-cover ratio climbs simultaneously, the conditions for a dramatic move become increasingly favorable — or dangerous, depending on your position. It’s critical to distinguish between a spike driven by informed institutional bearishness versus one driven by retail speculation or event-driven trading. The source of short pressure matters enormously when projecting what comes next. Short Squeeze Risk and the Opportunity Hidden Inside Heavy Shorting One of the most compelling reasons active traders monitor a short interest spike is the potential for a short squeeze. When heavily shorted stocks begin to rise — whether due to positive news, strong earnings, or simply buying pressure — short sellers are forced to cover their positions by purchasing shares. This creates a feedback loop: buying drives prices higher, forcing more shorts to cover, which drives prices even higher. The result can be explosive upside in a very short window. Historically, stocks with short interest exceeding 20% of their float and a days-to-cover ratio above 5 have shown the greatest squeeze potential. But the squeeze isn’t guaranteed, and mistiming the entry can be costly. Traders who chase a squeeze too late often buy at the peak, right as short sellers begin to find their footing. The best approach involves monitoring short interest trends over multiple reporting periods rather than reacting to a single data point in isolation. - Look for stocks where short interest has spiked more than 15% in a single reporting cycle - Cross-reference with options data — rising call volume alongside a short interest spike can signal institutional anticipation of a squeeze - Watch for catalysts: earnings dates, FDA decisions, contract announcements, or legal rulings that could trigger rapid short covering Using Short Interest Data as a Contrarian and Momentum Signal Short interest can serve both contrarian and momentum-based strategies, and skilled traders know when to flip between these approaches. From a contrarian perspective, a significant short interest spike in a fundamentally sound company with strong cash flow and manageable debt can represent an overreaction by the market. If the bearish thesis lacks compelling fundamental support, the crowded short position becomes a liability for those holding it — and an opportunity for bulls willing to build a position before the inevitable unwind. On the momentum side, a fresh short interest spike in a stock already in a downtrend can validate the bear case and provide confirmation for short sellers looking to add exposure. In this context, the spike is an alignment signal — institutions and traders are building the same position, reinforcing directional conviction. Momentum traders often use this confirmation to time their entries more precisely, waiting for the stock to break key technical support levels after a short interest increase is confirmed. The most disciplined traders treat short interest not as a standalone buy or sell signal, but as a layer of market intelligence that filters and strengthens other indicators they’re already watching. Where to Find Reliable Short Interest Data and How Often It Updates In the U.S. markets, FINRA requires member firms to report short interest data twice monthly — typically settling on the 15th and the last business day of each month. This means traders are often working with data that’s one to two weeks old, which introduces lag risk in fast-moving markets. Some financial data platforms now offer more frequent estimates or real-time approximations using borrow rate data and settlement flows, which can sharpen the picture considerably. title: Here’s how Trump has zig zagged with on-again, off-again strikes throughout the Iran war
text: Here’s how Trump has zig zagged with on-again, off-again strikes throughout the Iran war. President Donald Trump said late Saturday that he would halt new planned attacks on Iran pending renewed talks to wind down the war and revive stalled cargo traffic through the Strait of Hormuz . It was the latest in a pattern of announcements the U.S. president has made to first threaten massive strikes and then later call them off. The abrupt shifts have been a defining feature of the five-month conflict that has sent prices of oil and basic goods soaring — and the announcements to date have been upended by renewed attacks days or even hours afterward. Here is a look at some of Trump’s past major announcements about pausing strikes against Iran: April 7 The United States and Iran agree to a two-week ceasefire to end the intense fighting that began on Feb. 28 with Israeli and U.S. attacks . Trump makes the announcement less than two hours before a deadline he had set for Tehran to capitulate or face attacks on bridges and power plants — strikes he said would mean “a whole civilization will die.” April 21 Trump announces that the U.S. is indefinitely extending its ceasefire with Iran a day before it was to expire. He adds that he has been asked by mediators to hold off on attacks to give Iranian leaders time to come up with additional proposals. The fragile ceasefire lasts until May 8 , when the U.S. carried out strikes on Iranian tankers. May 18 After a weekend of dire threats against Iran, Trump says he is holding off on a major planned military strike because “serious negotiations” were underway. “There seems to be a very good chance that they can work something out. If we can do that without bombing the hell out of them, I’d be very happy,” he said. By May 27, U.S. strikes were back on after negotiations faltered. June 11 After two days of back-and-forth attacks, Trump threatens further escalation , saying the U.S. would hit Iran “VERY HARD TONIGHT” and take “total control” of its oil and gas industries . Then, a few hours later, Trump posts on social media that there had been a breakthrough in negotiations and called off the strikes. June 17 Trump signs an initial agreement with Iran that calls for a permanent end to hostilities and for reopening of the strait, and starts a 60-day negotiating clock to reach a final deal on the future of Iran’s nuclear program. Trump left the door open to abandoning it. “It’s a memorandum of understanding, and if I don’t like it, we’ll go back to shooting at them, dropping bombs,” he said. July 7 After Iranian attacks on commercial ships in the strait, Trump launches new strikes on Iran while he is in Ankara, Turkey, attending the NATO leaders’ summit. Later, he renews his threat to “just finish the job” on Iran after saying he believes the ceasefire is over. July 27 Trump says he has paused two weeks of intense, daily U.S. strikes on Iran to give negotiations another chance. During 13 days of strikes, the U.S. military had targeted key military and commercial sites as clashes continued to escalate over shipping routes. In response, Iran had launched missiles and drones across the Middle East at countries that host U.S. troops. Aug. 1 After telling reporters the U.S. would hit Iran “very hard,” Trump says on social media that he has canceled planned strikes, claiming Mideast allies had reached the parameters of a deal to end the war, including a reopening of the strait. “Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL,” Trump said. In response, Iran’s defense minister said that the country was “neither surprised nor passive” following Trump’s announcement and said Iran continues to remain alert in the face of threats. title: The Contrarian Setup That Could Trigger the Next Big Equity Surge
text: The Contrarian Setup That Could Trigger the Next Big Equity Surge. Markets have a way of humbling the majority just when confidence peaks — and right now, all the ingredients for a classic contrarian setup are quietly assembling beneath the surface of what looks like a calm, range-bound equity environment. While mainstream commentary fixates on rate trajectories and geopolitical noise, a growing body of sentiment data and positioning signals is telling a very different story to those paying close attention. A contrarian setup, at its core, emerges when market participants are overwhelmingly leaning in one direction while underlying conditions quietly favor the opposite outcome. The more crowded the consensus trade becomes, the more explosive the reversal tends to be. This is not speculation — it is a well-documented behavioral and structural dynamic that has preceded some of the most significant equity moves in modern market history. The current environment is beginning to exhibit those exact characteristics, and the evidence is difficult to dismiss. Sentiment surveys are flashing readings that typically accompany meaningful market bottoms or unexpected breakouts. The American Association of Individual Investors sentiment data, along with institutional positioning reports from futures markets, reveal that bearish bets have climbed steadily even as equities have held up with surprising resilience. When the crowd is positioned for decline but prices refuse to break, it creates a coiled-spring dynamic that forms the foundation of a textbook contrarian setup. The fuel for a sharp upside move accumulates precisely because so many participants are wrong-footed. What makes this particular setup compelling is that it extends beyond sentiment alone. Corporate earnings have continued to beat lowered expectations across multiple sectors, particularly in industrials and technology infrastructure, where capital spending tied to AI buildout remains robust. Revenue growth at the top-line level has outpaced what sell-side models projected entering the current earnings cycle, yet institutional money flows reflect a defensive posture that is more consistent with an economy on the brink of contraction than one delivering steady, if uneven, growth. This disconnect between fundamentals and positioning is exactly the kind of gap that a contrarian setup exploits. Volatility markets are adding another dimension to the picture. Implied volatility, while not at extreme lows, has compressed in a way that suggests the market is not pricing in the possibility of a large upside move — only downside risk is being actively hedged. Options skew data confirms this asymmetry. When the market is structurally unprepared for a rally, any positive catalyst can trigger a cascade of short covering and momentum-driven buying that accelerates gains far beyond what fundamentals alone would justify. This is the mechanical engine that powers contrarian moves into multi-week or even multi-month trends. It is also worth examining breadth conditions. Beneath headline index levels, small- and mid-cap stocks have been quietly stabilizing after a prolonged period of underperformance relative to large-cap peers. Historically, when breadth begins to improve from depressed levels while sentiment remains skeptical, it signals that institutional accumulation is occurring under the radar. Market breadth expansion is one of the most reliable early indicators that a contrarian setup is beginning to resolve to the upside, because it reflects genuine buying activity rather than a narrow, momentum-driven illusion of strength. None of this guarantees a specific outcome, and seasoned investors know that timing a contrarian trade demands patience and discipline. A contrarian setup does not hand you a precise entry date — it hands you a probability framework that tilts the risk-reward ratio meaningfully in one direction. The mistake most investors make is waiting for confirmation from the crowd before acting, at which point the trade has already largely played out. The edge in a contrarian setup is always front-loaded, extracted by those willing to act on data and structure before the narrative catches up. The equity market, by its nature, punishes complacency and rewards those who read positioning and sentiment with the same rigor they apply to earnings and economic data. The current contrarian setup may not resolve tomorrow, but the structural tension building beneath the surface suggests that when it does, the move will be sharp, fast, and largely unexpected by the majority who were looking the other way.

text: Stock futures rally as investors gear up for jobs report, key earnings: Live updates. U.S. equity futures rose Sunday evening as investors awaited the July jobs report and another busy week of earnings to kick off August trading. Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied 200 points, or 0.4%. S&P 500 futures advanced 0.5%, and Nasdaq-100 futures climbed 0.8%. President Donald Trump said early Sunday he canceled a planned attack on Iran. U.S. media reports on Friday said the president was gearing up for a new wave of strikes as hopes for a negotiated settlement to the war diminished and energy prices surged. The three major indexes closed higher on Friday, with the Dow advancing 276.97 points, or about 0.53%, to 52,485.03. The S&P 500 closed up 0.7% at 7,489.72, and the Nasdaq Composite surged 1% to 25,373.85. With the major averages wrapping up Friday near record highs, attention is turning to whether the catalysts that fueled the rally can continue to drive gains. While Big Tech companies largely delivered on earnings, investors are becoming less willing to overlook mounting AI-related spending without clearer evidence of earnings growth, according to Megan Horneman, chief investment officer at Verdence Capital Advisors. "The one takeaway that I had from those tech earnings is that investors don't have that appetite to just continue to pay and pay and pay without any clear insight into what this capex spending is going to do from an earnings perspective," Horneman told CNBC's "Fast Money" on Friday. "[With] big tech out of the way, what's the catalyst here that's going to get the market to continue to go higher? We just don't see it ... there are going to be more risks that we have going into August and the second half of this year." Meanwhile, earnings reports due out this week are coming from companies that could offer clearer insights into broader economic conditions. Results are expected from McDonald's, Kraft Heinz, Costco Wholesale and Walt Disney. Technology companies, including Palantir, and semiconductor giants like Advanced Micro Devices, are also on deck. Investors will also have a full slate of labor market data to digest next week, culminating with Friday's closely watched monthly jobs report. The U.S. economy is expected to have added 87,500 nonfarm payrolls in July, up from 57,000 jobs the previous month, according to FactSet consensus estimates. title: South Korea's July exports reach second-highest level
text: South Korea's July exports reach second-highest level. Aug. 1 (Asia Today) -- South Korea's exports reached their second-highest monthly level in July, driven by strong shipments of semiconductors and other information technology products, government data showed Saturday. Semiconductor exports exceeded $40 billion for the second consecutive month, while the country's monthly trade surplus remained above $30 billion for a second month. Exports rose 62.8% from a year earlier to $98.89 billion in July, according to data released by the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources. The total was second only to the record $102.25 billion registered in June, when monthly exports surpassed $100 billion for the first time. South Korea had 24 working days in July, one fewer than a year earlier. Average daily exports still rose 69.6% to $4.12 billion, remaining above $4 billion for a third consecutive month. Semiconductors led the increase. Chip exports surged 178.8% from a year earlier to $41.01 billion as fixed memory chip prices increased and investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure expanded. The figure marked the second-highest monthly total on record and the second consecutive month in which semiconductor exports exceeded $40 billion. Computer exports jumped 404% to $4.79 billion on rising demand for enterprise solid-state drives. Exports of wireless communications equipment increased 51% on stronger sales of premium smartphones, while display shipments rose 2.4%. Automobile exports increased 7% to $6.24 billion, supported by rising sales of hybrid and other environmentally friendly vehicles. Changes to summer vacation schedules at major automakers also affected the comparison with last year. Ship exports climbed 46.9% to $3.29 billion as deliveries of liquefied natural gas carriers and tankers increased. Exports of petroleum products and petrochemicals rose 34.1% and 10.3%, respectively, as higher international oil prices improved export prices. Steel exports increased 4.4%, supported by demand related to U.S. AI data center construction and pipeline replacement projects. General machinery exports rose 5.9%, while electrical equipment shipments increased 13.9%. Consumer goods also recorded strong growth. Biohealth exports reached $1.57 billion and cosmetics exports totaled $1.35 billion, both setting records for the month of July. Agricultural and seafood exports also reached a July record as overseas sales of instant noodles, snacks and kimchi increased. Exports rose in eight of South Korea's nine major overseas markets. Shipments to China jumped 96.2% to $21.68 billion, led by semiconductors, and exceeded $20 billion for a second consecutive month. Exports to the United States rose 68.7% to $17.43 billion on increased shipments of semiconductors, computers and electrical equipment. Exports to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations increased 73.7% to a record $18.8 billion. Shipments to the European Union also reached a record $9.38 billion. Imports rose 26.5% from a year earlier to $68.56 billion. Crude oil imports increased 54.2% to $9.3 billion because of higher prices and greater import volume. The trade surplus stood at $30.32 billion, remaining above $30 billion for a second consecutive month. South Korea accumulated a trade surplus of $168 billion during the first seven months of the year, an increase of $134.1 billion from the same period last year. "The strength of semiconductor exports continued, while exports of products other than semiconductors also increased, demonstrating an overall improvement in export competitiveness," Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said. Kim said the government would mobilize available policy measures to help companies respond promptly to changes in the international trade environment, including tariffs and nontariff barriers. -- Reported by Asia Today; translated by UPI © Asia Today. title: Markets signal investors are back in buying mode again after Kospi’s record surge while Trump gives peace a chance with latest Iran reversal
text: Markets signal investors are back in buying mode again after Kospi’s record surge while Trump gives peace a chance with latest Iran reversal. U.S. stock futures jumped on Sunday, continuing a bullish mood from late last week, as President Donald Trump balked at a major attack on Iran. Futures tied to the Dow Jones industrial average surged 189 points, or 0.36%. S&P 500 futures jumped 0.41%, and Nasdaq futures shot up 0.89%. South Korea’s Kospi index, which has been a bellwether for global stocks lately, soared 18% on Friday, marking its biggest single-day jump on record. That could signal Korean investors are dipping their toes back in the water, following a brutal selloff last month that prompted authorities to rein in the massive leverage that fueled wild swings earlier. Meanwhile, U.S. oil prices tumbled 4.5% to $80.85 a barrel, and Brent crude dived 4.6% to $83.90 on hopes for a deal that will reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield fell 2.7 basis points to 4.718%. In what has become a familiar pattern in the Iran war, Trump again threatened a massive attack then pulled back from the brink late Saturday. But while he attributed his latest reversal to U.S. allies pleading with him to give diplomacy another chance, experts also see signs Iran is gaining the upper hand . That’s as Tehran has used its proxies to expand the war across the region, most notably Houthis rebels threatening ships in the Red Sea that are trying to use the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. At the same time, Iran has warned its Persian Gulf neighbors they will be targets in the event of a renewed bombardment after demonstrating that its long-range weapons can evade U.S. air defenses. “Last night’s events underscore a reality that is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore: for now, Iran appears to hold the strategic advantage in deterrence,” Dennis Citrinowicz, a former Israeli intelligence official who specialized in Iran, posted on X . Meanwhile, Wall Street is also looking ahead to labor market data in the coming week amid doubts about the Federal Reserve’s willingness to rein in inflation. ADP’s private payrolls report comes out of Wednesday, and the Labor Department’s weekly jobless claims tally follows on Thursday. Then on Friday, the Labor Department’s monthly jobs report is due, and analysts expect a gain of 85,000 with the unemployment rate ticking up to 4.3% from 4.2%. The numbers come after Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh set off a central bank “ credibility shock ” last week, when he continued to offer zero forward guidance while also suggesting alternative data and market tools could be used to fight inflation. According to economists at Bank of America , the remarks were so dovish that they will likely force a hawkish outcome, meaning other members of the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee must pick up the pieces. A major test will come with Friday’s payroll data. Fresh signs that the job market remains robust could fuel more worries about inflation. BofA pointed to the bond yield curve as an indicator of the central bank’s perceived commitment to price stability. “Flattening of the curve would mean markets still believe the Fed will do what it takes to meet its mandate,” economists said. “But if the curve were to steepen on strong jobs/inflation data, that would indicate the Fed is behind the curve, raising more serious questions about its credibility.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

title: Inside the Moves Reshaping Global Finance Through Hedge Fund Position Shifts
text: Inside the Moves Reshaping Global Finance Through Hedge Fund Position Shifts. When the world’s largest pools of private capital quietly reposition themselves, markets rarely stay still for long. A single hedge fund position adjustment by a major player can ripple across currencies, commodities, equities, and bonds — often before retail investors even realize the tide has turned. Understanding what these funds are doing, and why, has become one of the most valuable edges any market participant can develop. Hedge funds collectively manage well over four trillion dollars in assets globally, and their influence has only grown as algorithmic strategies, leverage tools, and cross-border capital flows have become more sophisticated. These are not passive bystanders watching markets move — they are, in many cases, the force behind the movement. When institutional positioning data gets released through regulatory filings like the 13F reports in the United States, analysts and traders dissect every line looking for signals about where smart capital is flowing next. What makes the current environment particularly compelling is how dramatically hedge fund position activity has shifted across asset classes in recent cycles. After years of rotating in and out of tech-heavy long positions, many leading funds have meaningfully diversified into commodities, emerging market debt, and short volatility strategies. This isn’t random — it reflects a calculated response to inflationary pressures, geopolitical fragmentation, and the evolving interest rate landscape across developed economies. How Positioning Data Moves Markets Before the Headlines Do One of the most underappreciated dynamics in modern finance is the degree to which aggregate hedge fund position data acts as a leading indicator. When commitment of traders reports show funds building net long exposure to crude oil, or when prime brokerage data reveals elevated short interest in regional banking stocks, those signals often precede price moves by days or even weeks. Institutional positioning isn’t just a reflection of market opinion — it’s market-moving capital being put to work. Take the foreign exchange market as one vivid example. Hedge fund positioning in the Japanese yen has been a major driver of currency volatility in recent years. As funds built historically large short positions against the yen in anticipation of prolonged yield differentials, the resulting carry trades amplified exchange rate moves far beyond what fundamental models would have predicted. When those positions unwound — rapidly and simultaneously — the yen surged and equity markets across Asia felt immediate pressure. This is the cascading power of concentrated hedge fund positioning at its most visible. Equity markets tell a similar story. Crowded long positions in mega-cap technology stocks created a feedback loop where rising prices attracted more capital, compressing volatility and encouraging leverage. When sentiment shifted, the unwind was sharp and synchronized. Analysts who tracked hedge fund position crowding metrics were better prepared for those drawdowns than those focused purely on valuation multiples or earnings revisions. The relationship between hedge fund positioning and commodity markets has also intensified. Agricultural futures, energy contracts, and precious metals have all seen periods of sharp dislocation driven not by supply-demand fundamentals but by rapid shifts in speculative positioning. Funds with macro mandates increasingly treat commodities as a macro expression — going long oil to bet on geopolitical tension, or accumulating gold exposure to hedge against currency debasement and central bank credibility risks. What Global Investors Should Watch Going Forward For anyone trying to navigate global markets, monitoring shifts in hedge fund position data is no longer optional — it’s essential context. Several indicators deserve close attention. Prime brokerage reports from major investment banks track gross and net leverage across the hedge fund universe. CFTC commitment of traders data offers weekly snapshots of speculative positioning in futures markets. And 13F filings, while delayed, reveal long equity positioning from funds managing above the reporting threshold. What these data sources collectively reveal is a landscape where positioning is increasingly dynamic and less anchored to traditional long-term investment theses. Funds are quicker to rotate, quicker to hedge, and quicker to exit crowded trades than they were a decade ago. Liquidity management has become as important as idea generation, and that behavioral shift has real consequences for how markets absorb shocks. Emerging markets have felt this acutely. Capital inflows driven by hedge fund positioning can lift local equities and currencies within a matter of weeks, only to reverse sharply when global risk appetite shifts. Countries with strong macroeconomic fundamentals but high dependency on foreign portfolio flows have learned to monitor these positioning trends carefully, as central bank policy responses increasingly need to account for the behavior of institutional speculators as much as domestic economic conditions. The interconnected nature of modern markets means a hedge fund position change in one asset class can transmit pressure across seemingly unrelated markets within hours. Correlation assumptions built on historical data break down precisely when they’re needed most — during rapid repositioning events. For investors, that’s both the risk and the opportunity. Those who understand the mechanics of institutional positioning cycles are better equipped to anticipate dislocations rather than simply react to them. In a market where information asymmetry still exists but is narrowing fast, positioning awareness may be the most enduring edge left on the table.

title: Australia manufacturing PMI hits 52.0 as output growth returns in July
text: Australia manufacturing PMI hits 52.0 as output growth returns in July. The rise to 52.0 signals a modest but genuine improvement in Australian manufacturing conditions, with production and new orders both returning to growth for the first time in several months, a mildly positive read for domestic industrial activity and employment data in the near term. However, the recovery remains fragile: input cost inflation, though easing, is still running well above pre-conflict levels, with 40% of firms reporting higher costs tied directly to Middle East-driven fuel and shipping expenses. That keeps upside risk in play for producer price inflation readings, which the RBA will be watching closely alongside any further escalation in the region. The renewed fall in export orders, driven by rising prices and competition, points to a currency and competitiveness headwind that could weigh on trade-exposed sectors even as domestic conditions improve. Overall, the data supports a cautiously constructive read on the industrial economy, but the explicit warning from S&P Global's own economist that the recovery could prove fleeting if Middle East inflationary pressures reassert themselves should temper any strong directional conviction. Earlier, the latest on Trump's war: Reports of Iran firing cruise missile at US oil tanker, also UK Navy reports incident Trump claims Hormuz deal done, denuclearisation talks to start tomorrow --- Australian manufacturing is showing tentative signs of life, but the war in the Middle East still has its hand on the inflation dial. Summary: The S&P Global Australia Manufacturing PMI rose to 52.0 in July from 51.5 in June, its fourth straight month above the 50.0 growth threshold and the strongest reading since January Output and new orders both returned to growth, with production rising for the first time in six months, though growth rates in both were only marginal Employment rose at its fastest pace since January, marking the third consecutive month of staffing expansion, though some hiring was temporary New export orders fell again amid rising prices and competition, reversing a slight rise seen the previous month Input price inflation eased to its lowest rate since February but remained sharp, with 40% of respondents reporting higher costs, largely tied to fuel and shipping linked to the Middle East conflict Backlogs of work fell for a fifteenth straight month, though at the slowest pace in six months, while firms rebuilt input stocks for a second consecutive month Australia's manufacturing sector returned to output growth in July for the first time in six months, according to the latest S&P Global survey, offering tentative signs of recovery even as firms continued to grapple with elevated costs and supply disruption tied to the war in the Middle East. The headline seasonally adjusted S&P Global Australia Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index rose to 52.0 in July, up from 51.5 in June, marking the fourth consecutive month above the 50.0 no-change threshold and the most pronounced improvement in the sector's health since January. The gain was driven by renewed expansions in both output and new orders as the second half of the year began, with production growth recorded for the first time in six months on the back of the first increase in new orders since February. Growth in both measures was described as only marginal, reflecting still-muted demand and ongoing inflationary pressures. Job creation was a bright spot, with manufacturers expanding staffing levels for a third consecutive month at the fastest pace since January, although some firms noted that new hires were only on a temporary basis. Backlogs of work decreased for a fifteenth straight month as firms kept on top of workloads, though the pace of depletion was the slowest in six months. Stocks of finished goods edged down modestly, while firms rebuilt input inventories for a second consecutive month, supported by a renewed rise in purchasing activity, the first in three months. Price and supply pressures, while easing, remained a persistent drag on the sector. Input price inflation slowed markedly to its lowest rate since February, but costs still rose sharply, with 40% of respondents reporting an increase, driven chiefly by higher fuel and shipping costs linked to the Middle East conflict. Output price inflation also slowed, though only slightly, with charges continuing to rise at a much faster pace than before the outbreak of the war. Lead times on input deliveries lengthened again, with sea freight delays frequently cited, though the deterioration in vendor performance was the least pronounced in five months. New export orders fell once more, reversing a slight rise in June, as rising prices and competition for new work weighed on overseas demand. Andrew Harker, Economics Director at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said the renewed rises in output and new orders provided some reassurance that the sector was recuperating from the downturn triggered by the outbreak of war in the Middle East, but cautioned that the recovery remained only tentative, with growth still marginal amid ongoing price and supply pressures. He added that further deterioration in the Middle East situation left the forward path highly uncertain, warning that the nascent recovery could prove fleeting should inflationary pressures begin to strengthen again in the months ahead. Manufacturers themselves appeared cautiously optimistic, with confidence in the 12-month production outlook improving alongside planned capacity expansions, which rose for a third straight month but remained some way below levels seen before the conflict began. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
