title: Falling oil prices help calm worries about inflation, and Wall Street rallies
text: Falling oil prices help calm worries about inflation, and Wall Street rallies Oil prices are easing and helping to calm Wall Street’s worries that inflation could get even worse NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — Oil prices are easing on Monday and helping to calm Wall Street’s worries that inflation could get even worse. That has U.S. stock indexes rallying, though sharp swings are continuing to roil underneath the surface. The S&P 500 rose 1.5% following its wild July, where it swung up and down as oil prices shot higher because of the war with Iran and other worries. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 591 points, or 1.1%, as of 1:57 p.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 2.2% higher. Stocks got a lift as the price for a barrel of Brent crude sank 5% to $83.49. It dropped after President Donald Trump said over the weekend that he decided to hold off on new strikes against Iran at the urging of allies in the region. Brent's price careened between $72 and $102 last month as worries rose and fell about when the war with Iran would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again to deliver crude to customers worldwide. The latest acquiescence by Trump on Iran helped to ease worries about the global flow of crude, and Treasury yields correspondingly fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury sank to 4.69% from 4.75% late Friday. It, though, remains well above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran. Higher yields threaten to undercut prices for stocks and other investments, while slowing the economy by making borrowing more expensive for U.S. households and businesses. The average long-term U.S. mortgage rate has already leaped to its highest level in a year. Monday's ease in oil prices helped airlines and other companies with big fuel bills lead the market. United Airlines flew 5.2% higher, while American Airlines climbed 4.2%. Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings steamed 3.9% higher. Tyson Foods rose 2% after the meat company reported a slightly stronger profit for the spring than analysts expected. CEO Donnie King said strength is continuing in the company's chicken business and its prepared foods, which include brands like Jimmy Dean and Hillshire Farm. It joined a lengthening list of big U.S. companies to deliver a bigger profit for the spring than analysts expected. That's imperative for Wall Street because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate earnings over the long term, and worries were rising that stock prices may have already shot too high. Companies in the S&P 500 are on track to deliver earnings per share for the spring that are 47% higher than a year before, according to FactSet, with more than half of the companies having already reported. If that ends up being the case, it would be the strongest growth since the spring of 2021, when the economy was roaring out of the COVID pandemic. Also offering encouragement for profits was a report on Monday showing that growth for U.S. manufacturing accelerated to its strongest level since 2022. Keeping Wall Street unsettled, though, were swings for stocks of companies that make computer chips. They've been veering up and down for weeks on worries about whether their surging revenues because of the artificial-intelligence boom are sustainable. If AI ends up producing less profit and productivity than hoped, Big Tech companies could curtail their spending sprees on data centers that have helped chip stocks soar to tremendous heights. Micron Technology went from a drop of 6.4% to a gain of 0.7% during Monday's first 90 minutes of trading, for example. It's still up roughly 190% for the year so far. The manic swings for AI stocks have been most dramatic in South Korea, where the Kospi index is dominated by just two tech titans, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. Seoul’s Kospi fell 5.1% Monday, coming off Friday's 17.9% surge that was its best day in history. In neighboring Japan, Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 fell 0.9% after the United States and Japan confirmed they had moved together to to prop up the value of the Japanese yen against the dollar. A stronger yen would help to limit inflation in Japan, but it could also potentially hurt Japan’s exporters. ___ AP Writers Matt Ott, Elaine Kurtenbach, Mayuko Ono and Mari Yamaguchi contributed to this report.

title: Dividend stocks outperformed the S&P in July. Wall Street says these names will go higher
text: Dividend stocks outperformed the S&P in July. Wall Street says these names will go higher. Investors seeking shelter from the market volatility may want to consider dividend stocks. title: Food truck owners speak out about operating a mobile business
text: Food truck owners speak out about operating a mobile business. Food truck season is in full swing, and continues to be a popular staple at a number of community events and neighborhood gatherings. There's plenty of work and cost that goes into getting the truck ready before you head to the order window. Rick Faulkner and Amber Mason, owners of Taco Hut Food Truck, begin preparations a day before an event and finish the day of. Faulkner says these days he's paying $5.49 a pound for 100 pounds of 100% angus beef, up about $1.50 a pound since 2023. "Nobody has any idea how much work it actually is," Faulkner said. "And we didn't either. It's completely different than being in a restaurant." Faulkner also preps the outside of the truck. "Checking all the tires, make sure they're good on it," said Faulkner. As for fluctuating diesel prices, the truck's generator uses about four gallons an outing, and unlike other trucks that travel farther, Faulkner stays within a 10-mile radius and hasn't had to fill up the truck since June of last year. The truck's design reflects the tradition and legacy of the former and still empty Taco Hut restaurant in Jamestown, founded by Carlson's late dad, Jim. "Just being able to keep it going and keep the community happy, it's a great experience," said Carlson. The truck also requires city and county permits needed to run the business. "It is a lot of work. People do seem to think it's simpler than it is," said Jessica Wuerstle, director of environmental health services for Chautauqua County. Health leaders say while the state sets sanitary codes, requirements and regulations for the thousands of mobile food trucks in the state, municipal permitting and enforcement lies within each county. Chautauqua County has 90 permitted food trucks, that's down from 110 last year, but up sharply from 76, a decade ago. "By having each county be able to implement those regulations and permit the different facilities by themselves, it allows us to adapt the program best for what is going to work in our county," said Wuerstle. The state health department reports a little more than 5,400 permitted mobile food service establishments statewide, excluding New York City, yet the department says it does not collect data or track trends. To be compliant, Faulkner had to build a commissary for storage, install a fresh water line and drainage system, as well as secure waste water and sewer hookup, all separate from the main house. "You gotta make the health department happy. They kind of hold the keys to the castle for one," said Faulkner. Those improvements enable Faulkner and Carlson to serve their long-time customers. "It's unique and it's kinda fun. Prime example, I stood in line here for 15 minutes or so, talked to six people I've never seen before in my life," said customer Paul Mazzone. All part of the industry's long-standing following. "We're doing it as much for the community as anything and we enjoy doing what we're doing," said Faulkner. Health leaders also say not only do they do routine inspections, but also pre-operational checks for people thinking of owning a food truck. They urge people not to purchase a truck before contacting their local health department.

title: The Tariff Refunds Are Rolling in—but Gadget Prices Aren’t Dropping
text: The Tariff Refunds Are Rolling in—but Gadget Prices Aren’t Dropping. Consumers were always going to take the brunt of Donald Trump’s bungled “reciprocal tariff” scheme. The trickle-down of increased import costs has resulted in higher-priced gadgets, but the companies that originally hiked prices aren’t about to lower costs even after receiving their own tariff refunds. Apple seems to be one of the biggest beneficiaries of recent tariff refunds. A February Supreme Court decision nullified many of the White House’s tariffs. Instead of facing even more lawsuits, the federal government created a means for companies to apply for rebates on their extra tariff spending. Apple calculated the tariffs into its latest earnings report. In a press release, Apple said that money was worth “2 percentage points” of its 50.1% gross margin. That number allowed AppleInsider to put the profit at a tidy, approximated $2.2 billion. Apple has not revealed the actual number in its earnings report. While Apple is celebrating its margins, it won’t stop your next MacBook Air from becoming more expensive and more scarce. Last month, Apple increased prices for practically all its various products, from iPads to Macs to the lowly HomePod. Only iPhones, Apple Watches, and AirPods were spared price hikes caused by the ballooning price of RAM and SSD storage. In an investor Q&A, outgoing CEO Tim Cook said the tech giant has been forced to spend more on memory with each passing quarter. AppleInsider’s calculation may put Apple at the highest refund on tariffs so far. Still, the company never blamed import taxes for rising prices, though it did push the $1,100 iPhone 17 Pro for $100 more than the iPhone 16 Pro. Cook claimed at the time the hikes were not due to tariffs. And still, due to RAM costs, the iPhone 18 Pro will likely cost even more. A June report from the U.S. Federal Reserve said 15 to 20% of tariff costs were passed down to consumers. Prices on sites like Amazon were up close to 6%, according to analysis published in November last year. Some people are suing to try and get what they feel they’re owed. There is an ongoing class-action lawsuit against Amazon filed in May this year, arguing that Amazon needs to pass tariff refunds back to consumers. Similarly, beloved console maker Nintendo is currently being sued by some customers who think they deserve a piece of the tariff refund pie. In a response to that lawsuit, Nintendo’s lawyers made it perfectly clear that when customers purchase an item, they are accepting the current retail price. The company spiked costs for the original Switch consoles last year, and we likely won’t see a discount before the handheld reaches its end of life in the next few years. Some companies are using the tariff refunds to stay afloat. Sony also brought up the tariff refunds in its latest earnings report. The makers of PlayStation mentioned that the “impact of tariff refunds” was one of the main reasons its year-on-year revenue for its game and network services segment didn’t see a major dip despite declining console sales. Still, some companies claimed they’ll give customers a taste of these refunds. FedEx reported it’s received $800 million in refunds, and said it will pass that back to consumers. The shipping company is prioritizing people who sign up on an online portal. Walmart has promised similar kickbacks to consumers, though without any specifics on how that would happen. Amazon claimed in its latest earnings report it made a less significant $600 million from its earnings. In an investor Q&A, Amazon CFO Brian Olsavsky promised Amazon would give some consumers a refund under a “limited set of circumstances where we can trace what we passed specific import charges on to consumers.” It remains unclear how and when customers can expect refunds. Gizmodo reached out to Amazon about its refund plans, and we’ll update this post if we hear back. The CFO said the money it received from refunds was “limited” in part due to Amazon hoarding products before Trump first initiated his tariffs in early 2025. Olsavsky further claimed Amazon took some tariff prices on the chin rather than passing them to consumers. The fact of the matter, whether it’s due to tariffs, memory hikes, or inflation, nothing is getting any cheaper.

title: Newsom Pressures His Own AG to Drop Lawsuit to Stop Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger
text: Newsom Pressures His Own AG to Drop Lawsuit to Stop Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger. A report says California’s Democrat Governor Gavin Newsom is worried over job loss in his state if the lawsuit filed by his own Attorney General is successful at stopping the proposed merger between Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, and he has urged Rob Bonta to settle out of court and end his lawsuit. Radical, left-wing AG Rob Bonta is leading a coalition of 12 deep blue states in trying to stop the proposed merger claiming that the $111 billion plan is detrimental to the entertainment industry and the freedom of choice of consumers. But a new report by the Wall Street Journal says that Gov. Newsom — who is angling to run for the Democrat nomination for president in 2028 — is worried that if Paramount is stymied by Bonta’s lawsuit, Warner Bros. will shed thousands of jobs, or even completely shut down altogether. The massive loss of jobs just before the 2028 election would look very bad for Newsom. Consequently, Newsom has reportedly asked Bonta to change his track on the lawsuit. The Journal reported that “Newsom’s office has encouraged Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office, which has independent authority to file such suits, to find a resolution out of court.” In his lawsuit, Bonta asserts that “There is no debate here: This merger will snuff out competition, drive up prices, diminish content quality, and produce fewer movies and shows each year.” Joining California in the suit are the states of Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, and Washington. While Bonta’s suit is the biggest move to halt the merger, there are other suits in the works, as well, including one filed by the Writers Guild of America, which is also trying to head off the merger. Despite the lawsuits, though, officials in both the U.S. and Europe have given the greenlight to the merger, saying that the plans pass their regulatory hurdles. Still, Paramount agreed to temporarily pause the merger while Bonta’s lawsuit makes its way through the courts. Three Marvel superhero film actors also recently spoke out against the merger in the U.K., where regulators are still considering the deal. Actors Benedict Cumberbatch, Alan Cumming, and Benedict Wong joined together in an open letter to urge regulators in the U.K. to reject the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery claiming that the deal “threatens to inflict immense harm on the British public.” The actors claim that the merger will result in fewer films, canceled productions, and a tendency to avoid taking on risky projects. They insist that the decision over approving the deal will “prove one of the most important decisions any culture secretary has taken for UK film, television and media in a generation,” referring to U.K. culture minister Lisa Nandy who has the responsibility to OK the merger. title: Mass. seafood restaurant closes after 25 years, owners say they were ‘forced’ out
text: Mass. seafood restaurant closes after 25 years, owners say they were ‘forced’ out. A Central Massachusetts seafood restaurant that has been family-owned and operated for more than two decades has permanently shut down. Olde Time New England Seafood Company in Athol has closed after 25 years, according to a note posted in the Athol/Orange Area Information And More Facebook group. Mariette Richard, who wrote the note and whose partner Ed Drouin owns the establishment, confirmed the closure to MassLive Monday. Richard said that she has been “wanting to retire for a while,” but is now being “forced to do that” because of the restaurant’s landlord. “As you may know, the business has been for sale for a couple years. Our landlords have recently informed me that they no longer wish to have a restaurant on their property,” Richard wrote in the note. “They are currently showing the space to prospective renters who are not interested in running a restaurant.” Richard went on to name the many obstacles Olde Time New England Seafood Company overcame over the years, including, “9/11, which happened just before we opened, rising food costs (and) the fluctuations in the economy.” “Through all of the ups and downs, we’ve continued to serve our community to the best of our ability,” Richard wrote. “Although we have had so many tough times, it’s been a great 25 years. We have been blessed with so many friendships and amazing employees.” Located at 2294 Main St. in Athol, Olde Time New England Seafood Company was known for serving fresh seafood dishes in a casual and cozy atmosphere. Reviewers on Yelp frequently applauded the restaurant for its meal preparation, affordable prices and friendly service. “To every customer and the hundreds of employees who have walked through our doors over the past 25 Years, I would like to thank you all from my bottom of my heart for your unwavering loyalty and patronage,” she wrote. “It has been a pleasure serving you for all 25 years.” - Half marathon to be hosted in Worcester for 1st time in 10 years. title: Behind the Contrarian Setup: What Institutional Activity Really Signals
text: Behind the Contrarian Setup: What Institutional Activity Really Signals. When the crowd rushes in one direction, something quietly powerful tends to happen on the other side of the trade. That’s the essence of a contrarian setup — a moment in the market where prevailing sentiment has drifted so far from underlying fundamentals that professional institutions begin positioning themselves against the herd. Understanding how and why this happens can fundamentally change the way you read price action and market structure. Most retail traders treat sentiment and price as if they move in lockstep. In reality, institutional players — hedge funds, asset managers, and proprietary trading desks — are often building positions in the exact opposite direction of popular opinion. By the time mainstream financial media catches up to a trade idea, the real money has already been placed. That gap between public narrative and institutional behavior is where the contrarian setup lives. How Institutions Construct a Contrarian Position Large institutions cannot simply buy or sell enormous positions without moving the market against themselves. To accumulate shares in a beaten-down sector or asset class, they need cover — and that cover typically comes from retail panic, media-driven negativity, or an oversold technical condition that keeps ordinary investors away. This is precisely the environment that creates a textbook contrarian setup. Watch what happens during a period of sustained negative headlines around a particular sector. Volume patterns often tell a revealing story. As prices decline, you might expect volume to fade as sellers lose interest. Instead, in many contrarian setups, volume actually holds elevated or spikes on down days while institutional order flow quietly absorbs the selling. This is called accumulation, and identifying it requires looking beyond price alone into the depth of market data, dark pool activity, and options positioning. The options market is particularly telling. When institutions are building a contrarian position in equities, the options chain frequently shows unusual activity in out-of-the-money calls — contracts that only become profitable if the stock or index reverses sharply. This kind of positioning is not speculative noise. It reflects a calculated bet made with significant capital, often supported by proprietary research that the public simply doesn’t have access to yet. Another signal worth watching is short interest data. An extremely high short float in a stock or ETF can serve as rocket fuel for a contrarian setup. Institutional buyers entering a heavily shorted name understand that any fundamental catalyst — a better-than-expected earnings print, a regulatory decision, or a shift in macroeconomic data — can trigger a cascade of forced short covering. This mechanical buying amplifies returns well beyond what the fundamental catalyst alone would justify. Reading the Broader Context Around a Contrarian Setup Not every beaten-down asset deserves a contrarian trade. The distinction between a genuine contrarian setup and a value trap is critical. A contrarian opportunity is defined not just by negative sentiment, but by a meaningful disconnect between that sentiment and the actual underlying data. Institutions assess credit conditions, management quality, cash flow stability, and sector-level positioning before committing capital. Retail traders who simply buy what looks cheap often confuse cheapness with value. The macro environment adds another layer of complexity. A contrarian setup that emerges during a period of tightening liquidity carries significantly different risk than one forming during an easing cycle. Institutional desks factor in the cost of carry, correlation to broader risk assets, and the timeline over which a trade thesis might play out. This temporal dimension is something many individual investors underestimate — a contrarian position can be structurally correct while still being early by months, which requires either patience or precise entry timing. Positioning data from regulatory filings, such as 13F reports in the United States, offers a delayed but revealing look at where major institutions have been adding exposure. Cross-referencing these filings with price action around the same period can help traders reconstruct the logic behind institutional moves. It is not a real-time edge, but it trains the eye to recognize patterns that repeat across different market cycles and asset classes. One of the most reliable signals that a contrarian setup is maturing comes from sentiment surveys and retail flow data. When surveys like the AAII Investor Sentiment Report show extreme bearishness — particularly if that reading persists for multiple consecutive weeks — history suggests mean reversion becomes statistically more probable. Institutions track these surveys obsessively, not because sentiment drives markets directly, but because it maps the positioning of the retail crowd they often trade against. Ultimately, the contrarian setup is not about being contrarian for its own sake. Arguing against consensus without evidence is just noise. The real edge comes from identifying the specific moment when institutional capital — patient, data-driven, and structurally informed — begins accumulating against a narrative that has run further than the facts support. When price, volume, options activity, and sentiment all converge to tell the same story from opposite angles, you are looking at one of the most powerful configurations available in modern markets. Learning to see it clearly, before the crowd does, is what separates disciplined traders from those who are always one step behind.

title: Customers are embracing ‘friendly fraud’ to get free things
text: Customers are embracing ‘friendly fraud’ to get free things. Disputing credit card charges may be the new way to stick it to corporations. More consumers are engaging in friendly fraud, disputing real charges or purchases in order to get their money back. The trend reflects a distrust in corporations as well as overall economic instability. ‘Expensive, onerous process’ Friendly fraud involves the use of charge-backs, which are “when a customer goes to their bank, as opposed to the merchant, to dispute a charge,” said NerdWallet. “When the customer requests their money back, the bank contacts the business’s payment processor.” Then the “bank verifies whether the charge-back request is legitimate” and reverses the charge if it is, said NerdWallet. Most incorrect charge-backs tend to be honest mistakes as a “cardholder identifies a purchase on their transaction statement as fraudulent and disputes it,” when in reality, “they or someone else in their household may have made the purchase,” said Mastercard. Transaction disputes have also “traditionally been used to address certain types of crimes committed against consumers,” like if “someone steals your wallet and goes on a shopping spree, or if you put a deposit on a wedding venue that goes out of business before the big day,” said Bloomberg. The credit card issuer “claws the funds back from the offending merchant’s bank, on top of a charge-back penalty fee,” which is an “expensive, onerous process” that “incentivizes merchants to be honest transactors and resolve issues with customers before charge-backs are filed.” ‘Existential threat’ What was once an accidental error or a way to stop theft is now sometimes a tool to obtain free merchandise. Friendly fraud is a “costly form of charge-back abuse in which consumers dispute legitimate credit card transactions to recover their money while keeping the purchased goods or services,” said the technology publication Tekedia. Though the phenomenon is not new, it is becoming more common. There were “158 million transaction disputes in 2025, an increase of 29% from 2021, significantly outpacing general growth in card transactions,” said Bloomberg. The trend takes an economic toll. The “volume of disputes has become so cumbersome that more retailers are farming out the whole process of investigating and defending against fraud claims to third-party vendors that specialize in helping them hold on to more of consumers’ money,” said Bloomberg. Increased levels of chargebacks can also affect prices. “Large retailers fold the cost of lost revenue, lost product and lost labor that fraudulent charge-backs create into the prices everyone pays.” But “for small merchants those losses quickly become an existential threat to their ability to continue operating.” ‘Retaliate against retailers’ The rise of friendly fraud is directly tied to growing distrust of companies and corporations. Friendly fraud is a “way to retaliate against retailers over poor customer service, delayed deliveries, strict return policies or dissatisfaction with purchases,” said Tekedia. People may not even be aware they are committing fraud, as many small value disputes are approved quickly and without much investigation. There are “people that feel like, oh, this is just sticking it to the man, so to speak,” Jim Mortensen, a strategic adviser in the fraud and anti-money-laundering practice at the research firm Datos Insights, said to Bloomberg. Economic circumstances also contribute to the rise of stealing and fraud. “One thing in the last two to three years has been that the cost of living in most developed markets has put quite a significant squeeze on consumers, particularly younger consumers on lower income,” a senior research analyst at Juniper Research who focuses on digital payments, said to Bloomberg. While engaging in friendly fraud sounds intriguing, it is “unethical and, in some jurisdictions, may constitute fraud,” said Tekedia. “Repeated abuse can result in account closures, damaged relationships with financial institutions and even legal consequences.” Devika Rao has worked as a staff writer at The Week since 2022, covering science, the environment, climate and business. title: Woman Highlights Price Gap Between Whole and Pre-Cut Watermelon — ‘Convenience Comes at a Cost’
text: Woman Highlights Price Gap Between Whole and Pre-Cut Watermelon — ‘Convenience Comes at a Cost’. A viral video highlighting the price difference between whole and pre-cut watermelon prompted discussion online. The woman in this video shows the price difference when this concept is applied to something as simple as watermelon. The video was reshared on X by @ClownWorld and has since gotten over 200,000 views, with many commenters calling the price of the cut-up, packaged watermelon highway robbery, even if customers are paying extra for convenience. Commenters noted that, when you compare the price of a whole watermelon to the price of the cut-up watermelon, there’s no way you should be paying quadruple the price for the latter. This woman can’t believe a container of cut-up watermelon costs over $40 while a whole watermelon is only $8.99. Yes, that’s exactly how convenience works. You’re not just paying for the fruit. You’re paying for someone to cut it, package it, and have it ready to eat. If it’s not... pic.twitter.com/2MwoGoJD44 — Clown World ? (@ClownWorld) August 3, 2026 Although the video was less than a minute long, the message was still loud and clear: if you want convenience, prepare to pay the price for it. The video began with the creator, a woman shopping at the grocery store, filming a section stacked with whole watermelons. The watermelons were separated by size and price, with the smallest watermelons being sold for $3.99, the medium sizes being sold for $4.99, and the largest watermelons being sold for $8.99. Still, even the largest watermelons were nowhere near the price of the cut-up, packaged watermelon, which was being sold for over $40.00! The exact same fruit, minus the rind and bulk, costs more than quadruple the price of the largest whole watermelon being sold. But why such a huge difference? As the post said, “You’re not just paying for the fruit. You’re paying for someone to cut it, package it, and have it ready to eat.” The post argued customers are paying for convenience. The post argued that convenience accounts for the higher price. It’s similar to buying the raw ingredients needed to make a pasta dish, compared to going to a restaurant and ordering that same pasta dish. Or, better yet, ordering that dish and asking for it to be delivered to your door, like DoorDash. It would definitely cost less to buy the ingredients and make it at home yourself, but it would take more time. Convenience saves you time, energy, and the unnecessary trial and error that comes with doing things on your own. However, some X users in the comments said this particular grocery store is overpricing their “convenience.” One X commenter said, “There’s some sort of shenanigans going on. It is 5.99 a pound but listing nearly 7 pounds. Unless that little package has an inter dimensional portal, or maybe has a hidden gold bar, that ain’t happening.” Another person wrote, “In America cut watermelon averages 3 dollars a pound. Uncut watermelon averages about 50 cents a pound. Martin’s is just a rip off.” Several commenters said convenience has led shoppers to accept higher prices. Another X user wrote, “If people would just stop buying things that are ridiculously overpriced, the companies that pull this type of shit would be forced to bring their prices down. Too bad nobody seems to have any self control anymore.” While many commenters said the markup was excessive, others argued the higher price reflects the labor and convenience of buying fruit that’s already prepared. The Daily Dot was unable to independently verify the pricing shown in the video or where it was recorded. The reporting above is based on footage and claims shared in the viral X post. title: The Memory Chip Crunch Is Making a Beloved Apple Gadget Harder to Get
text: The Memory Chip Crunch Is Making a Beloved Apple Gadget Harder to Get. Right now, something pretty unexpected is happening with sales of some products from Apple. Despite the fact that Apple has decades of manufacturing expertise under its belt, it’s currently hard to get certain Apple products, especially the popular MacBook Air, in a timely way. It’s all because of a weird market distortion caused by memory chips. Apple, along with other hardware makers, is having difficulties sourcing enough memory chips to feed its voracious (though normally highly efficient) manufacturing supply chain. That’s because memory chips are a vital component of the super-powerful and often super-expensive processing boards needed to power AI systems. To perform the countless high-speed calculations needed to run AI models, these boards require lots of memory—and, as Bloomberg reported, the suppliers of these memory chips have switched production toward this lucrative market, where they can make more profit. You might scoff at this problem, which probably feels pretty in the weeds to most. But it’s a serious issue, and at the same time it’s so fundamentally basic it’s essentially a classic Economics 101 lesson in supply-and-demand. Making cutting-edge silicon chips, even relatively simple memory chips versus highly complex CPUs or GPUs, is difficult and requires large, phenomenally expensive and highly precise machines. For example, TSMC’s next-gen chip maker cost $400 million, MIT recently reported. But there are only a limited number of suppliers like TSMC in the world with the right kind of tech available to produce chips at the scale that companies like Apple need for Macs, or AI firms like Google need for their artificial intelligence data centers. As the demand for these memory chips stressed the available supply, it became a seller’s market: chip makers can charge premium prices and maximize their profits however they wish, including pivoting toward more profitable AI memory markets. This is why in recent months consumer tech firms like Apple have had to hike their prices—the rising memory chip cost means the cost of making Macs and iPhones has simply gone up, forcing Apple to boost its retail prices, sometimes as much as a few hundred dollars. Simultaneously, the memory chip supply shortage has forced Apple to dial back production of some of its most well-known products, like the Mac mini, the Mac Studio desktop computers, and now the popular MacBook Air laptop, as Bloomberg pointed out. Apple has always carefully controlled its public image, so you know the situation is dire when the company has to acknowledge problems like this in its ads. As Gizmodo pointed out, as part of Apple’s new ads for its back-to-school campaign the tech giant has had to add a disclaimer noting, “MacBook Air subject to availability.” What does this mean For you? The most obvious impact of this news is that if you’re looking to buy new Apple hardware for your workforce, you’re going to have a hard time finding certain products like the MacBook Air. You’re also going to have to pay more than you may have budgeted. Both of these points also hold if you’re looking for non-Apple hardware for the workplace, because the memory chip crunch has hit other tech names too. There’s also a lesson here in how your firm can pivot quickly so that you react to changing market conditions and maximize profits by taking advantage of trends, like the chip makers have. This idea holds even if your company delivers different products or services: scaling and pivoting in an agile way is your prerogative—assuming you don’t violate contracts with existing long-valued clients. The way Apple’s leadership has dealt with this issue is also worth paying attention to. They haven’t shied away from it, and have openly admitted they’ve had to boost their prices to maintain profitability. The company is also reportedly looking for alternative suppliers, including previously undesirable ones—like two Chinese chipmakers who are on a Pentagon blacklist, ChangXin Memory Technologies Inc. and Yangtze Memory Technologies Co. The company’s said to be lobbying the government to soften potential political blow-back from using these suppliers, especially at a time when U.S.-China relations on tech manufacturing are strained. Apple appears to be playing this game smartly, leaning on the supply chain expertise of outgoing CEO Tim Cook.

title: Nat-Gas Prices Gain on Higher US LNG Exports
text: Nat-Gas Prices Gain on Higher US LNG Exports. September Nymex natural gas (NGU26) closed up +0.034 (+1.24%) on Monday. Nat-gas prices settled higher on Monday as increased flows to liquefied natural gas export terminals reduced US domestic supplies. Estimated LNG net flows to US LNG export terminals on Monday were 18.0 bcf/day, the most in five days. More News from Barchart Gains in nat-gas prices were limited on Monday amid forecasts for cooler US weather, potentially reducing nat-gas demand from electricity providers to power air conditioning use. The Commodity Weather Group said on Monday that forecasts shifted cooler, with normal seasonal weather expected across the eastern US through August 17. Nat-gas prices tumbled to a 3.25-month nearest-futures (Q26) low last Wednesday as recent below-normal US temperatures have reduced air-conditioning demand and allowed nat-gas inventories to be rebuilt. A bearish factor for nat-gas prices in the medium term is speculation that a powerful El Niño weather system will bring warmer-than-normal temperatures to the Northern Hemisphere this fall and winter, reducing nat-gas heating demand. US (lower-48) dry gas production on Monday was 112.5 bcf/day (+2.6% y/y), according to BNEF. Lower-48 state gas demand on Monday was 78.7 bcf/day (+14.7% y/y), according to BNEF. Estimated LNG net flows to US LNG export terminals on Monday were 18.0 bcf/day (-0.8% w/w), according to BNEF. Projections for higher US nat-gas production are negative for prices. On July 7, the EIA raised its forecast for 2026 US dry nat-gas production to 111.2 bcf/day from a June estimate of 111.0 bcf/day. As a positive factor for gas prices, the Edison Electric Institute recently reported that US (lower-48) electricity output in the week ended July 18 rose +2.0% y/y to 101,391 GWh (gigawatt hours). Also, US electricity output in the 52 weeks ending July 18 rose +2.3% y/y to 4,350,346 GWh. Last Thursday's weekly EIA report was supportive for nat-gas prices, as nat-gas inventories for the week ended July 24 rose by +28 bcf, less than expectations of +37 bcf but above the 5-year weekly average increase of +26 bcf. As of July 24, nat-gas inventories were down -1.2% y/y, and +6.4% above their 5-year seasonal average, signaling adequate nat-gas supplies. title: A trio of positive developments has Boeing shares soaring
text: A trio of positive developments has Boeing shares soaring. Every weekday, the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer releases the Homestretch — an actionable afternoon update, just in time for the last hour of trading on Wall Street. Stocks are rallying to start the new week , putting the S & P 500 within striking distance of a record closing high. The market got a boost from a big drop in oil prices after President Donald Trump announced early Sunday that he called off a planned strike on Iran and would seek a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The drop in oil is driving interest rates down, with the yield on the 10-year Treasury falling about 6 basis points. Some of the biggest gainers in the market Monday were the hyperscalers. The group, which includes Amazon , Alphabet , Microsoft , and Meta Platforms , extended its rally into a second session as investors embraced Amazon CEO Andy Jassy's explanation of the expected returns on the company's AI spending and when that investment should begin generating meaningful cash flow. Boeing has been a strong performer all session , rallying roughly 6% on a trio of positive updates. First was the drop in oil prices. As we've written before, aerospace stocks tend to move inversely with oil prices because lower jet fuel costs improve airlines' profitability and reduce concerns that carriers could delay or cancel aircraft orders. We disagree with how tightly they trade off each other, but that's the relationship. The second piece of good news was a long-term bear flipping positive. Analysts at BNP Paribas doubled-upgraded their rating on Boeing to outperform from underperform, with a raised $300 price target. It's a notable call because the analyst had been bearish on Boeing since November 2025, maintaining a sell rating until now. The third positive development was the Federal Aviation Administration certifying the Boeing 737 Max 7 after a long series of delays. In a note to clients on Monday, analysts at Jefferies pointed out that Boeing has 282 orders for the Max 7, representing 6% of its total Max order book. With the Max 7 now certified, attention shifts to the 737 Max 10. Boeing has said certification of that aircraft should follow, though deliveries of both jets are not expected until next year. Still, the news adds credibility to CEO Kelly Ortberg's turnaround and free cash flow growth story. title: Nantucket shop's 'No Influencers' sign goes viral, prompts backlash
text: Nantucket shop's 'No Influencers' sign goes viral, prompts backlash A Nantucket gift shop is making a move to stop influencers from creating in-store content. The Four Winds Craft Guild in Nantucket, an island about 30 miles south of Cape Cod, Massachusetts, posted a picture of a new sign in their store stating "No Influencers" on Instagram on July 27, and it immediately went viral. It is unclear why the shop, which sells Nantucket "friendship baskets," a traditional handbag-style woven basket created in 1948 by basket maker José Formoso Reyes, doesn't want influencers in its establishment. USA TODAY has contacted The Four Winds Craft Guild on Aug. 3 for comment. What are people online saying? Stephanie Hanna, a home decor influencer with over 436,000 followers, took issue with the sign in a comment on the Instagram page. "I visited Nantucket for the first time with my family this summer. We fell in love with Nantucket. One day I walked into your store and saw that sign and immediately felt uncomfortable," wrote Hanna. "I thought to myself why would they have that sign on such a beautiful island where I felt magic around every corner. Made me feel bad for being me for a minute but I realized that anyone that would make anyone feel unwelcome is not where I should be. Maybe a no photos or video sign would be a good replacement," she continued. Another Instagram commenter argued the store was right to put up the sign. "Part of Nantucket’s magic is that it still feels like a real community. As someone who misses wandering little shops without ending up in someone else’s reel... I got the joke." According to the town's official website, year-round residents total around 14,000, while that number scales to 50,000 or more during peak summer months. Erin Gates, another home decor content creator based in New York City, defended the shop. "Nantucket was once a quaint island, but now feels only for the uber rich- the prices to stay in a hotel or rent a house are astronomical and the streets are packed with six figure cars, you can’t get dinner without a reservation months in advance, parking is non existent and the stores are all slowly turning from small businesses into chains," she said. The post continued: "If everyone is so upset about 'influencers invading the island' and robbing it of its charm then what about all of those other things that have, for me, made my visits less and less enjoyable over the years as well?" Michelle Del Rey is a trending news reporter at USA TODAY. Reach her at mdelrey@usatoday.com.

title: 'Cycles Line Up Like They Did Before 1929': Charles Nenner Warns Of "Very Big Downturn" In Stocks'
text: 'Cycles Line Up Like They Did Before 1929': Charles Nenner Warns Of "Very Big Downturn" In Stocks' Via Greg Hunter’s USAWatchdog.com , Renowned geopolitical and financial cycle expert Charles Nenner is usually way ahead of market moves. When nobody wanted silver ($29), he was buying it. When everyone wanted silver a few months ago ($120), he was selling it. So, what is Nenner seeing in the markets right now? Let’s start with the big surprise prediction coming in oil prices. Lots of people say oil is going higher, a lot higher. There are plenty of predictions of oil breaking over $200 a barrel. Heck, even President Trump thinks oil will hit $200, but Nenner says he’d be wrong. Nenner explains: “The crazy thing is, based on all my analysis, is crude oil looks weak for the next year. I am not sure what it means . . .. I see oil going down longer term. Maybe other countries are going to find oil because they cannot rely on oil (from the straight of Hormuz) anymore. By the way, Saudi Arabia has plans to make a pipeline through Israel to bring it to the sea. So, they won’t need the Strait of Hormuz anymore. Intelligence will find a solution. I think they are going to pump more oil. If people think they will flood the world with oil from other countries, then the price will come down. . .. there may be an outside chance of oil hitting $101 (per barrel).” On gold, Nenner predicts, “Some cycles are very interesting. The gold cycle came down at $5,300 (per ounce). We have a 30-day free subscription , and you can see those cycles. They are close to bottoming now." " Soon, there should be a new up move for gold. We had a (downside) price target of around $3,800 per ounce. We are very close. So, gold starts looking good into 2027.” Nenner says the next gold bull market starts next month in August. This is almost August, and big investors have time to be very defensive. I want to repeat my forecast of a very big downturn in the stock market.” Nenner likes cash, and he says watch out for big losses coming from some big banks. Nenner says: “ Real estate is a bad investment. I know big pension funds, and they have real estate in New York, and they are selling with a loss. I know it because I work with these people, and things don’t look very safe... I think we could have a banking crisis.” There is much more in the 40-minute interview. title: Here are some of JPMorgan's favorite stocks as August trading kicks off
text: Here are some of JPMorgan's favorite stocks as August trading kicks off. JPMorgan has an updated list of top ideas from its team of analysts as August kicks off a new trading month. The stock market sailed through choppy waters in July. The Iran war caused oil prices to remain volatile, companies began to report strong second-quarter profits and the Federal Reserve under new Chairman Kevin Warsh voted to keep benchmark lending rates unchanged even as Warsh pledged to bring down inflation . For all the drama, the S & P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average ended the month little changed. But JPMorgan sees dozens of stocks with potential upside. Each month, analysts at JPMorgan compile their top plays tied to one of the following investment themes: growth, income, value and short ideas. This month, the analysts didn't add any stocks to their top picks, while removing a pair of energy providers. Here are 10 stocks that made the JPMorgan list: Walmart is a growth-oriented consumer stock, the JPMorgan analyst says. Shares have fallen by 16% in the past three months after the Bentonville, Arkansas-based retailer issued a worse-than-expected outlook for the fiscal year in conjunction with its first-quarter earnings in May. But Mizuho echoes JPMorgan's positive view, choosing Walmart as a top pick in late July, and repeating an overweight investment opinion, citing improvements in its delivery network amomng other catalysts. "We undertook an extensive analysis of Walmart's (WMT) ultra-fast delivery network — relying heavily on AI to stress-test delivery times, identify pockets of opportunity and quantify the number of dark stores needed to facilitate 30-minute nationwide delivery," analyst David Bellinger said. "Our findings indicate WMT's network design is still underappreciated, and developing into an increasingly powerful competitive edge/demand consolidator." Another stock chosen by JPMorgan analysts is drug manufacturer Eli Lilly . For its part, Goldman Sachs reiterated a buy rating on Lilly in a July 24 note to clients in advance of the Indianopolis-based drugmaker's second-quarter earnings. Eli Lilly shares struggled earlier in the year as its new oral weight-loss pill, Foundayo, underperformed compared to competitors . But the stock has since rallied following impressive first-quarter results that topped analyst estimates thanks to strong Mounjaro sales. "LLY shares have rallied +39% since the company's 1Q26 print, which featured an impressive beat/raise driven by [outside the United States] Mounjaro and marked a turning point that served to shift the narrative toward the strength across the entire incretin franchise," Goldman analyst Asad Haider said. "Heading into 2Q26 earnings (Aug 5th), we anticipate the same themes will remain in focus, albeit on a more solid foundation given updates over the past 2 months have further boosted confidence on the company's rapidly evolving next-gen obesity engine." JPMorgan removed Cheniere Energy and Targa Resources from its monthly collection of stock recommendations.

title: Baggu sets opening date for Lincoln Park store
text: Baggu sets opening date for Lincoln Park store. Baggu announced the opening date of its second Chicago store. The California-based bag and accessories brand will open its Lincoln Park store , 2118 N. Halsted St., on Aug. 14, according to an Instagram post from Baggu last week. The 2,200-square-foot space was previously home to It’s A Secret Medspa. When Baggu opened its first Midwest store in Wicker Park in 2024, hundreds lined up to get inside on the first day. At the time, Baggu Director of Retail Stephen Stananhan said Chicago was its third largest market. The brand’s new location is in a highly trafficked retail and dining corridor. The shop is also about two blocks away from the CTA Armitage L stop, where trendy retailers like Buck Mason and Gorjana have outposts. The Lincoln Park store will be the brand's eighth location. It recently opened a store in Portland, Oregon, which joins five other locations in California and New York, as well as its Wicker Park store . Baggu has surged in popularity in recent years, leading to a brick-and-mortar expansion. Its reusable grocery bags in unique prints, often done in collaboration with other artists or brands, are particularly beloved by Gen Z. Its reusable shopping bag, which can fold into a small pouch, starts at $16. Most bags and purses are made from nylon, although recycled leather purses, starting at $90, have returned in recent years. Other products include socks, toiletry bags and glasses cases, at prices ranging from $10 to $46. Baggu didn't respond to a request for comment. title: Home Depot accused of using customers to boost profit
text: Home Depot accused of using customers to boost profit. After making several moves this year to win back customers, Home Depot is making headlines again over a lawsuit that alleges it violated customers' rights. In 2025, the home-improvement giant had a bumpy year, marked by several consumer boycotts over its decision to cut its diversity, equity, and inclusion policies; its alleged cooperation with ICE’s immigration crackdown; and price hikes to address tariff pressures. In 2026, it turned a new leaf by making several moves to lure shoppers back to its stores and offerings. Home Depot made a major expansion of its “Pro” ecosystem with high-tech tools such as an AI-powered Material List Builder and a first-of-its-kind real-time GPS delivery tracker for bulky materials. It also improved the physical store experience with Wahlburger’s food trailers and expanded its rewards program . Now, the home improvement retailer is facing legal challenges after being accused of using its customers' personal data without their consent. Home Depot accused of selling customer data without consent in new lawsuit A new class action lawsuit accuses Home Depot of selling customers' personally identifiable information ( PII ) to third parties without providing notice or obtaining their consent. Plaintiff William E. Wright filed the lawsuit in U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia on July 1, 2026. In the document, Wright alleges that the retailer used its retail media network, Orange Apron Media, to let brands advertise directly to its customers through the Home Depot website, social media channels and in stores, reported Top Class Actions . The lawsuit argues that by selling its customers' data to third parties without notifying them, the retailer had violated Virginia's Personal Information Privacy Act. “Home Depot profits handsomely from the unauthorized sale and disclosure of consumers’ purchasing patterns and other personal information and does so at the expense of its consumers’ statutory privacy rights,” the lawsuit read. Wright is seeking a trial by jury and asking the court to rule Home Depot's practices unlawful, order an immediate stop to the alleged data sharing, and award financial damages to affected consumers. Home Depot is accused of selling customer data without consent in a new lawsuit. UCG &sol Getty Images Why would Home Depot sell customers' personal data? Retail media has been a part of consumers’ everyday lives for roughly two decades now. It is a form of modern digital advertising where brands pay retailers to promote products and services directly to shoppers. “Given the strong brand demand, 49% of surveyed retailers view retail media as a top business priority. It can help them generate new revenue that is equivalent to up to 5% to 7% of e-commerce sales or 0.5% to 1.5% of total sales — with profit margins exceeding 65%,” reported Boston Consulting Group . Wright alleges that Home Depot generates additional revenue by offering detailed consumer profiles that allow Orange Apron Media to better target advertisements to customers. This isn’t the first time Home Depot has been accused of violating privacy rights. Home Depot's previous privacy lawsuit In May 2026, another class action lawsuit filed in California accused the retailer of running a "covert surveillance operation" by using cameras in parking lots to capture vehicle data. These data were then shared with law enforcement for various purposes, including theft investigations and immigration enforcement, according to Gadget Review . Related: Here’s what killed a 29-year-old fast-casual restaurant chain Home Depot and Lowe’s shared data from hundreds of Flock cameras with police, 404 Media’s investigation revealed. A coalition of 38 advocacy groups, including civil rights organizations Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), Fight for the Future, the ACLU of Ohio, and the American Federation of Teachers, along with shareholders from Home Depot, have expressed deep concerns over the technology, reported TheStreet’s Co-Editor in Chief, Daniel Kline. Then, a class action lawsuit was filed against Home Depot, claiming the retailer violated California law by failing to comply with several requirements of California’s Automated License Plate Recognition Privacy Act, wrote ClassAction.org . The document argued that the retailer also failed to identify training requirements for any employees and contractors who use that system, and that it has already contributed to wrongful law enforcement encounters. This reportedly included at least 12 misread incidents in which innocent people were stopped at gunpoint. Why consumers should care about Home Depot selling their personal information Modern consumers typically don’t even blink when they hear that their personal information is being used and sold, because data collection often feels invisible and harmless. This couldn’t be further from the truth. In the case of license plate and vehicle data, the California lawsuit argues that innocent people were stopped by police, suggesting the possibility of real-world physical consequences. “Your location data may cost a company less than a penny to buy, yet cost you your physical safety if it falls into the wrong hands... Privacy is a fundamental human right. It has no price tag. No person should be coerced or encouraged to barter it away,” Electronic Frontier Foundation noted. When it comes to the latest lawsuit against Home Depot, there are several angles to consider, starting with the law. “Through a series of groundbreaking cases, the FTC has made clear that there is a presumption against selling people’s sensitive data — and selling or sharing this data without getting people’s permission is an unfair practice that violates the FTC Act,” said Federal Trade Commission then-Chair Lina Khan at PrivacyCon. Additionally, the FTC's study on Commercial Surveillance & Dynamic Pricing said sharing or selling consumer data can contribute to surveillance pricing, which may directly affect consumers' wallets. “According to the FTC, surveillance pricing occurs when companies leverage advanced data collection technologies to adjust the prices of goods and services for individual consumers based on competitor pricing, precise location, browser history, purchase history, consumer preferences, demographics, and other sources of real-time data.” Home Depot did not immediately respond to TheStreet’s request for comment. title: Dow surges to record close after a fresh tech rally and a plunge in oil prices
text: Dow surges to record close after a fresh tech rally and a plunge in oil prices. Spencer Platt/Getty Images The Dow closed at a record high to kick off August as tech rallied and oil prices tumbled. President Donald Trump called off an attack on Iran, sending crude prices lower. Investors piled into beaten-down tech stocks, leading the Nasdaq 100 to rise nearly 2%. The Dow closed at a record on Monday, with stocks rallying and crude prices tumbling to start the month. Major indexes were sharply higher after the Donald Trump said he called off an attack on Iran and that peace talks were set to resume. The rally picked up steam as oil prices tumbled, with the Dow surging nearly 700 points to an all-time closing high. Brent crude , the international benchmark, fell about 5% to $83.75 a barrel. US oil prices were down 5% to $80 a barrel. The S&P 500 ended the day within striking distance of its own record high. title: Deutsche Bank sees gold's correction as largely done, holds US$4600 Q4 target
text: Deutsche Bank sees gold's correction as largely done, holds US$4600 Q4 target. Deutsche Bank's analysis suggests gold's recent pullback may already have run its course, with the bank pointing to a floor closer to $3,900/oz rather than the deeper retracement some technical models imply. That reading, paired with a fair value estimate still comfortably above spot, points to limited near-term downside risk and reinforces the bank's existing bullish stance into year-end. Traders parsing the note are likely to focus on the gap between model-implied fair value and the bank's official forecast, which suggests scope for gold to grind higher even after its historic run. The report also flags a longer-term valuation risk, with adjusted relative-price ratios implying a much lower equilibrium level near $2,600/oz, a divergence that could resurface in market debate if the current rally loses momentum. --- Earlier: - UBS forecasts gold at $5,200 by June 2027 despite near-term pullback risk - Gold price forecast: Why the $4,100 support zone could decide the next move Deutsche Bank argues gold's correction has likely bottomed near $3,900/oz and reaffirms its $4,600/oz year-end forecast. Summary: - Deutsche Bank identifies the current gold rally, dated from August 2024, as one of only five "explosive" price episodes in data going back to 1975, using a statistical filtering method that strips out isolated one-month readings. - The bank examines whether gold's rally is still intact by looking at the question from three separate angles. - A regression of gold prices against the bank's statistical test for explosive price behaviour suggests both the rally's upward extension and its recent pullback have been more muted than in past episodes, with gold potentially bottoming around $3,900/oz rather than falling toward a regression-implied $3,700/oz. - Deutsche Bank's fair value model, once adjustments for outsized official sector demand and real interest rate effects are unwound, still points to a fair value near $4,700/oz by year-end. - The bank maintains its existing Q4 2026 gold forecast of $4,600/oz on the back of this analysis. Deutsche Bank has reaffirmed its bullish outlook for gold, arguing that the metal's recent pullback has likely run its course and that fair value estimates continue to sit above the bank's own price target for the end of the year. In a note to clients, the bank's analysts said the current bout of rapid gold price appreciation, which they date back to August 2024, remains intact and represents just the fifth such episode identified in market data stretching back to 1975. The bank arrived at that count using a statistical method designed to isolate genuine episodes of explosive price behaviour from short-lived noise, filtering out single-month readings and grouping together observations that are temporally linked. That framing led the analysts to pose a direct question: if gold remains in an explosive phase, should prices not be falling further than they have? The bank tackled the issue from three separate directions. First, it examined gold's price relative to broader commodity markets, adjusting the ratio for long-run growth trends and indexing the result to a reference point from 1986. That approach implies a much lower long-term level for gold, near $2,600/oz, a figure that stands in sharp contrast to current spot prices and underscores how stretched valuations can look once the rally's momentum is stripped away. Second, the bank ran a regression of gold prices against its own proprietary statistical test for explosive price behaviour, known as the BSADF statistic. That analysis indicated both the rally's upward extension and its subsequent correction have been more subdued in this episode than in previous ones, leading the analysts to suggest gold may already have found a floor around $3,900/oz, rather than extending its decline toward a regression-implied level of $3,700/oz. Third, and most significant for the bank's near-term outlook, gold has closed the gap between spot prices and the bank's fair value model. Reversing adjustments made for unusually strong official sector buying and the convexity effects of real interest rates, the analysts still put fair value at around $4,700/oz by year-end, a level that sits above the bank's own Q4 2026 forecast of $4,600/oz. On that basis, Deutsche Bank said it is maintaining its existing gold price forecast, framing the metal's current pullback as a pause within an ongoing structural rally rather than the start of a deeper correction.

title: Which home upgrades lower energy bills? What experts say to do first
text: Which home upgrades lower energy bills? What experts say to do first - High energy bills can be a sign that your home has issues like poor insulation or air leaks. - Experts recommend air sealing and adding attic insulation as cost-effective ways to improve efficiency. - When replacing a roof or windows, choosing energy-efficient options can maximize long-term savings. If your energy bills are higher than ever, your home could be part of the problem. As record summer temperatures and rising energy costs put pressure on household budgets, less obvious problems can make your air conditioning work harder than it needs to. Inadequate insulation, air leaks and heat-absorbing materials can let cooled air escape and allow heat to enter, reducing your home’s efficiency. So, before spending thousands on a new HVAC system, try lower-cost improvements that can reduce energy waste and lower utility bills. And when it’s time for larger home upgrades, like roof or window replacements, choosing the most energy efficient options can help maximize long-term savings. Signs your home may be wasting energy There are several signs that your home is wasting energy. Here’s what to look for: - Your HVAC system runs continuously. If your air conditioning struggles to hold your thermostat’s setpoint, that usually means “the house is gaining heat faster than the equipment can remove it,” says Nicole Tomasin, chief commercial officer at Energy Access Innovations. - Some rooms are hotter than others. A several-degree difference between rooms can suggest HVAC distribution and air sealing problems, not necessarily that your system is lacking capacity. - Upstairs is hotter than downstairs. This can mean that your roof is not properly insulated and is letting heat through to your home’s upper floors. - Windows and doors are drafty. Feeling warmth or air flow around the edges of your windows and doors can point to inefficiencies and air leaks. Start with an energy audit If you suspect that your home is wasting energy, a home energy assessment can help you pinpoint the source of the issue. Many local utility companies will perform energy audits at little or no cost to homeowners. State and local governments also frequently offer energy-efficiency assessments and incentive programs. “A home energy audit with a blower door test and duct leakage testing will tell you in a few hours what a summer of speculation will not,” Tomasin says. Identifying the problem can help you understand what steps will be most effective for improving your home’s efficiency. Upgrades experts recommend most: air sealing and attic insulation If your home is leaking air, there are some relatively inexpensive steps you can take to improve efficiency. Two projects frequently offer a high return on investment: “Air sealing the attic floor and topping up the attic insulation,” says Kam Oveisy, owner of Desire Basements, a renovation company in the Greater Toronto area. In fact, the EPA estimates homeowners save an average of 15% on heating and cooling when they air seal their home and add insulation to attics and basements. These projects tend to cost much less than replacing your home’s roof or siding. “If you spend three grand insulating your attic, you could expect to recoup that in three to five years,” says Mitchel Dotson, owner of Indy Rooftops, an Indianapolis-based roofing company. He notes that proper insulation can also help your roof and HVAC unit last longer, compounding long-term savings. Larger projects that can pay off over time Air sealing and attic insulation tend to offer the best ROI for energy savings. But if you have another home project coming up, like roof or window replacements, there are ways that you can maximize your home’s long-term efficiency. Reflective roofing and roof replacements Replacing a roof solely to improve energy efficiency usually isn’t worth the upfront cost. “If the roof still has life left in it, insulation wins and it is not close,” Oveisy says. But if it’s time for a new roof anyway, upgrading to solar-reflective, or “cool roof,” shingles can offer more energy-saving benefits. “The extra cost of stepping up to solar-reflective shingles is modest, so replacement time is the right moment to buy that upgrade,” Oveisy says. These products are designed to reflect more sunlight and absorb less heat than traditional shingles. According to the EPA, cool shingles can help you reduce cooling demand during peak hours by 11% to 27%. They’re especially effective in hotter climates, where demand for AC is highest. Shingles with a high Solar Reflective Index might also offer durability benefits. “Solar reflective shingles lower a roof’s surface temperature and can help reduce UV degradation, which can extend the shingles' own lifespan and reduce maintenance costs over time,” says Lucas Hamilton, manager of applied building science at CertainTeed/Saint-Gobain North America. New siding systems Like roofing, replacing the siding on your home usually requires a larger upfront cost compared to the long-term energy savings. That said, if it’s time for a siding replacement, upgraded products can offer improved efficiency. “Modern siding materials, such as CERTAplank, are designed to provide better thermal resistance, which helps keep your home warmer in the winter and cooler in the summer,” Hamilton says. Window replacements The next time you need to replace your windows, consider an energy efficient option. Replacing single-pane windows with an ENERGY STAR certified option can reduce your energy bills by up to 13%. If you’re not ready to fully replace your windows, adding caulking or weatherstripping to existing windows can help reduce drafts and improve efficiency without the high upfront cost. Bottom line: The best home projects for energy efficiency An improperly insulated home can leak heating and cooling, making your HVAC work overtime to keep your space comfortable. An energy audit can help you identify where your home is leaking air and identify next steps. Experts widely recommend starting with air sealing and attic insulation, as these upgrades give you the best return on your investment when it comes to keeping energy costs down. The next time you need to replace your home’s roof, siding or windows, though, there are several energy efficient upgrades you can make that will maximize your energy savings in the long-run. Frequently asked questions Are cool roof shingles worth it? If you’re already replacing your roof, upgrading to cool roof shingles can be worth the upgrade, especially if you live in a warmer climate. These shingles absorb less sunlight than traditional roofing materials, which can help you save money on cooling costs. Can attic insulation improve roof energy efficiency? Yes. Attic insulation is one of the most effective ways to improve your roof’s energy efficiency. It helps keep your home cooler in the summer and warmer in the winter by slowing heat transfer between your attic and living space. What are the signs of poor attic insulation? Common signs of poor attic insulation include high energy bills, noticeable temperature differences between rooms and an HVAC unit that has to run almost constantly to keep up. Should I replace my roof for energy savings? Replacing your roof for the energy savings alone is usually not worth the large upfront cost. However, if it’s time to replace your roof anyway, it can be worth it to upgrade to more energy efficient materials, such as solar-reflective shingles. title: Momentum Acceleration Is Quietly Reshaping How Equity Markets Move
text: Momentum Acceleration Is Quietly Reshaping How Equity Markets Move. Something powerful is happening beneath the surface of global equity markets, and most investors are only beginning to understand it. Momentum acceleration — the phenomenon where rising assets begin to rise faster, and falling assets sink with increasing speed — is no longer just a theoretical concept favored by quants and algorithmic traders. It has become one of the dominant forces shaping price action across major indices, sectors, and individual equities alike. Understanding it may be the single most important edge available to market participants right now. At its core, momentum acceleration describes not just the direction of a price trend, but the rate at which that trend is intensifying. Think of it like a vehicle moving down a highway — momentum alone tells you the car is moving forward, but momentum acceleration tells you the driver just floored the gas pedal. In equity markets, this distinction matters enormously. A stock trending higher for weeks is interesting. A stock trending higher with an accelerating rate of gains signals something structurally different: capital is piling in with increasing urgency, often ahead of a significant catalyst or a broader repricing of expectations. Quantitative research has consistently shown that assets exhibiting momentum acceleration outperform simple trend-following strategies over medium-term horizons. The reason is largely behavioral. When institutional investors observe that a position is not just gaining but gaining faster, conviction builds. Portfolio managers who were previously neutral begin allocating. Those who were underweight scramble to close the gap. This self-reinforcing dynamic creates the kind of powerful, sustained price moves that can define entire market cycles. We have seen this pattern play out repeatedly in technology sectors, clean energy cycles, and more recently across artificial intelligence-adjacent equities where earnings revisions and capital flows have compounded on themselves in textbook fashion. What makes momentum acceleration particularly relevant today is the role of passive investing and ETF rebalancing in amplifying it. As index-tracking products grow in scale, stocks that outperform are mechanically purchased in greater quantities during rebalancing events, which pushes their prices higher, which in turn triggers further rebalancing purchases. This creates a feedback loop that pure momentum strategies of a prior era never had to contend with. The acceleration effect is baked into market structure itself, meaning the underlying mechanics that drive these moves are more persistent and more powerful than historical models alone might suggest. Identifying momentum acceleration before it becomes obvious to the broader market is where the real opportunity lies. Traders and analysts have developed several methods to detect early-stage acceleration: monitoring changes in the slope of moving averages, tracking volume-weighted price velocity, and comparing short-term rate-of-change indicators against longer-term trend baselines. When multiple signals converge — say, a stock’s 20-day price velocity sharply outpaces its 90-day trend while volume surges above average — it often signals that momentum acceleration is underway rather than merely possible. Risk management, however, cannot be an afterthought. Momentum acceleration works brilliantly in trending markets and brutally against you in reversals. Because prices have already moved significantly by the time acceleration becomes visible, entries can feel uncomfortably late. Position sizing, stop-loss discipline, and an awareness of broader macro conditions are essential guardrails. Markets driven by accelerating momentum can also be acutely sensitive to sentiment shifts — a single earnings miss, a change in central bank tone, or a spike in volatility can terminate an acceleration cycle almost instantly and with little warning. The traders and institutions who thrive in this environment are not simply chasing price. They are reading the velocity of capital flows, interpreting the rate of change in earnings revisions, and building frameworks that separate genuine acceleration from noise. They understand that momentum acceleration is not just a signal — it is a lens through which the entire structure of market conviction becomes visible. In markets where passive flows, algorithmic execution, and behavioral finance intersect more than ever before, mastering this concept is not optional for serious market participants. It is foundational. Those who learn to spot it early, size into it responsibly, and exit before the velocity collapses will find it to be one of the most reliable and repeatable edges available in modern equity investing.

title: Locksmith’s Rush-Service Pricing Sparks Debate After Customer Asks for a Discount: ‘You Want Fast, It’s More Money’
text: Locksmith’s Rush-Service Pricing Sparks Debate After Customer Asks for a Discount: ‘You Want Fast, It’s More Money’. A video shared on X has sparked debate after it showed a locksmith explaining his pricing to a customer locked out of a home, prompted discussion online. Re-shared by @TexasSpectator, the video was taken by a locksmith who recorded the conversation he had with a potential client. The client said that he and his family were stranded outside of their home in an affluent neighborhood because they locked the keys inside the house. But when they contacted the locksmith and he shared his price for immediate service, the gentleman seemed to have changed his mind, appeared to choose to stay stranded for longer than to pay a little extra for immediate access to his home. Foreingers lock themselves out of their affluent home and phone a locksmith. He quoted the rates. They said “come now.” He shows up... Them: “We never called you” Reason? They were calling around for cheaper prices ? The audacity is Olympic-level. Stop doing business with or... pic.twitter.com/cBsviZfQMf — Texas Spectator (@TexasSpectator) August 2, 2026 As the video began, a man with a foreign accent can be clearly heard speaking to the locksmith about being locked out of his home with his family. The locksmith said he understood his plight and asked him if he would like him to come right away to solve the issue. The client responded and asked how much he would charge for the service. That’s when the locksmith broke down his service prices. He said, “It all depends. So if you want someone to be there within five minutes, then it’s about $200 to let you in. If you wanna wait. . . between one hour and two hours, then it’s about $135. . . $120.” Immediately, the customer asked for a discount. He said, “Is there a reduced price or something?” And the locksmith replied that he had just explained that to him with the pricing options. He repeated, “You wanna wait, it’s less money. You want fast, it’s more money. It’s very simple.” A few moments later, when the locksmith arrived at the family’s location in response to his request for service, the man did not respond. He didn’t even lift his head to look at the locksmith. That’s when the customer’s daughter responded, “I think we’re good, sorry.” Without saying it outright, the foreigners refused to agree to the premium price of $200 for faster service, despite living in an upscale neighborhood. So the locksmith said, “You just wanna save money and stay outside in the heat? You wanna save? You just called us. . . How much do you wanna pay my friend?” He continued, “You can finish with this and that’s it. Easy. You’re just gonna pay a little bit more. It’s not like you can’t afford it, you know. “ But despite his efforts to bargain with him, the man refused to communicate. One X user wrote, “Don’t do business unless they prepay...they’re thieves. Want a Ferrari on a slipper budget.” Another person wrote this, “This is business 101. They’re haggling because they want shit for free or nearly free. Cheapest people on the planet that will shamelessly waste your time. If you’ve never run a business you won’t understand this.” The video drew mixed reactions on X. Some users sided with the locksmith, arguing that rush service commands a higher price, while others questioned the cost of the expedited fee. The Daily Dot was unable to independently verify the circumstances shown in the video or the claims made by those involved.
