title: These U.S. cities have the largest concentration of Gen Z homebuyers
text: These U.S. cities have the largest concentration of Gen Z homebuyers. Younger buyers are reshaping the housing market in unexpected cities. LendingTree found where Gen Z mortgage requests surged most A first-time buyer used to rent through their twenties, save for a few years, then buy once income caught up with home prices. That timeline has stretched later into adulthood for the newest generation of buyers. Mortgage rates hovering near seven percent, entry-level home prices that outpaced wage growth through most of the past decade, and student debt that delayed saving all pushed the typical first-time buyer further into their thirties. Young adults are still finding their way into mortgage applications, just not evenly across the map. In some cities, the youngest generation of buyers accounts for roughly one in four mortgage requests. In others, it's closer to one in ten. A mortgage payment scales with the price of the home, and home prices vary enormously from one city to the next, so the income and credit needed to qualify vary just as much. Younger buyers also tend to carry thinner financial cushions than the generations ahead of them. Nationally, buyers born after 1996 are putting down an average of $44,966 and borrowing roughly $274,794, tens of thousands of dollars less than buyers in their thirties and forties typically put down and borrow. Older Americans who locked in low mortgage rates years ago have also been reluctant to sell and take on a new loan at today's higher rates, leaving more room in some markets for first-time buyers to step in. Where housing costs stay modest and local incomes keep pace, that opening gets filled fastest. LendingTree analyzed mortgage purchase requests submitted through its platform in 2025, isolating the share that came from adults ages 18 to 28, and sorted the country's 50 largest cities by how large that share was. The data breaks down each city's average credit score, down payment, and loan amount for these buyers, along with how much their presence has grown or shrunk since 2024. Affordability, not ambition, is deciding where the next generation of homeowners gets its start. weston m / Unsplash Minneapolis, Minn., has the largest concentration of Gen Z homebuyers of any city LendingTree tracked. Adults ages 18 to 28 made up 26.4% of the mortgage purchase requests submitted there in 2025, up from 23.6% a year earlier. Matt Schulz, LendingTree's chief consumer finance analyst, points to income as the biggest driver behind that share. Minneapolis pairs relatively affordable housing costs with some of the stronger paychecks among the cities where young buyers are most active, a combination that widens who can realistically qualify for a mortgage. Gen Z buyers in Minneapolis also carry an average credit score of 690, well above the national Gen Z average of 674. Schulz notes that Minnesota residents generally carry stronger credit profiles, which makes it easier for young buyers there to close on a loan rather than just qualify for one on paper. Gen Z buyers in Minneapolis put down an average of $46,849 and take out loans averaging $288,483, both above the national Gen Z figures of $44,966 and $274,794 despite the city's relative affordability. Buyers there aren't stretching to the loan balances seen in pricier coastal cities, but they're bringing more money to the table than most of their peers elsewhere. Minneapolis added 2.7 percentage points of Gen Z share between 2024 and 2025, an 11.5% increase, as older homeowners hold onto mortgages locked in at lower rates and leave more of the available inventory to a generation just beginning to build equity. Minneapolis's gains also mirror what's happening nationally, just at a larger scale. Gen Z's overall share of mortgage requests climbed from 18.1% to 19.9% between 2024 and 2025, a trend Schulz ties partly to older homeowners staying put rather than trading a low mortgage rate for a higher one. Minneapolis has ridden that wave further than most cities, and the credit and income advantages its young buyers carry suggest the city has room to keep climbing even as competition for entry-level homes intensifies elsewhere. Compared with the typical millennial down payment of $72,412 nationally, Gen Z buyers in Minneapolis are still putting down far less, a reminder of how much ground the generation still has to make up even in its strongest city. Zachary Farmer / Unsplash Few cities have opened up to young buyers as quickly as Birmingham, Ala. Gen Z's share of mortgage purchase requests there jumped from 19.6% in 2024 to 25.7% in 2025, a gain of 6.1 percentage points and the second-largest share among the cities LendingTree analyzed. Only a handful of cities saw a faster percentage increase in that share, up 30.9% year over year. Home prices in Birmingham remain well below the national median, which keeps the math of a first purchase within reach for buyers who are still early in their careers. Gen Z buyers in Birmingham carry an average credit score of 667, the lowest of any city among the fastest-growing markets for this generation and below the national Gen Z average of 674, which points to the tradeoff behind that affordability. Matt Schulz, LendingTree's chief consumer finance analyst, describes Birmingham as affordable but at a lower income tier than cities like Minneapolis, which helps explain both the surge in Gen Z activity and the softer credit profile behind it. Buyers there put down an average of $37,932 and borrow $223,750, both well below the national Gen Z figures of $44,966 and $274,794, since that same affordability shapes the purchase itself and not just who can qualify for one. A young buyer priced out of a coastal city's entry-level market can still find a foothold in Birmingham, even without the strongest credit file or the biggest savings account. Birmingham's trajectory stands out against the national backdrop too. Gen Z's overall share of mortgage requests rose from 18.1% to 19.9% nationally between 2024 and 2025, an increase of less than two percentage points. Birmingham's 6.1-point jump dwarfs that pace, making it one of the fastest-moving cities in the entire analysis even though its buyers carry some of the weaker credit profiles among the cities where young buyers are most active. Rapid growth paired with a below-average credit score points to affordability, rather than buyer strength, as the real driver in Birmingham. The city's below-average down payment and loan figures back up that read, showing buyers stretching less financially even as their numbers grow. Kent Rebman / Unsplash Indianapolis, Ind., rounds out the top tier of cities where Gen Z is buying in the largest numbers. The generation made up 24.6% of mortgage purchase requests there in 2025, up from 22.6% the year before, a gain of 8.7%. Matt Schulz, LendingTree's chief consumer finance analyst, ranks Indianapolis between Minneapolis and Birmingham on income. Young buyers there aren't as flush as their counterparts in Minneapolis, but they earn more than buyers in Birmingham, which puts the city in the middle of the three on income. That middle position carries through the rest of the numbers. Gen Z buyers in Indianapolis average a credit score of 679, five points above the national Gen Z average of 674 and comfortably ahead of buyers in Birmingham. Down payments average $37,371, and loan amounts average $237,966, both figures that sit below the national Gen Z averages of $44,966 and $274,794 but reflect the city's below-average home prices rather than any strain on affordability. Steady population growth in the city and a diversified local economy anchored by health care, logistics, and manufacturing have kept entry-level inventory available even as buyers nationwide compete for a shrinking pool of starter homes. Young professionals settling into their first years of full-time work find real job opportunities there paired with a housing market that hasn't priced them out before they've had a chance to save. Indianapolis's growth also looks modest next to the fastest-moving cities on this list, even though the underlying numbers are solid. National Gen Z share grew from 18.1% to 19.9% between 2024 and 2025, and Indianapolis's own gain of two percentage points sits close to that national pace rather than far ahead of it. What sets the city apart is the steady combination of above-average credit and below-average home prices, not a sudden surge, which has kept a stream of new buyers arriving every year without the sharp swings seen in faster-growing Southern cities. Far Chinberdiev / Unsplash Gen Z's foothold in Kansas City, Mo., has grown quietly but consistently. The generation's share of mortgage purchase requests rose from 22.2% in 2024 to 24.5% in 2025, a gain of 2.3 percentage points and a 10.4% increase year over year, placing the city in a tie for the fourth-largest Gen Z share among the 50 cities LendingTree analyzed. Kansas City's housing stock skews toward moderately priced single-family homes, and its cost of living sits well below coastal benchmarks, which keeps a first purchase within reach for buyers who are just a few years into their careers. Gen Z homebuyers in Kansas City average a credit score of 677, just above the national Gen Z figure of 674, since their financial profile backs up that same affordability story. They put down an average of $38,459 and borrow an average of $247,056, both well below the national Gen Z figures of $44,966 and $274,794, evidence that buyers here aren't overextending to compete for homes. Kansas City's diversified economy, built on logistics, agribusiness, and a growing tech and startup scene, has kept job growth steady without the runaway price appreciation that's priced out young buyers in faster-growing Sun Belt cities. That balance between opportunity and affordability is exactly the combination that's let Kansas City's Gen Z share climb every year without the volatility seen in some coastal cities. Kansas City's climb also lines up closely with the national trend rather than outpacing it. Gen Z's overall share of mortgage requests rose from 18.1% to 19.9% nationally between 2024 and 2025, and Kansas City's own increase of 2.3 percentage points tracks that pace closely. Buyers here are neither pulling far ahead of the national curve nor falling behind it, which fits a city where affordability and income have stayed in balance rather than swinging sharply in either direction from one year to the next. Federico Ramirez / Unsplash Milwaukee, Wis., has held its position among the cities most popular with Gen Z buyers for two years running. The generation accounted for 24.5% of mortgage purchase requests there in 2025, tying Kansas City for the fourth-largest share nationally and essentially flat from 24.2% in 2024. Gen Z's presence in the Milwaukee market was already strong heading into 2025, so the city's share held roughly flat rather than climbing further last year. Gen Z buyers in Milwaukee average a credit score of 684, among the strongest of any city with a large Gen Z presence and 10 points above the national Gen Z average of 674, which helps explain why the city's share has stayed durable. Down payments average $43,777 and loan amounts average $257,503, both close to the national Gen Z figures of $44,966 and $274,794, which suggests Milwaukee buyers are neither straining their budgets nor getting an unusual discount relative to their peers elsewhere. Wisconsin's broader reputation for strong household credit, the same dynamic Schulz points to in nearby Minneapolis, appears to extend to Milwaukee's younger buyers as well. A stable manufacturing and health care base has kept incomes predictable, and predictable incomes make for buyers who can plan a purchase rather than rush one. Milwaukee's flat trajectory looks different set against the national trend, where Gen Z's overall share climbed from 18.1% to 19.9% between 2024 and 2025. Most cities on this list added at least two percentage points of Gen Z share over that span. Milwaukee added just 0.2 percentage points, a 1.0% increase and the smallest gain among the seven cities with the largest Gen Z presence. That reflects a market that had already absorbed much of its available first-time buyer demand the year before, leaving less room for further growth in a single year. Jake Blucker / Unsplash Cincinnati, Ohio, has settled into the middle of the pack among cities with strong Gen Z homebuying activity, and that consistency is itself notable. The generation made up 24.1% of mortgage purchase requests there in 2025, up only slightly from 23.6% in 2024, a modest 2.2% increase. Unlike Birmingham or Nashville, Cincinnati is simply sustaining a share that was already among the highest in the country a year earlier, rather than riding a sudden wave of new buyers. Gen Z buyers in Cincinnati average a credit score of 679, five points above the national Gen Z average of 674, since solid credit is part of what's kept the city's share so steady. Their down payment averages just $35,312, one of the smaller down payments among cities with a large Gen Z presence, and their loan amount of $222,219 is also well below the national Gen Z figure of $274,794. Cincinnati's cost of living ranks among the lowest of any major Midwestern city, and a mix of finance, health care, and consumer goods employers has kept the local job market resilient through recent economic swings. For a young buyer with a modest down payment saved up, Cincinnati remains one of the more forgiving paths into homeownership, without requiring the credit profile or savings cushion that pricier cities demand. Cincinnati's steadiness looks similar next to the national trend, where overall Gen Z share rose from 18.1% to 19.9% between 2024 and 2025, a gain of about two percentage points. Cincinnati's own increase of half a percentage point trails that national pace, yet its 24.1% share still ranks among the highest of any city in the analysis. That gap between fast national growth and a slower local gain suggests Cincinnati reached a high level of Gen Z activity earlier than most other cities on this list and has simply held that level steady since, without the sharp swings up or down seen elsewhere. Mike Gattorna / Unsplash Nashville, Tenn., has seen one of the sharpest jumps in Gen Z homebuying activity of any city LendingTree analyzed. The generation's share of mortgage purchase requests climbed from 19.6% in 2024 to 24.0% in 2025, a gain of 4.3 percentage points and a 22.1% increase, one of the fastest growth rates in the entire study. That surge comes even as Nashville's home prices have climbed well above what many of the other fast-growing Gen Z cities charge. Gen Z buyers in Nashville average a credit score of 685, well above the national Gen Z average of 674, and put down an average of $55,212 while borrowing an average of $331,382, both notably higher than the national Gen Z figures of $44,966 and $274,794, since Nashville's higher cost of entry demands more from every buyer regardless of generation. Nashville's job market, fueled by health care, music and entertainment, and a wave of corporate relocations over the past decade, has drawn a steady stream of young professionals with the income and credit to compete in a pricier market. Unlike the affordability-driven surges in Birmingham or Kansas City, Nashville's growth looks more like buyers with strong financial footing choosing the city on its merits, even at a higher price than they'd pay elsewhere in the region. Nashville's jump also stands out against the national pace, where overall Gen Z share grew from 18.1% to 19.9% between 2024 and 2025, an increase of less than two percentage points nationally. Nashville's gain of 4.3 percentage points is more than double that national pace, even as its buyers already carry some of the highest income and credit profiles among the cities with a large Gen Z presence. Few cities have managed that kind of growth without a corresponding drop in buyer quality, and Nashville's ability to do both at once sets it apart from cities like Birmingham, where growth has come alongside a softer credit profile rather than a stronger one.

title: New Reuters poll shows Democrats with key advantage over Trump’s GOP in 2026 midterms
text: New Reuters poll shows Democrats with key advantage over Trump’s GOP in 2026 midterms. The Democratic Party has the edge over the Republican Party when it comes to the economy for the first time in nearly a decade, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll. The poll, released Monday, found 37% of registered voters preferred the Democratic Party’s approach to the economy to the Republican Party’s. Another 36% of voters picked the Republican Party, while 27% said they were not sure either party had the better approach to the economy. The economy has been a sore point for Republicans in the wake of President Donald Trump’s decision to engage in military conflict with Iran. The war with Iran has sent U.S. gas prices skyrocketing as a result of a blockade on the Strait of Hormuz. Recent polls have suggested that disapproval on Trump’s handling of the economy and the cost of living has given a boost to Democrats ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. The Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 42% of voters would vote for a Democrat on the generic congressional ballot and 37% would vote Republican if the elections were held today. It also found that Trump continued to receive low ratings on how he is handling his job as president. His approval rating fell from 37% to 35% in the latest poll. The poll was conducted among 4,505 U.S. adults between July 29 and Aug. 3 and had a margin of error of 2 percentage points. The poll was released after Trump railed against recent polls showing negative numbers. “My REAL Polling Numbers, not those made up by the Fake News Media, are the best they have ever been, and why wouldn’t they be with the biggest tax cuts and employment numbers EVER, the biggest outside Investment in America in World history, a totally secure Border, a giant Victory in Venezuela, the Denuclearization of Iran, unparalleled respect and success throughout the World, and much more?” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “Don’t believe the Radical Left’s Fake Poll numbers. They are Crooked and Corrupt, just like the Country Destroying Dumocrats are Crooked and Corrupt. VOTE REPUBLICAN FOR GREATNESS IN AMERICA!” he added. It’s not clear what “real” polling numbers Trump was referring to.

title: ASUS, MSI, and Gigabyte motherboards could jump nearly 50% in price as PCB components exhibit surge
text: ASUS, MSI, and Gigabyte motherboards could jump nearly 50% in price as PCB components exhibit surge. In an unfortunate turn of events, it appears that Taiwan’s top motherboard manufacturers, including ASUS, Gigabyte, and MSI, are preparing to raise prices by nearly 50% in the third quarter of 2026. This report comes from a supply-chain-oriented outlet known as Board Channels. According to Board Channels, the PCBs used in motherboards are expected to see prices surge by at least 50% toward the end of 2026. This also includes other components such as surface-mounted capacitors, copper heatsinks, controller chips, and power-delivery VRMs. To offset rising costs of PCB components, ASUS, Gigabyte, and MSI are reportedly preparing to announce a fresh round of price increases in Q3 2026. This pretty much lines up with what other supply-chain reports have claimed this year. Taiwanese industry publication DigiTimes reported that memory now accounts for the largest share of a PC’s total cost, more than ever before, prompting brands to raise component costs or dial back specs. According to reports, ASUS is fighting a defensive battle to meet its already-lowered 2026 motherboard shipment target. Reduced demand does nothing to help matters DIY PC consumer demand has been slumping for months, and the shipment numbers back up this reality. ASUS previously shipped 15 million motherboards in a year and is now pacing well below that in 2026, with both MSI and Gigabyte seeing double-digit drops in shipments. This leaves the big three motherboard manufacturers with increasing development costs and lower production numbers, while they also struggle to pass those costs on to consumers and buyers who are already reluctant to build PCs. Another side to this problem is that CPU manufacturers haven’t offered much incentive for DIY PC builders to purchase new hardware on top of the exorbitantly high RAM prices. Intel’s Core Ultra 200 series has been the last major release for its current desktop lineup. AMD has stayed tight-lipped about Zen 6 chips at both Computex and its Advancing AI event and has instead decided to refresh its older SKUs, which are climbing in price, rather than catering to budget solutions. title: Oil companies are profiting from the US-Iran war. That’s a political headache for Trump
text: Oil companies are profiting from the US-Iran war. That’s a political headache for Trump. “They’re making too much money,” President Donald Trump said in the Oval Office on Monday. Oil companies — and their colossal profits — were the latest target of his ire. “I don’t like it. And I should be the last one to say because I’m a big free enterprise guy,” Trump told reporters. A tumble in energy prices is exactly what Trump needs three months ahead of midterm elections that current polling shows could bring big gains for Democrats in Congress. His war against Iran has sent global oil prices skyward, rippling out into higher costs for American consumers. But high prices are a boon for oil exporters. On Tuesday, Saudi Aramco — the world’s largest — reported a 33% surge in profit during the second quarter to $33.4 billion from $25.2 billion during the same period last year. Meanwhile, Americans continue to grapple with an affordability crisis that has seen the average price of a gallon of gas shoot up 37% since the start of the war. It’s tricky optics for a president who, with an eye to November, is in desperate search of a political win. “Too much money... I’ll say it loud and clear. I’m not happy about it,” he told reporters Monday. A familiar pattern Aramco joins a raft of oil majors reporting bumper earnings even as the US-Iran conflict has significantly reduced the flow of tankers through the Strait of Hormuz — making it, at times, all but impossible to export fuel from the region. On Friday, American oil giant ExxonMobil said its second-quarter profits had more than doubled to $14.5 billion from the same period in 2025. Rival Chevron reported $12.1 billion in profit, more than four times the amount it made during the same period last year. And, last week, British energy major Shell reported almost $10 billion in profit for the quarter — the second-highest quarterly profit in its history. Booming profits are part of a familiar pattern: When global supply is constrained, fear and physical scarcity will cause energy prices to rocket and politicians will protest. In the months following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, then President Joe Biden criticized what he called “war profiteering” by energy producers as global oil and natural gas prices soared, and floated the idea of a so-called “windfall tax” on their profits. The price of a barrel of Brent crude, the global benchmark, was trading a little under $70 before the US-Israeli war with Iran began, but has since climbed to triple digits, fallen sharply, and yo-yoed on any sign of progress or problems in peace talks. On Tuesday morning ET, Brent was trading close to $80 a barrel, up 14% from before the conflict. Rahul Choudhary, vice president of upstream research at Rystad Energy, said that Aramco’s latest earnings were also boosted by the company’s decision to export more high-value products like diesel. Still, “high revenue cannot hold forever,” Choudhary told CNN, noting that Aramco’s results were driven by oil sold from stockpiles, which are now lower. Prices, while volatile, also fell back in June after the US and Iran agreed to a since-broken ceasefire. While Saudi Arabia has found a workaround for a chunk of its oil exports, redirecting barrels west and loading them onto tankers in the Red Sea, this route has become another area of vulnerability. Last month, Iran-backed Houthi militants declared a blockade on Saudi ships exiting the Bab al-Mandeb strait at the base of the Red Sea and claimed responsibility for attacks on vessels. Saudi crude exports via the Red Sea have at least halved as a result, according to Choudhary. As long as oil price stay high, oil companies stand to make vast sums of money. That is, of course, if they choose to ignore Trump’s calls to “cut the retail price.”

title: Bank of Korea Just Bought Gold After 13 Years: Is a New Rally Coming?
text: Bank of Korea Just Bought Gold After 13 Years: Is a New Rally Coming?. The Bank of Korea will buy physical gold again after 13 years. Central banks bought 289 tonnes in the second quarter, their strongest second quarter on record. Gold traded near $4,086 an ounce on Tuesday, up 0.8%. It sits 27% below its January record. It is still up about 20% on the year. Korea Gold Purchases Resume After 13 Years Seoul stopped buying gold in 2013. It was mocked for the timing. The bank bought 90 tonnes between 2011 and 2013, at an average $1,629 an ounce. That came to about $4.7 billion, figures from Korea Economic Daily show. Then gold fell apart. The price had peaked at $1,920.30 in September 2011. By June 2013 it hit $1,180.71, a drop of 38.5%. That year was gold's worst since 1981. At that low, Korea's gold was worth 27.5% less than it paid. Lawmakers dragged in then-governor Kim Choong-soo. By 2015 the paper loss reached about 1.8 trillion won. Buying stopped. Here is the twist. Those same 90 tonnes are now worth roughly $11.8 billion. That is $7 billion more than Korea paid. So the bank is careful about how it explains itself. Jung Hee-sub, who runs its Reserve Management Group, denies any link to the recent price drop. "We did not decide the timing of purchases by looking at a specific price... we decide whether to proceed at that time based on domestic and international gold prices and market conditions," local media reported. Follow us on X to get the latest news as it happens The plan itself is tiny. Korea digs up 40 to 45 tonnes a year, mostly as a leftover from smelting copper and zinc. Only 4 to 5 tonnes get sold abroad. The bank will bid for that slice alone. So its reserves stay near 104.4 tonnes, ranking Korea 39th. It also bought its first gold exchange-traded funds (ETFs) last quarter, as South Korea's equity turmoil grips policymakers. Central Bank Gold Buying Hit a Record 289 Tonnes Korea is late to a crowded party. Central banks bought 288.9 tonnes in the second quarter, World Gold Council data show. That is 62% more than a year earlier. Poland bought the most, at 51 tonnes. Its stockpile hit a record 632 tonnes. It wants 700. Governor Adam Glapiński is blunt about how he does it. "We've been consistently buying gold, taking advantage of the recent price drops." China added 33 tonnes, keeping up a long buying streak. Russia sold 22. The rebound hides a slow start, though. Just 56.5 tonnes came in the first quarter. At 345 tonnes, the first half was the weakest since 2022. They are not losing interest. A record 45% plan to buy more within a year, and demand held firm through the price slump.

title: Canadian manufacturing PMI hits a four-year high
text: Canadian manufacturing PMI hits a four-year high. Highest reading since June 2022 Fourth straight month of expansion Input prices rise at fastest pace in four years New export orders down for a second month Business confidence falls to lowest since March Canada’s manufacturing sector enjoyed its strongest performance since June 2022 in the latest PMI from S&P Global. Output and new orders both accelerated, and employment rose for a fourth consecutive month. It seems to be a domestic story. New export orders declined for a second month running, with panellists again pointing to tariffs and the Middle East war as drags on international demand. The internal market is holding up despite the loonie near a four-year low. The inflation picture is the uncomfortable part. Input prices rose at the fastest pace in four years, extending an upward trend in place since late 2025. Companies flagged energy, transportation and steel as the core drivers, with tariffs and the Middle East conflict as root causes. Canada is steadily excluding imported steel. Manufacturers passed it along too — output charges rose strongly and well above trend, though below May's near four-year high. Vendor delivery times deteriorated considerably again, and there were signs firms are buying ahead to build stocks, with inventories rising at the steepest pace since the end of 2024. Despite the solid headline, confidence in the outlook fell to a four-month low and sits well below trend. S&P's Paul Smith summed it up: the current picture is positive, but whether growth can be sustained "at its current clip is doubtful" with international demand weak and prices rising rapidly. For the Bank of Canada, it's a low-tier but notable release. It shows four straight months of expansion and a four-year high in input costs. That's not going to quiet the rate-hike talk. These are the comments from Paul Smith, Economics Director at S&P Global Market Intelligence: "PMI data for July painted a positive picture of current growth, with output and new orders both rising at faster rates on the back of firmer domestic demand. Companies were suitably encouraged to take on additional workers, raising their staffing levels to bolster capacity and help support current workloads. "However, whether growth can be sustained at its current clip is doubtful. International demand remains weak, driven lower by tariffs and a highly uncertain geopolitical environment. These factors also continued to push up prices rapidly whilst adding to ongoing and widespread supply-side disruption. Subsequently, confidence amongst firms in the outlook and therefore near-term growth prospects - remains subdued, with sentiment in July its lowest for four months and well below trend." This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

title: U.S. stocks head toward a record as profits keep piling up and oil prices ease
text: U.S. stocks head toward a record as profits keep piling up and oil prices ease. NEW YORK — The U.S. stock market is rising toward a record on Tuesday as companies keep piling up profits and oil prices ease. The S&P 500 added 0.9% and is on track to top its all-time high set earlier in the summer. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 539 points, or 1%, from its own record set the day before, and the Nasdaq composite was 1.6% higher, as of 10:30 a.m. Eastern time. Despite worries about high inflation, the war in Iran and a possible bubble in stock prices because of euphoria around the boom in artificial-intelligence technology, Wall Street is nearing its latest apex in large part because profits are soaring for companies. That’s key because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate earnings over the long term. Palantir Technologies helped lead the way and jumped 25.5% after CEO Alex Karp said its overall revenue leaped 93% in what he called an “otherworldly” quarter. Besides reporting a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, the AI company also raised its revenue forecast for the full year of 2026. Caterpillar climbed 4.7% after the heavy-equipment maker likewise reported stronger profit and revenue for the spring than analysts expected. It was the first time Caterpillar made more than $20 billion in sales and revenue in a quarter, and CEO Joe Creed said it’s seeing strong order rates and a growing backlog across its main businesses. Caterpillar is also benefiting from the AI boom through increased orders for turbines used to power data centers, among other things. McDonald’s added 1.5% after topping analysts’ expectations for profit during the spring despite increased pressure on its customers from expensive gasoline and worries about the economy. They’re the latest companies to deliver even better profits for the latest quarter than investors expected, following strong results from Amazon, Microsoft and others. Coming into this week, companies in the S&P 500 index were on track to deliver growth in earnings per share for the spring of nearly 50% from a year earlier, according to FactSet. That would be the biggest such jump since the historic numbers of the spring of 2021, when the economy was roaring out of the COVID-19 pandemic. Also helping stocks on Tuesday was another drop for oil prices. Brent crude, the international standard, sank 4.7% to $79.87 per barrel as hope once again took over from fear in the oil market. It had swung sharply between $72 and $102 through July on uncertainty about when the war with Iran would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again to deliver crude around the world. It’s jerked up and down many times, as uncertainty built, receded and then built again, not only week to week but also hour to hour. That has many on Wall Street continuing to caution that “investors have seen similar headlines before,” including Tony Miano, global fixed income analyst at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. Even a signed agreement between the United States and Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to oil tankers “would not necessarily translate into an immediate or sustained increase in oil flows,” Miano said. The latest drop in oil prices nevertheless helped to ease Wall Street’s worries about inflation, which in turn pulled down yields in the bond market and relaxed pressure on the overall economy and on prices for stocks and other investments. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.64% from 4.70% Monday and from 4.75% at the end of last week. That’s a notable move for the bond market, but it remains well above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran. Higher yields make it more expensive for all kinds of Americans to borrow money, from homebuyers looking for a mortgage to big companies looking to build AI data centers. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose modestly across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi was an outlier and jumped 1.6%. Seoul has been home to some of the world’s sharpest swings recently because its stock market is dominated by two companies swept up in AI mania, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The Kopsi had dropped 5.1% and soared 17.9% in the prior two days. Stocks of computer chip companies also held firmer on Wall Street, where gains of 4.7% for Broadcom, 1.6% for Nvidia and 6.4% for Micron Technology were some of the strongest forces lifting the S&P 500. ___ AP Business Writers Yuri Kageyama and Matt Ott contributed to this report.

title: Why Ford believes its 10.2% July U.S. sales decline was still a 'good' month
text: Why Ford believes its 10.2% July U.S. sales decline was still a 'good' month. DETROIT — Despite reporting a 10.2% decline in its July U.S. vehicle sales Tuesday, Ford Motor is touting the results as a "good sales month." That's according to Rob Kaffl, Ford's director of U.S. sales, who said the steep decline from the previous year was "by design," as the Detroit automaker phases out two vehicles and lowered its daily rental fleet business. "July was a good sales month for a number of reasons. Our July results reflect a strategy that is working exactly as planned: we've intentionally been sunsetting select models and pulled back on low-margin rental fleet volume to make room for an onslaught of new-product introductions by the end of the decade," Kaffl said in an emailed statement. Many times, automakers do not cancel products — like Ford has done with its Ford Escape and Lincoln Corsair — until closer to production of newer models. Or they build up inventories to assist sales during the changeover in production for new vehicles. Kaffl said the company prioritized retail sales of its F-Series pickup trucks as the automaker continues to recover production after two aluminum fires last year at a major aluminum supplier. The company said rental sales, which are typically at lower profits, were reduced by 96% compared to a year earlier. Read more Without such actions, Ford contends its sales would be down less than 1%, slightly better than an estimated 2% fall for the overall industry compared to July 2025. Planned or not, the decline last month adds to a lackluster sales year for the automaker following the problematic F-Series production as well as a pullback in all-electric vehicle sales. Ford's sales year to date through July are down 9.7%. Ford's U.S. sales through June were already off 9.6% from a year earlier. That compares to an estimated 2.4% sales decline for the overall industry through the first half of the year, which doesn't include July, according to the most recent data from Cox Automotive's Kelley Blue Book. Higher prices and consumer economic concerns are weighing on the overall auto industry, which Cox and other forecasters expect to be off about 3% compared to last year to 15.8 million vehicles sold.

title: McDonald’s sales in the US are slowing after deal fatigue
text: McDonald’s sales in the US are slowing after deal fatigue. McDonald’s recently revved up the amount of deals and discounts it offers to attract more customers. That strategy seems to have hit a roadblock. The burger chain on Tuesday reported its slowest growth since 2025, with US sales rising just 0.8% in the second quarter. McDonald’s blamed the slowdown in visits on slower service because of the number of value offerings launched over the past few months. It now plans to re-evaluate its menu selection. CEO Chris Kempczinski said on the earnings call that is US business “slowed significantly” during the second quarter and that results were “below our expectations.” McDonald’s introduced several promotions in recent months, like limited time FIFA World Cup and KPop Demon Hunter meals, plus a revamped $3 menu. Kempczinski said that restaurants “were overwhelmed by too many deployments in the quarter, which led to less efficient restaurant operations... and impacted customer service times.” McDonald’s has doubled down over the past few years on value deals and lower-priced menu items in order to drive up business and convince consumers it’s affordable. Earlier this year, it phased out many digital promotions and its “Buy One, Get One for $1” deal in favor of a new McValue menu that sold many items under $3. But only about 65% of franchise restaurants participated in the deal. Some locations actually used the promotion to raise prices on some items while still keeping it under the $3 threshold. “In combination, all of these factors negatively impacted visits from some our most loyal customers,” McDonald’s Chief Financial Officer Ian Borden said on the call. As a result, Borden said McDonald’s will roll out new promotions next week in its app to “re-energize our high frequency customers.” The company will also increase marketing spending on proven value offerings like its Extra Value Meals. McDonald’s is also making leadership changes following the disappointing quarter. Joe Erlinger, its US president since 2019 that led the company through Covid-19 and its E. coli outbreak, is leaving the role immediately. He will be replaced by Skye Anderson, a 26-year veteran who is currently the chief operating officer for US operations.

title: NYC Egg Prices Soared. Officials Say Major Producers Rigged The Market
text: NYC Egg Prices Soared. Officials Say Major Producers Rigged The Market New Yorkers will receive relief after an investigation uncovered how egg producers influenced prices behind the scenes. NEW YORK, NY— Three major egg producers will send millions of eggs to food banks across New York after investigators found they illegally coordinated to influence prices, a settlement that will deliver direct relief to families facing high grocery costs. The first shipment arrived in Brooklyn, where more than 280,000 eggs were delivered to City Harvest for distribution through its network of food partners. The delivery is part of a multistate settlement involving Cal-Maine Foods, Versova and Hickman’s Egg Ranch after a joint investigation by New York Attorney General Letitia James, the U.S. Department of Justice and 16 other states found the companies manipulated egg pricing. Find out what's happening in New York Cityfor free with the latest updates from Patch. James said the companies secretly communicated beginning as early as 2022 to coordinate bidding activity and influence a daily egg price index used in supply contracts. The companies allegedly submitted higher bids that affected price quotes published by Urner Barry, a benchmark used throughout the egg industry. Find out what's happening in New York Cityfor free with the latest updates from Patch. The investigation found the conduct increased costs for retailers and consumers who bought eggs nationwide. Why Did Egg Prices Rise So Much? Egg prices climbed in recent years as the industry faced multiple pressures, including outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza, commonly known as bird flu, that forced farmers to kill millions of egg-laying hens. The loss of laying hens reduced the nation’s egg supply at a time when demand remained high, pushing prices higher at grocery stores. Farmers also faced rising costs for feed, transportation and other expenses that affected the price of producing eggs. But investigators said supply challenges were not the only factor affecting what consumers paid. According to the multistate investigation, three major egg producers also took steps to influence pricing by coordinating bids tied to Urner Barry, a benchmark pricing service used in egg supply contracts. Those benchmark prices are used throughout the egg industry to help set contract prices between suppliers and buyers. James said manipulating those quotes allowed the companies to increase prices beyond what normal market conditions would have produced. “It is unacceptable that New Yorkers paid higher prices for eggs because these companies were working together behind the scenes to raise prices,” James said. “My office has zero tolerance for big corporations breaking the law to boost their profits at the expense of working families.” Investigators said the companies communicated privately beginning as early as 2022 to coordinate bidding activity and influence daily egg price quotes. Where Will The Eggs Go? The companies will provide 53 million eggs to food banks and nonprofit organizations nationwide and pay $3.3 million under the settlement. New York will receive nearly 5 million eggs, which will be distributed through Feeding New York State. The eggs will be distributed throughout New York City to families through food pantries and community organizations. Additional deliveries across New York will continue through mid-October. The statewide distribution will be managed through Feeding New York State, which oversees the state’s network of food banks. “Protein-rich foods like eggs are among the most requested items by our neighbors experiencing food insecurity,” said Elizabeth Cooper, executive director of Feeding New York State. What Happens Next For The Egg Companies? In addition to providing eggs and paying $3.3 million, the companies agreed to adopt compliance measures designed to prevent future violations. The settlement was reached by New York, the U.S. Department of Justice and attorneys general from Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Florida, Hawaii, Iowa, Maryland, Minnesota, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas, Utah, Vermont and Wisconsin. title: The Bond-Salesman-In-Chief Has Fired The First Shot Of The Capital Market War That Follows The Trade War
text: The Bond-Salesman-In-Chief Has Fired The First Shot Of The Capital Market War That Follows The Trade War By Benjamin Picton, senior market strategist at Rabobank US equity markets approached record highs yesterday as traders basked in the afterglow of Donald Trump’s decision to (again) call off Iran strikes in favor of diplomatic efforts . The S&P500 closed almost 1.5% higher and the NASDAQ 100 was up by almost 1.8%. Sovereign yields pushed lower across Europe and North America with Treasuries likely encouraged by comments from Japanese Finance Minister Katayama yesterday that Japan intended to tap the Fed’s FIMA facility to defend the Yen in the future, thereby avoiding the necessity to sell Treasuries to fund Yen purchases. The front Brent crude future fell by more than 7%, despite the fact that there is no confirmation of material progress in loosening restrictions on global energy flows . ICE gasoil futures declined by more than 8.5% despite Russia’s ongoing diesel export ban, continued Ukrainian strikes on energy infrastructure, the Houthis’ recent decision to spread the Iran conflict to Saudi oil infrastructure in the Red Sea and low water levels in the Rhine disrupting energy shipping and forcing freight rates higher. Similarly, Singapore gasoil spot prices were down by almost 11% yesterday. On those figures you would think all of the problems in product markets are solved. This again highlights the capriciousness of markets; it was only a few weeks ago that I was reading articles making straight-faced suggestions of an emerging oil glut. While Hormuz certainly isn’t a Waterloo moment for Donald Trump just yet, he is obviously keen to find an offramp that satisfies key US strategic objectives of re-opening the strait without tolls, curtailing Iran’s nuclear program and regional influence, and – if at all possible – pushing Gulf states into the Abraham Accords and normalization of relations with Israel. Some progress has been made on the latter, but progress on the former two objectives continues to elude, giving this conflict more than a whiff of Middle-Eastern quagmires past. While the Commander in Chief plays Battleship in the Gulf, the self-described bond salesman in chief, Scott Bessent, has possibly fired the first shot of the capital market war that we have long warned would follow the trade war and the now numerous proxy wars. All of these developments can be contextualized through the strategic competition between the United States and China, with Russia, the European Union, Iran, the GCC, Japan, South Korea, North Korea, Israel, Australia and others playing the role of proxies, satellites, supplicants, vassals, junior partners and bit-players to the two great powers. In this respect, the US Treasury’s support of the Japanese Ministry of Finance and the BOJ in defending the Yen may have been a financial Fort Sumter moment. In supporting Japan’s efforts to defend its currency to stave off imported inflation pressures the USA not only takes out insurance against rising borrowing costs for the US Treasury while buying up assets that Bessent considers to be undervalued relative to Japan’s improving fundamentals, it also relieves competitive pressure on US manufacturers (currently in rude health according to yesterday’s manufacturing ISM) and pulls Japan closer into the US’ strategic orbit . This is important as the Trump administration views Japan as an important partner for countering China’s dominance in industrial production – particularly shipbuilding, steel manufacturing and rare earths processing – and both partners have an interest in preventing Japan’s reflating economy from becoming an outlet for China’s production surplus. Might we see further Japanese restrictions on Chinese imports? Could the US decision to sell EUR (even in relatively small amounts) rather than USD have been a subtle message to Europeans about US policy capabilities? Coordinated intervention between the Japanese Ministry of Finance and the US Treasury to manage the value of the Yen is perhaps the first concrete sign of the emergence of a new monetary order as foreshadowed by RaboResearch Global Strategist Michael Every several years ago in FX Wars . The post Bretton Woods system of mostly free-floating fiat with a constellation of international treaties intended to discourage state intervention and competitive devaluation has been on b orrowed time due to the rise of neo-mercantilist China and the QE-driven currency devaluations of the 2010s. Cooperation on managed exchange rates (and broader capital market dynamics) among allies may offer a path forward. However, intra-bloc accords only work if inter-bloc trade faces substantial barriers. Naturally, the US does not want to see a situation where the global role of the Dollar is undermined by developed market central banks holding larger and more diversified FX reserves, so watch as a system of “you scratch my back, I scratch yours” dollar swaplines emerges with common trade restrictions or other boons for US strategic interests as a kind of quid pro quo. Indeed, we have already seen this happen with the UAE’s decision to leave OPEC+ and coordinate with Israel on military matters following the extension of dollar swaplines. So, once again we are witnessing momentous structural changes unfolding with geopolitical tensions forcing the pace. While it is certainly relevant and important, one shouldn’t be too captivated by the up/down moves of this week. What really matters is the signal for the medium to longer term. title: These 5 Side Hustles Are Hot Right Now, and Each Could Become a Full-Time Business
text: These 5 Side Hustles Are Hot Right Now, and Each Could Become a Full-Time Business. Whether you want to eventually run your own business full-time or are just looking for some extra earnings to supplement your income, side hustles have become a popular option. Just as there are new fields opening in all corners of the startup world, there are new types of side hustles that can provide opportunities for profit. Many of these revolve around new technologies. Yes, that includes AI, but there are also emerging opportunities in other fields that require no knowledge of large language models or coding. And some have high earnings potential. Looking for something that could become a full-time business and doesn't yet have a lot of competition? Here are some fast-growing side hustle businesses to consider. Smart-home set-up Between smart thermostats, automated blinds, video doorbells and smart locks, setting up today's home can take more than just a basic knowledge of wiring. If you know IT and the major smart ecosystems (Alexa, Google and Apple lead the market), there's money to be made helping people set up and consolidate their home automation devices. The smart home business is valued at $30 billion and installers that have a sharp focus (i.e. installation services, device consultant or specialists in a specific area of automation) can see their side hustle grow quickly. "Many entrepreneurs are exploring how to start a smart home business to capitalize on connected technology trends," writes CEDIA, the association for smart home professionals. "Understanding the smart home business model early on will help you identify your target market, services, and long-term revenue opportunities - as home automation technology is fast becoming more affordable, widening the market for those looking to branch out." EV charger installation The market for electric vehicles has seem some fluctuation over the past few years as tax incentives have disappeared, but as gas prices remain high, more drivers are considering getting one. The rise in used EV car prices this year has highlighted that consumer interest, with vehicles retaining their value, versus gas-powered cars. (Prices for used EVs are up 5.1 percent from January to June 2026.) As that demand increases, there is a growing need for home chargers. Market research firm Research and Markets estimates the Smart EV Charger Home Installation Market will grow from $12.9 billion in 2026 to $22.4 billion in 2031. That makes this a good side hustle choice for licensed electricians, who can earn between $1,000 and $2,500 per install. AI consultant There are plenty of directions to take this side hustle. You can help businesses pick the best AI tools and models for their needs. You can help people or businesses integrate AI with their calendar, notes and local files. Or you can set up workflow audits that review how employees work to discover repetitive tasks that the AI could handle. If you're less tech-fluent, you can use AI to condense market breakdowns and competitor research into easily digestible insights or use it to assist with video editing. Rates for an AI consultant range from $150–$350 per hour for independent workers and people doing it as a side hustle. Should you find a robust customer base and turn this into a full-time business, those rates can go as high as $600 per hour. Personal data cleanup service We live in an online world, but there's often information about us on the Internet that we'd rather not share, especially with data brokers. A data cleanup side hustle helps people eliminate that online information, by submitting opt-out or deletion requests and setting up monitors in case it is republished at some point. It's a way to help people reduce the size of their online footprint or profile. You'll need to have a good bit of technical knowhow to do this side hustle and you'll have to do a fair bit of homework to know where to submit the opt-out requests for various data brokers. Only 6 percent of U.S. adults have used data removal services, but that number is expected to soar in the coming year, growing as much as 90 percent to an overall market size of $561 billion by 2029.. Pool and parking space rentals Sites like Airbnb and Vrbo have been around for a while, but if you don't have a second home or don't want to invite strangers into the house you live in, there are still plenty of alternate routes you can take. Swimply will let you rent out your pool to people looking to beat the heat. The founder appeared on a 2020 episode of Shark Tank to pitch the idea, failing to sway the Sharks, but later raised more than $50 million via venture capitalists. During the pandemic, the business began to take off, with a 4,000% increase in revenue. Today it operates in hundreds of U.S. markets as well as Canada and Australia. No pool? Platforms like Neighbor, Spacer, and SpotHero let you rent out an unused parking spot in heavy traffic and popular areas. And some entrepreneurs act as landlords, of sorts, for other people's parking spots, taking a cut of those fees and earning nearly $1,000 per month per space.

title: How to Shop at a Farmers Market Like a Pro and Actually Use What You Buy
text: How to Shop at a Farmers Market Like a Pro and Actually Use What You Buy. A weekly farmers market run sounds simple until the kale wilts by Wednesday and the strawberries mold by Thursday. If you have ever wondered how to shop at a farmers market and actually finish what you carry home, the answer is less about willpower and more about building a routine you can repeat. Nisha Vora , New York Times bestselling author of Big Vegan Flavor , and farmers market meal plan blogger Brittany Chang both walked through their approach with The Guardian . Their advice pairs with food safety guidance from the FDA to form a routine that actually sticks. Why the Farmers Market Habit Is Worth Building A repeatable trip pulls seasonal produce into your kitchen and supports local growers, but the real payoff is what happens after the haul. Without a plan, that gorgeous bunch of kale ends up in the compost bin. Pick one day that works with your local market’s schedule and pair the trip with something you already enjoy, like grabbing coffee on the way. That extra hook makes consistency easier than any rule about eating more vegetables ever will. Always Bloated? It May Be Food Sensitivities — Find Out With This Test When to Arrive For the Best Selection or the Best Deals Timing shapes what you bring home. Earlier hours mean fuller stalls and first pick of anything limited. Later in the day, prices often drop as vendors clear out inventory. “When you go later in the day, they are trying to get rid of stuff. They’ll be more eager to get things off their hands that they haven’t sold,” Vora told The Guardian . Either strategy works depending on what your goal is. Just decide which one fits your week before you go. How to Shop with Flexible Recipe Formats Rigid grocery lists collapse the moment you spot something better two stalls over. Loose formats hold up. Head in with categories rather than exact ingredients. Think two vegetables for a grain bowl, one to sheet-pan roast as a side and two fruits to slice into your yogurt. That structure keeps impulse buys in check while leaving room to swap based on what looks freshest. Give yourself one unplanned item each week. It keeps the trip fun and stretches your cooking without filling the fridge with rare finds that spoil. “I get excited when I see niche pepper varieties in the fall and fiddlehead ferns in the late spring. I know that sounds absurd to folks who don’t eat seasonally, but to me, it’s become a fun, creative hobby that has instilled a deep sense of gratitude for the food I get to eat,” Chang told The Guardian . Why Bangkok and Singapore Top the Best Street Food Cities List How to Prep and Store Your Haul So It Lasts Prep is where most farmers market trips succeed or fail. Wash everything, dry it well and store it according to what it needs. “Wash all produce thoroughly under running water before preparing and/or eating, including produce grown at home or bought from a grocery store or farmers’ market,” the FDA advises. The agency also warns that “Washing fruits and vegetables with soap, detergent, or commercial produce wash is not recommended. Produce is porous. Soap and household detergents can be absorbed by fruits and vegetables, despite thorough rinsing, and can make you sick.” Storage rules vary by item. Leafy greens last longest in an airtight container with a paper towel to absorb moisture. Carrots and celery stay crisp in a container of water. Tomatoes (unless super ripe) belong at room temperature, away from direct sunlight, not in the fridge. If you know you won’t get to something within a few days, freeze it. What to Bring and What to Ask the Vendors A few small habits round out the routine: Bring cash. Many stalls now take tablet payments, but some are still old-school. Pack reusable bags. Vendors often skip handing out single-use bags for environmental reasons. Ask questions. Vendors will tell you what is at its peak, how to cook something new or how long it will hold in your fridge. That last one might be the most underrated part of the whole ritual. The people who grew the food usually love to talk about it, so don’t be afraid to strike up a conversation.

title: Trump's 'credibility is shot' as he gets cold shoulder from massive industry execs: report
text: Trump's 'credibility is shot' as he gets cold shoulder from massive industry execs: report. text: LA’s biggest restaurant week is back with $15 meals and Michelin deals. California foodies are about to have 400-plus reasons to skip cooking. LA’s biggest restaurant week is back with $15 meals and Michelin deals, bringing two weeks of discounted prix-fixe menus to more than 400 restaurants across Los Angeles — from neighborhood classics and burger joints to exquisite, acclaimed dining destinations. Dine LA Restaurant Week returns Friday, Aug. 14, and runs through Aug. 28, transforming 84 neighborhoods into one giant dining room with deals spanning 26 global cuisines. Whether you’re craving ramen, barbecue, regional Chinese specialties, Mexican classics or an over-the-top tasting menu, there’s a seat at the table. The best part is you don’t even need a ticket. Unlike many food festivals, Dine LA is refreshingly simple: Just make a reservation, ask for the Dine LA Restaurant Week menu and dig in. The event is dine-in only, and organizers strongly recommend booking ahead before the hottest tables disappear. Sign up for the California Morning Report newsletter California's top news, sports and entertainment delivered to your inbox every day. Thanks for signing up! Prices range from wallet-friendly lunches to lavish Michelin-starred offers, making it one of the easiest ways to sample some of SoCal’s best restaurants without paying full freight. “This has been an extraordinary summer for Los Angeles, from welcoming the world during the 2026 FIFA World Cup to celebrating the incredible recognition our chefs and restaurants continue to earn,” Stacey Sun, Executive Director of Dine LA, said in a recent statement. “Dine LA offers a chance to experience the creativity, culture, and hospitality that define Los Angeles’ dining scene through the people and restaurants that bring our community together.” Held twice a year, the culinary celebration has cemented itself as one of La La Land’s tastiest traditions, spotlighting the city’s world-class dining scene. For bargain hunters, there are plenty of steals. Several restaurants are serving $15 lunch menus, including Hollywood Noodle House in Arcadia, Homegirl Cafe in downtown Los Angeles, Le Shrimp Noodle Bar in Glendale, Maple Block Meat Co. in Culver City, Sausal in El Segundo, The Cat and Fiddle in Hollywood, Descanso Restaurant in Mid-Wilshire, Delicious at the Dunbar downtown, Confections by Kirari West in Redondo Beach and multiple Hilltop Coffee + Kitchen locations across Eagle Rock, downtown Los Angeles, Inglewood and Slauson. If dinner is more your speed, you can also find $15 evening menus at a handful of establishments, including Le Shrimp Noodle Bar, Grand Central Market downtown and Highland Park’s For The Win. Looking to spend a little more? Many eateries are offering $25 dinner menus, including Canoe House in South Pasadena, Hollywood Noodle House, JINYA Ramen Bar in Topanga, Mixed Burgers & Bowls in Long Beach, NADC Burger in Westwood and Lei’d Cookies in Culver City. title: Back-to-school shopping tips to save money
text: Back-to-school shopping tips to save money. Back-to-school shopping can get expensive quickly. According to the National Retail Federation, families with K-12 students are expected to spend an average of $863.81 this school year, for a total of $43.3 billion nationwide. Families with college students are projected to spend even more—an average of $1,437.81, totaling $103.5 billion. Those costs can add up quickly, but there are several ways to stretch your budget before filling your cart. Shop your home first Before buying anything new, take inventory of what you already have. Brie Schwartz, editorial commerce director for Good Housekeeping, recommends checking last year's backpacks, binders, folders, calculators and other supplies before automatically replacing them. "Odds are the backpack will probably still be in good condition," Schwartz said. "Instead of reinvesting in a new one, buy a cute bag charm, which is really popular this year, which will give your child the opportunity to personalize without buying an entirely different backpack." Skip the pre-packaged school supply kits Those all-in-one school supply boxes may be convenient, but they aren't always the cheapest option. "Maybe they'll save you the headache," Schwartz said. "They're definitely not going to save you money." Instead, she recommends purchasing notebooks, folders, pencils and other classroom supplies individually at retailers such as Target or Walmart, where shoppers can compare prices and buy only what they actually need. Save on laptops and tech Technology is often one of the biggest back-to-school expenses. If you're buying a laptop or tablet, consider shopping for manufacturer-certified refurbished devices, which are typically inspected, tested, repaired if necessary and backed by a warranty. Before you check out, visit the manufacturer's website and look for an education store or student pricing. Many major tech companies offer exclusive discounts for students and educators during the back-to-school season. For example, Apple's Education Store is currently offering education pricing on qualifying Macs and iPads, along with a gift card worth up to $150. Start with the basics when shopping for clothes It can be tempting to buy an entirely new wardrobe before school starts, but Schwartz says parents should resist that urge and treat shopping like building a mini capsule collection. "Your kid will get to school. They'll start seeing trendy things on other children, and they'll probably want that," she said. "So, I would say don't go nuts buying a ton of things." You can also stretch your clothing budget by shopping resale marketplaces such as Poshmark, eBay and Facebook Marketplace or joining a local Buy Nothing group. Compare prices before you buy Before making a purchase, compare prices across multiple retailers and check an item's price history. Google Shopping lets shoppers compare prices and, for many products, view historical pricing across retailers. Amazon shoppers can also use price-history tools, including Amazon's built-in price history feature and third-party services such as CamelCamelCamel. CamelMart, created by the same developers, provides historical pricing for Walmart products. Looking at an item's pricing history can help you determine whether today's discount is truly a bargain or simply a return to a previous sale price. Understand price-matching policies Take a few minutes to review the retailer's price-matching or price-adjustment policy. Policies vary widely. For example, Target no longer matches competitors' prices, but it will adjust the price if an eligible item goes on sale at your local Target store or on Target.com within 14 days of your purchase. Walmart will match the price of identical items sold on Walmart.com for purchases made in its stores. Staples, Best Buy and Office Depot also offer price matching on many qualifying items from competing retailers. No matter where you shop, save your receipt and read the fine print. Price-matching policies often include restrictions on eligible products, competing retailers and the amount of time you have to request a refund or adjustment. title: Trump to visit California to boast about the economy, White House confirms
text: Trump to visit California to boast about the economy, White House confirms. President Donald Trump is making a rare visit to California and Nevada this week to try to draw contrasts with Democrats on the economy, border security and crime, seeking to shore up support for Republicans in November elections that will determine whether his party keeps control of Congress. The Republican president has struggled to connect with voters on the economy as elevated inflation and feelings of uncertainty have overshadowed the stock market gains he often talks about, along with a low national unemployment rate. Trump will visit the Los Angeles area on Tuesday to speak at a fundraising dinner for the Republican National Committee at a golf club his family owns in the suburb of Rancho Palos Verdes. Trump is likely to take aim at Democratic Gov. Newsom During the trip, Trump is likely to throw barbs at California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat eyed as a likely candidate for his party's presidential nomination in 2028. Newsom has become one of the president's highest-profile opponents. White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said the president plans to "draw a sharp contrast between his commonsense agenda and the radical policies of Democrats like Gavin Newsom," touting his own efforts to cut taxes, reduce fraud in government programs, and crack down on immigration and crime. On Tuesday, Newsom's office sent the following statement in response to Trump's visit. “Donald Trump is coming to Los Angeles to raise money while wildfire survivors are still waiting for the federal recovery funding he promised 18 months ago. Californians deserve a President focused on helping families rebuild — not raising money for himself at his golf course.” California was one of Trump's first domestic stops after returning to office in January 2025. He surveyed the aftermath of wildfires that had wiped out whole neighborhoods of Los Angeles County, left thousands of people homeless and killed more than two dozen. Newsom greeted Trump at the airport on that trip, and they chatted amiably and gestured toward cooperation despite a bitter history. But the comity did not last. Six months later, Newsom argued in a speech that "democracy is under assault" by Trump after the president sent National Guard troops and U.S. Marines into Los Angeles without Newsom's consent. This came after protests following a series of immigration raids by federal authorities. Trump routinely mocks Newsom and refers to the governor using a derogatory nickname, while Newsom taunts the president with frequent social media posts. The Democrat wrote on social media on Monday that California is raising its minimum wage next year to $17.40 an hour, more than double the federal minimum wage of $7.25. "Donald Trump and the GOP are still defending a $7.25 minimum wage while workers scrape by. Pitiful," Newsom wrote. Housing prices are a big issue at Trump's second stop: Nevada On Wednesday, Trump will discuss the economy during an event at Red Rock casino in Las Vegas. Only 32% of U.S. adults approved of Trump's handling of the economy in an AP-NORC poll conducted in late July. In the same poll, most Americans, 69%, characterized the state of the economy as "poor," and many said the cost of everyday essentials like groceries and gas was a "major" source of stress in their lives. Trump's overall approval rating is at 33%, slightly below where he stood at this point in his first term. Nevada, where Trump will be on Wednesday, is led by a Republican governor, Joe Lombardo, who faces Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford in a battle for reelection in November. The contest is considered one of the most competitive governor's races in the country. The Nevada State Democratic Party is putting up billboard signs about Trump's visit that tie him to Lombardo and higher costs. The state is grappling with a shortage of affordable housing, exploding energy demand from artificial intelligence data centers and federal cuts to key state programs. Trump has tried for several months to sell voters on his income tax cuts and claims of a manufacturing renaissance. But interest rates are high, a gallon of gasoline costs more because of the Iran war, tariffs are still reshaping the economy and by the White House's own estimates, there is a national shortage of housing. The president called his own housing bill a "yawn," and past speeches advertised by the White House as being about the economy, including one he delivered at a General Motors facility in Michigan last week, gave way to Trumpian weaves about his political enemies and construction projects in the nation's capital. ___ Associated Press writers Josh Boak in Washington and Jessica Hill in Las Vegas contributed to this report. -KCRA 3 contributed to this reporting. title: These 10 Metros Have The Most Negotiating Power For Home Buyers—Should You Consider Buying?
text: These 10 Metros Have The Most Negotiating Power For Home Buyers—Should You Consider Buying?. Where you choose to buy your home matters, as some metros have better deals than others. Detroit, San Antonio and Austin, Texas, offer the most negotiating power to prospective home buyers, with each metro having a high percentage of active price-drop listings (19.8%, 28.2%, and 26.5%, respectively), among other buyer-market perks. This is according to a July 27 report from Best Interest Financial, a real estate company that reviewed Redfin data of the 50 largest U.S. metros. Other cities with a substantial amount of active price-cut listings include Pittsburgh (18.3%), Houston (24.8%), Tampa, Florida (26.4%), Memphis, Tennessee (21.8%), Dallas (26.1%), Indianapolis (26.6%) and Philadelphia (21.1%). In these areas, there are more homes available to buy. As a result, sellers are making their properties more competitive by significantly trimming the home asking prices, putting more power in buyers’ hands. House hunters could score a better deal in these metros—and save even more if they choose a lender that doesn’t charge an origination fee. But you should always consider your finances and other relevant factors before sending in an offer. An Expert’s Home-Buying Tips While the housing market is improving in some metros, experts warn you shouldn’t jump to buy a home based on deals alone. “The right market still depends on employment opportunities, affordability, lifestyle and long-term housing goals. Negotiating power is a bonus, not the primary reason to choose where you live,” says Jim Gruler, licensed real estate broker and co-founder of Seeking Agents, an independent real estate comparison platform. Still, Gruler confirmed today’s buyers have more opportunities to negotiate than they’ve had in years, which could make now a good time to shop. Before doing so, look at your finances to make sure you’re ready to take on the long-term costs of homeownership. If you’re uncertain, consider speaking to a home mortgage consultant. “Buyers who are financially prepared shouldn’t try to perfectly time the market. They should focus on purchasing a home they can comfortably afford when the numbers make sense for their situation,” adds Gruler. Other Ways To Save On Housing There are other strategies to make your dream house affordable beyond shopping in a more affordable metro—like choosing a lender that doesn’t charge origination fees, which are usually around 1% of the loan amount. While 1% can sound small, it can cost you thousands of dollars. For example, the median home list price in San Antonio is $315,696, according to the same report, which would make a 1% origination fee about $3,156. Consider that this is a home on the cheaper end: $94,518 less than the national median listing price of $410,214. If your home is pricier, the origination fee will cut into more of your budget. Here are a few of the best lenders with no origination fees to consider. Make sure to review all the loan terms and administrative costs before applying. Some may qualify for a more favorable deal with another lender, even if it does charge an origination fee. Bottom Line Select metros are seeing home asking prices drop substantially, with more overall homes available, creating a market more favorable to buyers. If you’re planning on buying a home in these areas, this could be a good time, especially if you find a lender that doesn’t charge an origination fee. However, buyers should look beyond a deal and consider all factors before signing.

title: McDonald’s US sales miss estimates as CEO taps new leader in major shake-up: ‘We simply didn’t execute’
text: McDonald’s US sales miss estimates as CEO taps new leader in major shake-up: ‘We simply didn’t execute’. McDonald’s on Tuesday missed US sales growth expectations for the second quarter, blaming execution lapses that blunted its value push aimed at lower-income consumers who have been cutting back restaurant spending. CEO Chris Kempczinski said weak promotion of value deals and a pullback in digital deals, including its buy-one-add-one promotion, led to a drop in visits from loyal customers, which accounted for about two-thirds of the traffic shortfall in the quarter. Comparable sales in the largest market for McDonald’s grew 0.8%, below analysts’ estimates of a 1.06% rise, according to data compiled by LSEG. The pace of growth in the US was 2.5% a year ago. Higher prices for basic goods and fuel have left lower-income consumers, a key customer base for McDonald’s, with less money to spend on eating out. “We don’t have a strategy problem, we simply didn’t execute at the level we needed to in the second quarter,” Kempczinski said on the earnings call. New US leader In a push to revive growth in the US, McDonald’s named insider Skye Anderson to lead the business, replacing Joe Erlinger and betting on an executive with extensive experience across operations and international markets. The appointment is a sign of management’s dissatisfaction with recent performance and could result in faster execution of sales and profit growth initiatives, Citi analysts said. The company has begun restoring national digital offers, rolling out more targeted promotions for loyalty members and redirecting marketing spending to proven value platforms. McDonald’s shares, which have fallen nearly 13% this year, were nearly 2% higher in early trading after the burger chain reported better-than-expected quarterly profit. The softer demand also comes as a multistate cyclosporiasis outbreak tied to contaminated produce impact store visits to Taco Bell amid uncertainty about food safety. McDonald’s expanded its McValue platform in April with a new under-$3 menu and a $4 breakfast meal deal, but executives said the offerings generated less incremental traffic than expected. Sales of beverages improved as Kempczinski said the new beverage platform was running ahead of plan, lifting average spending per visit and drawing customers at new times of the day. Globally, comparable sales rose 1.3%, slowing from a 3.8% jump a year ago. Sales in McDonald’s international operated markets segment, which includes major European nations, rose 1.5%, down from 4% a year ago. Adjusted earnings per share increased to $3.38 from $3.19 a year earlier, beating expectations of $3.32.
