title: Japan's Honda reports robust results after its first ever annual loss
text: Japan's Honda reports robust results after its first ever annual loss. TOKYO (AP) — Honda’s profit for the fiscal first quarter more than doubled from a year ago, as the Japanese automaker continues to tackle a turnaround from the first full year loss in its history. Tokyo-based Honda Motor Co. said Wednesday its April-June profit totaled 456.9 billion yen ($2.9 billion), up from 196.6 billion yen for the same period a year ago. Quarterly sales rose 13.5% to 6.06 trillion yen ($38 billion), as vehicles sold well in the U.S. and India, according to the maker of the Accord sedan, Fit subcompact and Super Cub motorcycle. Honda previously recorded a 423.9 billion yen ($2.7 billion) loss for the fiscal year ended in March, acknowledging heavy costs for its electric-vehicle plans, which didn’t measure up to the original ambitions, partly because of U.S. President Donald Trump’s policies. Analysts say many consumers weren’t ready to go electric. Honda has abandoned many of its plans for EV models. The Trump administration has pulled back on incentive programs for EVs and withheld money to states wanting to add more EV charging stations, even as gas prices have soared over the war in Iran. Trump’s tariffs on imported autos and auto parts, lowered to 15% from the initial 25%, also worked to dent Honda’s profitability. For the latest quarter, Honda’s motorcycle operations were highly lucrative with sales going strong in Brazil and India. Car sales grew in Japan and the U.S., while struggling in China. Chief Financial Officer Masao Kawaguchi said Honda was working to offer the kinds of models that appeal to Chinese buyers, which are different from those in other markets. “For that, we must fully utilize our resources in that market,” he told reporters. That may still take another year or two, he added. Kawaguchi said Honda’s overall first quarter results were very healthy, thanks partly to a favorable exchange rate. Although the recent U.S.-Japan joint intervention has boosted the yen’s value somewhat, the U.S. dollar traded higher during the fiscal first quarter, compared with the previous year. A cheap yen is a boon for Japanese exporters like Honda because it raises the value of its overseas earnings when translated into yen. Honda is expecting a return to profit for this fiscal year and raised its profit forecast to 400 billion yen ($2.5 billion) from an earlier 260 billion yen ($1.6 billion). All the Japanese automakers have been impacted by last week’s 7.1 magnitude earthquake in Kumamoto in southwestern Japan. Some production lines were temporarily halted and supply chains disrupted. Like other Japanese companies, Honda is going on a summer break later this month. Officials said they’re hoping things will have returned to normal by the time they’re back at work, and the exact impact of the quake on vehicle production is still unclear. Honda shares jumped 3.9% in Tokyo trading after the financial results were released. ___ Yuri Kageyama is on Threads: https://www.threads.com/@yurikageyama

title: U.S. Treasury yields fall as traders monitor possible Iran war deal
text: U.S. Treasury yields fall as traders monitor possible Iran war deal. Yields on U.S. Treasurys continued to move lower Wednesday, as investors eye how a potential deal to unlock the Strait of Hormuz is likely to shape the U.S. economic picture and inflation path. The 10-year U.S. Treasury note yield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — was more than 1 basis point lower at 4.6086% in early dealmaking. The longer-dated 30-year Treasury bond yield, which is more sensitive to geopolitical risks, was down 2 basis points at 5.1617%. The 2-year Treasury note yield, which tends to react in line with short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was up 1 basis point at 4.2061%. One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC Tuesday that a deal to allow commercial ships to pass through the Strait of Hormuz could be struck this week. That sent U.S. government bond yields sharply lower, with U.S. crude oil prices tumbling almost 6% during Tuesday's session. Later, U.S. Central Command in a post on X declared the Strait of Hormuz's southern route "free and open." Oil prices edged higher in early trade Wednesday, with West Texas Intermediate futures for September delivery trading at $76.21, a 0.58% rise, and Brent crude, the global benchmark, up almost 1.1% at $80.20. Traders are now looking to a flurry of upcoming data releases to gauge how the evolving situation in the Middle East is shaping the U.S. inflation picture and the Federal Reserve's interest rate path. Ahead of Friday's key non-farm payrolls data and unemployment rate for July, the Institute for Supply Management's services PMI print, due later Wednesday, is expected to come in at 54.5, up from 54.0 in June, according to consensus forecasts.

title: Brands Want Their Product Launches to Be Front-Page News. So They’re Printing Newspapers
text: Brands Want Their Product Launches to Be Front-Page News. So They’re Printing Newspapers. Last month, dog food brand Maev teased the launch of its newest product, a Nordic fish formula, by posting a picture of a person cracking open a newspaper. Splashed across the front page was a shot of the frozen cod, haddock, and salmon blend in a dog bowl, along with the words, “Perfect Fish.” As a direct-to-consumer business, “so much of the world that we build is digital,” Maev’s senior director of brand Maddy Tank says. That’s why her team wanted to use something she calls more “real and tactile” to announce the limited-edition formula to customers. They gravitated toward the newspaper concept in particular because it both felt nostalgic and would allow Maev to showcase a close-up of the ingredients. Plus, Tank says: “A launch at its core is news.” It took the Austin, Texas-based brand—which ranked No. 38 on Inc.’s list of the fastest-growing private American companies in 2024—about a month to draft the newspaper. While the Maev team primarily created it to serve as a social media teaser, they also included copies in PR mailers, handed them out in New York City dog parks, and dropped them off at local doggy daycares and Nordic cafes. Photo: Courtesy Maev Going all-in on print paid off. Maev’s social media accounts saw an 87 percent higher engagement rate during the two week launch period compared to its last limited-edition formula rollout in October 2025. And while Tank says it’s difficult to measure the impact of handing newspapers out in-person, she thinks doing so helped create “the sustained hype we were looking for, which contributed to that very high engagement rate number.” As unlikely as it may seem—with U.S. daily newspaper circulation plummeting from 55.8 million in 2000 to 24.2 million in 2020, causing revenue to slide for publishers—print is facing a renaissance. Over the past two years, brand marketers have become increasingly obsessed with creating newspapers or magazines to announce product launches, decorate pop-ups, and build community with their customers. Fast-growth at a printing press Maev tapped Glasgow, Scotland-based Newspaper Club for its project. It’s in good company. According to chief marketing officer Kaye Symington, the company's small-batch print production services have been in high demand from brands such as Asics, New Balance, Linktree, and Stella McCartney. She recalls the newspaper-as-marketing trend began taking off on social media in 2024. But brands weren't the only ones turning to print then—people were also using newspapers to share personal news like engagements or birth announcements. The trend's popularity had “a huge impact” on Newspaper Club, Symington says. The business got its start in 2009 when founders Ben Terrett, Tom Taylor, and Russell Davis attempted to turn their friends’ blog posts into a newspaper and discovered just how difficult small-batch printing was. They set out to make the process as easy as possible, allowing customers to create newspapers through online templates, order anything from one to tens of thousands of copies, and ship them anywhere in the world in two to nine days. Prices range depending on the number of pages, newspaper format, type of paper, shipping location, and number of copies. One four-page digital tabloid, for example, costs $67. Maev ordered 500 copies of an eight-page broadsheet, according to Tank, an order that’s priced at $1,649 total ($3.30 per copy) on Newspaper Club’s website. Newspaper Club now has nine staff members and has produced a total of 40 million newspapers in its lifetime. From 2023 to 2024, Symington says the business saw a 50 percent increase in revenue. The do-it-yourself crowd Not every brand participating in the trend seeks out a partner. Earlier this year, Bala, a Los Angeles-based workout equipment brand known for its wrist and ankle weights called Bangles, teamed up with Dunkin’ for the launch of its protein milk. Photo: Courtesy Bala Brooke Konzelmann, Bala’s chief brand officer, thought creating a branded newspaper would be a fun way to promote the collaboration. Bala has “a very nostalgic, vintage, retro vibe,” she says. “So anytime we can incorporate those types of elements in our marketing, we do.” The company had created branded newspapers twice before, once in November 2024 and once in February 2025, so it knew how to do it quickly and efficiently. In just 24 hours, Konzelmann and her team drafted the text, uploaded pictures of its pink and orange Bala x Dunkin’ bangles to Canva, created a design, and printed it out at Office Depot for about $36. “We're super scrappy,” Konzelmann says. “I love that we have a team that, if we have an idea, it really doesn’t take long for us to execute.” Bala posted pictures of the newspaper, which says “America Runs on Bala” on its front page, on social media. In less than 48 hours, the $65 Dunkin-branded bangles sold out, becoming the brand’s fastest-selling collaboration to date. Magazines as brand building Since 2024, Symington says consumer interest in the newspaper trend has cooled. Brands, however, have only leaned in further. “They’re actually printing editions that are much thicker,” she says. “They’re printing multiple copies, and what they're using them for is to engage long-term with their community offline.” In 2025, Newspaper Club printed a total of 3.5 million newspapers. Cat food brand Smalls made its first branded publication last year after serving as a sponsor for two volumes of the independent magazine Catnip and seeing great results. “Smalls is craving something lasting,” says Melody Park, director of brand marketing, “where we can show up as a brand beyond just 30 seconds on your Instagram feed or a [product page] you visited once.” Smalls teamed up with Broccoli, the publisher of Catnip, to produce the 40-page zine, Cat Parenthood, which serves as a comprehensive guide for first-time cat parents. It went into production about a year ago and arrived in Smalls’ warehouses last fall. Priced at just $5 online, Park says the brand doesn’t expect Cat Parenthood to drive a significant amount of revenue. In fact, she estimates that it only mentions Smalls products twice. Photos: Courtesy Smalls Her team is instead aiming to use the zine to build brand equity, increase brand awareness, and offer “something different to our customers,” Park says. Smalls’s ultimate goal, after all, is to become “so uniquely tied to cats” that “when you think of Smalls you think cat, when you think of cat you think Smalls,” she adds. So far, Park says, directional signals point to Cat Parenthood resonating with customers. The zine has also gotten “quite a lot of interest” from local bookstores through online wholesale marketplace Faire, she adds. Park’s advice to other marketers is to first ask yourself, “What can you only do with print that you can’t do with something else?” While creating a newspaper or magazine can sound fun, it’s also time-intensive and might not be the right fit for your brand or specific project. “Could you achieve the same emotional feeling, response, effect if you made a 90-second TikTok or if you made a really beautiful landing page or blog post?” she says. If the honest answer is no, do it.

title: New York bets on factory-built homes to ease Long Island's housing crunch
text: New York bets on factory-built homes to ease Long Island's housing crunch. As Long Islanders struggle with rising housing costs, New York State and local homebuilders are betting one part of the solution will be delivered via flatbed trucks, hauling homes from factories in Pennsylvania and upstate New York. Modular and manufactured housing offer potential to create housing faster and cheaper than traditional homebuilding, according to local builders and national research studies. Now, New York State hopes to spur factory-built housing to create affordable starter homes that have fallen out of favor as builders focus on luxury houses and new apartments, said RuthAnne Visnauskas, who leads the state's affordable housing agency. With manufactured homes, the state is trying "to step into what we see as the missing middle," said Visnauskas, commissioner of New York State Homes and Community Renewal. The state recently awarded East Hampton Town $7 million to build 16 manufactured, three-bedroom homes that are expected to be priced below market value. But there are limitations to the promise of factory-built housing on Long Island, where land is scarce and expensive. Long Island builders who spoke with Newsday said homebuyers interested in modular skew toward the luxury end of the market. Research comparing the costs of factory-built and site-built homes showed a roughly 27% savings when building CrossMod manufactured homes compared with traditional building methods, according to a 2023 analysis by researchers at the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies. The study compared costs using a nearly 1,600-square-foot house and factored in building, foundation, transportation, installation and administrative costs. However, the researchers noted the cost advantage declines as land cost rises. In a scenario where a ready-to-build lot costs $185,000, the savings fell by almost half, to just 14%. Listings on OneKey MLS show it can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars to acquire a vacant lot in Nassau or Suffolk counties and cheaper options often require clearing land or seeking a zoning variance. "If the cost of land is very high, it could be that you can't justify putting a lower-price home on that piece of land," said Laurie Goodman, founder of the Housing Finance Policy Center at the Urban Institute in Washington, D.C. Building modular Everything is solid. It's just really efficient and well-built. — Armando Polanco, of Massapequa When Armando Polanco and his wife, Debra, considered building modular, it was a Christmas tree that sold them. The Polancos had purchased a nearly 100-year-old house on an 80-by-250-foot lot in Massapequa, which they planned to replace with their dream home. When they closed in 2020, at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, they expected to use traditional building methods. But then worries started to creep in that they'd made a mistake. The price of lumber rose more than 300% because of surging demand and supply shortages, and the cost of new construction rose sharply as well. That led Polanco, 50, to consider modular building on the advice of a friend. He and his wife toured several factories in Pennsylvania and upstate New York but a conversation with Westchester Modular based in upstate Dutchess County sealed the deal. The couple had always wanted a double-height living room to fit a 14-foot Christmas tree and worried that wouldn't be possible with a modular home. But the company showed them in a digital rendering how the tree would fit. "We're big Christmas junkies, and he was able to give us the height on the tree that we wanted," Polanco said. Polanco said the cost to build modular was about 25% lower than the quote he had received from a Long Island builder — he declined to share the full construction cost — and it cut down the construction timeline by about half. Polanco, who served as his own general contractor, obtained a building permit in late November 2022. By February 2023, his house arrived aboard a flatbed truck in pieces with Sheetrock, plumbing fixtures, electrical wiring, windows and cabinets already installed. Once it arrived, plumbers and electricians helped connect the house to water and electricity, and contractors installed flooring and completed upgrades to the primary bathroom. The family moved into their new home that April, Polanco said. That created significant savings by cutting in half the time the family of five needed to live elsewhere in a rental house. It also allowed Polanco to convert his construction loan to a home mortgage, which had a lower interest rate, more quickly than with a longer construction period. "The time is the biggest savings," he said. The quality of the build also won the approval of Polanco's father, who spent his career in construction and was initially skeptical of his plan to build modular. Polanco's father was impressed with the thickness of the Sheetrock, the plywood used for flooring and how straight the floors were, even where the different pieces used to build the house connected. "Everything is solid," Armando Polanco said. "It's just really efficient and well-built." Westchester Modular completes about 20 projects a year on Long Island, said Michael Marano, the company's regional sales manager for Long Island in Westhampton. Those projects range from 600-square-foot accessory apartments to 10,000-square-foot mansions in Amagansett, Marano said. Some of modular companies' key advantages include construction inside a climate-controlled warehouse where materials aren't exposed to the elements, as well as tighter control over labor and material costs. "It helps homeowners really be able to control their budgets," Marano said. But it would be tough for first-time homebuyers looking to save money compared to today's market prices unless they have a way to acquire land cheaply, Marano said. Modular building also offers advantages for second-floor additions, said Scott Boerckel, owner of East Coast Dormer in Bethpage, who has been completing dormers using factory-built modules for more than 30 years. He estimated modular renovations can result in about 5% savings but installation takes only two weeks and he has delivered renovated homes to clients in about three months compared with about six months experienced contractors could complete a traditional renovation. The factory building process allows for a greater focus on insulation that can also help homeowners save on energy costs, Boerckel said. "A stick framer can't build like you build indoors," Boerckel said. "There is no air penetration whatsoever." Interest in modular homebuilding is growing but still hasn't taken off yet despite evidence of lower costs and faster construction, said Mike Florio, CEO of the trade group Long Island Builders Institute in Melville. The quality of new modular homes will be important for the technique to gain wider adoption, he said. "You're dealing with the perception issue also," Florio said. "Modular homes — is it like a trailer? It's not that. It looks like a real home. It has to seamlessly blend into the surrounding community too if they're going to be accepted." [A modular home] has to seamlessly blend into the surrounding community too if they're going to be accepted. — Mike Florio, CEO of Long Island Builders Institute in Melville Ben Jackson, president of Ben's General Contracting Corp. in Freeport, has built modular homes on the South Shore of Nassau County but said it's not the right fit for everyone. Jackson said the savings could be 10% to 20% compared with traditional construction, but the more a homeowner wants to customize after delivery, such as cabinets, countertops or kitchen tiling, the less sense it makes to build modular, he said. "The more things you change after the fact, you're losing your savings," he said. He sees modular as a great fit for speculative homebuilders who know exactly what they want, but he doesn't believe the process gives a homeowner enough flexibility if they're pursuing a high-end new build. "It's still, in my opinion, easier to give someone exactly what they want if you build traditionally," he said. An affordability fix? Uniondale Community Land Trust, an affordable housing nonprofit, offered one example of what modular building looks like on Long Island last year, when they sold a single-family home on Uniondale Avenue for $275,000 to a Queens family. The nonprofit worked with Pennsylvania-based Simplex Homes and said the new home, built on land purchased for around $86,000 from the Nassau County Land Bank, cost $650,000 to build. The land trust covered the rest using federal funds administered by Nassau County, state affordable housing funding and private fundraising, Newsday previously reported. That gap between the cost to build and the price buyers can afford helps explain why modular building has prove, proved, proving more popular in multifamily housing than single-family construction, said Goodman, at the Urban Institute. Research from the Urban Institute found modular homes represented 7% of all completed multifamily units nationwide compared with just 2.7% of completed single-family homes in 2023. Glen Cove-based affordable housing developer Georgica Green Ventures has used the process for developments in East Hampton, New Cassel, Roslyn Heights and for its latest building in Central Islip. While modular building can offer savings, it also requires extensive coordination with factories to avoid costly changes as well as logistics on-site to accept deliveries of massive modules and hoist them into place by crane, said David Gallo, president of Georgica Green Ventures. "We have seen some limited savings. More of what we have is the savings in time," Gallo said. "I am hopeful that with continued experience, we are going to see more savings on the construction side." Visnauskas, the state housing official, said she hopes New York's support of the 16 modular homes in East Hampton will help convince private Long Island homebuilders that building smaller homes can be a viable business. "We would love to see the market fill in," on Long Island, she said, "and be able to provide more starter homes. Modular vs. manufactured vs. mobile homes Prefabricated or factory-built homes: Any home built in a controlled factory setting, including both manufactured and modular homes, that are transported to their final site. Modular homes: This type of factory-built home is built and transported in pieces called modules and attached to a permanent foundation. They must adhere to the same state and local building codes as traditional new construction homes built on-site and offer more customization options than manufactured homes. Manufactured homes: Houses built in a factory that tend to be smaller and less expensive than modular homes. They conform to U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development building codes and some can be moved. Manufactured homes previously were required to be built on a chassis, which distinguished them from modular homes but that federal requirement was removed in July with Congress’ passage of the 21st Century Road to Housing Act. Mobile homes: These homes are a type of factory-built home built before June 1976, when HUD building codes took effect. Any home built on a chassis after that date is considered a manufactured home and must comply with federal standards. Sources: International Association of Certified Home Inspectors, GEICO and NerdWallet

title: The hottest luxury neighborhoods in the U.S. housing market right now
text: The hottest luxury neighborhoods in the U.S. housing market right now Luxury home shoppers are running into a serious supply crunch this year. Redfin found the fiercest competition concentrated in unexpected ZIP codes Mortgage rates sitting near multi-year highs have pushed much of the U.S. housing market into buyers' territory this year, with inventory piling up and sellers cutting prices to close deals. Luxury buyers are moving through that same market in the opposite direction. In dozens of ZIP codes with median sale prices well above their metro's typical home, competition for available inventory hasn't eased at all. Bidding wars are still common, homes are selling in weeks rather than months, and prices keep climbing even as the broader market cools around them. The numbers behind that split are stark. In some of these high-end ZIP codes, three-quarters of home sales are closing above the asking price, a rate that would be unheard of in a typical buyer's market. Elsewhere, median sale prices in luxury ZIP codes have climbed more than 30% in a single year, even as home sales volume in those same areas has fallen by double digits, a sign that fewer homes are changing hands but for much more money. Days on market in several of these pockets have dropped into the teens, while listing views have jumped by triple digits year over year, evidence that demand for a shrinking pool of listings keeps intensifying. Redfin tracked this divide across ZIP codes in the country's 100 most populous metro areas, ranking them by year-over-year growth in listing views and by Redfin Compete Score, a measure of how difficult it is to win a bid on a home. Every neighborhood that made the cut had a median sale price in the 65th percentile or above for its metro and at least 50 home sales recorded during the first two months of the year. The following neighborhoods posted the sharpest jumps in buyer demand even as the housing market around them tilted toward buyers. Park Slope, Brooklyn Ashe Walker / Unsplash Park Slope's median sale price hit $1,770,000 in early 2026, more than double the $795,000 median across the broader New York City market, and it's still climbing. Prices in the neighborhood rose 10.6% year over year even as the number of homes sold there dropped 17.9%, a combination that points to fewer sellers testing a market that keeps rewarding them anyway. Listing views jumped 34.4% year over year, and homes are moving in a median of 44 days, fast for a market with prices this high. Only 6.3% of sales closed above the asking price, a modest figure next to some of the other neighborhoods on this list, suggesting sellers here are already pricing in the demand rather than waiting for a bidding war to push them higher. The draw comes down to a mix that's hard to find elsewhere in the city. Park Slope's brownstone-lined blocks sit next to Prospect Park, Brooklyn's second-largest park, giving residents easy green space without leaving a dense, walkable neighborhood. Redfin agents say the schools rank among the best in the city, which matters most to the young families increasingly choosing Park Slope over Manhattan's Upper West Side and Upper East Side. Remote work has widened that pool further, letting professionals who no longer need a Manhattan commute settle in Brooklyn instead. Local agents describe a wave of buyers actively avoiding Manhattan altogether, drawn to a neighborhood where the amenities of the city sit alongside the feel of a residential block rather than a dense commercial corridor. That shift, accelerated since the pandemic, has turned what was once considered an alternative to Manhattan into a first choice for many house hunters with young families. That preference shows up directly in the price data. Buyers who once treated Park Slope as a fallback for those priced out of Manhattan now compete for it on its own terms, which helps explain why prices keep rising even as fewer homes change hands each year. With Prospect Park, strong schools and brownstone housing stock all concentrated in one neighborhood, agents don't expect that competition to ease anytime soon. Highland Park, Illinois Leo Heisenberg / Unsplash Highland Park sits about 25 miles north of downtown Chicago, and its housing market is behaving nothing like a typical suburb 25 miles out. The median sale price reached $762,500, more than double the $354,000 median for the broader Lake County market, and 42.6% of homes there sold above their asking price, the highest share of any neighborhood on this list. Prices still climbed 5.2% year over year even though the number of homes sold fell 34%, the steepest sales decline among these ZIP codes. Listing views rose 23.8%, and homes typically sell in 41 days. That combination of falling sales volume and rising prices suggests owners are in no hurry to list, while the buyers who do show up are competing hard for what little comes on the market. Highland Park's appeal rests on a mix local agents describe as increasingly rare among Chicago suburbs. It pairs a walkable downtown with direct access to the Lake Michigan shoreline and schools that consistently rank among the state's best, all inside a community built around an easy commute. The housing stock leans older, with century-old homes lining tree-lined streets that give the area an established feel newer developments can't replicate. That mix of suburban space and lake access has kept demand strong for decades, agents say, and it's holding up now even as mortgage rates keep many other buyers on the sidelines. Families weighing a move outside the city find a version of small-town living in Highland Park that still puts Chicago within reach. The falling sales count is worth watching closely, too. With 34% fewer homes changing hands than a year earlier, current owners appear content to stay put rather than test a market that keeps setting new price records. That kind of reluctance to sell, paired with steady demand from families relocating from the city, is a large part of why buyers are willing to pay above asking on more than four in 10 homes here. Overland Park, Kansas Far Chinberdiev / Unsplash Overland Park's numbers tell a different story than most of the neighborhoods on this list. Its median sale price of $840,000 is roughly in line with the broader Kansas City metro, not a steep premium over it, which means the demand surge here isn't about outbidding rivals for a scarce slice of the market's priciest homes. Instead, it shows up almost entirely in buyer interest. Listing views rose 158.8% year over year, by far the largest jump of any neighborhood in this ranking, while the median sale price still climbed 8.5% year over year. Home sales actually rose 3.3%, a rare increase among these ZIP codes, most of which saw sales volume shrink even as prices grew. About one in four homes here, 25.4%, sold above asking, and the typical home takes 64 days to sell, longer than most neighborhoods on this list but still brisk given the price point and the sheer volume of interest driving it. One of Kansas City's largest suburbs, Overland Park is pulling in buyers with newer housing stock, much of it built within the last 25 years, alongside highly rated schools and an expanding retail and job base. Redfin agents describe a market where homes move quickly once listed, forcing buyers to act fast to secure a spot. The individual neighborhoods within Overland Park each carry their own identity and social fabric, agents say, the kind of close-knit character that keeps residents from wanting to leave once they've settled in. That reputation is spreading well beyond people already living in the Kansas City area. The scale of the jump in listing views, more than double the second-fastest riser on this list, points to buyers discovering Overland Park from further afield rather than simply longtime residents shifting between neighborhoods. A growing job market in the metro is adding to that pull, giving newcomers a reason to look at Overland Park specifically rather than treating it as one option among several Kansas City suburbs. Belmar, New Jersey Ryan Loughlin / Unsplash Belmar's median sale price climbed to $725,000, up 12.9% year over year and well above the $545,000 median for the surrounding New Brunswick metro. What sets Belmar apart from most of the other neighborhoods on this list is its sales volume, which rose 27.5% year over year even as buyer competition intensified, a sign that more homes are trading hands here rather than fewer. Nearly a third of sales, 31.4%, closed above asking, and homes typically sell in just 38 days, one of the fastest paces on this list. That speed reflects how tight inventory has become in a town built around a narrow strip of coastline. Belmar draws buyers with a walkable downtown, direct ocean access and a restaurant scene that keeps the town lively well beyond the summer season. Remote workers and second-home buyers make up a large share of the demand, agents say, drawn by the ability to work from a beach town year-round rather than treating it as a seasonal getaway. Inventory in Belmar remains limited, and demand for larger beach houses has only grown. Local agents describe buyers seeking homes on quieter residential streets that still sit close to private beach access, trading the density of nearby shore towns for a slower pace with room to host and entertain. That combination of coastal living and year-round livability is what separates Belmar from towns that empty out once summer ends. Its rising sales volume also sets it apart from most of the rest of this list, where sales counts mostly fell even as prices climbed. That contrast suggests Belmar's inventory, while tight, hasn't tightened as severely as it has in some of the priciest neighborhoods here, giving more buyers a real chance to close a deal even in a competitive market. Second-home buyers in particular are treating Belmar less like a seasonal purchase and more like a year-round residence, agents say, a shift that's helping keep both sales and prices climbing together. Coronado, California Ryan Loughlin / Unsplash Coronado carries the highest median sale price of any neighborhood on this list at $2,449,020, well above the $899,500 median for the San Diego metro it sits within. That price kept rising, up 6.8% year over year, even as the number of homes sold fell 8.9%, a pattern seen across several of the priciest neighborhoods here, where fewer sales are closing but each one commands a steeper price. Listing views climbed 36% year over year, homes typically sell in 47 days, and 9.8% of sales closed above asking. The appeal is a peninsula lifestyle that's hard to replicate on the mainland. Buyers get golf courses, yacht clubs, tennis and pickleball courts and fine dining within a small-town setting minutes from downtown San Diego. Local agents describe the peninsula as feeling like a private island escape, lined with multimillion-dollar historic mansions and custom-built estates, many with private yacht slips. That geography is also Coronado's biggest constraint. A peninsula can't expand its housing stock the way a landlocked suburb can, so every new listing draws outsized attention from affluent buyers seeking a version of Southern California living that feels removed from the mainland's pace. With supply already this tight, agents expect competition for whatever does come up to keep intensifying rather than ease. That scarcity is part of why Coronado's price sits so far above the rest of this list even as its year-over-year growth rate looks modest next to faster-climbing neighborhoods elsewhere. A market already this expensive doesn't need rapid growth to stay competitive. It just needs a buyer pool large enough to absorb whatever limited inventory does hit the market, and Coronado has that in spades. The 8.9% drop in home sales alongside continued price growth points to owners who feel little pressure to sell, content to wait for a buyer willing to meet their price rather than negotiate. That patience from sellers, paired with a fixed and unchangeable supply of land, is likely to keep Coronado among the priciest and most competitive markets on this list for years to come. East Orlando, Florida Talia / Unsplash East Orlando posted the sharpest price growth of any neighborhood on this list, with its median sale price jumping 37.8% year over year to $477,000, a smaller premium over the Orlando metro's $400,000 median than most other entries here carry. Listing views rose by that same 37.8% margin, and home sales held flat year over year rather than falling the way they did in most of the pricier neighborhoods on this list. Homes sell in a median of 50 days, and 20% of sales closed above asking. Growth here is tied to master-planned communities like Waterford Lakes and Avalon Park, along with the area's proximity to the University of Central Florida and to Orlando's biggest draws, including Walt Disney $DIS World Resort. Newer housing stock and highly rated schools have pulled in buyers looking for space without leaving easy reach of the region's amenities, from golf courses to fields built for organized youth sports. Avalon Park in particular functions almost as a self-contained township. Restaurants, gyms, dentists, eye doctors and medical offices sit packed inside a one-mile radius, letting residents handle daily errands and entertainment without leaving the neighborhood. That self-sufficiency, paired with prices that still undercut much of the rest of this list, is drawing buyers who want Orlando's amenities without paying Orlando's steepest premiums. East Orlando's flat sales count, unchanged from a year earlier, stands out against a backdrop of price growth this steep. Most neighborhoods on this list saw sales volume drop as prices rose, a sign that some buyers were priced out even as demand held. East Orlando's ability to keep the same number of deals closing while prices jumped nearly 38% suggests the buyer pool here is still growing rather than simply competing harder over the same limited group of homes. Families relocating from pricier parts of Central Florida, and from out of state, appear willing to pay significantly more than they would have a year ago to land in a neighborhood built around schools and amenities rather than proximity to downtown. That willingness to pay up for a newer, family-oriented suburb is a big part of why East Orlando's growth rate outpaces every other neighborhood on this list. Noe Valley, San Francisco Anthony Sebbo / Unsplash Noe Valley posted the fastest sales pace and the highest share of homes selling above asking of any neighborhood on this list. Homes there sell in a median of just 14 days, and 73.1% of sales closed above their asking price, more than double the rate in all but a handful of other neighborhoods here. The median sale price reached $2,250,000, up 18.3% year over year, well above the $1,545,000 median for the broader San Francisco market, even as the number of homes sold fell 7.1%. Local agents describe a neighborhood where buyers aren't shopping around. Many want Noe Valley specifically and are competing over a limited supply of move-in-ready single-family homes, with much of that demand landing in the $2 million to $4.5 million range. That kind of loyalty to one neighborhood, rather than a willingness to consider several nearby options, helps explain why so many sales are closing well above asking even as the total number of transactions declines. A wave of newly wealthy tech workers is a big part of that push, agents say, as compensation packages from the city's AI companies put more buyers in a position to bid aggressively for a small pool of listings. That combination, a longtime cultural draw paired with a fresh injection of tech money, has kept prices climbing quickly even as sales volume slows across the rest of the market. The 14-day median for time on market is the fastest of any neighborhood on this list by a wide margin, more than three times quicker than several other entries here. Paired with a 73.1% overbid rate, it points to a neighborhood where buyers aren't just willing to pay more. They're also moving fast to make sure they don't lose out. For a market already defined by tight supply, that speed is likely to keep pushing prices higher through the rest of the year.

title: Corporate America got billions of dollars in tariff refunds. Where’s your cut?
text: Corporate America got billions of dollars in tariff refunds. Where’s your cut?. Apple got an estimated $2.2 billion tariff refund last quarter. Amazon got $600 million. Nike got $300 million. But American consumers who paid higher prices as President Donald Trump’s tariffs filtered through the economy are getting almost nothing back. Those corporate payouts may be just the beginning as the government continues processing refund claims after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s most sweeping levies earlier this year. In total, the government is on the hook to refund hundreds of thousands of importers a total of around $166 billion. A little more than half of that has already been paid out, according to a Customs and Border Protection court filing. The levies cost households an estimated $1,000 on average last year, according to the Tax Foundation. Before the Supreme Court weighed in, the Trump administration had floated the idea of $2,000 tariff rebate checks to redistribute some of the revenue the government had collected. Those, however, never materialized. You aren’t owed a tariff refund The tariff refund system is structured so that only the parties who directly paid the tariffs — or the customs brokers acting on their behalf — can file for a refund. That means that if you bought, for example, a pair of Nike sneakers that became more expensive as the company passed along some of its increased tariff costs, you have no legal way to get that money back. In many cases, it’s nearly impossible to figure out how much of a company’s tariff refund came out of consumers’ pockets. That’s because Trump during his second term has layered on multiple rounds of tariffs besides the ones struck down by the Supreme Court. So, even when a company raised prices, it can be difficult to determine which tariffs those increases were designed to cover. Adding another wrinkle: Many businesses didn’t pass the full cost of tariffs on to shoppers in the first place, absorbing some of the impact themselves. The big outlier Amazon has been an outlier, saying it will give customers a direct refund in certain cases. “We have identified a limited set of circumstances where we can trace that we passed specific import charges on to customers, and when we receive those refunds, we will proactively contact affected customers and automatically issue refunds to them,” Amazon chief financial officer Brian Olsavsky said last week during the company’s earnings call. “Otherwise, like other large retailers, we’ll utilize refunds to continue to invest in low prices for customers,” he said. Amazon, however, has not disclosed what circumstances would qualify customers for a tariff refund, whether the process has begun, or how much money it expects to return. A company spokesperson declined to comment to CNN. Returning ‘value’ to customers Costco CEO Roland Vachris said in May that the company intends to “return to our members in some form the portion of tariffs that were passed on to them” on its first-quarter earnings call. But that doesn’t necessarily mean issuing refunds to customers. Back in March, Vachris said, “Our commitment will be to find the best way to return this value to our members through lower prices and better values.” Like Amazon, Nike and others, Costco is not only facing pressure to pass down a share of its refund to customers but is also the subject of a class action lawsuit from customers compelling it to do so. (Costco and Nike didn’t respond to CNN’s requests for comment.) A slew of other companies, including Walmart and BJ’s, have promised to use their refund to lower prices for customers. Meanwhile, Apple CEO Tim Cook shared that the tech giant is using the money to expand its American manufacturing footprint. However, higher energy and freight costs tied to the war with Iran are making it even less likely that tariff refunds will flow directly to consumers. Instead, companies are saying they’re using the money they received to offset those rising costs. “The tariff refund comes [in], obviously, very handy” for that, said PepsiCo CEO Ramon Laguarta in an earnings call last month.

title: A Wall Street CIO shares his ideal stock portfolio as he sees signs that the economy is set to slow
text: A Wall Street CIO shares his ideal stock portfolio as he sees signs that the economy is set to slow. Spencer Platt/Getty Images Cyclical sectors like energy, industrials, and materials have lead the market in 2026. But Alessio de Longis predicts a slowdown in growth, leading quality stocks to outperform. He prefers exposure to the tech, consumer staples, utilities, and healthcare sectors. It's been a banner year for cyclical pockets of the market. Energy, industrials , and materials are among the market's top-performing sectors in 2026. But according to Alessio de Longis, the chief investment officer of active investments at ProShares, which manages $114 billion in assets, the impressive run for economically sensitive areas of the market will soon start to fade. de Longis sees a slowdown in economic growth ahead — not a recession, just a more muted pace of growth. That's because economic expansion over the last year has generally been strong, he said, and it will be difficult to continue to keep pace. In Q2 and Q3 2025, US GDP grew by 3.8% and 4.4%, respectively. Some other signs that growth could be peaking are: 12-month forward earnings revisions approaching historically high levels, and the ISM manufacturing and services survey being on the decline. That doesn't mean de Longis is bearish on stocks as a whole, but shifts will start to happen under the surface of the broader market, he said. If growth does indeed start to slow, he said investors would likely turn to quality stocks , as they'll start to place greater emphasis on strong balance sheets, low debt, and a track record of robust earnings. "These normal growth slowdowns are absolutely part of the cycle, and in that environment, equities can continue to do very well," Alessio de Longis told Business Insider on Monday. "They typically do, and they're led by quality stocks." De Longis got a bit more granular with his views. In terms of sectors with the most overlap with the quality factor, de Longis said to look to information technology. The sector is heavily concentrated in some of the market's most formidable juggernauts: Nvidia ( NVDA ), Apple ( AAPL ), and Microsoft ( MSFT ) collectively make up just under 37% of the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF ( XLK ). Those three stocks are also the top three holdings in the iShares MSCI USA Quality Factor ETF ( QUAL ). Part of de Longis' preference for the tech sector also ties in with his views on interest rates and inflation. He sees inflation remaining fairly tame alongside energy prices, and that will allow short-end rates to stay put and long-end rates to come down. Right now, market consensus has one or two Federal Reserve rate hikes penciled in; if that scenario doesn't come to pass, it will be a positive for stocks, he said. And falling long-term rates are typically a boon for long-duration growth stocks, and they'll allow tech firms to borrow money in the bond market at cheaper rates, boosting their free cash flow levels. On the other side of the portfolio, de Longis said he'd barbell his tech exposure with three traditionally defensive sectors: consumer staples, utilities, and healthcare. These are areas of the market that tend to outperform when economic growth weakens, giving investors a bit of cushion in case of a more severe decline in growth, de Longis said. They also usually outperform in the falling-interest-rate environment he sees, which is associated with a slowing economy. Examples of funds that offer exposure to the trades de Longis mentioned include the JPMorgan US Quality Factor ETF ( JQUA ), the Vanguard Information Technology ETF ( VGT ), the iShares U.S. Healthcare ETF ( IYH ), the Fidelity MSCI Consumer Staples Index ETF ( FSTA ), and the Utilities Select Sector SPDR Fund ( XLU ). title: Oil prices and world shares gain after Wall Street hits fresh records on strong corporate earnings
text: Oil prices and world shares gain after Wall Street hits fresh records on strong corporate earnings. BANGKOK (AP) — Shares advanced in Europe and Asia on Wednesday after the U.S. stock market rallied to records, helped by strong corporate earnings reports and hopes for a deal setting the stage for talks that might eventually lead to an end to the war in Iran. Oil prices resumed their ascent, with Brent crude gaining more than 1%. In early European trading, Germany's DAX rose 0.3% to 26,268.90, while the CAC 40 in Paris edged less than 0.1% higher. Britain's FTSE 100 was up 0.2% at 10,898.40. The futures for the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were up 0.2%. Benchmarks jumped more than 3% in Tokyo and Seoul as shares in computer chipmakers and other AI-related companies advanced. Japan's Nikkei 225 gained 3.7% to 66,300.44, with chipmaker Kioxia surging 4.2% while chip testing equipment maker Advantest soared 8.8%. The Kospi in Seoul shot up 3.8% to 6,598.26, led by a 5.8% gain for memory chipmaker SK Hynix. Tech giant Samsung Electronics advanced 2.5%. Taiwan's Taiex advanced 2.9% as major chipmaker TSMC gained 3.7%. “Clearly today the market is rallying on the back of AI stocks. You look across the other sectors, there’s a bit of activity here and there, but really the focus has been back on semiconductors, technology and AI," said Neil Newman, head of strategy for Astris Advisory Japan. Elsewhere in the region, the Shanghai Composite index picked up 1.5% to 3,878.43, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng added 0.4% to 25,915.82. In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 rose 0.9% to 9,227.80. The Sensex slipped 0.2% after the Reserve Bank of India chose to keep its key repo rate unchanged at 5.25%, saying the economy was resilient despite shocks from the Iran war, but risks remained. Declines in oil prices have buoyed shares. Brent crude, the international standard, reversed early losses, gaining 1.4% to $80.45 per barrel early Wednesday. On Tuesday, it sank 5.3% as hopes rose for progress toward a full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices swung between $72 and $102 through July on uncertainty about when calm in the Middle East would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again to deliver crude around the world. Iran and Oman were inching toward a deal to reopen the strait, though that appears to be contingent on the United States lifting its blockade on Iran’s ports. "All in all, it’s looking much brighter. We’re still not completely out of the woods yet, but I think we’re seeing some route out of this now and it’s been reflected in the markets,” Newman said. U.S. benchmark crude picked up 0.7% to $76.29 per barrel. On Tuesday, the S&P 500 shot up 1.8%, topping its prior all-time high set in June. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 1.7% to its own record set the day before, while the Nasdaq composite jumped 2.6%. Profits are piling up for companies as easing oil prices assuage worries about inflation. Palantir Technologies helped lead the way, surging 29.5% after its CEO Alex Karp said its overall revenue leaped 93% in what he called an “otherworldly” quarter. Such reports have helped to allay worries over a possible bubble in stock prices because of the AI boom. Shares in Chipotle Mexican Group tumbled 9.7%, however, on fears that its future profits could be hurt after the chain removed jalapeños from some of its restaurants following a salmonella outbreak. Chipotle said that Minnesota health officials have no ongoing concerns with it. Reports on the U.S. economy showed it remains resilient even though inflation is worse than anyone would like. U.S. employers were advertising nearly 7.4 million job openings at the end of June, the Labor Department said, a slight slowdown from May’s level but close to economists’ expectations. In other dealings early Wednesday, the U.S. dollar slipped to 157.81 Japanese yen from 157.74 yen. The euro rose to $1.1535 from $1.1532. ___ Associated Press writer Mayuko Ono in Tokyo contributed to this report.

title: Meijer Slash Prices on More Than 1,000 Items: List of Biggest Savings
text: Meijer Slash Prices on More Than 1,000 Items: List of Biggest Savings. Meijer has announced price cuts on more than 1,000 grocery and household products through September 8, offering discounts across categories including meat, produce, cereal, snacks and household essentials. The six-week promotion is available in stores, online and through the retailer's app, with no coupons or special memberships required. "Midwesterners work hard for their money, and we believe they shouldn't have to work equally as hard to save money on their groceries," said Don Sanderson, chief merchandising & marketing officer at Meijer. "We're proud of the value we offer customers 365 days a year and this is our way of saying thank you as families make the most of the last few weeks of summer." The move makes Meijer the latest major grocery chain to roll out a large-scale discount campaign as retailers compete for budget-conscious shoppers. Which Grocery Items Are Getting Cheaper? Some of the biggest discounts are on fresh foods. In the produce department, 16-ounce containers of strawberries have fallen from $2.99 to $2.50, while whole seedless watermelons have been reduced from $8.99 to $4.99. Kellogg's Frosted Flakes cereal has been cut from $4.29 to $2.99, while 24-ounce jars of Vlasic pickles are now $2.50 instead of $3.49. Meijer said the discounts are part of a rotating selection of more than 1,000 products spanning hundreds of categories, meaning additional items will be added throughout the promotion. Meat, Produce and Pantry Staples Lead the Biggest Savings Among the standout reductions are meat products, with a whole pork shoulder butt roast reduced to $1.79 per pound from $2.99, while family-pack chicken drumsticks are now 99 cents per pound, down from $1.39. Discounts extend beyond groceries too. Meijer Soft & Strong 18 Mega Roll toilet paper is now priced at $10.49, down from $13.99. Rather than focusing on a handful of loss-leader products, Meijer said the campaign covers hundreds of categories across grocery and household departments, from fresh produce and meat to cereals, snacks and paper goods. Meijer Joins Growing List of Grocers Cutting Prices The announcement follows Giant Eagle's decision to lower prices on more than 300 products through Labor Day, a move publicly praised by Trump in a Truth Social post. The president described Giant Eagle as a "GREAT American Grocery Company" and urged other retailers to follow its example. Walmart, Stop & Shop and Kroger have also announced grocery price rollbacks this summer, making Meijer the latest retailer to highlight savings on everyday staples as food costs remain a key concern for consumers. How Inflation Impacts Groceries Meijer's latest round of grocery discounts comes as food prices remain a major issue for American consumers and a closely watched measure of President Donald Trump's economic performance. According to the latest Consumer Price Index report released on Tuesday, food prices were 3.1 percent higher in July than a year earlier. Food consumed at home, a category that includes groceries, rose 2.7 percent over the same period, while the index for meats, poultry, fish and eggs increased 3.5 percent. That means many shoppers are still paying more for groceries than they were a year ago, even as overall inflation has cooled significantly from the levels seen earlier in the decade. Retailer promotions, like this one from Meijer, may help ease some of that pressure by lowering prices on popular household staples. Inflation played a decisive role in Trump's 2024 election victory. Throughout the campaign, Trump argued that Americans were struggling with higher living costs after prices surged during 2021 and 2022 amid pandemic-related supply chain disruptions and broader inflationary pressures. Lowering the cost of everyday necessities, including groceries and gasoline, became a central part of his economic message. Several major pollsters' surveys in recent weeks have shown that Trump’s approval rating has fallen to a record low. David Stebenne, professor of history and law at Ohio State University, previously told Newsweek: “[Trump] has a kind of populist appeal with a lot of white working class voters and the heartland, but they're the kind of people who are very sensitive to increases in the price of gas and groceries.” The issue remains politically important for the White House. While inflation has fallen markedly from its post-pandemic peak, surveys continue to show voters closely tracking the cost of essentials. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Rebecca Flood and Emma Lee-Sang

title: Current price of oil as of August 5, 2026
text: Current price of oil as of August 5, 2026. At 5:30 a.m. Eastern Time today, the price of oil sits at $83.72 per barrel, using Brent as the benchmark (we’ll explain what that means shortly). That’s a decrease of $6.09 since yesterday morning and roughly $15.38 more than at this time last year. oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $89.81 -6.78% Price of oil 1 month ago $72.65 +15.23% Price of oil 1 year ago $68.34 +22.50% Will oil prices go up? Nobody can predict the future path of oil prices with certainty. A range of factors influence how oil trades, yet supply and demand remain the main drivers. When fears of economic slowdown, conflict, or similar shocks rise, oil prices can move sharply. How oil prices translate to gas pump prices The price you see at the gas pump reflects more than just crude oil. Also built in are the costs of refining, distribution through wholesalers, various taxes, and the margin your neighborhood station charges. Crude oil is still the largest single driver of the final pump price, typically representing over half of each gallon’s cost. Spikes in oil prices tend to push gas prices higher in short order. But when oil prices decline, gas prices often ease down gradually, a behavior known as “rockets and feathers.” The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve In the event of an emergency, the U.S. maintains a stockpile of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its main goal is to safeguard energy security when disasters strike—think sanctions, severe storm damage, or war. It can also do a lot to ease the pain of sudden price jumps when supply gets disrupted. It’s not a permanent fix, as it’s more meant to provide immediate support for consumers and ensure critical parts of the economy like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, and so on can keep operating. How oil and natural gas prices are linked Both oil and natural gas play key roles as major sources of energy. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by proxy. If oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, increasing the demand for natural gas. Historical performance of oil Oil prices are often measured by two key benchmarks: Brent crude oil is the main global oil benchmark. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) is the main benchmark of North America. Between the two, Brent is a better representation of global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. It’s also often the best way to review historical oil trends. In fact, the U.S. Energy Information Administration now leans on Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook. When you look at the Brent benchmark across multiple decades, you’ll see that oil has been anything but consistent. It has experienced spikes driven by wars and supply cuts, as well as crashes linked to global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example: The early 1970s brought the first big oil shock when the Middle East cut exports and imposed an embargo on the U.S. and others during the Yom Kippur War. Prices dropped in the mid-1980s for reasons such as weaker demand and more non-OPEC oil producers entering the industry. Prices spiked again in 2008 with rising global demand, but soon crashed alongside the global financial crisis. During the 2020 COVID lockdown, oil demand collapsed like never before, bringing prices to under $20 per barrel. In short, oil’s historical performance has been far from steady. It’s massively affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more. Energy coverage from Fortune Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage: Oil rebounds as Iran war de-escalation, yen intervention worries ease Could a UN-backed plan to reopen Hormuz break the deadlock? Fortune gets exclusive access to a UN-backed plan to reopen the strait Frequently asked questions How is the current price of oil per barrel actually determined? The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic. How often does the price of oil change during the day? The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing. How does U.S. shale oil production affect the current price of oil? In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply. How does the current price of oil impact inflation and the broader economy? When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf. title: S&P 500, Dow at record highs on Mideast deal hopes; SpaceX, AMD drag - Wed, 05 Aug 2026 PST
text: S&P 500, Dow at record highs on Mideast deal hopes; SpaceX, AMD drag - Wed, 05 Aug 2026 PST. The S&P 500 and the Dow traded at all-time highs on Wednesday on hopes of a Middle East peace breakthrough, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq struggled to stay afloat, limited by a slide in SpaceX and AMD after the upbeat forecasts issued by the companies failed to impress investors. Elon Musk-led SpaceX’s revenue nearly doubled and operating losses narrowed in its first earnings report since going public, fueled by its booming Starlink satellite communications and AI businesses. But the rocket company’s shares slid 7.3% after executives flagged the spending spree underpinning its lofty ambitions was far from over. Shares could face additional pressure from the expiry of the stock’s post-IPO lock-up period starting on Thursday. Musk’s other company, Tesla, slipped 1.3%. “This is the culmination of the story of this entire earnings season. SpaceX beat analysts’ expectations on revenue, but spending on AI is getting out of hand, with no signs of slowing down anytime soon,” said Nic Puckrin, cross-asset analyst and founder of Coin Bureau. Advanced Micro Devices forecast quarterly revenue above estimates, reflecting strong AI demand. However, shares slipped 6.5%, suggesting investors were looking for a stronger outlook to justify the stock’s 142% jump this year. Rival Nvidia’s shares, which have lagged AMD this year, rose 3.7%, also underpinned by SpaceX’s plans to use the company’s hardware exclusively to build its data centers. Five of the 11 S&P sectors were trading higher. Materials led the gains with a 1.5% rise, tracking a 4% jump in gold and silver prices. Energy stocks lagged with a near 2.1% fall. Wednesday’s moves built on Wall Street’s recent rally that took the benchmark S&P 500 and the blue-chip Dow to record highs following strong forecasts from AI-hyperscalers including Microsoft and Amazon in the previous week. At 11:38 a.m. ET, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 435.60 points, or 0.81%, to 54,521.48, the S&P 500 gained 8.34 points, or 0.11%, to 7,744.86 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 10.68 points, or 0.04%, to 26,574.32. Investors also weighed a slew of earnings from other sectors. Drugmaker Eli Lilly was up 2.8% after raising its full-year revenue forecast, while Disney rose 2.2% after beating third-quarter profit expectations. Arista Networks jumped 3.8%, as the networking equipment maker forecast third-quarter revenue above estimates. Uber lost 6.2% after forecasting current-quarter adjusted earnings below estimates. On the data front, U.S. private payrolls growth slowed in July, as per the ADP national employment report. The bigger focus will be on the official non-farm payrolls figures on Friday. Data has broadly reflected robust economic performance, but with Middle East tensions keeping energy costs elevated and the Federal Reserve offering no forecasts on monetary policy, uncertainty persists. Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari in an interview with CNBC said he believed now is the time to start slowly moving interest rates higher. At least two more top Fed officials are expected to speak later in the day. Among others, drug developer Charles River Laboratories jumped 11.8% after raising its annual profit forecast, while medical device maker Insulet tanked 20% after lowering its annual sales growth forecast. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.2-to-1 ratio on the NYSE and by a 1.37-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq. The S&P 500 posted 33 new 52-week highs and two new lows, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 86 new highs and 50 new lows.

title: States Where Retirees Pay No Sales Tax on Groceries and Everyday Essentials
text: States Where Retirees Pay No Sales Tax on Groceries and Everyday Essentials. Key Takeaways - Five states have no statewide sales tax, but local taxes in three of them can still raise your final bill. - Grocery taxes vary widely by state, with some charging full rates, others reduced rates, and many offering exemptions. - Retirees weighing a move should compare sales, income, property, and estate taxes—not just one tax advantage. Contemplating relocating after retiring? Don't underestimate sales tax. Charged as a percentage of the purchase price every time you buy something, it makes everyday essentials more expensive and varies widely from place to place. In some municipalities, you'll pay nothing; in others, up to 10%. For retirees living on Social Security, pensions, and investment withdrawals, those extra costs can quickly add up—and turn a comfortable budget into a tight one. States With No Statewide Sales Tax According to the Tax Foundation, five states impose no statewide sales tax: Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire, and Oregon. However, that doesn't mean no sales tax is charged in any of these places. Only Oregon and Delaware levy no state or local sales tax whatsoever on consumers. The other three states carry the following caveats: - Alaska allows local governments to levy their own taxes, with rates averaging 1.82% and climbing as high as 7.85%. - Montana has no statewide or local sales tax, but certain designated resort communities, including Big Sky, West Yellowstone, Whitefish, and Red Lodge, charge a local resort tax of up to 3% on lodging, food, alcohol, and other tourist-oriented goods and services. - New Hampshire exempts all retail purchases but applies an 8.5% tax on restaurant meals, room rentals, and motor vehicle rentals. Why This Matters Sales tax is often overlooked in retirement planning guides, despite having a significant impact on day-to-day finances. Live somewhere with high rates and you could end up spending hundreds of dollars more each year on basic essentials. States That Don't Tax Groceries Of all sales taxes, the one that hits retirees hardest is often the one levied on groceries. Fortunately, many states exempt groceries entirely. Others apply a reduced rate, and a few tax groceries at the full rate. States that still tax groceries at their full rate include: - Idaho: 6% - South Dakota: 4.2% (reverts to 4.5% in July 2027) Note Hawaii's General Excise Tax on businesses is often considered a sales tax, as it's typically passed on to consumers in the form of higher prices. A reduced rate, meanwhile, is levied in: - Mississippi: 5% - Tennessee: 4% - Alabama: 2% - Utah: 3% (1.75% state + 1.25% local) - Missouri: 1.225%
