title: I've Been Wrong About Coca-Cola Stock for 5 Years. Here's Why I'm Finally Changing My Mind.
text: I've Been Wrong About Coca-Cola Stock for 5 Years. Here's Why I'm Finally Changing My Mind.. For years, I filed Coca-Cola (NYSE: KO) stock under "fine, but why bother?" on my list of investment options. I saw a 130-year-old soda company facing a world turning against sugar, and I assumed it would plod along while faster-moving names sprinted past it. After watching Coca-Cola lately, I have had to admit I was reading it wrong. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » The growth I said wasn't there The story I told myself was that soda is a shrinking business. The company's July quarter made that story hard to defend. Organic revenue rose 6% year over year, and unit case volume grew across every single operating segment, not just one lucky region. More telling was where the growth came from. Coca-Cola Zero Sugar jumped 16%, and Fairlife, its high-protein dairy brand, climbed in the first half of the year. That is not a company clinging to old habits. It is one quietly reshaping what it sells, meeting the health shift rather than getting run over by it. Management was confident enough to raise its full-year outlook. Why the durability finally won me over What changed my mind is not one quarter but what it revealed. In a jittery market, Coca-Cola kept nudging prices higher without driving customers away, the kind of pricing power most companies would envy. It generates enormous free cash flow, is on track for roughly $12 billion this year, and has raised its dividend for more than six decades straight. I used to see that steadiness as boring. Now I see it as rare. The push into no-sugar and protein-forward drinks tells me the real moat is not just the brand, but the willingness to keep evolving it. I am not pretending the risks vanished. The stock is not cheap, currency swings can dent reported results, and the longer-run question of how weight-loss drugs and health trends reshape beverages is a real one. This is still a slow-and-steady compounder, not a rocket. But that is exactly the point I missed for five years, and I'm tired of falling behind. For investors who want dependable growth, a fortress balance sheet, and a rising dividend to hold through whatever the market throws next, Coca-Cola has earned a fresh look. I would rather admit I was wrong to dismiss it than keep overlooking a business that is this consistent and profitable. It will not double overnight, but for the patient, that reliability is starting to look like the feature, not the flaw.

title: How much can debt forgiveness save on a $20,000 balance this August?
text: How much can debt forgiveness save on a $20,000 balance this August?. Borrowers have spent the last few years adjusting to higher borrowing costs amid elevated inflation and rising prices, but many are discovering that the biggest challenge they're facing isn't avoiding new debt — it's getting rid of the debt they already have. At today's nearly 22% average rates, even the borrowers who have stopped using their credit cards are finding that the steep interest charges on their cards can keep their balances stubbornly high, making the payoff process a frustratingly slow endeavor. That, in turn, has prompted many borrowers to rethink their credit card payoff strategies.For example, rather than asking how long it will take to eliminate their credit card balances, many borrowers are now asking whether there are ways to reduce the amount they owe altogether to make it easier to get their debt issues under control. As more borrowers explore their debt relief options, debt forgiveness has become an increasingly common part of that conversation. The appeal of debt forgiveness is obvious: Settling a debt for less than the full balance could potentially help borrowers save a lot of money compared to traditional payoff strategies.But the amount you might save with debt forgiveness isn't as straightforward as you may think. The savings depend, in large part, on how negotiations unfold and what fees are involved. So, how much can you actually save by pursuing debt forgiveness if you're carrying a $20,000 balance this August? That's what we'll calculate below.Find out if you qualify to enroll in a debt forgiveness program now.How much can debt forgiveness save on a $20,000 balance this August?Debt forgiveness, which can be pursued on your own or through a debt settlement program, generally results in creditors agreeing to accept 30% to 50% less than the amount originally owed. That said, the outcomes can vary, and depend, in large part, on factors such as your financial hardship, how delinquent the account is, the type of debt you owe, the creditor's policies and your ability to fund settlement offers. If you're considering the average, though, here's what the savings could look like on a $20,000 balance:30% debt reduction: If your creditors agree to forgive 30% of the balance, you'd pay $14,000 instead of $20,000, resulting in $6,000 in gross savings.40% debt reduction: A 40% settlement would reduce your repayment to $12,000, creating $8,000 in gross savings.50% debt reduction: If you secure a 50% reduction, you'd repay $10,000, producing $10,000 in gross savings before fees.Those aren't necessarily your final savings if you're working with a professional debt relief company during the settlement process, however. Debt relief companies charge fees for their services, which vary, but generally range from 15% to 25% of the enrolled debt. On a $20,000 enrolled balance, that typically works out to $3,000 to $5,000 in fees. For example:A 40% settlement saves you $8,000 before fees. If your debt relief fee totals $4,000, your net savings would be approximately $4,000.A 50% settlement creates $10,000 in gross savings. With a $3,500 fee, you'd still save about $6,500 overall.Those figures don't account for potential tax consequences, though. In many cases, the forgiven debt will be considered taxable income unless you qualify for an IRS exception.Learn more about the debt relief strategies available to you today.How to determine if debt forgiveness is worth pursuing nowDebt forgiveness can be a powerful tool for borrowers who qualify, but it isn't automatically the best solution simply because you owe a substantial amount on your credit cards. Before enrolling in a program, it's important to consider your overall financial picture.Start by evaluating whether you're actually unable to repay your debts through traditional methods. If your monthly payments have become unmanageable, you're relying on credit cards to cover everyday expenses or you're falling behind despite making a genuine effort to keep up, debt forgiveness may deserve consideration.You should also compare it against other forms of debt relief. If your credit is still relatively strong, a balance transfer card or debt consolidation loan could lower your interest costs without damaging your credit as significantly. Or, a debt management plan through a credit counseling agency could reduce your interest rates while allowing you to repay your balances in full over time.You'll also want to think about the timing. Because debt forgiveness generally works best after accounts have become delinquent, borrowers who are still current on their payments should carefully weigh whether intentionally falling behind makes sense. The temporary credit damage and collection activity can be substantial, particularly if your financial situation may improve in the near future.The bottom lineDebt forgiveness has the potential to generate meaningful savings on a $20,000 balance, with settlements often reducing what borrowers ultimately repay by 30% to 50% before fees are calculated into the equation. But even after accounting for debt relief company costs, many borrowers still save thousands of dollars with this strategy. Those savings come with tradeoffs, though, including credit score damage, possible tax implications and months of negotiations.That's why debt forgiveness shouldn't be viewed as a shortcut. Rather, it should be evaluated alongside other debt relief strategies based on your income, financial hardship and long-term goals. Taking the time to compare your options now can help ensure that the money you save today doesn't create bigger financial challenges tomorrow.

title: U.S. Services Sector Optimism Rises as Sales and Activity Accelerate
text: U.S. Services Sector Optimism Rises as Sales and Activity Accelerate. Business at U.S. service companies picked up sharply in July, and executives grew more optimistic about the months ahead, surveys released Wednesday showed, a sign the economy entered the second half of the year on firmer footing than expected. The service sector—restaurants, banks, hospitals, truckers, software firms and the rest of the roughly two-thirds of the economy that doesn’t make physical products—grew at its fastest pace in nine months, according to S&P Global. Its index of services activity rose to 54.6 from 51.2 in June. Any reading above 50 signals growth. The figure came in stronger than the preliminary estimate S&P Global published two weeks ago, which had put the reading at 53.6. Companies surveyed later in the month, in other words, reported better conditions than those surveyed early. The survey points to “an encouraging acceleration in economic growth” at the start of the quarter, said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. He estimated the results are consistent with the economy growing at a 2.3 percent annual rate this quarter, up from 1.5 percent in the spring. New orders climbed at the fastest rate since November, and across the private economy—services plus manufacturing—new business grew the most in 19 months. Because orders come in before the work gets done, that points to activity holding up into August and September. Firms also reported the biggest buildup of unfinished work since February. Companies hired to keep up. Service firms added workers at the fastest rate in eight months, and private employers as a group added staff for the first time since April. A different survey, from the Institute for Supply Management, found the same surge in activity. Its overall services index barely moved, ticking up to 54.1 percent from 54 percent. But the measure of actual business activity leapt 3.7 points to 59.1 percent, the second-highest reading in more than two years, and new orders rose to 57.2 percent. Thirteen of 18 industries reported growth, led by retailers, truckers and wholesalers. The two surveys clashed on jobs. ISM’s employment gauge fell to 47.4 percent, the lowest since March and back below the 50 percent line separating growth from contraction. It has been below that line in 12 of the past 18 months. They disagreed on exports, too. ISM found foreign orders rising for a sixth straight month, while S&P Global’s companies reported one of the steepest drops in overseas business since late 2022, blaming tariffs and the war in the Middle East. Costs kept climbing in both surveys. Service firms told S&P Global their expenses rose at the fastest pace since May 2025, citing tariffs, raw materials and fuel. ISM’s price gauge rose to 70.3 percent, topping 70 percent for the fourth time in five months. But companies are having a hard time making customers pay for it. S&P Global said firms raised their own prices where they could—and the increases they managed were far smaller, by the survey’s measures, than the increases they absorbed. What isn’t passed along comes out of profits. Executives described the squeeze in their own words. A construction firm said sales kept sliding even after it cut prices, while costs mounted from every direction. A wholesaler said homebuilders were pushing back hard against price increases. A trucking executive said fuel and labor were driving prices up while demand held flat. The cost pressure was also narrower than the headline suggests. ISM said six commodities got cheaper in July, double the number in June, with copper and aluminum flipping from the list of goods rising in price to the list of those falling. Oil-related products and plastics kept climbing. Steve Miller, who runs ISM’s services survey, said the sector remains “resilient” and pointed to the recent run-up in oil prices as the source of the pricing pressure still working its way through. Companies mentioned tariffs and the Middle East conflict far less often than in past months, he said. Some of July’s strength won’t repeat. Both surveys found companies crediting the World Cup and expanded Fourth of July events for a burst of consumer spending. And S&P Global gathered its responses between July 9 and July 29; Williamson warned that the calm in the Gulf and the lower oil prices that helped businesses early in the month had reversed by the end of it. Still, the surveys describe a service economy moving faster than it was in the spring, with orders piling up and companies adding workers rather than cutting them.

title: Gold IRA or ETF? How to choose the right investment
text: Gold IRA or ETF? How to choose the right investment - A gold IRA allows for physical gold ownership within a tax-advantaged retirement account but has higher fees and less liquidity. - Gold ETFs offer a low-cost, highly liquid way to invest in gold's price movements without owning the physical metal. - The best gold investment option depends on an individual's goals, such as retirement planning, portfolio diversification, or direct ownership. When it comes to investing in gold, there are three common options that can easily be confused: owning physical bullion, holding physical gold in a gold IRA and investing in a gold ETF. While each can provide exposure to gold, they're designed for different goals. Before choosing how to invest in gold, first determine why you want to own it. Are you looking for a retirement investment, a long-term portfolio diversifier or direct ownership of physical bullion? The answer will help determine which option makes the most sense. Understanding these differences in ownership, storage, taxes and costs can help you determine which option best fits your investment strategy, risk tolerance and long-term financial goals. "Decide the purpose before the vehicle," says Leo Chen, Ph.D., of the University of South Florida's Muma College of Business. Gold IRA vs. gold ETF vs. physical gold at a glance One way to understand the difference is to think about stock investing. Buying an individual stock means you own shares of a specific company. Buying a mutual fund or ETF means you own shares of a fund that holds investments on your behalf. Gold investing works in much the same way. When you buy physical gold, you own the bullion itself. When you buy a gold ETF, you own shares of a fund designed to track the price of gold rather than taking direct possession of coins or bars. You benefit when gold's price rises, but you don't personally own or store the underlying bullion. Although they're often discussed alongside physical gold and ETFs, gold IRAs are different. A gold IRA is a type of individual self-directed retirement account (IRA) that can hold IRS-approved physical precious metals, including gold. Investors who hold gold in a gold IRA own the underlying metal, but it must be stored by an approved custodian rather than kept at home. Here’s a brief look at how these three types of gold investing work: | Feature | Gold IRA | Gold ETF | Physical Gold | | Owns physical gold | Yes | Generally no (owns shares) | Yes | | Retirement account | Yes | Optional | No | | Tax advantages | Yes | Only in retirement accounts | No | | Storage required | Depository | None | Owner responsible | | Liquidity | Moderate | High | Moderate | | Annual fees | Moderate | Low | None (but storage may apply) | | Best for | Long-term retirement | Easy investing | Direct ownership | Gold IRAs A gold IRA allows you to hold physical gold — and, in many cases, other IRS-approved precious metals such as silver, platinum and palladium — as part of your retirement savings. Unlike a traditional IRA that typically holds stocks, bonds or mutual funds, a gold IRA holds physical bullion while offering the same tax advantages and following the same IRS contribution and distribution rules as other IRAs. "A gold IRA only matters if you want the physical metal itself inside the wrapper," says Chen. While you choose the investments, a custodian administers the account, and an IRS-approved depository provides secure storage, making the process more specialized than a standard brokerage IRA. That additional oversight comes with tradeoffs. "If you want to hold gold in a retirement account, the gold IRA is the best option there, but it's important to understand the rules, the friction and the costs associated with that type of holding," says Evan Mills, associate financial advisor and commodities specialist at Scholar Advising. Tax benefits and implications One of the biggest advantages of a gold IRA is that it offers the same tax benefits as other individual retirement accounts while allowing you to invest in physical precious metals. Because the gold is held inside a tax-advantaged retirement account, buying and selling metals within the IRA generally doesn't trigger immediate capital gains taxes. Instead, taxation depends on the type of IRA and when you take distributions. "Putting bullion in an IRA does avoid that 28% collectibles tax, but every single dollar you take out is treated as regular income," says George Dimov, CPA and founder of Dimov Partners. Key tax considerations include: - Tax-deferred or tax-free growth: With a traditional gold IRA, investment gains grow tax-deferred until retirement. With a Roth gold IRA, qualified withdrawals — including investment growth — are generally tax-free. - Potential tax deduction: Contributions to a traditional gold IRA may be tax deductible if you meet IRS income and eligibility requirements. Roth IRA contributions are made with after-tax dollars. - No immediate capital gains taxes: Buying and selling IRS-approved precious metals within the IRA generally doesn't create a taxable event. Instead, the account follows the tax rules for traditional or Roth IRAs. - Collectibles tax treatment: Physical gold held in a taxable account may be subject to the IRS's collectibles tax rules when sold at a gain. Those rules generally don't apply to transactions that occur within a gold IRA. - Annual contribution limits: Gold IRAs are subject to the same annual contribution limits as other traditional and Roth IRAs. - Distribution rules: Traditional gold IRA withdrawals are generally taxed as ordinary income, while qualified Roth IRA withdrawals are typically tax-free. - Early withdrawal penalties: Taking money from a traditional or Roth gold IRA before age 591⁄2 may trigger taxes and a 10% early withdrawal penalty unless an IRS exception applies. - Required minimum distributions (RMDs): Traditional gold IRAs are subject to RMD rules beginning at the applicable IRS age. Roth IRAs are not subject to RMDs during the original owner's lifetime. Ownership and risk profile A gold IRA gives you ownership of physical precious metals, but unlike bullion you keep at home, the assets must meet IRS requirements and be held by a qualified custodian in an approved depository. This structure offers additional oversight and tax advantages but also introduces third-party involvement. "You're buying the coins or bars to put in your retirement account, but you don't have the easy control and possession you'd have if you just bought physical bullion outside the IRA," Mills explains. Key considerations include: - Physical ownership: Your account owns IRS-approved physical gold, rather than shares of a fund tied to gold prices. - IRS-approved metals only: Only certain coins and bullion that meet IRS purity standards are eligible for a gold IRA. - Secure storage: The metals must be stored in an IRS-approved depository. Home storage generally isn't permitted for IRA-owned precious metals. - Different risk profile than ETFs: Because the account holds physical bullion, its value is tied directly to the price of gold rather than the performance or management of an investment fund. However, investors still rely on custodians and depositories to administer and safeguard the assets. - Choosing reputable providers matters: Since multiple companies are involved — including a custodian, precious metals dealer and depository — it's important to evaluate each provider's reputation, fees and customer service before opening an account. Liquidity and accessibility Gold IRAs are designed for long-term retirement investing rather than frequent buying and selling. While you can liquidate assets or take distributions, the process is generally more involved than selling a stock or ETF. Ryan Maynard, managing partner at Vaquero Private Wealth, says selling physical gold isn't always as straightforward as investors expect. "I've worked with clients on selling large physical gold positions, and it's not easy." Key considerations include: - Built for retirement savings: Gold IRAs are intended as long-term investment vehicles, not active trading accounts. - Selling your metals: If you decide to sell, you'll typically work through your dealer or custodian to liquidate the holdings. - Distribution options: Upon reaching retirement age, you may be able to sell the metals for cash or, in some cases, take an in-kind distribution of the physical bullion. Taxes may apply depending on the account type and distribution. - Less liquid than ETFs: Transactions generally take longer than selling shares of a gold ETF, making gold IRAs less suitable for investors who need immediate access to their money. Fees and costs Because gold IRAs involve physical assets, they typically carry more ongoing costs than traditional brokerage IRAs or gold ETFs. These fees vary by provider and should be reviewed carefully before opening an account. Common costs include: - Account setup fees: Some custodians charge a one-time fee to establish the account. - Annual custodial fees: Ongoing administrative fees cover account maintenance and IRS reporting. - Storage fees: Depositories charge annual fees to securely store your precious metals. - Insurance costs: Storage fees often include insurance to protect the metals while they're held in the depository. - Dealer markups: Dealers typically charge a premium above the spot price of gold when you purchase coins or bars. - Shipping fees: Shipping costs may apply when purchasing metals or taking an in-kind distribution of your bullion. Benefits and drawbacks of gold IRAs Pros - Own physical, IRS-approved gold in a tax-advantaged retirement account - Potential tax-deferred or tax-free growth, depending on the account type - Can help diversify a retirement portfolio - Professional storage and insurance reduce the burden of safeguarding bullion Cons - Higher fees than most gold ETFs - Requires an IRA custodian and approved depository - Less liquid than exchange-traded investments - Limited to IRS-approved coins and bullion - Subject to IRA contribution limits and withdrawal rules Gold ETFs A gold exchange-traded fund (ETF) is an investment fund that provides exposure to the price of gold without requiring you to buy, store or insure physical bullion yourself. Instead of owning coins or bars, you own shares of a fund that typically holds physical gold or uses other strategies to track gold's market price. Unlike a gold IRA, a gold ETF is an investment — not a retirement account. Gold ETFs can be purchased through a taxable brokerage account or held inside many traditional and Roth IRAs, making them one of the simplest and most accessible ways to invest in gold. As Chen points out, "An ordinary IRA can hold a gold ETF and get the same tax deferral for far less cost and complexity." Tax benefits and implications How a gold ETF is taxed depends largely on where you hold it. In a taxable brokerage account, physically backed gold ETFs are generally taxed differently than stock ETFs. When held inside a traditional or Roth IRA, however, they follow the same tax rules as other retirement investments. Key tax considerations include: - Taxable brokerage accounts: Long-term gains on physically backed gold ETFs are generally subject to the IRS's collectibles tax rules rather than the lower long-term capital gains rates that apply to most stocks. - Retirement accounts: Gold ETFs held inside a traditional or Roth IRA receive the same tax treatment as other investments held within those accounts. - Capital gains considerations: Selling ETF shares in a taxable account may trigger capital gains taxes, while buying and selling within an IRA generally does not create an immediate taxable event. - Different tax treatment than stocks: "Many people don't realize that the IRS taxes physical gold. But physically backed ETFs are capped at 28% on long-term gains in a taxable account, versus 20% for stocks," says Chen. Ownership and risk profile Gold ETFs offer exposure to gold prices without direct ownership of physical bullion. Instead, investors own shares of a fund whose value is designed to closely track the market price of gold. Key considerations include: - Fund shares instead of bullion: ETF investors own shares of the fund rather than specific gold bars or coins. - Fund structure: Many of the largest gold ETFs hold physical bullion in secure vaults on behalf of shareholders, although investors generally cannot claim individual bars. - Tracking error: While gold ETFs are designed to mirror gold's performance, returns can differ slightly because of fund expenses and operational factors. - Counterparty and management considerations: Investors rely on the fund sponsor, custodian and other service providers to manage the ETF and safeguard its holdings. - Limited redemption rights: Individual investors generally cannot redeem small holdings for physical bullion. Instead, shares are bought and sold on a stock exchange. Liquidity and accessibility One of the biggest advantages of a gold ETF is its liquidity. Because ETFs trade on stock exchanges, investors can buy and sell shares throughout the trading day at market prices. Key considerations include: - Trades like a stock: Gold ETFs can be bought and sold through most brokerage accounts during normal market hours. - Intraday pricing: Share prices update continuously while markets are open. - Easy buying and selling: "If you own a gold ETF in your brokerage account, you can just go sell it," says Mills. - Low investment minimums: Investors can often begin with the cost of a single share, making gold ETFs accessible to a wide range of budgets. Fees and costs Compared with physical gold and gold IRAs, gold ETFs typically have lower ongoing costs because investors aren't paying for storage, insurance or custodial administration. Common costs include: - Expense ratios: Most gold ETFs charge an annual management fee that's automatically deducted from fund assets. - Brokerage commissions: Many brokerages offer commission-free ETF trading, although fees may still apply depending on your platform. - Bid-ask spreads: Investors should consider the difference between the highest price buyers are willing to pay and the lowest price sellers are willing to accept. - No storage responsibilities: Investors don't pay directly for home storage, insurance or depository fees because those responsibilities are handled within the fund structure. - Lower overall costs: "A gold ETF gives people most of what they are looking for at a fraction of the transactional and holding costs, and none of the logistical complexities," says Maynard. Advantages and disadvantages of gold ETFs Pros - Easy to buy and sell through a brokerage account - Highly liquid with intraday pricing - Lower ongoing costs than most gold IRAs - No need to store or insure physical bullion - Can be held in taxable accounts or many retirement accounts Cons - You own shares of a fund, not physical gold - Physically backed ETFs held in taxable accounts may be subject to the IRS's collectibles tax rules - Small investors generally cannot redeem shares for bullion - Expense ratios can modestly reduce long-term returns - Still subject to fluctuations in gold prices What about owning bullion outright? Buying physical gold means purchasing coins or bars outright and storing them yourself or through a private vaulting service. Unlike a gold IRA, there are no retirement account rules, contribution limits or custodians involved. And unlike a gold ETF, you own the bullion directly rather than shares of a fund. Physical gold may appeal to investors who value direct possession or want to hold assets outside the traditional financial system. "If you want more physical control outside of the traditional financial system, then physical bullion is your best bet," says Mills. That ownership comes with additional responsibilities. Investors are responsible for securing, insuring and eventually selling their bullion, and dealer markups can add to the total cost. "The friction with physical gold is high, and most people underestimate it. The cost of transport, assay, secure storage and insurance can be surprisingly high," Maynard adds. Bottom line: Which option is right for you? For most investors, the decision comes down to why they want gold. If the goal is low-cost exposure to gold's price, a gold ETF may be the simpler option. If the goal is holding physical metal in a tax-advantaged retirement account, a gold IRA may be a better fit. But if having direct possession of bullion is the priority, buying physical gold outright may be worth the additional costs and logistical considerations. Here's how each option may fit different types of investors: - Retirement-focused investors: A gold IRA may be a good fit if you specifically want to hold physical gold within a tax-advantaged retirement account and are comfortable with the additional rules, fees and storage requirements. - Long-term wealth preservation: Investors looking to diversify a long-term portfolio may choose either a gold IRA or a gold ETF, depending on whether they value direct ownership of bullion or lower costs and greater liquidity. - Active traders: A gold ETF is generally the better choice for investors who anticipate frequent buying and selling, as it trades on stock exchanges throughout the day. - First-time investors: A gold ETF may offer the easiest entry point thanks to its low investment minimums, straightforward trading and relatively low ongoing costs. - Investors wanting direct possession: Buying physical bullion outright may appeal to those who want to own and control their gold outside of the traditional financial system, though they'll also be responsible for storage, insurance and security. - Investors prioritizing simplicity and low costs: A gold ETF typically offers the most cost-effective and convenient way to gain exposure to gold without managing physical assets. Often, the answer is choosing more than one option. Alternative investments generally shouldn't dominate a portfolio, and some investors combine physical gold with a gold ETF to balance direct ownership with liquidity. The right approach ultimately depends on your financial goals, risk tolerance, time horizon and how you expect gold to fit into your broader investment strategy. FAQs Is a gold ETF backed by real gold? Many of the largest gold ETFs are backed by physical gold stored in secure vaults, but investors don't own specific gold bars or coins. Instead, they own shares of a fund whose value is designed to track the price of gold. Not all gold ETFs use the same structure, so it's important to review a fund's prospectus before investing. Can I own physical gold in an IRA? Yes, but only through a self-directed gold IRA. The IRS allows certain gold, silver, platinum and palladium coins and bullion that meet specific purity standards to be held in an IRA. The metals must be stored by an IRS-approved custodian at an approved depository rather than at home. Are gold ETFs taxed differently than physical gold? It depends on how you own them. In a taxable brokerage account, physically backed gold ETFs and physical gold are generally subject to the IRS's collectibles tax rules. If they're held inside a traditional or Roth IRA, they follow the tax rules that apply to those retirement accounts instead. Which has lower fees: a gold ETF or a gold IRA? In most cases, a gold ETF has lower ongoing costs than a gold IRA. Gold ETFs typically charge an annual expense ratio, while gold IRAs may include setup fees, annual custodial fees, storage costs and dealer markups. However, investors who want to own physical bullion inside a retirement account may find those additional costs worthwhile. Should retirees own physical gold or gold ETFs? There's no one-size-fits-all answer. Retirees who want a simple, low-cost way to diversify may prefer a gold ETF, while those who specifically want physical bullion in a tax-advantaged retirement account may consider a gold IRA. Investors who value direct possession may prefer owning physical gold outright. The right choice depends on your investment goals, risk tolerance and income needs. Can I hold a gold ETF in my IRA? Yes. Gold ETFs can generally be held in traditional and Roth IRAs through most brokerage firms. If your goal is simply to gain exposure to gold's price inside a retirement account, a gold ETF may be a simpler and lower-cost alternative to opening a self-directed gold IRA. title: The Contrarian Setup That Has Equity Traders Watching Very Closely
text: The Contrarian Setup That Has Equity Traders Watching Very Closely. Markets have a long and humbling history of punishing the crowd at exactly the wrong moment. Right now, a textbook contrarian setup is emerging across equity markets — one that seasoned traders recognize as the kind of alignment that tends to precede outsized moves. Whether that move resolves to the upside or the downside depends on how you read the signals, but one thing is clear: ignoring this setup would be a costly mistake. At its core, a contrarian setup occurs when sentiment, positioning, and price action diverge in ways that suggest the market is leaning too hard in one direction. When too many participants are positioned the same way, the conditions for a violent reversal become structurally sound. This isn’t speculation — it’s mechanics. Markets need liquidity to move, and that liquidity is often found by running stops on the crowded side of the trade. Right now, the crowded side is looking increasingly exposed. Sentiment data has been flashing warning signs for weeks. Retail investor surveys show elevated bullish readings that have historically coincided with near-term market tops, while institutional positioning in equity futures has quietly shifted toward a more defensive stance. This divergence between retail optimism and institutional caution is one of the clearest hallmarks of a maturing contrarian setup. The smart institutional money isn’t necessarily bearish — but it is hedged, and that tells you something important about conviction levels at current prices. Volatility markets are adding another layer to this picture. Implied volatility has been compressed for an extended period, and when volatility stays suppressed for too long, it tends to mean-revert sharply. Options traders have been selling premium into a calm market, collecting yield in a low-vol environment. That strategy works — until it doesn’t. A volatility spike in this environment would force rapid position unwinds, amplifying whatever directional move triggers the reset. This dynamic is baked into the current contrarian setup and shouldn’t be underestimated. Technical analysis reinforces the case. Several major indices have been grinding higher on declining volume, with breadth deteriorating even as headline numbers remain elevated. When a smaller number of stocks carry the index higher, it creates a deceptive picture of market health. Internals are weakening beneath the surface, and historically, this kind of narrow leadership — followed by a sentiment extreme — has been one of the most reliable precursors to a meaningful repricing. The contrarian setup doesn’t demand a crash, but it does suggest that the path of least resistance is shifting. It’s worth noting that contrarian signals are not timing tools. They identify conditions, not catalysts. A setup can persist for longer than most traders expect before the market finds its trigger. That trigger could come from a macro data surprise, a shift in central bank language, or simply the weight of accumulated positioning unwinding on its own. The setup creates the kindling; the catalyst lights the match. Right now, there’s no shortage of potential catalysts circling the market — from geopolitical uncertainty to evolving inflation dynamics — any of which could serve as the spark. For investors, the practical implication of recognizing a contrarian setup is not to panic or go aggressively short. It’s to reassess portfolio risk with clear eyes. If your equity exposure was built during a period of easy gains and low volatility, it may be larger than your actual risk tolerance allows. Hedging strategies, rebalancing toward quality names with strong balance sheets, and maintaining some cash optionality are all rational responses to a market environment where the contrarian case is building credibility. The equity market is not broken. Fundamentals still matter, earnings still drive long-term value, and bull markets have survived countless contrarian setups without rolling over. But the signal in the noise right now is unusually loud. The alignment of stretched sentiment, weakening breadth, compressed volatility, and divergent institutional positioning doesn’t guarantee a correction — but it does mean the risk-reward calculus has shifted. Traders and investors who recognize a contrarian setup for what it is — an opportunity dressed in uncertainty — will be far better positioned for whatever comes next.

title: An economist says there a 3 reasons Kevin Warsh is right to nix Fed guidance, and flags one thing he can do to calm markets
text: An economist says there a 3 reasons Kevin Warsh is right to nix Fed guidance, and flags one thing he can do to calm markets - Apollo economist Torsten Sløk said Kevin Warsh is right to nix forward guidance from the Fed. - He said it gives the Fed flexibility, though at the cost of greater volatility in markets. - Sløk says there's one thing Warsh can do to help quell bouts of volatility in reaction to Fed decisions. The market may have freaked out after the last Fed meeting, but a top economist says chairman Kevin Warsh is getting it right when it comes to how the central bank communicates. Warsh's decision to end forward guidance from the Fed has been met with criticism, but Apollo's chief economist Torsten Sløk praised the new chairman's call, even if markets don't appear to like it. Sløk wrote in a blog post that he supports Warsh's call, and that there are three reasons it's way for the central bank to go about conducting monetary policy. "Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has been unfairly criticized," he wrote. "The decision to eliminate forward guidance isn't reckless. It's pragmatic." Here's why Sløk is onboard: - It can prevent policy inertia by not locking the central bank into rate paths. - It can improve real market signals by letting prices adjust as new data comes available. - It can stop false certainty by ending predictability and forcing investors not to treat a rate path as a certainty. In Sløk's view, the central bank should prioritize flexibility and market accuracy over the old forward guidance framework. However, he does see one change Warsh could make that that would soothe jittery markets ahead of future policy decisions. "Warsh could dampen this newly introduced volatility by providing clearer framework guidance," he said. "Without it, markets struggle to understand how the Fed will reach 2% inflation. Is it through higher rates, a smaller balance sheet or tighter financial conditions? This uncertainty has steepened the yield curve and pushed up risk premiums." When Sløk responded to Warsh's July press conference, he noted that a critical component of the Fed's credibility depends not just on stating its goals for the economy, but making it clear how they intend to accomplish them. Warsh's announcement that they would continue withholding forward guidance triggered a selloff in markets, making it clear that investors were not happy with the new communications style. But Sløk maintains that if the Fed prioritizes clearer framework, eliminating guidance can end up benefiting markets. "By eliminating forward guidance, the Fed gets more flexibility," he said. "But higher volatility is the cost, and the cost can be minimized by providing clearer framework guidance." If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

title: The Case For Fundamental Analysis in Shaping Modern Corporate Strategy
text: The Case For Fundamental Analysis in Shaping Modern Corporate Strategy. Something significant is happening in corporate boardrooms around the world. Executives who once relied on gut instinct, short-term market signals, or surface-level competitive benchmarking are increasingly turning to a more disciplined framework — one rooted in the principles of fundamental analysis. What was once largely a tool for equity investors evaluating individual stocks has quietly evolved into a strategic compass guiding some of the most consequential business decisions made at the highest organizational levels. The shift is not accidental. In an era defined by macroeconomic volatility, geopolitical disruption, and rapid shifts in consumer behavior, companies that anchor their strategy in rigorous financial and operational analysis are outperforming those that don’t. The data is telling a clear story, and corporate leaders are starting to listen. From Investment Tool to Strategic Framework Traditionally, fundamental analysis was the domain of portfolio managers and equity analysts. It involved dissecting a company’s financial statements — income statements, balance sheets, and cash flow reports — to determine intrinsic value relative to market price. But the same analytical discipline that helps investors decide whether a stock is undervalued is now helping companies decide whether an acquisition makes sense, which markets to enter, and where to allocate capital over the next five to ten years. Corporate strategists are now applying core principles of fundamental analysis — including earnings quality assessment, debt-to-equity evaluation, return on invested capital (ROIC) analysis, and free cash flow modeling — directly into their planning cycles. This approach brings a level of financial rigor that complements traditional strategy tools like SWOT analysis or Porter’s Five Forces. When combined, these frameworks give leadership teams a far more complete picture of competitive positioning and long-term viability. Mergers, Acquisitions, and the Due Diligence Revolution Nowhere is the influence of fundamental analysis more visible than in mergers and acquisitions. Companies are increasingly applying deep fundamental scrutiny before pursuing targets, moving well beyond surface-level revenue comparisons. Analysts inside corporate development teams are now expected to build detailed intrinsic value models, normalize earnings for one-time items, and stress-test cash flow assumptions under multiple economic scenarios. This shift has measurably improved acquisition outcomes. Research consistently shows that deals preceded by thorough fundamental analysis tend to generate better post-merger returns and fewer write-downs. Companies that acquire based on momentum or market buzz alone — without grounding the decision in fundamental metrics — have historically overpaid and underdelivered for shareholders. Today’s environment, where capital is more expensive and investor tolerance for strategic missteps has narrowed, makes this discipline not just valuable but essential. - Earnings quality reviews help identify accounting risks before a deal closes - ROIC benchmarking ensures acquired assets meet internal hurdle rates - Cash flow stress testing reveals resilience under adverse conditions - Valuation modeling anchors offer prices in financial reality rather than speculation Capital Allocation and Long-Term Value Creation Beyond M&A, fundamental analysis is reshaping how companies think about internal capital allocation. CFOs and board members are increasingly adopting a portfolio management mentality — treating business units the way an investor treats a portfolio of securities. Units that consistently generate strong returns on capital are funded aggressively, while those showing structural deterioration in margins or cash conversion are restructured or divested. This investor-minded approach to internal strategy has become particularly prominent among large conglomerates and diversified industrials, but it is spreading across sectors. Technology companies, consumer brands, and healthcare organizations are all embedding fundamental metrics into their annual strategic planning processes. The goal is consistent: ensure that every dollar deployed internally generates a return commensurate with the risk taken — the same standard a disciplined investor would apply to an external position. The growing availability of real-time financial data and advanced analytics tools has further accelerated adoption. Companies can now model intrinsic value scenarios dynamically, adjusting assumptions as macroeconomic conditions evolve rather than relying solely on annual planning cycles that quickly become outdated. Investor Relations and Strategic Credibility There is another powerful reason companies are embedding fundamental analysis into strategy: their investors demand it. Institutional shareholders — pension funds, sovereign wealth funds, and large asset managers — evaluate management teams using the same fundamental frameworks they apply to stock selection. When executives speak the language of ROIC, free cash flow yield, and intrinsic value, they build credibility with the capital markets community in ways that narrative-driven presentations simply cannot. Companies that demonstrate a fundamental understanding of their own financial drivers are rewarded with lower costs of capital, more stable shareholder bases, and greater tolerance for long-term investment cycles. Those that lack this discipline often find themselves reactive — responding to activist pressure or analyst downgrades rather than proactively shaping their own financial narrative. The broader lesson is clear: fundamental analysis has outgrown its origins as a stock-picking tool. It has become a core competency for any organization serious about creating durable, compounding value. Companies that internalize this discipline across their strategic functions — from capital allocation to M&A to investor communication — are better positioned to navigate uncertainty, allocate resources wisely, and earn the trust of the markets that ultimately determine their cost of growth.

title: After sailing on over 55 cruises, there are 6 things I never waste my money on when I'm at sea
text: After sailing on over 55 cruises, there are 6 things I never waste my money on when I'm at sea. As a frequent cruiser, I've got a few tricks for saving money, and I know which onboard add-ons aren't a good value for me. Allie Hubers After taking 58 cruises across 26 years, I've got a list of things I won't pay extra for on board. Most spa services and unlimited drink packages never feel like a good value for me. I take my own photos and do laundry in the sink instead of paying for these services on a ship. I took my first cruise as a toddler, and after 58 sailings, I've watched the onboard experience change significantly. Gone are the days of midnight buffets and endless lobster nights in the dining room. Although cruise fares are still largely inclusive, it's easy to feel nickel-and-dimed once you're on board. From specialty restaurants to drink packages, spa treatments, and professional photos, the cost of your cruise can climb quickly after embarkation. I'm still happy to splurge on certain add-ons that enhance my cruise experience. For instance, I won't hesitate to pay for a memorable specialty dining meal or upgrade to a balcony cabin on a scenic itinerary. But after 26 years of cruising, I've also learned that some add-ons are rarely worth the money. Regardless of the ship, itinerary, or cruise line, these are the onboard extras that I never waste my money on. Most onboard spa treatments don't feel like a great value. Thermal Spa on Celebrity Edge Allie Hubers Spa treatments might seem like a tempting way to relax during your cruise, but I've rarely found them worth the high price. After splurging on massages across multiple cruise lines, I've always left disappointed. My husband is a sucker for the spa, but after we spent more than $400 on a couples massage during a cruise to New Zealand , even he agreed it wasn't worth the splurge. Although the massages themselves were perfectly fine, the upselling afterward always makes me uncomfortable. Therapists often encourage you to buy expensive products, but the pushy sales tactics can quickly offset the post-massage relaxation. Instead, I'd rather splurge on a thermal spa pass. It's often cheaper than a couples massage and it lets me enjoy the spa's amenities throughout the cruise without feeling pressured to buy anything. Drink packages never feel like a good value for us. Allie Hubers Although unlimited cocktails might sound appealing, purchasing a drink package has actually made my cruises less relaxing. I've splurged on drink packages with Royal Caribbean and Carnival, but I can't drink enough alcohol to justify the cost. Often, they can cost upward of $70 per person, per day. Whenever I've purchased one, I've found myself constantly calculating how many drinks I need to order just to break even. This completely defeats the convenience of having a drink package in the first place. I also don't have the stamina to drink consistently throughout a cruise, especially on longer itineraries. Even when my husband and I cruised with friends who had drink packages, we struggled to get our money's worth. Instead, we ended up drinking more than we normally would, which left us feeling bloated and hungover. Now, the only time I'll cruise with a drink package is when it's bundled with a fare, such as with Norwegian's Free at Sea or Celebrity's All Included. On-board art auctions and pricey paintings don't tempt me. Allie Hubers Almost every cruise ship I've been on has had a dedicated art gallery where guests can browse and purchase artwork to bring home. Throughout the sailing, the galleries host art auctions and entice guests with the promise of free Champagne. I've never been tempted to attend one — not even for a free drink. Buying expensive artwork isn't my style, and I've heard horror stories from cruisers who regret getting caught up in the excitement of a competitive auction. If I'm going to buy artwork during a trip, I'd rather support local artists in port. In fact, many of my walls are covered with beautiful pieces of art from all over the world. I don't bother with professional photos when I can take my own. Allie Hubers On most cruise lines, photographers repeatedly ask you to pose for pictures, whether that's during embarkation, while you're eating at a specialty restaurant, or as you're stepping off the gangway in port. These photos can be fun keepsakes, but each printed photo usually costs around $25 — and that often doesn't include a digital copy. Photo packages can be an even bigger expense, often costing more than $100. Some cruisers buy a package before they even know whether they'll like enough photos to make it worthwhile. Although this is a convenient way to get posed photos, I don't think professional cruise photos are worth the price. My phone takes excellent pictures, and there's almost always another guest who's happy to snap a quick group photo for me. If room service costs extra, I'm skipping it. Allie Hubers I love ordering room service for a complimentary continental breakfast, especially during busy port mornings. But when it comes to paying extra for room service, I always skip it. Continental breakfast is perfect for enjoying coffee and a pastry before heading ashore. However, most cruise lines charge a flat delivery fee for other orders. For instance, Royal Caribbean charges $7.95 per delivery for room service, which can add up quickly over the course of your cruise. For me, it's just not worth the extra cost. There's almost always a complimentary dining venue open somewhere on the ship for snacks, late-night bites, or pizza. I'd rather take a short walk than pay to have food delivered to my cabin. Laundry services can get pricey, and I don't mind washing clothes at sea as needed. I've had luck with travel-sized detergent packets and a sink. Allie Hubers I've taken plenty of longer itineraries, including a 15-night repositioning cruise from Sydney to Singapore. Laundry can pile up on these long sailings, but I've never paid to have the cruise line do it for me. Cost is the biggest reason I avoid using this service while cruising. For example, on my most recent Celebrity cruise, prices ranged from about $12 to launder a dress to nearly $24 for a suit. A full laundry bag can easily turn into a hefty bill. Instead, I pack a few travel-size laundry-detergent packets and hand-wash smaller items in my cabin sink or shower. I'll typically wash undergarments and socks in warm water before hanging them to dry in the shower. After hand-washing my clothes for 100 days during Semester at Sea in college, washing a few items in my cruise cabin is no big deal. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: US only has 43-day emergency buffer of crude oil left in 45-year low
text: US only has 43-day emergency buffer of crude oil left in 45-year low. U.S. crude oil supplies have fallen to their lowest level in 45 years as President Donald Trump continues to wage war against Iran — with only 43 days of global supply left. There now exists a thinner cushion against any potential disruptions should the fighting in the Middle East escalate further. According to Bank of America Global Research Data, compiled by Bloomberg, the U.S. has just 43 days of crude oil supply, including that of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, compared with a long-term average of about 65 days. The data shows the measure falling to its lowest level since the 1980s. The decline comes as markets fear tightening crude supplies as the U.S. continues to bomb Iran, raising concerns over shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. It comes after an embarrassing final video of Lindsey Graham exposed him humiliatingly mocking Trump over his Iran war flip-flopping. After Trump, who has been accused by his own staff of 'letting his appearance go' on purpose after a sloppy discovery, launched the initial strikes against the Islamic Republic at the end of February, Iran seized control of the strait, closing it to through-traffic, stymying the flow of about 20% of the world's oil supply. Any further disruptions to the strait could cause a greater impact on global oil supplies, which are already at multi-decade lows. Lower inventories don't necessarily mean there's an immediate shortage, however. The market has been left with smaller buffers after unexpected supply disruptions in the past. Click here to follow the Mirror US on Google News to stay up to date with all the latest news, sports and entertainment stories. Oil prices have always been sensitive to geopolitical developments, and the situation unfolding as a result of the Iran war isn't any different. Brent crude jumped to over 2% and cleared the $90-per-barrel mark in early Asian trading in mid-July, while the U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude price stood at about $84.48 per barrel, about a 2.4% rise since June 12, per Seeking Alpha. Stocks rose in morning trading on Wall Street Wednesday and added to their records set a day earlier, while oil prices held steady. The S&P 500 climbed 0.4%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 584 points, or 1.1%, as of 10:45 a.m. Eastern time. The Nasdaq composite rose 0.1%. The S&P 500 and the Dow both set records on Tuesday, while the Nasdaq is less than 2% from its record. Every major index has been surging this week, giving August a strong start. The market is leaping as companies head into the closing stretch of their latest round of earnings reports with sharp overall gains. Three-quarters of the companies within the S&P 500 have reported results so far, and Wall Street expects profit growth of 50% when they are all finished. The Walt Disney Co. rose 3% after easily beating Wall Street’s profit forecasts, helped by a $1 billion box office haul from “Toy Story 5” and theme park revenue. Booking Holdings jumped 6.6% after reporting that strong travel demand drove profit and revenue growth during its most recent quarter. SpaceX fell 8.8%, despite reporting a smaller loss than Wall Street expected late Tuesday in its first quarterly report as a public company. The company did help give semiconductor giant Nvidia a 3.7% boost after announcing it would exclusively use that company’s chips for its artificial intelligence technology. Treasury yields held relatively steady in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury remained at 4.63% from late Tuesday. Markets in Asia rose. Benchmarks jumped more than 3% in Tokyo and Seoul as computer chipmakers and other AI-related companies climbed. European markets also gained ground. Strong corporate profits and expectations for more growth ahead have been steering stocks higher. Wall Street has also been worried about stock prices becoming unjustifiably high, especially within the technology sector and for companies focused on artificial intelligence. Profit growth, especially for some of the big chipmakers, like Nvidia, could help justify some of the big investments those companies are making in AI. AI-focused companies have been behind many of the big market swings and most of Wall Street's gains. That remained the case on Wednesday, with Nvidia leading the market higher. Micron Technology rose 1.8% to help support the gains. Uncertainty about the direction of the U.S. war with Iran continues hanging over the market. President Donald Trump said a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz could come as early as Wednesday. But there have been many stops and starts during the five-month old conflict that has stifled the global supply of oil and rattled energy markets. The price of Brent crude, the international standard, fell 0.6% to $78.81 a barrel. Oil prices have been swinging for months and were as high as $102 per barrel at one point during the conflict, jolting already stubbornly high inflation. Higher oil prices pushed gasoline prices higher and increased shipping costs for a wide range of products. Inflation concerns have been hanging over markets and the Federal Reserve. The central bank has been holding its key benchmark rate steady as it monitors the costs and the impact on the economy. Wall Street expects the central bank to raise rates at least once before the end of 2026. Household spending remains resilient, despite the stress from higher costs on everything from gas to groceries. The jobs market has been one of the stronger areas of the economy, though growth has been slowing. Wall Street will get another update on Friday with the monthly employment report for July. It comes after disrespectful Trump was slammed for a 'disgusting' act during Lindsey Graham's funeral.

title: 17-year-old Mexican restaurant chain closes all locations
text: 17-year-old Mexican restaurant chain closes all locations. Another Mexican restaurant chain has abruptly shut down all its locations, leaving customers searching for answers after the company has not provided an immediate explanation for the closures. The shutdowns come as restaurant operators across the industry continue facing pressure from rising costs, changing consumer habits, and increased competition for dining traffic. Founded in Orlando, Florida, in 2009, Gringos Locos is a Tex-Mex restaurant chain known for its homemade salsas, marinades, and sofrito, along with menu items such as nachos, tacos, and burritos. Gringos Locos closes all restaurants Gringos Locos has closed all of its Orlando-area restaurants, according to News 6 . The affected locations include: SoDo: 517 E Michigan St Downtown Washington: 20 E Washington St Milk District: 2405 E Robinson St UCF: 4258 W Plaza Dr The company has not publicly explained the reason behind the shutdowns . As of publication, all locations remain closed, and Gringos Locos' website does not list any restaurants accepting pickup or delivery orders. TheStreet reached out to all Gringos Locos locations by phone for comment on the closures, but did not receive a response before publication; calls were routed straight to voicemail. An individual identifying themselves as a Gringos Locos employee commented on a local report , stating that they were unemployed after receiving a closing notice from management on July 31. The individual also claimed that locations would shut down permanently after running out of food. A person who identified themselves as a Gringos Locos worker told Knight News that the restaurants are closing while the company navigates its finances. TheStreet could not independently verify the individuals' employment statuses or identities. Customers have also turned to Gringos Locos' Instagram and Facebook page seeking answers about whether the shutdowns are permanent and asking the company to provide an update. The restaurant's social media accounts have not posted new feed content since 2025, and no public response regarding the closures has been provided. Gringos Locos reportedly closes all restaurants. RJ Sangosti&solThe Denver Post via Getty Images Mexican restaurants face continued pressure While the reason behind Gringos Locos' closures remains unclear, the shutdown comes as several Mexican restaurant chains have faced financial challenges, closures, or restructuring efforts. On the Border Cantina Mexican Grill & Cantina , owned by Pappas Restaurant Group, closed all remaining locations in June 2026. The company acquired the chain out of Chapter 11 bankruptcy in May 2025. Tijuana Flats filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in April 2024 and shuttered 11 restaurants as part of its restructuring before being sold to new ownership in 2025. Abuelo's Mexican Restaurant filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in September 2025 and now operates 16 locations, down from a peak of about 40 restaurants. Del Taco has closed several restaurants and exited multiple markets following separate franchisee bankruptcies. Restaurant industry navigates ongoing challenges The Gringos Locos closures come as restaurant operators across the U.S. continue navigating elevated costs and changing consumer behavior. Although inflation has eased from its peak, restaurants are still dealing with higher food, labor, occupancy, and operating expenses. At the same time, consumers have become more selective with discretionary spending , creating additional challenges for traffic and sales. According to the National Restaurant Association survey, 60% of restaurant operators reported lower customer traffic in December 2025. Here’s some of my previous coverage of restaurant closures: Popular breakfast chain closes more restaurants Popular beverage chain closing multiple locations nationwide 30-year-old restaurant chain confirms more closures in 2026 The National Restaurant Association has also reported that food and labor costs have each climbed roughly 35% over the past five years, putting additional pressure on restaurant profit margins. Meanwhile, prices for food away from home increased 3.4% in the 12 months ending June 2026, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics . "The restaurant industry is battling for its share of shrinking consumer wallets," said The New York Times food industry writer and expert Julie Creswell . "Last year, most chains raised menu prices, and lower-income consumers were the first to cut back on eating out." Related: Popular Mexican chain closing all locations after Chapter 11 rescue

title: Middle East War Triggers New Global Refining Boom
text: Middle East War Triggers New Global Refining Boom Submitted By Tsvetana Paraskova of OilPrice.com For the second time this decade, a war has upended global oil markets and sent oil prices and refining margins to multi-year highs, benefiting the world’s biggest oil companies and top refiners. The war in Iran has tightened fuel supply as crude oil has struggled to move through the Strait of Hormuz, triggering reduced refining throughput in Asia and a temporary Chinese ban on exports. The fuel markets tightened even more than the crude market to send refining margins to record highs. And the biggest refiners benefited from the new refining boom, with Big Oil reporting their highest second-quarter earnings since the previous outbreak of a war, the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The bumper earnings were driven not only by the jump in oil prices between April and June—the contribution of the refining and trading divisions was also fundamental for fueling the high profits. Record Refining Margins Despite the slump in crude prices and the extreme volatility in the past five months, t he refined product market continues to tighten with refining margins at record highs because the supply of petroleum products is much tighter than crude supply. Refining margins held at record highs even as crude oil prices soared to $100 per barrel and above. That’s because global gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel supply is tightening and has been tightening for months amid a combination of factors, most stemming from the wars in Iran and Ukraine. Last month, refining margins for gasoline and diesel jumped to new record highs amid on-and-off escalation in the Middle East, Russia’s ban on diesel exports, and crumbling global fuel inventories. In a rare statement last month, Fatih Birol, the executive director of the International Energy Agency (IEA), said that “There is no room for complacency on oil security amid the escalation in hostilities and a continued drawdown of available commercial inventories.” While assuring markets that IEA countries still hold more than 1 billion barrels of government-controlled stocks, Birol said that “Refinery activity and product supplies have not picked up as much as crude deliveries, meaning that markets for refined oil products, including diesel and gasoline, are considerably tighter than those for crude.” Big Oil’s Bumper Profits As a result of the tight fuel markets and soaring refining margins, the world’s biggest international oil companies reported their strongest earnings for the second quarter since at least 2022. They also expect refining to continue providing high earnings in the short term amid distorted fuel markets with restricted supply and refining capacity. Shell, for example, more than doubled its second-quarter earnings from a year earlier, as higher oil and gas prices, record refinery utilization, and strong trading boosted profits to above analyst expectations. Refinery utilization at Shell was 102% in April to June, compared with 99% in the first quarter of 2026, mainly due to lower planned and unplanned maintenance activities. Strong refining and chemical margins also boosted Shell’s earnings in the past quarter. Shell’s global indicative refining margin rose to $24 from $17 per barrel in the first quarter, while the global indicative chemical margin doubled to $270 per ton, from $139 per ton. “The operational performance of Refining has been excellent,” CEO Wael Sawan said on Shell’s earnings call. TotalEnergies’ adjusted net income jumped by 68% from a year earlier to $6 billion for the second quarter of 2026 as the jump in oil prices and refining margins boosted earnings and cash flows. The European Refining Margin Marker for the supermajor rose by 19% quarter-to-quarter and soared nearly threefold year-to-date compared to the first half of 2025, to $12.4 per barrel, up from $4.3 a barrel. “Refining and Chemicals performed in an exceptional way leveraging market conditions, managing well the tensions on supply of refined products to maximize captured margins,” TotalEnergies CEO Patrick Pouyanné said on the earnings call. The U.S. supermajors, ExxonMobil and Chevron, also reported their highest earnings in years, drawing criticism from U.S. President Donald Trump, who this week said they are making “too much money” and “They’re going to give some of that back to the public and they better cut the retail price, the consumer price.” Chevron had record refinery throughput of over 1 million barrels per day for the second quarter, CEO Mike Wirth said on the earnings call on Friday. “Middle distillates are really the tight spot right now. Initially, it looked like jet, now diesel,” the executive noted, saying that European diesel demand could soon start rising from relatively weak levels in Q2 amid restocking of heating oil ahead of winter. “That lands on top of the export ban from Russia, refinery outages in Russia, the obvious constraints that exist in the Strait,” Wirth added. China and its demand is a big unknown for the market now, but Chevron doesn’t see a significant scale of demand destruction, said the executive, adding “I think we're going to see some upward pressure on product pricing here into the third quarter and perhaps beyond that.” Exxon’s CEO Darren Woods said the supermajor expects continued “very robust refining market with very high margins.” Even if supply disruptions are resolved by the end of the year and crude and fuels flows from the Middle East are restored, low global inventories and the need to restock could support the global refining complex for a few more quarters. title: What's behind the sudden surge in gold buying
text: What's behind the sudden surge in gold buying. What's driving today's $180 rally in gold prices to $4257 -- the highest six weeks? I wish there was an easy answer. Firstly, gold has been forming a base for the past five weeks, bouncing around near $4000. It briefly dipped below several times but was able to keep from breaking down. The signal from the time spent there and the price action was that the bears were running out of reasons to sell. There has been a huge wave of profit taking since $5400 in March but some strong hands finally appeared near $4000. I've written about that before and speculated that Chinese official buying might be taking place near $4000. In any case, gold has been slowly finding a bottom there and testing it. If you look closely, there has been a series of higher highs since the low on June 30 in another positive sign. All that sets the stage for a bounce but why today? That's far from clear. Zooming in, the buying started in Asia and that might be a hint. Gold bulls have been looking for signs of Asian demand as it's that part of the world that largely fuelled the prior rally. From there, a short squeeze might have kicked off to do the rest of the work. Gold ran though some technical levels to maintain the momentum. Behind the scenes, there have also been positive developments, though not exactly today. The US has been actively devaluing its currency versus the Japanese yen in the strongest sign yet that Trump's Treasury department wants to pursue a weak dollar policy. In addition, we got another TACO from Trump this week on Hormuz. Gold topped at the start of the war and has been struggling since because of fears that emerging oil importers would be forced to sell gold reserves to pay for oil (or use it to stabilize their currencies). With WTI falling back to $75 and Trump showing no appetite for escalation, the broader market is signalling a true end to the war (whether that's wise or not is a question for another day). Finally, it appears that bullish sentiment on gold was simply washed out. In a situation like that, it doesn't take much to swing momentum and with broader markets in a 'buy everything' mode since late last week, gold has been swept up in the enthusiasm. What next? The rally is obviously stretched in the short term but we have seen what momentum and FOMO can do in the gold market. The 38.2% retracement of the Jan-June fall is at $4590 and that's a reasonable target over the next two months. This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

title: Long Branch Gets A New Coffee Shop, Almost Home At The Inkwell Lofts
text: Long Branch Gets A New Coffee Shop, Almost Home At The Inkwell Lofts Almost Home CEO Robbie Doran said he hopes his version becomes just as much of a community gathering place as the original Inkwell was. LONG BRANCH, NJ — There's a new coffee shop in Long Branch, and it's at the location of the former legendary Inkwell Coffee House. The new coffee shop is Almost Home, a popular coffee shop/breakfast spot that started in Lincroft. The coffee shop opened last week and it's located on the ground floor of Inkwell Lofts, a 22-unit condo building at Second Avenue and New Court, one block from the Ocean Avenue beach. When it first opened in the 1960s, the original Inkwell Coffee House became a popular hangout spot in Long Branch. Almost Home founder and CEO Robert "Robbie" Doran got nostalgic talking about it: Find out what's happening in Long Branch-Eatontownfor free with the latest updates from Patch. "It was a cafe, a poetry house, a place for live music where kids went after the bar to chill out," he said. "The Inkwell would be open until the wee hours of the morning, and they built a cult following. My parents went there in the '70s and '80s, and Bruce (Springsteen) wrote the 'Born to Run' album right around the corner. So it's really wild to be opening here today." Hours for Almost Home Long Branch are 7 a.m. - 4 p.m. Sunday-Wednesday and 7 a.m. - 9 p.m. Thursday, Friday and Saturday. Almost Home Long Branch will sell coffees, pastries, and have prepared sandwiches and salads to go, prepared by the Blonde Shallot. Find out what's happening in Long Branch-Eatontownfor free with the latest updates from Patch. Doran said he hopes his version becomes just as much of a community gathering place as the original Inkwell was. "I envision it to be a European-style cafe, with good coffee, amazing French pastries and grab-and-go salads, wraps and prepared foods," said Doran. "I love exploring Paris and other European cities, and one of the things I love about those cities is the ability to get a great cup of coffee or cappuccino after 3 p.m. Most coffee shops in American close in the afternoon. I want the Inkwell to be a late-night coffee cafe ... I'm a people person. I love taking care of people. And I love the idea of building a place that has longevity and contributes to the community around it." Doran said he next plans to open an Almost Home somewhere in Ocean County, where exactly he did not reveal. "Ocean County is a market I do want to enter," he said. "At this point, the location has to meet something to me. I really believe you find true success and passion when you believe in a place, and I'm willing to put my reputation up for it." Doran also called all the development that's happened in Long Branch in the past five years "phenomenal." "With Netflix opening and so much happening in Monmouth County right now, I think Long Branch is going to be huge over the next 10 years," he said. "You're going to see a major, major investment in overall growth here." Doran, 37, grew up in Highlands and Rumson. But he said home prices in those tiny towns have priced out most young buyers. "All my friends I grew up with would move back to Rumson tomorrow. But there's no availability in those towns," he said. "So they're looking elsewhere to buy. And Long Branch is only the natural next trajectory." "It's going to be all high-rise condos with really nice amenities all along Ocean Avenue," he predicted. "And all those people don't want to get in their car and drive 30 minutes away for a good sandwich and good coffee." The Inkwell Lofts was built and is owned by Ralph Zucker, CEO of Somerset Development, and the owner of Bell Works in Holmdel. Designed by Minno & Wasko Architects and Planners, condos have either one-bedroom-plus-den or two-bedroom floor plans, with select homes featuring additional dens. Each condo has private balconies, hardwood flooring, oversized windows and open-concept layouts filled with natural light. See inside units here. There's a rooftop terrace with an outdoor kitchen and ocean views and an indoor parking garage next door with EV charging stations. There are six condos left still on the market, with prices ranging from $830,000 to $1,125,000. Louis Critelli of Critelli Realtors is the broker of record and exclusively doing the sales.
