title: I tried frozen custard from Culver's, Freddy's, and Shake Shack — and there's only one chain I'm rushing to return to
text: I tried frozen custard from Culver's, Freddy's, and Shake Shack — and there's only one chain I'm rushing to return to. I ordered frozen custard from Culver's, Freddy's, and Shake Shack. The winning dessert came from a Midwest favorite. Savannah Born I visited chains Culver's, Freddy's, and Shake Shack in search of the best frozen custard . Freddy's seemed to have solid prices, and Shake Shack's portion size felt generous. In the end, Culver's left me most impressed with its frozen-custard desserts. Nothing beats a sip, spoon, or bite of anything cold on a hot summer day — especially frozen custard. Best described as ice cream's rich cousin, frozen custard is made with egg yolks, which are meant to give it a thick, dense consistency. Culver's, Freddy's Frozen Custard & Steakburgers , and Shake Shack are all known for their custard, including blended concoctions, and I was curious which had the best. There was only one way to find out. I spent the same Wednesday night at all three chains, ordering a plain vanilla custard and (when possible) an Oreo-themed custard concrete. To keep things fair, I opted for the smallest size of each. Here's how they measured up in taste, value, and price. I started at Culver's, a Midwest staple. Savannah Born Culver's is a beloved Midwest staple based in Wisconsin. What started as a regional specialty operates over 1,000 locations across 26 states, though Midwesterners (myself included) still claim it as their own. I grew up in Illinois just five minutes from a Culver's. The chain is known for its ButterBurgers, and of course, its custard. Culver's seemed moderately busy for a weeknight. Savannah Born The first thing I noticed when I arrived at my local Culver's was a partially full parking lot and kids peeping at me from the windows. Diners occupied about six tables, and judging by appearances, a significant portion were under the age of 10. As much as I enjoyed the family vibe, the restaurant itself wasn't anything special. I kind of felt like I was in a healthcare setting, thanks to the plain gray tables, generic carpet, and fluorescent lighting. Freddy's is also a Midwest staple, but it's pretty new to me. Savannah Born Another Midwest favorite , Freddy's began in Kansas and has since expanded to 37 states and Canada. It has over 500 stores, including a few near my current home in Indiana. As the name suggests, Freddy's is famous for its signature steakburgers and frozen custard. I'd only ever been here one other time, and it was quite recently. Freddy's seemed much busier than Culver's. Savannah Born A long line awaited me at Freddy's. It stretched not quite to the door, but halfway there. Whereas kids dominated Culver's, Freddy's seemed to have a much older clientele. This might be because of its senior meals , which launched earlier this year and offer discounts to the over-55 crowd. The inside looked notably cute, with a retro red-and-white theme that made it feel like a vintage diner. This was my first time at a Shake Shack. Savannah Born Shake Shack is based in New York, where it started as a hot-dog cart in Madison Square Park. It operates over 350 restaurants in the United States and abroad, yet somehow, I'd never been. From what I've heard, Shake Shack has pretty tasty burgers and custard-based treats. This Shake Shack had a chic, modern vibe. Savannah Born Unlike Culver's and Freddy's, both a few miles from downtown Indianapolis, Shake Shack had a location in the heart of the city. The interior still seemed chic, modern, and industrial, with colorful wall murals, exposed-pipe ceilings, and shiny floors that appeared to be concrete. Much to my surprise, only a few of the tables were in use during my visit. I also liked the convenient self-ordering kiosk. Culver's custard was super customizable. Savannah Born With Culver's create-your-own option, I could choose a vanilla or chocolate custard base, either in a dish or as a Concrete Mixer, and add toppings. For those wondering, a Concrete Mixer is just Culver's trademarked version of a custard concrete — a frozen custard with toppings blended in. Per my plan, I ordered the smallest-size dish of vanilla custard ($3.39) and a vanilla-based Concrete Mixer with Oreo pieces ($4.59). The concrete included two free mix-ins, but I only opted for Oreos. I ordered the same thing at Freddy's. Savannah Born The large menu screens on televisions were out of service when I arrived, but luckily, there were paper menus. I already knew what I wanted, anyway: a small dish of vanilla custard ($3.39) and an Oreo-themed custard concrete ($4.69). Like Culver's, Freddy's concrete custard had a create-your-own option, which included one free mix-in. Mine, of course, was Oreos. Unfortunately, Shake Shack didn't have custard concretes on the menu. Savannah Born Since Shake Shack is partially known for its custard, I expected to find custard concretes. However, they weren't available to order when I asked. Turns out this fan-favorite specialty dessert was removed from US menus in 2020. I was disappointed I didn't get to taste one, especially after reading about the chain's past unique mix-ins, like cereal and, at one point, bits of regional local pies . Without the option for a concrete, I just ordered a small vanilla custard ($4.49). Culver's vanilla custard reminded me of soft-serve, but better. Savannah Born Light in color and dense in texture, the dessert seemed like a thicker version of soft-serve ice cream . It had a velvety mouthfeel and sweet, vanilla-bean-like flavor. The plain vanilla felt anything but plain. That said, I was incredibly disappointed in the portion. I know I ordered the smallest size, but the 8-ounce cup arrived barely half full. I liked the flavor of Freddy's custard, but not the texture. Savannah Born For those seeking a classic vanilla flavor, Freddy's delivered. It was tasty and decadent yet not overpowering. However, the custard itself had a drippy consistency in the bowl and a grainy one in my mouth. Far from smooth, it lacked what defined custard: a luscious, full-bodied texture. Again, I was disappointed in the portion I was served. This one seemed even more scant than Culver's, and my 8-ounce cup had plenty of room left in it. In terms of taste and portion size, Shake Shack's custard impressed me. Savannah Born Shake Shack's vanilla custard wasn't overly sweet, but it still had a strong vanilla taste, and I appreciated the creamy texture. It didn't feel too heavy, either. Shake Shack's small custard seemed like a great value. My portion size felt massive compared to the other chains, to the point where I wondered if the staff had given me extra by mistake. Later, a Shake Shack spokesperson told BI that, in the US, its custard comes in a single scoop (5 ounces) or a double scoop (8 ounces). Although I ordered a small, and that's what I was charged for, I felt like I was served more than 5 ounces. It looked like maybe I'd been given two scoops, too. Culver's Concrete Mixer was worth the hype. Savannah Born When my Concrete Mixer arrived looking as thick as ever, I knew I was in for a treat. The concrete custard was so firm that I could flip the cup like a Dairy Queen Blizzard without anything spilling out — and the texture mirrored it, too. It was even silkier than Culver's plain vanilla custard. I didn't expect to find substantial chunks of Oreos, either, yet the concrete was peppered with large and small bits that fell apart in my mouth. The Concrete Mixer checked every box and more. Freddy's concrete custard had a solid taste, but a too-soft texture. Savannah Born Similar to its plain vanilla custard, Freddy's Oreo-themed concrete had a nice vanilla flavor. And like Culver's, it had real cookie pieces. But the custard itself didn't seem firm enough to me. Soft and liquidy, it mimicked a shake rather than a concrete. As I ate it with a spoon, I wondered if I could drink it with a straw. (Later, I tested it and confirmed that I could.) Comparing the prices and value of the custards was surprisingly tricky. Savannah Born I was unable to find the portion sizes for the custards and concretes at each chain on the menu or online — eventually, I just reached out to local stores and company headquarters directly to confirm. As I mentioned, my small vanilla custards at Freddy's and Culver's should have been served in 8-ounce dishes, and my Shake Shack custard should have been a 5-ounce single scoop. I paid $3.39 for a small vanilla custard at Culver's and Freddy's. Shake Shack's version cost me $4.49 — $1.10 more — but to be fair, my custard portion seemed almost double the size ... even though, on paper, it was supposed to be smaller. In terms of custard concretes, Freddy's had a slight price advantage. At Culver's, my small 8-ounce Concrete Mixer came to $4.59, or $0.57 per ounce. Freddy's small 10-ounce concrete mixer cost $4.69, or $0.47 per ounce. All in all, though, prices felt pretty comparable and fair across the board. Two chains were almost tied for best plain vanilla custard, but neither was my favorite dessert I tasted. Savannah Born In terms of plain vanilla custard, it was a toss-up between Culver's and Shake Shack. In my opinion, Shake Shack dominated in the value department, considering the generous portion I received (though I'd have to try ordering it again to see whether it was just my lucky day). For the best taste and texture, however, I'd still recommend Culver's plain vanilla custard. It had the densest, most unique consistency and the sweetest flavor. Still, there's only one dessert I tried that really blew me away ... In the end, Culver's Concrete Mixer was my favorite custard dessert by a landslide. Savannah Born Out of the desserts I tried, Culver's Concrete Mixer was the only one I'd order again. It dominated in taste and value, and even though it cost a smidge more per ounce than Freddy's, I'd gladly pay a little extra. Plus, I liked the 8-ounce size, especially for such a rich treat. Any more would have been too much of a good thing — for me, anyway. Business Insider reached out to Freddy's, Shake Shack, and Cuver's for comment. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Oil prices jump after Iran publishes restrictive draft plan for Strait of Hormuz
text: Oil prices jump after Iran publishes restrictive draft plan for Strait of Hormuz. Crude oil prices rose Thursday after Iranian state news published a draft plan with restrictive conditions for ship traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose about 4% to $82.72 per barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate was up about 3.5% to $77.83. Prices have fallen about 8% this week after President Donald Trump, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said a deal was near to increase traffic through the strait. The Iranian state news agency Fars on Thursday published the text of what it described as an "initial draft of the strategic plan for managing Strait of Hormuz." Under the apparent draft plan, Iran would ban U.S. and Israeli ships from transiting the strait. Other nations that have harmed Iran would not be allowed to transit until compensation is paid, according to the draft. Tehran will impose penalties on violators equivalent to 20% of the value of cargo aboard a ship. The plan is under review by an Iranian parliamentary committee, according to Fars. Meanwhile, a tanker reported hearing two explosions off the coast of Oman while transiting Hormuz, according to a Wednesday incident report from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre. The crew and vessel are safe. Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen claimed Thursday to have attacked Saudi Arabian troop concentrations there. The Houthis said Wednesday that they attacked a Saudi tanker in the Red Sea off the coast of its Yanbu export terminal.

title: Saudi Crude Shipments to US Plunge to Zero as Oil Refiners Pivot
text: Saudi Crude Shipments to US Plunge to Zero as Oil Refiners Pivot. US imports of Saudi Arabian oil dropped to zero in July, the first time that’s happened for an entire month since 1985, according to preliminary government data. Saudi oil exports have been disrupted for months as the US-Iran conflict all but shut down Persian Gulf crude flows. Last month, US-bound shipments of the kingdom’s crude ground to a halt, according to US Department of Energy data released Wednesday. It’s a significant decline given that US refiners were buying more than 800,000 barrels of Saudi oil a day earlier this year.

title: Rents are down in the Miami area but many still can't afford it
text: Rents are down in the Miami area but many still can't afford it - Rental prices in South Florida have continued to trend downwards, according to a report by Realtor.com. - According to the company's June 2026 Rental Report, June marked the 35th consecutive month of year-over-year decline for properties with 0-2 bedrooms "across the 50 largest metros" in the U.S. Rental prices in South Florida have continued to trend downwards, according to a report by Realtor.com. According to the company's June 2026 Rental Report, June marked the 35th consecutive month of year-over-year rent decline for properties with zero to two bedrooms "across the 50 largest metros" in the U.S. In the Miami-Fort Lauderdale-West Palm Beach area, the median asking rent was $2,277 in June, down 2.6% year-over-year, according to the report. Still, the region is notoriously expensive — a report analyzing 2024 data recently listed the Miami area as having surpassed New York in cost of living expenses. Overall, rent for properties of up to two bedrooms "across the 50 largest metropolitan areas dropped by 1.5% compared to the previous year." The median asking rent also dropped slightly to $1,692, $25 lower than the prior year. The median asking rent is still $238, or 16.4%, higher than pre-pandemic levels recorded in June of 2019. Rental homes out of reach for 'millions' Rental homes are out of reach for "millions" of low-wage workers — in Florida alone, you'd have to work 91 hours per week to afford a one-bedroom at minimum wage. That's according to the 2026 Out of Reach report, published by The National Low Income Housing Coalition, a self-described nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. The report lists "housing wages" by state and metro area, which it defines as estimates of the income required to afford a rental home at HUD’s Fair Market Rent without spending 30% of one's wages on housing. Nationally, the housing wage for 2026 was $34.73 per hour for a "modest" two-bedroom rental, and $29.19 for a one-bedroom rental. The average hourly wage for renters was $24.84. How Florida rent prices compare Florida ranked as the 10th most expensive state overall, with an hourly housing wage of $37.93 required to afford a two-bedroom apartment, for which the fair market rent was listed as $1,973. That means, to "afford this level of rent and utilities" without spending more than 30% of their income on housing, a renter in Florida must earn $6,575 per month, or $78,905 per year. Within the state, Monroe County, home of the Florida Keys, was first on the list of most expensive areas, requiring a housing wage of $48.15 to afford a two bedroom at fair market rent. Monroe County also ranked as the second most expensive nonmetropolitan county or county equivalent nationally, beat only by Nantucket town in Massachusetts. The Miami-Miami Beach-Kendall area followed closely, with a housing wage of $46.85 required to afford a two-bedroom. The Fort Lauderdale area required an hourly wage of $44.87, and the West Palm Beach-Boca Raton area required a wage of $43.35. Meanwhile, the state's minimum wage is $14, while the average renter's wage is $24.27, according to the report. title: Californians revealed as awfully cheap tippers in new national rankings
text: Californians revealed as awfully cheap tippers in new national rankings. Golden State diners may be all about sunshine — but when it comes to tipping, they’re leaving servers in the shade. California diners tipped less than any other state in the nation, according to a new report that ranked the Bear Flag State dead last in restaurant generosity. The state’s overall tip rate came in at 17.3%, about 1.5 percentage points below the national average of 18.8%, according to Toast’s Q1 2026 Restaurant Tipping Trends report. That means Cali’s customers were the biggest wallet squeezers at the table — at least when it comes to card and digital payments tracked by the restaurant technology company. Toast analyzed aggregated tip transactions from restaurants using its platform, which serves roughly 171,000 locations nationwide. Sign up for the California Morning Report newsletter California's top news, sports and entertainment delivered to your inbox every day. Thanks for signing up! The report did not include cash tips, meaning the findings don’t capture every dollar diners may have slipped servers under the table. Still, California couldn’t catch a break in either major category. At quick-service restaurants, Golden State diners tipped just 14.8%, trailing the national average of 15.8%. Nationwide, tipping habits have remained relatively steady over the past two years, with full-service restaurant tips hovering between 19.1% and 19.4% and quick-service tips holding around 15.8% to 16%, according to Toast. Industry observers say California’s lower tip numbers may have less to do with stinginess and more to do with its unique restaurant landscape — including higher menu prices, a requirement that servers receive the full state minimum wage before tips, and the growing use of service charges at some restaurants. In other words: diners may be tipping differently — not necessarily skipping out entirely. Still, the numbers put California at the bottom of the tipping totem pole. It was followed by the District of Columbia, where diners tipped an average of 17.5%, Washington at 17.8%, Nevada at 18.2% and Florida at 18.3%. Meanwhile, Delaware diners proved the most generous tippers in the nation, leaving an average overall tip rate of 22.1%. For comparison, New Yorkers landed closer to the middle of the pack, with an overall tip rate of 18.7% — just below the national average. The report also found that Americans are far more likely to reward sit-down service than grab-and-go orders. Full-service restaurants averaged a 19.3% tip, while quick-service restaurants averaged 15.8%. Takeout customers were the least generous of all, with an average tip of just 13.7%. As The Post previously reported, a recent Popmenu survey found that 78% of consumers believe tipping practices have “become ridiculous,” while 74% said they’ve noticed restaurants raising the suggested gratuity amounts displayed on digital payment screens. Those prompts may be influencing behavior: 59% of the 1,000 adults surveyed said they feel compelled to leave a tip when faced with a suggested gratuity screen. The pushback has fueled a growing backlash against so-called “tip creep” — the expansion of tipping requests into places where customers traditionally weren’t expected to leave gratuities. Still, restaurant owners say Americans continue to support tipping when it’s tied to actual service. “It’s kind of ingrained in American culture that if you go out to dinner at a restaurant, and you sit down and you’re served, I think that a 20% tip is a good tip,” Vicki Parmelee, owner of Jumby Bay Island Grill in Jupiter, Florida, previously told Fox News Digital. But Parmelee said customers are increasingly frustrated by payment screens that ask for tips in situations where gratuities were once uncommon — like grabbing a coffee or ordering at a counter. “It is pretty annoying to go up to a service counter and order a coffee and then have them turn around a terminal and expect a tip just for handing you a coffee,” she said. More than a third of consumers surveyed — 36% — said they typically skip the preset options and enter a custom tip instead, suggesting diners are looking for more control over when and how much they give. “A tip is always something that’s earned,” Parmelee said. “It’s not something they should ever expect.” So while California may have plenty of five-star views, perfect weather and beachside dining spots, its tipping habits earned a decidedly less glamorous ranking. title: ConocoPhillips CEO Ryan Lance departs as oil producer posts best profit since 2022
text: ConocoPhillips CEO Ryan Lance departs as oil producer posts best profit since 2022. ConocoPhillips said on Thursday that CEO Ryan Lance will retire after 14 years, with CFO Andy O'Brien set to succeed him on September 1 after the oil and gas producer posted better-than-expected quarterly profit. The departure caps a tumultuous period for ConocoPhillips. The company cut 20-25% of its workforce in September after it hired management consulting firm Boston Consulting Group to advise on the restructuring. Lance took responsibility for the job cuts at the time, telling employees that the company had become less competitive as it focused on swallowing smaller rivals. ConocoPhillips struck two multibillion-dollar deals in recent years: buying smaller peer Marathon Oil in 2024 for $22.5 billion and acquiring Concho Resources for $9.7 billion in 2021. It also acquired Permian assets from oil major Shell for $9.5 billion. Despite those challenges, the company on Thursday posted its highest net income since 2022 on the back of sturdy oil prices in recent months, which have also boosted other oil majors like ExxonMobil XOM.N and Chevron Corp CVX.N. Shares of ConocoPhillips, the largest U.S. independent oil and gas producer, rose about 1% to $116.13 at midday. "This has been coming for a while. Ryan's done, I think, a great job ... It's a volatile environment and the financial results are good, the Marathon acquisition's mostly integrated and you've got Andy — a well-tenured executive," said Dan Pickering, chief investment officer at Pickering Energy Partners. Fourteen years at the helm Lance took the helm of the company in 2012 after ConocoPhillips split from refining business Phillips 66 PSX.N, leaving it as a pure exploration and production company. During his tenure, ConocoPhillips emerged as one of the largest independent oil and gas producers globally, with operations spanning North America, Europe, the Asia-Pacific region and the Middle East. Lance also oversaw a series of major portfolio moves, including the sale of billions of dollars of noncore assets following the 2014 oil price collapse and massive oil price drops in 2020 after the COVID-19 pandemic crushed demand. O'Brien takes over as CEO Lance will become executive chair and O'Brien will take over as CEO on September 1, the company said. Konnie Haynes-Welsh, who joined ConocoPhillips in 2012 as a finance vice president and controller, will become senior vice president and chief financial officer. "Andy (O'Brien) very much fits the mold of a large company executive — thinks before he talks, measured," Pickering said. "He's managed and handled a lot of different roles and responsibilities within the company. He understands the technical nature of what ConocoPhillips is doing, and he's very familiar with the assets." Current and former employees described O'Brien as smart, driven and thorough, with one saying he was unafraid to make difficult decisions. He joined the company in 1997 and has held roles in finance, planning and strategy, in addition to overseeing the company's Alaskan and international businesses, commercial, LNG and mergers and acquisitions. Amid the other leadership changes, Khoa Dao, currently chief commercial officer, will become the senior vice president of commercial and strategy, according to an internal company memo seen by Reuters. "I don't see any change in COP's strategy under O'Brien as O'Brien had been in lock-step with Ryan on all key strategic decisions ... I believe O'Brien is the right person to lead the company going forward," said Simon Wong, a portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds The company recently agreed to acquire a 42% stake in a joint venture in the Kirkuk oilfields in northern Iraq and signed an agreement to re-enter Syria. Second-quarter results exceed forecast ConocoPhillips posted an adjusted profit of $3.24 per share for the second quarter ended June 30, beating average analyst estimates of $2.88 per share, according to data compiled by LSEG. Revenue rose 32.4% to $19.5 billion in the quarter, beating estimates of $18.8 billion. Production dipped nearly 6% to 2.25 million barrels of oil equivalent per day (boepd), however, while the company's average realized price was $62.33 per barrel of oil equivalent (boe), 36% higher than a year earlier. Rival producers Occidental Petroleum and Diamondback as well as oil majors Chevron and Exxon Mobil have all reported multiyear high profits on the back of high oil prices stemming from the Iran war. ConocoPhillips shares have gained over 24% so far this year, largely in line with Diamondback's stock, but weaker than Occidental's, which has risen about 37.5%. Benchmark Brent crude averaged about $93.58 per barrel during the April-to-June period, up more than 32% from a year earlier, driven by geopolitical tensions in the Middle East that raised concerns about global oil supplies. The company forecast third-quarter production between 2.29 million boepd and 2.32 million boepd.

title: We're adding a critical enabler of AI computing to our Bullpen watchlist
text: We're adding a critical enabler of AI computing to our Bullpen watchlist. Every weekday, the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer releases the Homestretch — an actionable afternoon update, just in time for the last hour of trading on Wall Street. Stocks are dipping on Thursday, led to the downside by the Dow Jones Industrial Average . The S & P 500 is digesting its run to new highs for the second session in a row. Oil and bonds are a slight headwind, with energy prices moving higher as the market awaits more clarity on a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and allow safe passage of oil tankers. Bond yields are up, with the yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury pushing back above 4.65% We're looking to add new names following some recent adjustments. Honeywell Aerospace and Procter & Gamble are out of the portfolio, while our remaining Dover position is held for sale. Against this backdrop, we're adding the memory-chip maker Micron Technology to the Bullpen. This was an idea we suggested after learning that the forced selling by a highly levered, AI-focused hedge fund had ended, creating a clearing event to repurchase many AI stocks that had fallen between 30% and 50% from their highs. Micron has had a strong rebound since the morning of July 30, but shares are still 25% below their record close of $1,213.56 on June 25. The broader memory semiconductor market is dominated by three big companies: Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix in South Korea, and Idaho-based Micron here in the U.S. Within the memory market, the main two products to know are NAND and DRAM. Think about NAND as more of a longer-term storage, like a flash drive. DRAM is what's considered working memory, like the RAM in your computer. A specialized form of DRAM is HBM, or high-bandwidth memory, which is the key enabling technology for modern AI workloads. AI accelerators, such as the graphics processing units (GPUs) made by Club name Nvidia and rival Advanced Micro Devices , do the math that underpins AI computing, but they rely on HBM to store and feed them data. Since the AI boom took off, DRAM and NAND industry demand has significantly exceeded industry supply, and this ongoing shortage has led to huge price increases and exceptional margins at Micron. The company said on its earnings call in June that these tight industry conditions are expected to persist beyond calendar 2027 because of AI-driven demand and structural supply constraints. The key concern with Micron is that the memory industry has historically been a boom-and-bust business, and many investors believe this cycle won't be any different. That skepticism helps explain why the stock trades at an extremely cheap price-to-earnings multiple of less than 9 times calendar year 2027 estimates despite strong fundamentals. However, Micron has been trying to ease those concerns by signing strategic customer agreements, or SCAs, to fundamentally change its business model. The company has signed 16 agreements so far, and the typical deal is a five-year term from calendar 2026 through the end of 2030. These agreements represent about 20% of its DRAM volume and 33% of its NAND volume. They are structured as take-or-pay agreements, with the largest contracts featuring a price ceiling set at the second-quarter market price and a floor that still guarantees Micron strong margins. While the pricing structure puts a ceiling on margin expansion, it also provides greater durability, allowing margins to remain elevated for longer than in previous cycles. title: Decoded: What an Earnings Catalyst Actually Does to a Stock’s Trajectory
text: Decoded: What an Earnings Catalyst Actually Does to a Stock’s Trajectory. Few forces in financial markets move as decisively — or as fast — as an earnings catalyst. When a company reports results that materially diverge from expectations, the ripple effects can reshape valuations, trigger institutional repositioning, and redefine the narrative around an entire sector. Yet for many investors, these events remain poorly understood, treated as binary bets rather than structured intelligence opportunities. Getting serious about how earnings catalysts work is one of the most leveraged moves any market participant can make. At its core, an earnings catalyst is any earnings-related event — a quarterly report, a pre-announcement, a guidance revision, or even a post-earnings analyst call — that causes a meaningful and sustained shift in a stock’s price and investor sentiment. The word “catalyst” is key here. It signals a change agent, not merely an event. Just as a chemical catalyst accelerates a reaction without being consumed by it, an earnings catalyst doesn’t just move a stock temporarily — it creates conditions for a new price equilibrium to establish itself. That’s the business intelligence angle most retail participants miss entirely. Understanding what separates a true earnings catalyst from routine earnings noise requires digging into the architecture of market expectations. Wall Street analysts publish consensus estimates ahead of every earnings release. These figures — revenue, earnings per share, gross margins, forward guidance — become embedded in a stock’s current price through a process of continuous discounting. When results hit exactly in line with consensus, the market often shawws almost no reaction, because the information was already baked in. The earnings catalyst phenomenon emerges when there is a genuine surprise — either dramatically better or dramatically worse than what the market had priced. The magnitude of that surprise, combined with the credibility of the forward outlook, determines how explosive the catalyst becomes. Business intelligence tools have fundamentally changed how sophisticated investors approach earnings season. Alternative data providers now offer satellite imagery of retail parking lots, credit card transaction aggregates, app download metrics, and web traffic trends — all feeding into proprietary models designed to forecast earnings outcomes before the official report drops. Hedge funds and institutional desks have built entire research infrastructure around the idea of front-running the earnings catalyst by developing better information — legally — than what the consensus reflects. For individual investors, understanding this intelligence ecosystem is itself a form of competitive advantage, even if they can’t replicate the full data stack. One of the most overlooked dimensions of any earnings catalyst is the guidance component. A company can beat estimates handily on the top and bottom line and still see its stock sell off sharply if forward guidance disappoints. This dynamic is especially pronounced in high-growth sectors where the market prices companies based on future cash flow potential rather than current profitability. The earnings catalyst, in these cases, isn’t the beat — it’s the reset of the growth trajectory. Investors anchored only to the headline EPS number frequently get blindsided by post-earnings moves that seem contradictory until you understand what actually moved the needle. Sector context matters enormously when evaluating an earnings catalyst. In defensive sectors like utilities or consumer staples, earnings surprises tend to produce muted price responses because the growth profiles are stable and expectations don’t swing dramatically. In technology, semiconductors, or biotech, the same magnitude of surprise can produce double-digit percentage moves in hours. This variance is captured in a metric called Earnings Response Coefficient, or ERC, which measures how sensitively a stock’s price responds to unexpected earnings information. Tracking ERC over multiple quarters gives investors a calibrated sense of how reactive a given name is likely to be — a critical input for positioning around potential catalysts. Timing and positioning strategy around an earnings catalyst requires discipline. Options markets often price in elevated implied volatility heading into earnings, which means simply buying calls or puts can be expensive even when the directional thesis is correct. Experienced traders frequently use spread structures to reduce the cost of participation, or they focus on post-earnings momentum rather than trying to predict the immediate reaction. The business intelligence framework here is less about guessing the number and more about assessing whether the stock’s current valuation already reflects a best-case or worst-case scenario — and where the asymmetry of surprise actually lives. What makes earnings catalyst analysis genuinely powerful is its compounding nature. Investors who develop structured, repeatable processes for evaluating earnings setups — analyzing expectations gaps, studying historical response patterns, monitoring alternative data signals, and reading management credibility through transcript analysis — build an edge that strengthens over time. Markets are not perfectly efficient around earnings events, and that inefficiency is where informed, disciplined investors earn disproportionate returns. Treating every earnings season as a business intelligence exercise rather than a guessing game is the shift that separates reactive market participation from proactive, thesis-driven investing.

title: Fed’s Lisa Cook ready to hike rates if ‘too high’ inflation stays elevated
text: Fed’s Lisa Cook ready to hike rates if ‘too high’ inflation stays elevated. Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook warned Wednesday that she is prepared to hike interest rates if inflation doesn’t start to cool off – as an increasing number of officials signal a readiness to tighten policy. “I am prepared to act by raising rates, if necessary,” Cook — whom President Trump tried to fire over alleged mortgage fraud — said at the Economic Luncheon of the Anchorage Economic Development Corporation in Anchorage, Alaska. “I would support an increase, if it becomes necessary, to bring inflation down. It may not.” She argued that the risks to the price stability side of the Fed’s mandate are higher than risks to its goal of full employment, as the US faces “too high” levels of inflation. Cook also said that the Fed is running out of time to deal with stubborn inflation, which has been running above its 2% goal for more than five years – easing slightly to 3.5% in June. “Inflation may become entrenched in price- and wage-setting behavior, leading to persistence that would be much harder for us to attack,” Cook said. “While we might be able to afford to wait for longer in a different environment, we do not have that luxury in this one.” At the Fed’s meeting last week, Cook was among the nine officials who voted to hold interest rates in the key 3.5% to 3.75% range – though three officials preferred to hike rates, a sign of deepening dissent within the board over how aggressively they should tackle inflation. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack and Minneapolis’ Neel Kashkari tried to raise rates by a quarter point. Others – like New York Fed President John Williams and Philadelphia’s Anna Paulson – have also signaled an openness to raising rates. “I felt it was appropriate not to change rates while we see how” inflation pans out, Cook said Wednesday – nodding to uncertain elements like tariffs, the Middle East conflict and massive AI spending. However, she said: “I am firmly committed to restoring price stability.” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who has been on the job for less than three months, repeatedly emphasized the committee’s promise to lower prices at the Fed’s meeting last week – but he also refused to answer when he would be ready to raise rates. Inflation eased slightly in June on falling energy prices, but oil prices have since spiked and dipped several times amid back-and-forth reports over negotiations with Iran. The debate for officials has become whether one good inflation report is enough to shake off concerns around prices – and whether they would be raising interest rates too soon as a result, potentially stunting economic growth. The opposite concern is that officials could wait too long to raise rates, allowing inflation to run rampant. Last August, Trump attempted to fire Cook, a Biden appointee, over allegations of mortgage fraud. Powell – who Trump called “stupid” and “hardheaded” for not slashing interest rates faster – and one of his predecessors, Ben Bernanke, attended oral arguments in the case earlier this year to show solidarity with Cook. title: 8 things to know before starting a backyard renovation
text: 8 things to know before starting a backyard renovation Before you break ground on a backyard renovation, check permits, fix drainage and plan the layout so the project stays on budget and on schedule A backyard renovation looks simple from the curb. Pick a style, hire a crew, add a patio or a pool, and enjoy the results by summer. But the parts that actually decide whether the project goes well rarely show up in inspiration photos. They show up in a permit application, a utility locate ticket, a soil test, or a grading plan. That is the unglamorous groundwork that determines whether the visible upgrades hold up over time. Skipping that groundwork is where most backyard renovation problems start. A deck built without a permit can become a liability when the home is sold. A patio poured without checking the slope can send water toward the foundation instead of away from it. A fence post sunk without calling the utility locate service can knock out power or gas service to an entire block. None of these mistakes show up on a mood board, and none of them are cheap to fix after the fact. The upside is that almost all of this groundwork is knowable in advance. Building departments publish permit thresholds. The national utility locate service is a free phone call. Soil tests, drainage slopes, and plant hardiness data are all public information, and looking them up takes only a few minutes. None of it requires design expertise. It requires knowing which questions to ask before the shovels come out. The eight items below cover the planning steps that landscapers, contractors, and building departments treat as standard practice for a backyard renovation. They run from permits and utility lines to drainage, soil, and the order in which the work should happen. Some apply to every project, regardless of budget. Others matter most for specific additions, like a pool, a retaining wall, or an irrigation system. Together, they cover decisions that are far easier to get right at the planning stage. Fixing them later, once the concrete has set or the plants are already in the ground, costs far more. Check permits and HOA rules before you break ground Credit: Ivan S / Pexels Most permanent backyard structures need a permit. Skipping that step can create problems well after the renovation is finished. Decks above a certain height, sheds over a certain square footage, pools, tall retaining walls, and some fences typically require sign-off from the local building department before work begins. The exact thresholds vary by city and county. That is why the first call in any backyard renovation should go to the local building or planning department, not to a contractor. Some places exempt small, low decks or sheds under 120 square feet. Others require a permit for any structure attached to the house, since it affects the building's structural load or drainage path. A short phone call or a look at the department's website settles the question for a specific project. Homeowners associations add a second layer, and it runs separately from city permits. An HOA can require approval for a fence style, a paint color, a shed's placement, or even a change to plant beds visible from the street. That approval process can take weeks on its own. Submitting to the HOA and the building department at the same time, rather than one after the other, keeps a renovation timeline from stalling. Unpermitted work causes the most damage later, not during construction. When a home goes up for sale, many states require disclosure of unpermitted additions. A buyer's lender or inspector can flag a deck or pool that was never signed off. That can delay a sale, reduce an offer, or force the seller to get the work retroactively permitted. Sometimes that means tearing out finished construction just to expose it for inspection. Homeowners insurance can also deny a claim tied to an unpermitted structure, such as storm damage to a deck that was never inspected. Permits exist to catch real safety issues before they become expensive ones. A retaining wall that is not engineered for the soil behind it is one example. A pool barrier that does not meet code is another, along with electrical work for outdoor lighting that was never inspected. A building inspector's visit during a backyard renovation is not a bureaucratic hurdle. It is one of the few free, independent checks a homeowner gets on the quality of the work. Call 811 before you dig Credit: Nelson Axigoth / Pexels 811 is a free, federally designated national phone number. It connects a caller to a local one-call center, which notifies utility companies to mark buried gas, electric, water, sewer, and cable lines before any digging starts. It applies to a backyard renovation just as much as it applies to a construction site. Dialing 811 from anywhere in the U.S. routes the call to the correct regional center based on the caller's location. A representative asks for the address, the boundaries of the work area, and a description of the project. The center then notifies every utility operator with lines in that area. Each one sends a locator to mark the approximate position of buried lines with flags or spray paint. That typically happens within a couple of business days, though the exact window varies by state. The list of projects that require a call is longer than most homeowners assume. Installing a mailbox post, building a deck, planting a tree, or putting in a fence line all count as digging under most state one-call laws. So does laying a paver patio or trenching for a sprinkler system. Utility lines are often buried just a few inches below the surface. That means even shallow digging for flowers or shrubs can strike one. Calling 811 is free in every state, and in a number of states, including California and Nevada, it is a legal requirement before any excavation. Skipping the call is not a minor risk. Striking a gas or electric line can cut off service to an entire block, cause injury, and leave the homeowner liable for repair costs and, in some states, fines. Once the utilities respond and the lines are marked, it is worth waiting for every operator on the list to confirm before breaking ground. A line that has not yet responded is a line that has not yet been located. The flags and paint marks should stay in place, undisturbed by pets, mowing, or foot traffic, until the digging for that project is finished. If the project changes or expands later in the renovation, a new call is worth making. Erosion, prior digging, or root growth can shift where lines actually sit compared with where they were marked before. Get the drainage and grading right before anything else Credit: Denys Razumovskyi / Pexels The ground within 10 feet of a house's foundation should drop at least six inches. That is the drainage standard set by the International Residential Code, and it exists so rainwater flows away from the house instead of pooling against it. That single number is worth checking before any backyard renovation adds a patio, raised bed, or retaining wall. A backyard renovation changes the shape of a yard, and shape determines where water goes. A new patio, an added set of garden beds, or a retaining wall can unintentionally flatten a slope that used to carry water away from the house. It can also redirect that water toward a neighbor's yard instead. Impervious surfaces like concrete and pavers are held to their own standard under the same code: a minimum two percent slope away from the building. Hard surfaces shed water faster than soil or lawn, so the standard is stricter. Fixing a drainage problem is far cheaper before hardscaping and planting begin than after. Regrading a bare yard means moving soil with a shovel or a small excavator. Regrading a yard with a finished patio, an irrigation system, and new plantings already in place means tearing some of that work out first. Then it has to be rebuilt a second time. A few signs point to a drainage issue worth addressing at the planning stage. Standing water that takes more than a day to drain after a normal rain is one. A soggy patch that never fully dries out is another, along with water visibly pooling near the foundation or a basement with a history of dampness. Any of these should shape where a deck, patio, or planting bed goes, not just how it looks. Common fixes include a swale, a shallow, sloped channel that redirects surface water around a problem area. A French drain is another option: a buried perforated pipe surrounded by gravel that carries water to a lower point. Downspout extensions help too, carrying roof runoff several feet away from the foundation instead of dumping it at the base of the house. A landscaper or drainage contractor can usually diagnose which fix a yard needs with a single site visit. That visit is worth scheduling before the rest of the renovation gets designed around it. Confirm your property lines and easements Credit: Muharrem Alper / Pexels A survey or a recorded plat map is the only reliable way to know exactly where a property line falls, not a fence, hedge, or a neighbor's word. Confirming that line before a backyard renovation starts is one of the simplest ways to avoid a dispute with a neighbor later. Older fences and hedges are frequently off from the actual property line by a foot or more. Sometimes the original owner guessed. Sometimes the boundary was never marked precisely in the first place. Building a new fence, shed, or retaining wall along what looks like the line, rather than the surveyed line, can be a costly mistake. A neighbor or a title search may later prove it sits on the wrong side, and it has to come out. Most counties keep plat maps and property records on file with the recorder's office or assessor's office, and many now post them online by parcel number or address. That record shows the legal boundary, but not always its exact physical location on the ground. For a project that involves permanent construction close to the line, such as a fence, a detached structure, or a pool, hiring a licensed surveyor is worth the cost. Staking the actual corners removes any guesswork for a price that is small next to moving a finished structure. Setback rules add another layer on top of the property line itself. Most municipal codes require a structure to sit a minimum distance back from the line, often measured in feet from the rear and side boundaries. That minimum can differ for a shed, a fence, a pool, or an addition to the house. An HOA can add its own setback requirement on top of the municipal one, and the stricter of the two applies. Utility easements are the least visible constraint and the easiest to miss. An easement gives a utility company or the local government the legal right to access part of a property, often along the rear or side boundary. The land underneath still belongs to the homeowner, but access to it does not. Building a shed, planting a tree, or installing a fence over an active easement can mean it gets removed at the owner's expense if the utility needs access. A plat map or a call to the local utility will show whether an easement runs through the section of yard a renovation is planned for. Test your soil before you plant anything Credit: Kampus Production / Pexels A soil test reveals pH level, nutrient content, and texture. It is a far more reliable guide to what a yard needs than judging by how the ground looks or feels. Most state land-grant universities run a cooperative extension office that offers this testing to homeowners for a modest fee. The process itself is simple. A homeowner collects a small sample of soil, usually from several spots around the yard mixed together. It gets mailed to the extension lab along with a short form describing what they plan to grow. Results typically come back within one to two weeks. They cover pH, which measures how acidic or alkaline the soil is, along with levels of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium, the three nutrients most plants need in the largest amounts. Most lawn grasses, vegetables, and ornamental plants grow best in soil with a pH between 6.0 and 7.0. That is the range where nutrients are most available to plant roots. Soil that is more acidic or more alkaline than that can lock up nutrients even when they are technically present in the ground. A struggling lawn or garden bed is sometimes a soil chemistry problem, not a watering or sunlight problem. Texture matters as much as chemistry for a backyard renovation. Clay-heavy soil drains slowly and compacts easily under foot traffic or equipment. That makes it a poor base for a lawn or a planting bed without amendment. It can work well, though, for a pond or a rain garden designed to hold water. Sandy soil drains quickly and dries out fast, which suits drought-tolerant plants. A vegetable garden in sandy soil will need more frequent watering and added organic matter to retain moisture and nutrients. Testing before construction begins also flags compaction problems that construction itself can make worse. Heavy equipment, stored materials, and repeated foot traffic during a renovation compress soil, squeezing out the air pockets roots need to grow. A test taken before work starts gives a baseline. Amending compacted soil with compost or other organic matter before planting is far more effective than trying to fix it after sod or shrubs are already in the ground. Know your USDA plant hardiness zone Credit: Enrique / Pexels The USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map divides the U.S. into 13 zones based on average annual extreme minimum winter temperature. Looking up a specific zone by ZIP code is the fastest way to avoid planting something that will not survive winter in a given yard. The USDA released the current version of the map in November 2023, the first update since 2012. Each zone spans a 10-degree Fahrenheit range and splits into "a" and "b" half zones covering five degrees each. A plant tagged as hardy to zone 7a needs a slightly milder minimum winter temperature than one tagged for 7b. The map is built from 30 years of weather station data. The 2023 update used records from 1991 through 2020, pulled from more than 13,000 stations, nearly double the number used for the 2012 version. That update pushed roughly half the country into a warmer half zone than before. The shift came partly from actual warming trends and partly from the added precision of thousands of new weather stations. A plant that struggled in a specific yard under the 2012 map might now be a reasonable choice. But a plant that was already borderline for the old zone is worth rechecking, rather than assuming the shift helps every case. Hardiness zone data matters most for perennials, shrubs, and trees, the plants a backyard renovation expects to survive multiple winters, not just one growing season. An annual flower or a vegetable planted for a single summer does not need to survive winter at all. Hardiness zone is far less relevant to that choice than sunlight and soil are. A yard's hardiness zone, as mapped, is a regional average, not a guarantee for every square foot of a specific property. Microclimates inside a single backyard can push real conditions warmer or colder than the map suggests. A spot next to a south-facing wall or a paved patio tends to run warmer. A low area where cold air settles, or an exposed spot with no windbreak, can run colder than the mapped zone would predict. Build hardscaping before you plant Credit: William Adams / Pexels Structures and utility lines should go into a backyard renovation before soil amendment, sod, or planting begins. Heavy equipment and repeated foot traffic during construction can compact soil and damage plants that are already established. This order, often called hardscape before softscape, is standard practice among landscape contractors for a reason. A typical sequence starts with excavation and grading, which sets the slopes that control drainage for the entire yard. Underground work comes next: irrigation lines, drainage pipe, lighting conduit, and any utility work, all installed and tested while the ground is still open and accessible. Doing this after a patio or lawn is in place means cutting into finished work to reach the pipes and wiring underneath it. Hardscaping follows the underground work. Patios, decks, retaining walls, walkways, and fences are the structures that define how a backyard functions. They are far easier to build on bare or rough ground than around fragile new plantings. Those plantings need protection from foot traffic, dropped tools, and delivery trucks driving over root zones. Soil preparation and planting come last, after the heavy construction is finished. Topsoil, compost, and other amendments perform better when they go down after grading and hardscaping are complete. Regrading later can bury or wash away amendments added too early. Sod and new plantings are also the most vulnerable part of a renovation to construction traffic, so installing them last protects the investment in root establishment and lawn growth. Skipping this order tends to cost money twice. A homeowner who plants first and builds a patio afterward often ends up replacing plants that got crushed, compacted, or buried in construction debris. A yard graded around finished plant beds, rather than before them, sometimes needs those beds dug up again once a drainage problem becomes obvious. Planning the full layout before any single piece of the renovation starts is the safer approach. Following hardscape-to-softscape order during construction is the most reliable way to make each dollar spent hold up through the finished project. Get multiple contractor quotes and verify licensing and insurance Credit: Thirdman / Pexels Getting at least three written quotes from licensed, insured contractors is the most reliable way to gauge a fair price for a backyard renovation. Landscaping and hardscaping costs vary widely by region, by material, and by the scope of a specific project. A single quote gives no basis for comparison, no matter how reasonable it sounds on its own. Verifying a contractor's license is a separate step from getting a quote. It takes only a few minutes through the state contractor licensing board's website, which most states maintain and make searchable by business name or license number. That same search often shows whether a license is active, whether it covers the type of work being quoted, and whether any complaints are on file. Insurance matters as much as licensing. A contractor should be able to provide proof of general liability insurance, which covers property damage during the project, and workers' compensation coverage for their crew. Without both, a homeowner can end up personally liable for an injury on their property or for damage the work causes to a neighboring yard or utility line. A detailed written quote should break down labor, materials, permit fees, and equipment separately, rather than presenting one lump number. A line-item breakdown makes it possible to compare quotes on an apples-to-apples basis and to see where one contractor's price differs from another's. It should also include a payment schedule tied to project milestones, rather than a large payment due upfront before any work has been done. Timing affects pricing more than most homeowners expect. Spring and summer are the busiest season for landscaping and hardscaping contractors in most parts of the country, which tends to push prices higher and booking windows longer. Scheduling a backyard renovation for fall or winter, where climate allows, can bring lower pricing and a shorter wait for the crew to start. Asking to see photos or addresses of a contractor's completed projects, ideally ones similar in scope to the current job, adds one more check before signing a contract.

title: Chevron Turned $3.1 Billion Loss Into A Gain In One Quarter Amid ‘Heightened Volatility’ During Iran War
text: Chevron Turned $3.1 Billion Loss Into A Gain In One Quarter Amid ‘Heightened Volatility’ During Iran War. Topline Chevron’s commodity derivatives—financial contracts used to hedge risks associated with oil shipments—trended upward for the company in its latest quarter after recording a $3.1 billion loss in the previous one amid “heightened volatility” during the Iran war. Key Facts Chevron’s commodity derivatives raked in $368 million in the company’s second quarter, a significant jump from the $3.1 billion loss posted in its first quarter, according to an SEC filing. Chevron disclosed $870 million in margin calls posted as cash collateral in its first quarter, which dropped to $139 million by the quarter ended June 30 and marked a cash recovery that came as oil prices dropped from their highs in March. A footnote in the filing’s derivatives section said “heightened volatility in commodity prices associated with the ongoing conflict in the Middle East” created large losses and forced Chevron to pay out cash to cover its trading accounts. Chevron stock traded up 1.4% to around $188 per share as of Thursday afternoon. Big Number $12.1 billion. That was Chevron’s reported net income in its latest quarter, far above the $2.5 billion it reported in the same period last year. The figure was driven by increased production volumes and the Iran war, which sent commodity prices higher. Tangent Energy firm Phillips 66 said in an earnings call Wednesday it became the third-largest buyer of Venezuelan crude oil, benefiting from maritime trading exemptions doled out by the Trump administration. Phillips 66 was excluded from President Donald Trump’s scrutiny of oil giants this week, as he has blasted Chevron and Exxon for “making too much money” amid the Iran war. Key Background Brent crude, one of the global pricing benchmarks for crude oil, averaged $81 per barrel in the first quarter and surged to an average of $92 per barrel as fears surged around the Iran war. Prices for the oil are up 33% since the start of the year, when the cost for a barrel was about $60. Chevron’s net short position in commodity derivatives means the company profits when oil prices fall. So, as Brent crude surged to well above the $100 mark in March and April, the company eventually benefited from a drop down to about $73 that came in the nick of time for its earnings window. Trump’s anger with Chevron and Exxon’s profits come as gas prices remain stubbornly high despite the recent slump in oil prices, with the president threatening to have the companies “give some of that back to the public,” though Trump did not elaborate on how that could be done.

title: 15 Colleges That Students Can Attend Tuition-Free
text: 15 Colleges That Students Can Attend Tuition-Free. Money Research Collective’s editorial team solely created this content. Opinions are their own, but compensation and in-depth research determine where and how companies may appear. Many featured companies advertise with us. How we make money. 15 Colleges That Students Can Attend Tuition-Free By MONEY RESEARCH COLLECTIVE Rice University just expanded a free tuition program to cover more students. Here are other colleges with similar scholarships. Rice University just made it easier for middle-income families to afford one of the country’s most selective colleges. The Houston-based university announced this week that, beginning with students entering in fall 2027, families earning up to $200,000 a year will qualify for free tuition through its expanded Rice Investment financial aid program. Students from families earning less than $100,000 will receive grants covering tuition, mandatory fees, room and board. Rice will also continue meeting 100% of demonstrated financial need without requiring student loans. While published tuition at many private universities now exceeds $65,000 a year, an increasing number of schools expect many admitted students to pay far less. A number of public universities also offer tuition waivers for in-state students, and some mission-focused colleges have offered free tuition for decades. Here are some of the popular colleges that qualifying students can already attend tuition-free. Harvard University Harvard substantially expanded its aid program in 2025. Students from families earning up to $200,000 generally qualify for free tuition, while many families earning $100,000 or less receive comprehensive aid packages covering tuition, housing, food, health insurance and travel costs. Harvard also doesn’t require loans as part of its financial aid packages, helping many graduates leave school debt-free. Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) MIT now provides free tuition to students from families earning up to $200,000, provided they have typical assets. Families with incomes below roughly $100,000 often qualify for packages that cover the full cost of attendance, including housing, meals and other expenses. Like many elite universities, MIT uses a need-blind admissions process for U.S. applicants, meaning decisions are made based solely on grades, test scores, essays and achievements without looking at your financial data. Once the list of qualifying students is finalized, the university promises to meet 100% of their demonstrated financial need. Princeton University Princeton has long been considered one of the nation’s most generous financial aid providers. Students from families earning up to about $150,000 typically receive grants covering the entire cost of attendance. Families with significantly higher incomes — including many earning well above $250,000 — may still qualify for substantial grant aid depending on assets, family size and other financial circumstances. The university eliminated student loans from financial aid packages more than two decades ago. Yale University Yale offers some of the most generous need-based aid in higher education. Families earning under $100,000 generally pay nothing toward tuition, room or board, while many middle-income families earning up to $250,000 can also receive free tuition. Yale meets 100% of demonstrated financial need without requiring loans. Duke University Beginning with students enrolling in fall 2023, Duke expanded its financial aid so students from North Carolina and South Carolina families earning up to $150,000 qualify for free tuition. Students from those states with family incomes below $65,000 generally receive full financial support covering tuition, housing and meals. Duke has also broadened aid for students from across the U.S., although eligibility varies by income and assets. Berea College Unlike most schools on this list, Berea has offered free tuition for generations. Every admitted student receives a Tuition Promise Scholarship that covers 100% of tuition. Students are still responsible for housing, meals and fees, although financial aid often helps with those costs as well. Located in Kentucky, Berea also requires students to participate in a campus work program, giving every student a paid job while enrolled. College of the Ozarks Nicknamed “Hard Work U.,” College of the Ozarks in Missouri charges no tuition to full-time students. Instead, students work on campus through a required labor program that helps offset educational costs. Many graduates leave with little or no student debt thanks to the school’s model. Students from families earning less than $200,000 annually, with typical assets, can generally expect financial aid packages that fully cover tuition. Those from families earning under $100,000 typically receive grants covering tuition, fees, housing and meals, allowing many students to attend at little or no cost. Caltech also meets 100% of demonstrated financial need for admitted students. Columbia University Columbia has one of the nation’s most generous need-based financial aid programs. Beginning with students entering in fall 2025, families with annual incomes under $150,000, and typical assets, generally qualify for free tuition. Families with incomes below roughly $66,000 often receive aid covering the full cost of attendance, including housing and meals. Columbia also meets 100% of demonstrated financial need without requiring student loans. Emory University Emory recently joined the growing list of colleges expanding aid to middle-income families with the launch of Emory Advantage Plus. Beginning in fall 2026, undergraduate students from families earning up to $200,000, with typical assets, will qualify for grants covering the full cost of tuition. The program applies to Emory College, Oxford College, the undergraduate business program and the nursing school, and builds on Emory’s longstanding commitment to meeting demonstrated financial need. Tufts University Tufts introduced the Tufts Tuition Pact for students entering in fall 2026. Under the program, U.S. undergraduates from families earning less than $150,000 annually, with typical assets, receive grants covering the full cost of tuition. The university continues to meet 100% of demonstrated financial need, and many lower-income students receive additional aid for housing, meals and other educational expenses. University of Chicago The University of Chicago has steadily expanded its financial aid program. Starting in the fall of 2027, students from families earning less than $250,000 can attend tuition-free, while students from families earning up to $125,000 will receive enough aid to also cover room, board and other expenses. The university also offers generous need-based aid to students from across the country, although the tuition guarantee specifically applies to qualifying Illinois residents. University of Michigan Through the Go Blue Guarantee, the University of Michigan offers free tuition to eligible in-state students. Michigan residents whose families earn $125,000 or less and have assets below established limits qualify for four years of free tuition, regardless of academic major. University of Virginia The University of Virginia provides free tuition for qualifying Virginia residents through its AccessUVA financial aid program. In-state students from families earning less than $100,000 generally receive grants covering tuition and mandatory fees, while many also receive assistance for housing and other expenses. The university meets 100% of demonstrated financial need without relying heavily on student loans. Curtis Institute of Music One of the most selective music conservatories in the world, the Curtis Institute of Music in Philadelphia provides every admitted student with a full-tuition scholarship regardless of financial need. Free tuition is especially rare among conservatories, where many aspiring musicians face high costs for specialized training and limited scholarship opportunities. Students are still responsible for living expenses, but the tuition scholarship makes the institution one of the few colleges in America where every student receives the same tuition benefit. Don’t assume a college is too expensive Sticker prices continue to climb, but they often tell only part of the story. Elite private colleges increasingly use financial aid to compete for talented students, meaning families with six-figure incomes may qualify for grants that would have been unimaginable a decade ago. Even households earning well above the national median income can sometimes receive free tuition or significant discounts. The key is looking beyond the published price. Most colleges now offer net price calculators that estimate what your family would actually pay after grants and scholarships. For many students, the most expensive-looking college on paper may end up costing less than an in-state public university once financial aid is factored in.
