title: With loss of another grocery store, North Charleston’s food desert grows drier
text: With loss of another grocery store, North Charleston’s food desert grows drier. NORTH CHARLESTON — One of the last stores offering fresh produce and meat in the city’s south end closed its doors, further limiting food access in an area already facing few options. The Save A Lot on Durant Avenue served its last customers Aug. 5 before moving all operations to the Dorchester Road store five miles away. Shannon McPherson, a North Charleston resident who owns both discount stores, said the decision was not made in haste. He spent the last six months working to keep the store open, but declining profits made it unsustainable. He said a lot of regular customers shop at both locations, so consolidating the stores made sense. Most of the staff is transitioning to the other location, he added. “We’re part of the community and this was a very difficult decision to make,” he said. The Dorchester Road location opened nearly three years ago in the Oak Ridge Plaza shopping center that’s home to Planet Fitness, Dollar General and several restaurants. McPherson said this store is one-third bigger than the Durant Avenue one, providing a larger produce section, more space for meat and dairy, and wider aisles. He said it offers a better shopping experience for customers. “This was not entered into lightly, but we really do think that it’s the best path forward to be able to continue serving North Charleston,” he said. The city’s food desert Richard Fludd, who has lived in the area most of his life, visited the Durant Avenue store during its final week open. He said the closure leaves no grocery options stretching from the lower end of Rivers Avenue to Remount Road. The impact will likely fall hardest on low-income and elderly residents. “That’s what we’re concerned about as a community, what’s the plan to bring in another grocery store?” he said. The city’s south end has struggled to lure a full-service grocery store for nearly two decades, forcing residents in Chicora-Cherokee, Union Heights, Accabee, Dorchester Waylyn and neighborhoods off Rivers Avenue to travel farther for groceries. The area is considered a food desert, a U.S. Department of Agriculture designation identifying low-income areas with limited access to fresh and affordable food. In some of these neighborhoods, nearly 30 percent of residents are in poverty, according to data from Policy Map. Small corner stores and dollar stores attempt to fill the gaps, occasionally offering cartons of eggs or gallons of milk, along with canned food and snacks. Community gardens and urban farms provide small batches of fresh produce. A small, neighborhood grocery store is in the works on Reynolds Avenue. The closest full-service stores include the Walmart Supercenter near the Tanger Outlets, Piggly Wiggly or Food Lion off Remount Road or Food Lion off Dorchester Road. For residents without transportation, getting to any of these stores is difficult. “That’s quite a distance to be toting groceries without personal transportation, and who’s got money for Uber when you can just barely afford food,” said resident Glenn Douglas, who lives off McMillan Avenue. While he has a car, he said he thought of residents who don’t have reliable transportation when he heard about the Durant Avenue store closing. Finding a solution Mayor Reggie Burgess, who has been working to bring a grocery store to the area since taking office in 2024, remains optimistic based on conversations with major retailers. Though none has committed to opening a store, yet. A June 2024 third-party study, initiated by the city, assessed four sites near Rivers Avenue as potential locations for a grocery store. The study identified two locations as the best options: a vacant Kmart on Rivers and McMillan Avenues and a 10.5-acre piece of land near the former Navy Hospital on Rivers Avenue. While local government is not in the business of building grocery stores, Burgess said officials will offer help and guidance when a grocer decides to open in the area. “We’re going to support them as much as we can to get them settled into the southern part of the city so they can actually help that part of the city prosper,” he said. He is hopeful that growth in the area will lure a major supermarket chain. Higher density and higher area median income are the keys to attracting a store, he said. Since grocery stores operate with thin profit margins, around 1 to 3 percent, a store needs to reach a weekly sales benchmark to remain profitable. Burgess pointed to plans for the area’s first bus rapid transit system along the Rivers Avenue corridor, reinvestment into Reynolds Avenue and the ongoing Navy Base redevelopment project. He said the team developing the former base has been in conversations with major grocery chains too. Still, some residents say simply waiting for a retailer to come to the area is not enough. Okeeba Jubalo, the founder of the community-led North Charleston Arts District, said the community lacks basic infrastructure, like quality, affordable grocery stores, despite some home prices in Park Circle soaring above $1 million. “What we need now is creative, local-first leadership,” he said. “And a community willing to champion its own solutions instead of waiting on municipal excuses.”

title: The 7 best U.S. cities for single parents to own a home
text: The 7 best U.S. cities for single parents to own a home Raising kids alone already stretches a single paycheck thin. LendingTree ranks large U.S. cities where homeownership costs the least Raising a child without a second income already means stretching every dollar across rent or a mortgage, child care, groceries and health care. There's no partner's paycheck to absorb a bad month. Housing sits at the center of that balancing act. A monthly payment that runs even a little too high can crowd out everything else a family needs. For a single parent, buying a home carries the promise of stability once the mortgage is signed, but getting there and staying there both depend heavily on how much of that income the housing payment actually eats up. In some cities, that math leaves plenty of room for savings and emergencies. In others, it leaves almost none. Nationally, single parents who own their homes spend just over a quarter of their income on housing, a share that climbs above 40% for those who rent instead. That split shapes which families can eventually make the leap from renting to owning. A smaller housing burden leaves more money free for a down payment, closing costs and the reserves lenders expect to see. Local wages and home prices drive most of the difference from city to city, but property taxes, insurance costs and the pace of new construction all factor into the final number too. A single parent doing the same job in two different cities can end up with housing costs that differ by 10 percentage points or more, a gap wide enough to change the type of home, school district or neighborhood a family can actually afford. LendingTree analyzed U.S. Census Bureau data across the 50 largest American cities to measure exactly what share of income single-parent households spend on housing, breaking the numbers out separately for owners and renters. The gap between cities is stark. Single-parent homeowners in the most expensive markets hand over close to a third of their paycheck every month, while those in the most affordable cities keep that share below a quarter. These seven cities put the least strain on a single parent's budget once the mortgage is signed. Indianapolis Kent Rebman / Unsplash Indianapolis holds the top spot on this list because single-parent homeowners there spend less of their paycheck on housing than anywhere else in the country. LendingTree found that a single parent who owns a home in Indianapolis puts 21.7% of household income toward housing, more than four full percentage points below the next closest city on this list and well under the national average of 25.7% for single-parent homeowners overall. That gap between Indianapolis and the national figure is roughly a full mortgage payment's worth of breathing room every few months. The distance from the most expensive cities is even wider. A single parent who owns a home in Los Angeles spends 31.8% of income on housing, and one in New York spends 31.6%. Indianapolis homeowners keep roughly 10 cents of every dollar that those families don't. LendingTree's affordability index for ownership gives Indianapolis a perfect score of 100 among the 50 cities in the analysis, the only city to hit that ceiling. Indianapolis also posts a single-parent homeownership rate of 42.2%, above the national rate of 39.2%, though wages there haven't caught up with the biggest coastal cities any more than home prices have. Renting tells a different story. Single-parent renters in Indianapolis hand over 41.3% of income, close to the middle of the pack among the 50 cities LendingTree studied and nearly 20 percentage points higher than what owners there pay. That gap between renting and owning is wider in Indianapolis than in almost any other city on this list, which makes the leap into ownership carry unusual financial weight for a single-income family trying to build equity instead of paying it to a landlord. Indianapolis's homeownership index of 64.2 puts it in the middle of the pack on that particular measure, which is why the city ranks lower on LendingTree's broader single-parent housing index, at 74.7, even as it tops this list for ownership costs specifically. The two rankings answer different questions. LendingTree's combined index rewards cities where both the rate of single-parent homeownership and overall affordability score well, while the ownership cost figure isolates something narrower, how much of the paycheck the mortgage takes every month once a single parent actually buys. Indianapolis answers that second question better than any other city in the country. Louisville, Kentucky Joshua Michaels / Unsplash A single parent buying a home in Louisville, Ky., keeps more of the paycheck than in all but one city on this list. LendingTree puts the ownership cost share there at 22.0%, just three-tenths of a point behind Indianapolis and still more than three and a half percentage points under the national average for single-parent homeowners. Louisville also happens to be the only city on this list that ranks near the top for renters and owners alike. Single-parent renters in Louisville spend 36.6% of income on housing, the lowest rent burden among the 50 cities in LendingTree's analysis and a full 4.3 percentage points better than what Indianapolis renters pay. Combine that with the low ownership cost, and Louisville earns a combined affordability score of 97.6 out of 100, the highest of any city ranked here. Only Salt Lake City posts a higher overall single-parent housing index once homeownership rates get factored back in, and that's driven mostly by a homeownership rate Louisville doesn't match. That homeownership rate sits at 42.9% in Louisville, a hair above Indianapolis and close to two points above the national rate of 39.2%. Kentucky's largest city has spent years absorbing manufacturing and logistics jobs without home prices climbing at the pace seen in faster-growing Southern cities, and that combination keeps monthly payments within reach of a single income. For a single parent weighing whether to rent another year or take on a mortgage, Louisville offers one of the rare markets where neither option carries much financial risk. Louisville's homeownership index sits at 66.7, a modest score on its own, but paired with the city's affordability performance it produces a single-parent housing index of 82.1, the third-highest of any city in LendingTree's full 50-city ranking. That's a reminder that the ownership cost figure driving this list and LendingTree's broader combined ranking aren't always measuring the same thing. Louisville performs well by both standards at once, which turns out to be rarer than it sounds. Raleigh, North Carolina TJ Wallace / Unsplash In Raleigh, N.C., the ownership math looks different from the story playing out in most fast-growing Southern cities. Single-parent homeowners there spend 22.5% of income on housing, the third-lowest share among the 50 cities LendingTree studied, even as Raleigh's population and job base have both expanded rapidly over the past decade. That combination of growth and affordability is unusual. Cities that add jobs and residents as quickly as Raleigh has typically see home prices, and therefore ownership costs, climb right along with them. Renting hasn't kept pace with the same restraint. Single-parent renters in Raleigh spend 41.5% of income on housing, the highest rent burden of any city on this list and nearly 20 percentage points above what Raleigh's homeowners pay. LendingTree's data shows an affordability index of 92.1 for ownership in Raleigh against just 69.4 for renting, one of the widest gaps between the two figures anywhere in the analysis. That imbalance means a single parent's financial picture in Raleigh depends heavily on which side of the rent-or-own line they land on. Raleigh's single-parent homeownership rate stands at 40.8%, slightly above the national figure of 39.2% but the lowest among the seven cities on this list. Research Triangle employers have kept incomes relatively strong even as the region's population has grown, and that income growth appears to be helping single parents who already own homes more than it's helping renters trying to break into the market. For a single parent who can clear the initial hurdle of qualifying for a mortgage in Raleigh, the payoff shows up quickly in a lighter monthly burden. On LendingTree's homeownership index, Raleigh scores just 59.1, the lowest of the seven cities on this list, which drags its overall single-parent housing index down to 69.9, also the lowest ranking among these seven. The ownership cost figure that puts Raleigh on this list measures something narrower than that broader score. It captures how far a paycheck stretches once a mortgage is already signed, not how many single parents in the city have managed to sign one in the first place. St. Louis Kenny Nguyễn / Unsplash St. Louis home prices haven't caught up with the rest of the market, and that lag is exactly what benefits single-parent buyers. LendingTree calculated an ownership cost share of 22.7% for single-parent homeowners in St. Louis, more precisely the fourth-lowest figure among the 50 largest American cities and more than three full percentage points under the national average of 25.7%. That distance holds up even against St. Louis's rent burden, which at 37.8% is itself the sixth-lowest rent share on record in the analysis. Because both ownership and rental costs run low in St. Louis, the city posts a combined affordability score of 90.6, the third-highest of any city LendingTree ranked. Only Louisville and Kansas City, Mo., score higher on that combined measure, and both trail St. Louis on the ownership figure specifically. A single parent moving between renting and owning in St. Louis faces less financial disruption than in almost any other market in the country. Neither side of that decision carries an outsized cost. St. Louis carries a single-parent homeownership rate of 43.0%, nearly four percentage points above the national rate and the third-highest among the seven cities on this list. Decades of population loss left St. Louis with a larger housing stock than its current population needs, and that oversupply keeps a lid on prices even as other Midwestern cities see values climb. For single parents priced out of faster-growing cities elsewhere in the country, that combination of low costs on both sides of the housing ledger is rare. St. Louis's homeownership index sits at 67.0, and its combined single-parent housing index reaches 78.8, the fifth-highest among the 50 cities LendingTree studied. Both figures track closely with the city's ownership cost ranking, which is unusual. Several cities on this list post a strong cost figure while lagging on the broader index, or the reverse, but St. Louis performs consistently well across every measure LendingTree calculated. Pittsburgh Vidar Nordli-Mathisen / Unsplash Pittsburgh's aging housing stock keeps prices low, and low prices are what keep the city in the top five on this list. LendingTree's analysis puts single-parent homeowners in Pittsburgh at 22.9% of income spent on housing, a figure that lands almost exactly three percentage points under the national average for single-parent owners. That cost advantage holds even though Pittsburgh's economy has shifted heavily toward health care and education in recent decades, industries that don't always pay as well as the steel and manufacturing jobs the city once relied on. Renters in Pittsburgh do reasonably well too, spending 38.6% of income on housing, a share that ranks in the better half of the 50 cities LendingTree studied. That balance between ownership and rental costs gives Pittsburgh a combined affordability score of 87.3, fourth-highest among the cities on this list behind Louisville, St. Louis and Kansas City. Few cities manage to keep both figures this low at once, which is part of why Pittsburgh keeps showing up near the top of affordability rankings across different demographics. Pittsburgh's single-parent homeownership rate sits at 43.2%, the second-highest among the seven cities ranked here and nearly four points above the national figure of 39.2%. Much of Pittsburgh's housing was built decades before the current construction boom priced other cities out of reach for single-income buyers, and that older stock still trades at prices that a single parent's income can realistically cover. The tradeoff comes in the form of higher maintenance costs on older homes, but LendingTree's cost figures suggest that tradeoff hasn't outweighed the savings on the purchase price itself. That consistency shows up across Pittsburgh's other numbers too. The city's homeownership index of 67.7 and its combined single-parent housing index of 77.5 both land comfortably in the upper half of LendingTree's 50-city ranking, reinforcing what the ownership cost figure alone already suggests. Few cities balance a low cost burden with a genuinely high homeownership rate the way Pittsburgh manages to. Detroit Alex Brisbey / Unsplash Few cities have changed as much over the past two decades as Detroit, and that history now works in favor of single-parent buyers. LendingTree found that single-parent homeowners in Detroit spend 23.4% of income on housing, the sixth-lowest figure among the 50 cities studied and more than two full percentage points below the national average of 25.7%. Home values in Detroit fell so far during the city's population decline that even a recovery in recent years hasn't pushed ownership costs back up to where other Midwestern cities now sit. Detroit's single-parent homeownership rate tells an even bigger part of the story. At 47.5%, it's the third-highest rate among all 50 cities LendingTree analyzed and the second-highest among the seven cities on this list, trailing only Grand Rapids, Mich. That combination of a high ownership rate and a low cost share pushes Detroit's overall single-parent housing index to 80.5, the second-highest of any city ranked here. Renting is a tougher proposition in Detroit than owning. Single-parent renters there spend 41.0% of income on housing, nearly 18 percentage points more than what Detroit's homeowners pay and among the higher rent burdens LendingTree recorded. That gap between renting and owning in Detroit is almost as wide as the one in Indianapolis, and it points to the same underlying pattern. In cities where decades of population loss left more homes than buyers, ownership costs stayed low even as rents, driven by a smaller pool of available units, climbed at a different pace entirely. Detroit's homeownership index of 83.2 ranks fourth-highest nationally, and combined with its ownership cost figure, the city posts a single-parent housing index of 80.5, also the fourth-highest of any city in LendingTree's full ranking. Only Salt Lake City, Grand Rapids and Louisville score higher on that combined measure, and Detroit's rate of ownership actually outpaces two of those three cities. Grand Rapids, Michigan Ad Telic / Unsplash Grand Rapids, Mich., rounds out the list with the highest single-parent homeownership rate of any city ranked here except one. LendingTree recorded a rate of 48.1% in Grand Rapids, trailing only Salt Lake City nationally and edging out Detroit for second place among all 50 cities in the analysis. Single-parent homeowners there spend 23.8% of income on housing, the seventh-lowest share on this list and still nearly two full percentage points under the national average. That combination of a high ownership rate and a below-average cost share gives Grand Rapids a single-parent housing index of 82.3, the highest of any city on this list and third-highest nationally behind only Salt Lake City and Louisville, Ky. Renters in Grand Rapids pay 39.8% of income toward housing, a figure that sits almost exactly in the middle of the 50-city range LendingTree studied and roughly 16 percentage points above what the city's homeowners pay. Grand Rapids has built a reputation over the past decade as a furniture and manufacturing hub that never fully lost its industrial base the way some larger Midwestern cities did, and steady employment appears to be translating into steady homeownership for single-parent households specifically. Median home values in Grand Rapids remain well below the national figure even after years of steady price growth, and that gap between local wages and local home prices is exactly the kind of balance LendingTree's data points to as the difference between a city where single parents can realistically buy and one where renting becomes the only option. Grand Rapids' homeownership index of 85.3 ranks second nationally, trailing only Salt Lake City, and its single-parent housing index of 82.3 is the highest of any city on this list. That makes Grand Rapids the rare market where a single parent is more likely than average to already own a home and pays less than average once they do.

title: Bank of America says the midterm elections could be a major turning point for the stock market
text: Bank of America says the midterm elections could be a major turning point for the stock market. - BofA is eyeing a potential upheaval in stocks following the midterms in November. - The bank flagged a scenario where economic worries cause investors to dump stocks and buy bonds. - Higher yields are a "canary in the coalmine" for the bull market, the bank said. The bull market could run into its next big hurdle in a few months' time, Bank of America says. Strategists flagged the risk of a "big" reversal in stocks following the midterm elections in November. In a recent note to clients, the bank pointed to the possibility of a Democratic sweep in Congress as the election amounts to a "referendum on populist capitalism vs populist socialism." A team led by Michael Hartnett wrote in a note on Friday that investors should eschew risky assets and head into defensive investment in the near-term. He added that the bank likes gold as an investment to hedge risks of the K-shaped economy and an electorate that delivers an "it's the economy, stupid" midterm result. Economic dissatisfaction has been a growing concern for the lower leg of the K-shaped economy, which refers to the widening gap between the top earners and lower- to middle-income households. While top earners are benefiting from higher stock and real estate prices, many lower- to middle-income Americans are feeling the cumulative effects of hotter inflation and a tough job market. Recent growth in the economy has largely been fueled by the wealth effect from higher stock prices, BofA strategists said, pointing to the $9 trillion in market gains investors have seen over the past two years. A reversal in the market is a risk to economic growth, as dwindling wealth on paper could cause consumers to rein in spending. Separately, the bank floated the possibility that yields could move higher as investors continue to worry about inflation and the country's fiscal outlook. In a bear-case scenario, yields could reach levels that would materially weigh on risk assets, leading the AI bubble to pop. "Bonds end booms and bubbles, and this one ends once 'higher yields-lower dollar' vigilante event forcing fiscal policy U-turn, and asset allocation from stocks to bonds rise," strategists said, adding that rising yields are a "canary in the coalmine" they're watching. Yields have already started to rise as investors fret over hotter inflation, though the increase so far has been tolerated by markets. The 10-year US Treasury yield is sitting at around 4.67%, above the 4.5% psychological threshold closely watched by investors. Other forecasters on Wall Street have flagged the potential for a surge in volatility as the midterm election approaches.

title: Is Micron Stock Too Cheap to Ignore?
text: Is Micron Stock Too Cheap to Ignore?. Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) is an odd stock. While it has risen an incredible amount this year (up 214% in 2026), its valuation on multiple metrics still looks dirt cheap. There are a few reasons for this, and it raises the question: Has the stock become too cheap to ignore? Let's take a look at why Micron's stock appears as cheap as it does and see whether this is a generational buying opportunity or a value trap. Micron's business is cyclical Micron produces memory chips, which are used in just about every computing device. It produces both types of memory: DRAM and NAND. DRAM is high-speed memory that's utilized in computing devices for rapid memory access, while NAND is often used in long-term storage applications. Regardless, both types are in high demand thanks to AI data center build-outs. The primary issue here isn't demand. There isn't one factor that sets Micron's product apart from its competitors. Most memory products are interchangeable, and end users don't care if they're using memory from Micron or another supplier. This makes the memory chip industry commoditized, which can be difficult to operate and invest in. The reason for Micron's latest success is soaring memory chip prices. There is currently a supply shortage, so prices are moving higher. Micron is building some additional production capacity, but not enough to meet the growing demand. So its revenue and profits are soaring as customers outbid each other to gain access. This supply/demand imbalance won't last forever, as either demand will drop or supply will increase enough, and prices will stabilize. Micron is actively working to increase its production capacity and plans to have another factory online between mid-2027 and late 2028. This increase in production capacity is the right thing to do, although it could cause the price of its products to fall. As a result, the market doesn't fully value Micron's stock because it's worried about an inevitable demand drawdown. So, it has a low valuation of 5.7 times fiscal year 2027 earnings (ending August 2027). However, if you look at Micron's average trailing P/E ratio over the past decade, it's 22. So, even if Micron's stock rises to half of its average valuation, the stock could double by the end of fiscal year 2027.

title: States with the least—and most—housing market inventory heading into the fall
text: States with the least—and most—housing market inventory heading into the fall. Want more housing market stories from Lance Lambert’s ResiClub in your inbox? Subscribe to the ResiClub newsletter . Nationally aggregated inventory is up just 2.1% on a year-over-year basis from July 31, 2025, to July 31, 2026. While that’s up a tad from the +1.9% year-over-year pace last month, it’s decelerated significantly since last year. If you go back 12 months, that year-over-year national inventory growth rate was much higher (+24.7.%). After a period of a burst of softening in which leverage shifted more toward homebuyers, the supply-demand balance in the nationally aggregated housing market has been more stable over the past year, settling into what ResiClub considers a “soft” market. Note, however that there’s a lot of nuance regionally and locally. Nationally, we’re still below pre-pandemic 2019 inventory levels (9.1% below July 2019), and some resale markets, in particular chunks of the Midwest and Northeast, still remain, relatively speaking, tight-ish. July inventory/active listings total, according to Realtor.com : July 2017 -> 1,322,659 July 2018 -> 1,261,916 July 2019 -> 1,239,534 July 2020 -> 822,834 July 2021 -> 546,686 (pandemic housing boom overheating) July 2022 -> 691,652 July 2023 -> 647,135 July 2024 -> 884,273 July 2025 -> 1,102,787 July 2026 -> 1,126,252 From July 2024 to July 2025, U.S. active inventory across the country rose by 218,514 homes for sale. From July 2025 to July 2026, U.S. active inventory across the country rose by 23,465 homes for sale. Right now, we’re looking at state inventory data. ResiClub members (paid tiers) can get our monthly interactive deep-dive analysis looking at inventory shifts and signals for 800-plus metro areas, 3,000 counties, and 25,000 zip codes. ResiClub PRO details here . Below is the year-over-year active inventory percentage change by state. Click here to view an interactive version of the year-over-year map below . While active housing inventory is rising in most markets on a year-over-year basis, the pace of growth continues to decelerate across much of the country (see the side-by-side maps below). In fact, Florida—home to many of the weakest regional housing markets over the past two years—is now seeing active inventory edge down a little year-over-year (-14%). From left: Year-over-year active inventory shift from July 2024 to July 2025 ; year-over-year active inventory shift from July 2025 to July 2026 And while active housing inventory is rising in most markets on a year-over-year basis, some markets still remain tight-ish. As ResiClub has been documenting, both active resale and new homes for sale remain the most limited across huge swaths of the Midwest and Northeast. That’s where home sellers in the summer are likely, relatively speaking , to have more power than their peers in many Southern markets. In contrast, active housing inventory for sale has neared or surpassed pre-pandemic 2019 levels in many parts of the Sunbelt and Mountain West, including metro-area housing markets such as Punta Gorda, Florida, and Austin. Many of these areas saw major price surges during the pandemic housing boom, with home prices getting stretched compared to local incomes. As pandemic-driven domestic migration slowed and mortgage rates rose, markets like Punta Gorda and Austin faced challenges, relying on local income levels to support frothy home prices. This softening trend was accelerated further by an abundance of new-home supply in the Sunbelt. Builders are often willing to lower prices or offer affordability incentives (if they have the margins to do so) to maintain sales in a shifted market, which also has a cooling effect on the resale market: Some buyers who would have previously considered existing homes have opted for new homes with more favorable deals over the past couple of years—which then put additional upward pressure on resale inventory. Click here to view an interactive version of the map below . At the end of July 2026, 16 states were above pre-pandemic 2019 active inventory levels: Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Hawaii, Idaho, Nebraska, North Carolina, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, and Washington. (The District of Columbia is also back above pre-pandemic 2019 active inventory levels.) Click here to view an interactive of the chart below (best done on desktop) . Big picture: Over the past year the post-boom softening hasn’t been as strong as it was in 2024 or 2025, and inventory growth has decelerated on a year-over-year basis. That said, the nationally aggregated housing market remains soft. While home prices are declining in some parts of the Sunbelt , large parts of Northeast and Midwest markets are still eking out small year-over-year gains. At the national level, home prices are essentially flat year over year. Click here for an interactive version of the table below . Below is another version of the table above—but this one includes every month since January 2017. If you’d like to further examine the monthly state inventory figures, use the interactive below. As ResiClub has been closely documenting, Florida—which has been the epicenter of housing market weakness over the past 2.5 years, particularly in Southwest Florida—is no longer seeing the same upward burst in inventory. Indeed, the intensity of Florida’s housing market correction is easing across many pockets of the state . There are still pockets of weakness, particularly in Southwest Florida, but the burst of softening has let up. Some builders have also reported that their affordability adjustments have helped them better meet the market in the state. title: Tensions flare as $34-billion Charter-Cox cable deal nears finish line
text: Tensions flare as $34-billion Charter-Cox cable deal nears finish line. Spectrum owner Charter Communications is nearing the finish line in its long-awaited $34.5-billion purchase of Cox Enterprises to form the nation's largest internet and cable television company. California's Public Utilities Commission is scheduled to vote next week to approve the merger that would bolster Southern California's dominant provider with more than 5 million customers. Securing the approval of California regulators — the deal's final hurdle — has been a slog as federal officials gave Charter their consent months ago. Customers of privately held Cox, the Atlanta-based company that serves Rancho Palos Verdes, Rolling Hills Estates, Las Vegas and large parts of Orange and San Diego counties, would be switched to Spectrum service. Charter is the industry leader, providing Spectrum internet, phone and cable TV packages for Los Angeles, Riverside, San Bernardino and Ventura counties. It's been more than a year since the companies unveiled their proposed union, and they hope to combine operations this month. But flaps have flared up in the last lap. Public interest groups have argued that the PUC's proposed settlement with Charter doesn't go far enough to ensure long-term affordable internet for low-income residents or accommodations for customers reeling from natural disasters such as last year's Eaton and Palisades fires. In addition, advocates have asked utilities commissioners to demand that Charter commit to fostering workplace diversity, equity and inclusion among its proposed 9,000-member workforce in California. Such programs have been under siege since President Trump returned to the White House. "State regulators like the CPUC have an important role to play — they have a voice and leverage if they choose to use it," said Jason Solomon, director of the National Institute for Workers’ Rights, a Bay Area group that is lobbying for Charter to renew its commitment to a diverse workplace. "It's important that California stand up for its own laws, policies and values," Solomon said. The five-member commission is set to vote on the Charter-Cox merger Thursday. The panel will consider two competing proposals; both would allow the merger to go through with various conditions. Charter years ago pledged to create a diverse workplace but scaled back its public statements amid Trump's vocal demands that companies dump DEI programs. Trump's Federal Communications Commission chairman, Brendan Carr, also has championed eliminating diversity programs, saying they are discriminatory. The FCC in February approved Charter's proposed purchase of Cox's residential cable, commercial fiber, cloud and information technology businesses. To win Carr's approval, Charter agreed to "new safeguards to protect against DEI discrimination," according to the FCC. Charter is in a bind. It disavowed diversity efforts to win the FCC's blessing but now is facing calls in California to embrace such commitments. "In a state as diverse as California we should protect diversity in the workplace," said Jessica J. González, co-chief executive of advocacy group Free Press. "We have a responsibility to stand up to what's been going on in the federal government, and in the Trump administration, to force companies to roll back their policies." In its public filings, Charters said it would reach out to diverse suppliers and work with business groups, including the Women's Business Development Council, the California LGBTQ Chamber of Commerce, the African American Chamber, the California Hispanic Chamber and the Cal Asian Chamber. “This transaction will be good for consumers, community leaders, and businesses across California as it will provide them with lower prices, greater value, better service, and support from Spectrum's 100% U.S.-based employees," the Stamford, Conn. company said in a statement. Concerns heightened among activists after one of the two proposed settlements, hashed out between Charter and Commissioner Matthew Baker, the commission's Public Advocates Office and the California Emerging Technology Fund, failed to include diversity efforts. Advocates viewed Baker's proposal as weaker on broadband access provisions too, including commitments to provide low-cost internet for disadvantaged residents and communities that lack service. "For us, it's really about making sure everyone in Cox's and Charter's service territory benefits from this transaction," said Paul Goodman, counsel for the Berkeley-based Center for Accessible Technology. "We want to make sure that communities that have been historically overlooked get the same benefits from the transaction as everyone else," Goodman said. For example, a coalition of advocacy groups is seeking to prevent Spectrum from tacking on equipment charges for customers on low-income plans. Commissioners will be asked to select from Baker's draft decision or last month's proposal from the agency's administrative law judge, Jamie Ormond. Advocates are urging the panel to adopt Ormond's version because it contains more compliance conditions, including mechanisms to foster an inclusive workplace. Commissioners have "a statutory duty" under the state's utilities code "to deny the transaction outright rather than approve a weaker deal," the advocates argued in a recent filing. Solomon's group is pushing for an "organizational infrastructure for equal opportunity compliance," including reporting compensation and promotion data for Charter's California workforce and pay equity audits. The state has required diversity measures before — despite such initiatives being out of favor in Washington. In January, the commission approved Verizon Communications' purchase of Frontier Communications. In that proceeding, Verizon pledged to "further California’s public policy goals of diverse supply chains and workforces, including a $10 million partnership with the California State University system," the PUC said. Under both Ormond's and Baker's proposals, Charter would be required to offer affordable broadband to low-income residents, including California LifeLine service tiers. It would have to sell stand-alone broadband plans for five years, although advocates would like to see that extended to 10 years. The company has agreed to spend at least $275 million to upgrade its California network and complete its 1-gigabit service capability across its legacy service areas within three years. Charter also agreed to invest at least $30 million in customer outreach initiatives, such as digital literacy training and device access for low-income communities. The company also is being asked to provide free broadband and Wi-Fi service for about 50 eligible institutions, including schools, libraries and community centers for several years. Charter was criticized after the January 2025 fires for charging fees for equipment that burned, said Natalie Gonzalez, director of Digital Equity Los Angeles, one of the advocacy groups that is asking for Charter to "improve disaster response and customer service standards ... during life's most challenging moments." Charter pushed back on that contention, saying it helped residents in the burn areas. "We opened all our wifi hot spots to anyone (non Spectrum customers) and were deeply involved in the restoration efforts," the company said in its documents. The advocates, including Digital Equity LA and the California Alliance for Digital Equity, compiled evidence to help commissioners determine whether the merger was in the public interest. Should the deal go through, Cox subscribers will soon see changes. Charter plans to roll out its Spectrum products and fees to Cox customers next month. Subscribers can opt for their existing pricing or switch to a Spectrum bundle that includes such apps as Disney+, Hulu, ESPN and Paramount+. Charter has also said it would offer Cox subscribers a year of free service when they switch their cellphone carrier to Spectrum. The Charter name will be dropped in one year and the combined company will become Cox, although consumer products will keep the Spectrum brand. The switch is because the Cox family — descendants of an Ohio press baron who bought his first newspaper in 1898, began acquiring cable systems in 1962 — will become the firm's largest shareholder group, with about 23% of the stock. In a recent earnings call, Charter Chief Executive Chris Winfrey told investors the combined company would have nearly 37 million customers nationwide. It expects to generate $67 billion a year in revenue and about $28 billion in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization.

title: Granite Point Mortgage Trust Q2 Earnings Call Highlights
text: Granite Point Mortgage Trust Q2 Earnings Call Highlights. Key Points - Granite Point reported a $62 million GAAP net loss in Q2, or $1.29 per share, driven by a $47 million credit-loss provision and a $6.1 million impairment on real estate owned assets. Book value fell $1.35 to $5.70 per share. - The company increased its CECL reserve to approximately $166 million and is prioritizing legacy-loan resolutions. About $160 million of repayments, resolutions and asset sales reduced the loan portfolio by roughly $122 million, while three of five risk-rated five loans were placed in active sale processes. - Granite Point strengthened its financing position by extending key facilities and refinancing legacy CLO assets, lowering funding costs from SOFR plus 238 basis points to SOFR plus 200 basis points. Management expects the move to reduce annualized interest expense by about $2 million and plans to keep shrinking the portfolio before resuming originations. Granite Point Mortgage Trust (NYSE:GPMT) reported a second-quarter GAAP net loss attributable to common stockholders of $62 million, or $1.29 per basic common share, as the commercial real estate lender increased credit-loss reserves and recorded an impairment on real estate owned assets. The company said the quarterly loss included a $47 million provision for credit losses, a $6.1 million impairment loss on REO, and a distributable loss of $37.7 million, or $0.79 per basic common share. Book value declined to $5.70 per share as of June 30, down $1.35 from the prior quarter. President and Chief Executive Officer Jack Taylor said commercial real estate credit conditions continued to improve during the quarter, though geopolitical developments tied to the Iran war, energy prices and tariffs increased uncertainty around inflation and interest-rate expectations. While potential rate hikes could pressure property values, Taylor said capital has continued flowing into commercial real estate and lending spreads have tightened. Reserves Increase as Company Focuses on Legacy Loans Granite Point's aggregate current expected credit loss, or CECL, reserve totaled approximately $166 million at quarter-end, up about $17 million from the first quarter. Chief Financial Officer Blake Johnson said the increase included a $10 million rise in specific reserves, largely related to one newly risk-rated five loan, partially offset by a write-off tied to a loan resolution. General reserves increased $7 million because of downgraded macroeconomic forecasts in the company's CECL model and changes in loan attributes.

title: Forget the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Capex Bubble: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk Says the Memory Shortage Will Drive Costs Even Higher
text: Forget the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Capex Bubble: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk Says the Memory Shortage Will Drive Costs Even Higher Although some skeptics frame demand for memory chips and the acceleration in capital expenditures (capex) by artificial intelligence (AI) hyperscalers as a bubble, recent remarks from Elon Musk cut through this narrative with unusual clarity. During the recent earnings call for Space Exploration Technologies, otherwise known as SpaceX, Musk said that "memory output is increasing by around 20% per year" while "demand is increasing by 200% a year, maybe higher." Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » This dynamic positions pure-play memory producers like Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU) for outsize gains, making now a compelling entry point for investors who understand the forces of bringing next-generation AI applications into production amid the rising demand for the infrastructure that supports these developments. Memory specialists are in an advantageous position right now In a mature industry, 20% annual growth in output would normally be celebrated. The explosion of AI workloads has, however, shifted adoption of specialized chips into an exponential regime. Training large language models and inference deployments consumes ever-larger volumes of high bandwidth memory (HBM) chips, with each new generation multiplying the requirement. When demand grows by an order of magnitude faster than supply, scarcity becomes inevitable. Under these conditions, basic economics suggests that prices rise and profit margins expand for the businesses that can deliver the resource in question. Micron focuses on advanced DRAM and HBM, placing it directly in the center of the bottleneck Musk cites. Smart investors have already recognized how rising capex is affecting Micron, as the company's pricing power is directly fueling improved profitability and helping fund aggressive manufacturing scale. Why now is the time to buy Micron stock The stock market often overreacts to short-term signals even when longer-term fundamentals remain intact. Micron stock reached an all-time high in late June, only to sell off considerably shortly after. Micron's decline reflects both a familiar pattern of profit-taking after a strong rally and ongoing skepticism surrounding AI infrastructure spending. Musk's observation about memory prices reframes Micron's decline as noise rather than a signal that shares should continue to plummet. If memory remains the binding constraint for data center build-outs, this would imply Micron is in the early phase of capacity expansion rather than the late phase of excess supply. Against this backdrop, capital will continue to flow toward the memory bottleneck, benefiting the companies that produce it.

title: Ramstad: How Peter Carter, Delta’s new president, sees the airline’s next era
text: Ramstad: How Peter Carter, Delta’s new president, sees the airline’s next era. Imagine walking into an airport, stopping for a coffee or bite, then heading to your gate without ever having to line up for a security check. “You just walk through, and there’ll be this sort of virtual security queue that you don’t even perceive,” Peter Carter, the new president of Delta Air Lines, mused as we were wrapping an interview recently. So much about air travel has changed during the past 30 years that I wasn’t surprised to hear Carter say he wants to change the part that people dislike most. “The Holy Grail at the airport of the future,” he added, “is one that you’ll walk with your phone through some sort of arch, and you don’t have to put your stuff on a belt or take your shoes off.” People love to complain about flying and airlines and airports. But air travel is in higher demand than ever. And here’s something that may seem hard to believe: Even with airfares spiking because of the U.S. war against Iran, ticket prices, adjusted for inflation, are lower today than when the industry deregulated in 1983. In that time, executives at Minnesota airlines like Northwest (and by extension Delta) and Sun Country have played a huge role shaping the industry. Carter looks to be the next one to do so. Carter took the No. 2 position at Delta four months ago after serving as its chief legal officer for the past 11 years, a period when Delta transformed itself and the industry by segmenting planes to directly align customers’ flying experience with the price they pay.

title: 5 Small Business Ideas With Strong Margins
text: 5 Small Business Ideas With Strong Margins. 5 Small Business Ideas with the Best MarginsBy Chris Morris If you’re looking for a small business idea with room to grow, it’s helpful to look at businesses with a strong margin. Those profits can make it easier to add staff, and expand into new products, services, or locations without taking on extra debt. When it comes to margins, not all businesses are equal. Elements like pricing and overhead costs are important, of course, but it can also come down to the industry you choose. Higher startup costs can lower your initial margins. Plus, if the tools you use in that business need to be regularly updated, whether it’s a new AI model or a specialized piece of equipment, that will have an impact as well. Here are several small businesses that have high gross margins, according to industry experts. (For more inspiration read Inc.'s full guide to 25 small business ideas for 2026.) Bookkeeping firm Solopreneurs and small businesses are increasingly looking for outsourced financial assistance. Financial specialists can increase their earnings by not limiting themselves to a single company, whether as a stand-alone bookkeeping business or as a fractional CFO or bookkeeper Census Bureau data shows the finance and insurance sector as having the best projected performance for at least the next six months, notably exceeding the national business average. Areas of particular interest for these clients are often things like payroll and managing transactions. Solo businesses have the highest margins, writes Madras Accountancy, an international Certified Public Accounting (CPA) and management consulting firm, because they have a minimal cost structure. Smaller firms of two to five people have a slightly lower margin. Typical gross margin: 35 to 55 percent for a solo practitioner, 25 to 40 percent for a small firm Commercial cleaning company There's a low barrier to entry with commercial cleaning companies due to their fairly muted startup costs. You'll need equipment and cleaning supplies (which can be purchased in bulk for a low price) along with transportation, which you likely already have. The amount you can charge for your services will vary widely depending on location and the size of your clients. This small business idea can scale easily, too, as you connect with local commercial real estate agents and property managers. Gross margin levels will come down to your staffing, operational efficiency and client retention, writes FieldServicely, a field service management (FSM) software provider. Typical gross margin: 50 to 70 percent Junk removal business Whether you work with commercial businesses or a recurring residential customer base, the junk removal field is showing growth potential. Data from Market Reports World finds that more than 63 percent of residential households generate bulky waste at least twice per year, while 58 percent of small businesses have need of junk removal services. It's not a small business idea for people who prefer office attire, but it's expected to be a $1.2 billion industry this year and grow to $3.4 billion by 2034. Your gross margins will vary depending on a number of factors, such as the disposal fees you're able to negotiate and the wear and tear on your vehicle, writes Junk Removal Authority, a consulting, marketing, and business support company for the junk removal industry. Typical gross margin: about 40 percent Online courses E-learning reached a market size of $314 billion in 2024 and is expected to grow to $615 billion by 2029. That presents an opportunity for people who can find the right niche, preferably one that's not overly crowded. You'll need to create content that’s both informative and interesting, with video lessons, downloadable resources, and quizzes. Platforms to consider include Etsy, Skillshare, Udemy, Teachable and Kajabi. These lessons can generate passive income for you as you plan follow-up courses and grow your business. Real world experience in any number of fields can be the bedrock of an online education business. And small business ideas that focus on digital course sales typically achieve very strong gross margins. "Self-paced digital courses are the highest-margin format because production is a one-time cost spread across unlimited students," writes Revenue Map, a financial-modeling tool for startup founders. "Cohort-based programs carry instructor and community-management costs that scale with enrollment, compressing margins to 50 to 65 percent even though they command higher prices. Bootcamps sit lower still, at 30 to 50 percent, because intensive instruction is a true marginal cost per student." Typical gross margin: 75 to 82 percent Pool service Your margins on a pool service business will vary depending on the services you offer, writes specialty insurance provider Nip Group. Pool cleaning is on the low-end, ranging from 15-30 percent, but if you offer pool equipment and repair, they can go significantly higher. Evolving your business into a full-service operation not only increases your margins, but your potential revenue streams—and could make your business more appealing to commercial operations. "A solo cleaning route can net $75,000 to $120,000 annually," Nip Group writes. "Multi-truck businesses can produce $200,000 to $400,000 or more." Typical gross margin: 30 to 45 percent
