title: China July factory-gate inflation eases to 3-month low, CPI slows
text: China July factory-gate inflation eases to 3-month low, CPI slows. By Kevin Yao and Yukun Zhang BEIJING, Aug 9 (Reuters) - China's producer price inflation eased more than expected in July to its weakest in three months, while consumer inflation also cooled, official data showed on Sunday, as global energy prices retreated despite the U.S.-Israel war against Iran. China's leaders, confronting a two-speed economy of strong factory output and exports but weak domestic demand, have pledged to bolster growth by accelerating fiscal spending on already budgeted infrastructure projects through year-end. "Lower oil prices, combined with weakening demand, caused both (consumer and producer price inflation) in July to come in below expectations. Oil price trends remain uncertain, meaning their impact on inflation is also likely to be uncertain," said Zhaopeng Xing, ANZ's senior China strategist. "On the demand side, the effect of faster fiscal spending in the second half of the year is likely to be felt with a lag of about one quarter. We maintain our view that inflation will follow an M-shaped trajectory this year." FISCAL LAG, LIMITED EFFECT ON QUELLING PRICE WARS The producer price index rose 3.5% from a year earlier in July, National Bureau of Statistics data showed, easing from 4.1% in June to its lowest in three months. It was below economists' expectations for a 3.8% increase in a Reuters poll. The core consumer price index, which excludes volatile costs for food and energy, rose 0.9% on year, food prices fell 1.5%. From the previous month, CPI edged down 0.1%, compared with an expected 0.2% gain and following a 0.3% dip in June. Zhiwei Zhang, chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, said the slower inflation was consistent with other activity data such as the PMI reading. "The economic momentum softened in Q2," Zhang said. "The Politburo in July signalled stronger fiscal spending as the policy response. The transmission of the fiscal spending will take time." ANZ forecasts full-year PPI of 2.5% and CPI of 1.0%. Although some of China's upstream and high-tech sectors have maintained strong profit growth, more domestic market-facing manufacturers struggled against sluggish demand as overall economic growth lost steam. Rising input costs risk further squeezing their profit margins and dampening confidence. Higher producer prices were driven mainly by increases in the mining and raw materials sectors, the statistics agency said. By contrast, prices declined for food and daily consumer goods. Price shocks stemming from the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the key oil and gas passage, have lifted producer prices and helped flip China's years-long deflationary streak. Government efforts to curb fierce price wars in major industrial sectors and stabilise prices had previously achieved only limited effects.

title: Here's how much your Social Security benefit could rise in 2027
text: Here's how much your Social Security benefit could rise in 2027. Social Security benefits are projected to increase by as much as 3.8% in 2027, according to initial estimates of advocacy groups. The Senior Citizens League, or TSCL, projected a one-percentage point increase in the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment to 3.8% from 2.8% in 2026. Meanwhile, AARP, a nonprofit, nonpartisan organization, said its projected cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, for 2027 could be 3.6%. More than 71 million Americans receive Social Security benefits, averaging close to $1,938 per month, according to a report by the Social Security Administration in June 2026. The estimated 3.8% cost-of-living adjustment could mean a $73.60 increase to the average retired worker's monthly benefit. The Get the Facts Data Team has created a calculator that shows how much your Social Security monthly benefit could increase based on the 3.8% COLA forecast for next year. Calculate how much your benefit may change Is this the final COLA for 2027? The Social Security Administration recalculates benefits annually by factoring in what's called the cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA. This is to ensure that the purchasing power of benefits does not fall behind the current cost of goods. COLA is computed by comparing the current year's third-quarter inflation average, July through September, against the prior year's third-quarter average. The final COLA number for the upcoming year is announced by the SSA in October. Alex Moore, a statistician for The Senior Citizens League, said its forecast 3.8% for the 2027 COLA can still change as there has been a lot more economic uncertainty throughout the year. "We've seen with oil prices being really unstable this year, and that's the number one thing to watch," said Moore. "If we start seeing oil do better and fossil fuels do better over these next two months, and we see the Consumer Price Index go down, that means that will probably get a little bit lower COLA. If those inflationary fuel pressures stay really high, we'll probably get a higher COLA because that will continue to push prices higher in the market," said Moore. Is COLA keeping up with Medicare? Aside from inflation, seniors also face rising health care costs. In November 2025, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced that the standard monthly premium for Medicare Part B enrollees, which is deducted from the Social Security benefit payment, has risen to $202.90 per month in 2026 from $185 in 2025. The 9.7% increase was the second-largest premium increase in the program's history and particularly impacts seniors on fixed incomes. This is evident in a trend that Moore said he has seen in TSCL's research. According to Moore, 57% of seniors have skipped a health care procedure of some kind due to cost in the last year. "They just can't afford it, and they're skipping things like the dentist, which obviously has a lot of preventative value and you end up paying more later," Moore said. Russell Gloor, a Social Security Advisor at AMAC Foundation, said health care expenses are rising more than the average Social Security benefit amount. Gloor said this is a problem seniors continue to face and the cost-of-living adjustment is "never enough." "The actual cost of living happens before the cost of living is provided, so it's based on the third quarter of the previous year, so as a result you've already spent a lot of money on goods and services that you can't get back," Gloor said. What is the Social Security bill reintroduced in Congress? A bill reintroduced in Congress called the Social Security 2100 Act would change the way the government computes annual cost-of-living adjustments. Instead of computing COLA using the Consumer Price Index based on the spending patterns of urban wage earners and clerical workers, the bill requires the government to use what's called CPI for the Elderly, or CPI-E. The CPI for the Elderly index tracks spending of persons 62 years of age or older and puts more importance on categories such as housing and medical care. "What we our research has shown time and again is that seniors tend to experience inflation differently," said Moore. "They disproportionately spend more on housing and healthcare, which are two of the heaviest hit parts of the economy when it comes to inflation." The Social Security 2100 Act was first introduced by U.S. Rep. John Larson in the U.S. House of Representatives in July 2014. It has been routinely reintroduced in subsequent sessions of Congress and has not been passed. 

title: China's July CPI cools to six-month low as producer prices also ease
text: China's July CPI cools to six-month low as producer prices also ease. Softer than expected CPI and PPI readings reinforce the picture of a two-speed Chinese economy, with strong exports and factory output offset by weak domestic demand, adding to the case for the accelerated fiscal spending Beijing's leadership signalled at July's Politburo meeting. The data suggests deflationary pressure has not been fully resolved despite the earlier boost to producer prices from the Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz disruption, leaving analysts expecting an M-shaped inflation path through the rest of the year. Continued softness in household demand, tied to the property market slump and job security concerns, points to limited near-term upward pressure on prices, a mildly negative signal for Chinese consumer-facing equities. The lag before fiscal stimulus feeds through, expected around one quarter, means markets are likely to look past near-term inflation weakness toward the pace and scale of implementation over the second half of the year. Chinese inflation cooled further in July on cheaper oil and weak demand, leaving Beijing's promised fiscal push to do the heavy lifting on growth over the second half of the year. The National Bureau of Statistics said the consumer price index rose 0.5% year on year in July, a six-month low, edging down 0.1% on a month-on-month basis. Core CPI, which strips out food and energy, rose 0.9% year on year, while food prices fell 1.5%. The producer price index rose 3.5% year on year, easing from 4.1% in June and coming in below economists' expectations for a 3.8% increase in a Reuters poll. Higher producer prices were driven mainly by increases in the mining and raw materials sectors, the statistics agency said, while prices for food and daily consumer goods declined. Price shocks stemming from the US-Israeli war on Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil and gas passage, had previously lifted producer prices and helped flip China's years-long deflationary streak, though government efforts to curb fierce price wars in major industrial sectors had achieved only limited effect before this latest easing. China's leaders are confronting a two-speed economy of strong factory output and exports alongside weak domestic demand, and have pledged to bolster growth by accelerating fiscal spending on already budgeted infrastructure projects through year-end. One analyst said lower oil prices combined with weakening demand caused both consumer and producer inflation to come in below expectations in July, though oil price trends remain uncertain, meaning their effect on inflation is also likely to stay uncertain. The same analyst noted that economic momentum softened in the second quarter, and that July's Politburo meeting signalled stronger fiscal spending as the policy response, though the transmission of that spending into demand is expected to take around a quarter to materialise, consistent with a view that inflation will follow an M-shaped path for the rest of the year. With household demand for goods still subdued by a property market slump and weak job security, economists said deflationary pressures are likely to persist. Factory activity contracted in July according to an official survey and slowed to a four-month low in a private-sector survey, with both showing weakening new orders. China's top leaders, at their late-July meeting, signalled stronger support for the economy and vowed to continue cracking down on price wars among manufacturers competing for market share at the expense of profits, while pledging to introduce pragmatic new policies in a timely manner and more forcefully expand domestic demand. The latest inflation figures follow trade data released two days earlier showing exports and imports both surging, boosted by strong overseas demand for AI-related technology products, underscoring the divergence between China's resilient external trade performance and its more subdued domestic economy. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

title: RAMageddon? 2027 Memory Capacity Reportedly Sold Out
text: RAMageddon? 2027 Memory Capacity Reportedly Sold Out. IGN reports: [A] new report suggests that all three memory manufacturers — Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron — have collectively sold through their 2027 memory manufacturing capacity to, you guessed it, AI companies. According to a report from Digitimes and spotted by TweakTown, all DRAM and HBM capacity has been sold through for 2027, with no further supply planned. (The companies themselves have not yet confirmed this to be the case.) Of course, that only means that retail prices are going to go up even further in the near future. Selling through all the capacity for next year would be bad enough for consumers, but the problem is that most of the companies buying up this capacity have done so through long-term purchasing agreements, essentially pre-ordering memory that hasn't even been manufactured yet over a five-year term. Unless more capacity opens up somewhere in the next few years, it's hard to imagine that RAM will become more affordable and less scarce any time soon. It's not just memory that's affected. According to that Digitimes report, NAND storage is growing in demand too. Luckily, NAND capacity hasn't been completely absorbed, because there are more companies supplying the stuff. title: Crude, FPI Outflows Threaten Indian Market Stability
text: Crude, FPI Outflows Threaten Indian Market Stability. India’s financial markets have a strong domestic foundation, but geopolitical tensions, elevated crude oil prices and foreign investor outflows remain key risks, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) said in its annual report for 2025-26.The assessment comes after a difficult year for Indian equities, with global uncertainty weighing on market performance despite resilience in the domestic economy..Equities Fall 14% in Dollar Terms.The Nifty 50 and broader indices declined by around 14% in US dollar terms during 2025-26. Sustained foreign portfolio investor (FPI) selling, rupee depreciation, valuation concerns and slower earnings growth affected Indian markets. title: 7 U.S. cities where minimum wage can't get you a 1-bedroom apartment
text: 7 U.S. cities where minimum wage can't get you a 1-bedroom apartment Rent has outpaced minimum wage across the country. Best Interest Financial found seven cities where a full paycheck doesn't cover one apartment Grocery bills, gas prices, and rent have all climbed for more than a decade and a half while pay for minimum-wage workers stayed exactly the same. The federal minimum wage has sat at $7.25 an hour since 2009, even as the typical one-bedroom apartment turned into a luxury that few full-time minimum-wage workers can rent on their own. In a handful of U.S. cities, a full-time minimum-wage paycheck now falls short of a typical one-bedroom by hundreds of dollars every month. Some states have raised their own minimum wage well above the federal floor, giving workers there more breathing room. But 17 of the 50 largest U.S. cities still pay workers only the federal $7.25 an hour, even as rent has grown far faster than paychecks for the lowest earners nationwide. A single full-time worker on the federal minimum brings home about $1,160 a month before taxes, well short of covering a typical one-bedroom apartment in any of the nation's largest cities. In several cities, the shortfall is severe enough that a worker would need to log well over 100 hours a week just to cover rent alone. Best Interest Financial compared local minimum wages with fair market rent data from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development across the 50 largest U.S. cities. Housing is considered affordable when it costs no more than 30% of gross income, and a single full-time minimum-wage worker cannot rent a typical one-bedroom within the 30% threshold in any of the 50 cities studied. The firm's analysis found seven cities where the shortfall runs steepest, with rent alone consuming well over 100% of a minimum-wage worker's entire monthly paycheck. State minimum wage laws played a heavy role in the results, and cities stuck at the federal floor consistently landed among the worst off. Atlanta Ben Dutton / Unsplash Full-time workers earning Georgia's minimum wage take home roughly $1,160 each month before taxes. A one-bedroom apartment at fair market rent costs $1,660 a month in Atlanta, a $500 shortfall no minimum-wage paycheck alone can close. Rent consumes 143% of a minimum-wage worker's gross income here, the steepest imbalance Best Interest Financial found among the 50 largest U.S. cities. The math doesn't improve by working more hours, either. Someone earning $7.25 an hour would need to log close to 191 hours in a single week, nearly five weeks of standard full-time work squeezed into seven days, to cover Atlanta's rent through hours alone. Georgia's own minimum wage law technically sets a lower rate, but federal law overrides it for nearly every employer in the state, so $7.25 an hour is what most minimum-wage workers in Atlanta actually earn. The federal minimum hasn't moved since 2009, while Atlanta's rental market has kept climbing as corporate relocations, film production work and a broader population boom have drawn in higher earners who can absorb rising rents. For a barista, retail clerk or fast-food worker making minimum wage, those transplants compete for the same shrinking pool of affordable apartments, and low-wage renters haven't seen matching pay gains. None of this leaves workers with many good options. Full-time minimum-wage employees in Atlanta typically make up the difference by moving farther from the city core, where older apartment stock rents for less, or by living with family rather than qualifying for a lease on their own. Others spend far more than the recommended 30% of their income on housing, leaving less for food, transportation and health care. Atlanta's own housing market makes clear that a $7.25-an-hour paycheck was never designed to cover a $1,660 rent, and nothing about the local job market for minimum-wage work has closed the shortfall. Retail clerks, home health aides and fast-food workers make up much of Atlanta's minimum-wage workforce, and they keep the city's service economy running even as housing costs leave them further behind every year. Dallas R K / Unsplash Minimum-wage workers in Dallas fare only slightly better than those in Atlanta, and only on paper. Best Interest Financial's analysis puts rent at 142% of a minimum-wage worker's gross income in Dallas, the second-steepest imbalance among the 50 cities the firm studied. Texas sets its own minimum wage at the same $7.25 an hour as the federal floor, so a full-time worker here takes home roughly the same $1,160 a month as counterparts in Atlanta, Raleigh or Philadelphia. One-bedroom apartments in Dallas rent for around $1,416 a month on average, RentCafe data shows, leaving minimum-wage workers roughly $256 short every month before a single utility bill or grocery run enters the picture. Dallas has spent the past decade absorbing corporate headquarters relocations from higher-cost states, and the jobs those moves bring pay well above minimum wage. Those relocations have pushed median household income in Dallas to about $70,518 a year, comfortable enough for a typical two-income household to clear the 30% rent threshold with room left over. Low-wage service and retail workers haven't seen matching pay increases. They compete for the same limited stock of one-bedroom units against young professionals relocating from California, the Northeast, and Austin, and landlords have little reason to hold rents down when demand keeps arriving from out of state. The report's own fair market rent benchmark for Dallas ran even higher than the $1,416 average asking rent RentCafe tracks today, only widening the shortfall a minimum-wage paycheck has to close. Dallas workers earning the minimum wage typically respond the same way workers do elsewhere on this list, by moving farther from the urban core or leaning on family and informal arrangements rather than qualifying for a lease alone. Occupancy limits in many Dallas apartment complexes cap units at two unrelated adults per bedroom, ruling out most workarounds beyond a single tenant or couple on the lease. For a single minimum-wage worker without those options, the realistic path in Dallas runs through the suburbs, where older apartment stock still rents well below the citywide average. Raleigh, North Carolina TJ Wallace / Unsplash It's no accident that Raleigh, N.C., lands among the seven U.S. cities where the shortfall between minimum wage and rent runs steepest. North Carolina's minimum wage matches the federal floor of $7.25 an hour, so a full-time worker here takes home about $1,160 a month before taxes, the same baseline income as counterparts in Atlanta or Dallas. Typical asking rent for a one-bedroom in Raleigh runs around $1,391 a month, RentCafe data shows, and the federal fair market rent figures used in the wage study run higher still in a market where new supply hasn't kept pace with demand. Either way, a single minimum-wage paycheck doesn't come close to covering it alone. Raleigh sits at the center of the Research Triangle, an economic engine built on universities, biotech firms and technology employers that pay well into six figures for engineers and researchers. High salaries in those fields have pushed the city's median household income to roughly $85,395 a year, one of the strongest figures among the cities on this list. Rents have climbed as new arrivals with tech salaries bid for the same apartment stock that fast-food workers, retail clerks and home health aides depend on. Pay for those service jobs hasn't kept pace, widening the split between what Raleigh's economy pays its highest earners and what it pays everyone else. Best Interest Financial's own fair market rent benchmark for Raleigh ran higher than the asking-rent average RentCafe tracks, only reinforcing how far a single minimum-wage paycheck falls short here. Workers earning $7.25 an hour in Raleigh typically close the shortfall the way low-wage workers do across this list, by moving toward outlying suburbs, doubling up with family or simply spending well beyond the recommended 30% of their income on housing. Most Raleigh apartment complexes and the city's own occupancy codes limit a one-bedroom to two or three unrelated adults, narrowing the workaround even for those willing to share housing informally. For minimum-wage workers priced out of central Raleigh, the more common answer is a long commute from Wake County suburbs like Garner or Wake Forest, where older rental stock still runs meaningfully cheaper than the city core. Nashville, Tennessee Mike Gattorna / Unsplash Tennessee has no state minimum wage law of its own, leaving employers there to default to the federal floor of $7.25 an hour, the same rate that leaves workers in Atlanta and Raleigh short on rent. A full-time minimum-wage worker in Nashville, Tenn., takes home roughly $1,160 a month before taxes. A typical one-bedroom apartment in Nashville rents for around $1,690 a month, RentCafe data shows, meaning rent alone would consume close to 146% of the worker's gross income, a wider shortfall than Atlanta's already severe 143%. Nashville's economy runs heavily on tourism, live music venues, hospitality and health care, industries that generate enormous numbers of jobs at or near minimum wage even as the city's population and visitor numbers keep climbing. Hotel housekeepers, restaurant servers relying on tipped minimum wage, and retail workers on Broadway or in the surrounding entertainment district compete for housing against a wave of newcomers drawn by the same growth, including remote workers and retirees relocating from higher-tax states. Rents have risen faster than wages for the service workers who keep the tourism economy running, and Tennessee's lack of a state income tax, often cited as a draw for higher earners, does nothing to offset rent for someone earning $7.25 an hour. Best Interest Financial's fair market rent benchmark for Nashville reinforces the same point already visible in the average asking rent. A single minimum-wage paycheck here isn't close to enough. Workers earning $7.25 an hour in Nashville typically respond by moving to outlying counties, taking on a second job in the same tourism and hospitality sector that pays them so little, or spending well beyond the recommended 30% of income on rent alone. Nashville's own occupancy codes and tight rental market leave little room for informal workarounds either because most apartment leases restrict how many unrelated adults can occupy a single unit. For a minimum-wage worker in Nashville without family nearby to fall back on, a lengthy commute from Rutherford or Wilson County remains one of the few paths to rent that a single paycheck can actually cover. Austin, Texas Mitchell Kmetz / Unsplash Austin, Texas, ranks second worst among the four Texas cities in Best Interest Financial's study, with rent consuming 135% of a minimum-wage worker's gross income, trailing only Dallas's 142%. Texas caps its own minimum wage at the federal $7.25 an hour, so a full-time worker in Austin takes home the same roughly $1,160 a month as workers in Dallas, Atlanta or Raleigh. One-bedroom apartments in Austin rent for around $1,417 a month on average, RentCafe data shows, tracking closely with the 135% figure the firm calculated using federal fair market rent benchmarks. Austin's population and cost of living both surged over the past several years as technology companies expanded operations in the city and thousands of new residents arrived from California and other high-cost states. The boom has cooled somewhat from its peak, but rents remain well above where they stood before the influx, even as the minimum wage stayed frozen at $7.25 an hour the entire time. Service workers who staff Austin's restaurants, music venues and retail corridors, the same industries that draw tourists and new arrivals to the city, have watched their purchasing power shrink even as the city around them grew wealthier. The report's own fair market rent benchmark for Austin ran above the $1,417 average asking rent RentCafe tracks today, another sign of how far a single minimum-wage paycheck falls short in this market. Workers earning $7.25 an hour in Austin typically respond by moving to outlying suburbs, picking up extra shifts in the same restaurants and venues that already pay them minimum wage, or spending well beyond the recommended 30% of their income on rent. City code typically limits occupancy in a one-bedroom to two unrelated adults, leaving little legal room for informal workarounds. For minimum-wage workers priced out of central Austin, commuting in from Pflugerville, Kyle or other outlying suburbs remains the most realistic path to affordable rent in the area. Charlotte, North Carolina Wes Hicks / Unsplash Charlotte, N.C., sits among the seven cities in Best Interest Financial's study where the shortfall between minimum wage and rent runs steepest. North Carolina's minimum wage tracks the federal floor of $7.25 an hour, the same rate paid to minimum-wage workers in Raleigh, so a full-time worker in Charlotte takes home roughly $1,160 a month before taxes. A typical one-bedroom apartment in Charlotte rents for around $1,470 a month, RentCafe data shows, more than the entire monthly paycheck of a full-time minimum-wage worker before a single other expense enters the picture. Charlotte built its modern identity as a national banking hub, home to Bank of America $BAC's headquarters and a major regional presence for Truist and Wells Fargo $WFC, and those institutions pay well above minimum wage for the professionals who staff their towers. Finance salaries have helped push Charlotte's median household income above $82,000 a year. Workers in retail, food service, and hospitality see little of it. Those lower-wage jobs have grown just as fast as the finance sector in raw numbers, filling call centers, restaurants, and retail floors that serve the city's growing professional class, but pay hasn't kept pace with rents that finance salaries can absorb far more easily. Best Interest Financial's fair market rent benchmark for Charlotte ran high enough to leave a single minimum-wage paycheck well short, even before utilities or groceries enter the picture. Workers earning $7.25 an hour in Charlotte typically respond by moving away from the city's core neighborhoods, picking up extra shifts in the same retail and hospitality jobs that already pay them minimum wage, or spending well beyond the recommended 30% of their income on housing. North Carolina's building and fire codes, like those in most states, limit how many unrelated adults can occupy a typical one-bedroom, narrowing the informal workarounds available to anyone trying to share costs. In practice, minimum-wage workers priced out of Charlotte's core neighborhoods tend to move outward toward Gastonia, Concord or Rock Hill, S.C., trading a longer commute into the city for rent that a single paycheck can actually cover. Philadelphia Catherine Kerr / Unsplash Philadelphia rounds out the seven cities in this list, and Pennsylvania's minimum wage sits at the same federal floor of $7.25 an hour that leaves workers short in Atlanta, Dallas and every other city here. A full-time minimum-wage worker in Philadelphia takes home about $1,160 a month before taxes. A typical one-bedroom apartment in Philadelphia rents for around $1,856 a month, RentCafe data shows, meaning rent alone would consume close to 160% of a minimum-wage worker's gross income, the widest shortfall of any city in this list. Pennsylvania hasn't raised its minimum wage above the federal floor since 2009, even as every state that borders it, including New Jersey, New York, Delaware, and Maryland, has moved its own minimum wage well above $7.25 an hour. Philadelphia workers earn less than counterparts doing the same jobs a short drive away in Camden or Wilmington, while paying rent in a city built around large hospital systems and universities, an economy often nicknamed "eds and meds" that employs enormous numbers of lower-wage support staff alongside its highly paid doctors and researchers. Food service workers, janitorial staff, and home health aides are the ones left absorbing rent that has climbed well ahead of a wage frozen for a decade and a half. Best Interest Financial's fair market rent benchmark for Philadelphia was already the toughest on this list. The $1,856 average asking rent RentCafe tracks today runs even higher still, suggesting the shortfall here has only grown since the report's data was collected. Philadelphia's own housing code and most private leases limit how many unrelated adults can occupy a one-bedroom, leaving little room for workers to close the shortfall by sharing costs informally. Workers earning $7.25 an hour here are left choosing between a long commute from cheaper Pennsylvania suburbs, doubling up with family or simply devoting most of a paycheck to rent alone. Whatever the choice, the math leaves little room for the food, transportation, and health care costs that come with holding down a full-time job in one of the nation's largest cities.

title: Costco confirms 7 new locations are opening across the country in August – one state is getting two
text: Costco confirms 7 new locations are opening across the country in August – one state is getting two. COSTCO has confirmed seven new locations will open across the US this August. The new warehouses will open in Albany, New York; Oconomowoc, Wisconsin; Otsego, Minnesota; Stone Mountain, Georgia; and Lee’s Summit, Missouri. Texas residents will also get two new branches, with Costco opening locations in Mansfield and Celina. A further warehouse is coming to Camarillo, California, although shoppers there will have to wait until the autumn. Costco Wholesale is one of the world’s biggest warehouse retailers, known for selling groceries, household goods and electronics in bulk. The retail giant operates more than 650 warehouses across the US, as well as locations in several other countries. Read more in Money Shoppers pay an annual membership fee to access its stores and typically buy products in much larger quantities than they would at traditional supermarkets. Costco has built a fiercely loyal following thanks to its low prices, generous portions and famously wide-ranging selection. The latest openings come as Costco works to overhaul checkouts at its US warehouses this year. Several locations are now piloting advanced “Automated Pay Stations”, which feature large digital screens and plenty of space for shoppers to scan bulky items. But it is employee assistance that is helping slash checkout times to around eight seconds. A staff member starts by scanning a customer’s membership card while they wait in line for an Automated Pay Station. They then scan every item in the customer’s cart. By the time the shopper reaches the payment station, they only need to scan their membership card. All of the merchandise in their cart then appears on the screen, allowing them to pay almost instantly. The checkout changes are just one of several ways Costco is looking to improve the shopping experience for its members. The retailer has also revealed that around 14,000 residents have already signed up for memberships since they became available in June. Building on this popularity, company bosses hope to bring more than 25 new stores to the US in 2026.

title: Will the COLA announcement be delayed again this year? What to know
text: Will the COLA announcement be delayed again this year? What to know. Predictions for the annual Social Security cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) have been out since last month. However, the official announcement doesn’t typically occur till the fall. And since it was delayed last year, many Social Security beneficiaries might be wondering if the same thing’ll happen this year. The Motley Fool explains that last year’s COLA announcement was pushed back because a key inflation report was released later than expected due to the government shutdown. COLAs are based off of specific Consumer Price Index (CPI) information, according to the Social Security Administration (SSA). So, since that report didn’t come in when it was supposed to, the 2025 COLA announcement was also released at a different time. But since there’s no shutdown this year — and since there’s currently no impending flies-in-the-ointment for the release of that CPI data — there’s no reason to believe that this year’s COLA announcement will be delayed, too, The Motley Fool states. The most recent COLA projections from the Senior Citizens League (TSCL) estimates 2027’s COLA to be at 3.8 percent. Should this come to pass, it’d be the largest COLA increase seen since 2022. A league press release notes that this would bring the average retiree monthly benefit amount from $2,026.41 to $2,103.41, a $77 bump. Still, TSCL Executive Director Shannon Benton warns that still might not be enough given current prices. “We’re seeing inflation on the rise when more than half of seniors already can’t afford basic living standards,” said Benton via the release. “We’re talking about food, a roof over their heads, and transportation. “Many seniors already have to skip doctor’s appointments due to costs, which costs all of us more in the long run when we swap preventative care for emergency care. A 3.8 percent COLA might sound like a lot compared to last year’s 2.8 percent, but it won’t be enough to make up the difference between what seniors bring in and what they need to live with dignity.” This year’s COLA announcement is expected to take place on Oct. 14.

title: Rents are falling across the country. But not here.
text: Rents are falling across the country. But not here.. Something strange has been happening this year in Los Angeles, San Diego, Washington D.C., and Denver: In some of the nation’s most expensive places to live, rents have fallen, offering residents a rare reprieve. But not in Boston. For all the challenges facing Boston’s economy right now — cuts at universities and research labs, sluggish job growth, people moving away — rents both in the city and the broader metropolitan area have defied economic gravity, either rising modestly or remaining flat year over year, depending on which numbers you look at. And while other markets have seen an influx of new construction driving rents downward, that hasn’t been nearly as much the case here. In other words, while rents fall elsewhere, even in higher-cost cities where prices have historically been stubborn, Boston’s housing market is so out of whack that it’s in a class largely by itself. “There are two big factors at work here: People really want to live in Boston, and the Boston area has one of the largest housing shortages in the country,” said Adam Guren, an associate professor of economics at Boston University. “Those two things together make it pretty difficult for rents to go down.” By multiple measures, rents have ticked up here lately. The median rent for a two-bedroom apartment in Boston in June was $2,524, according to the rental listing website Apartment List, which estimates rents based on census data and a formula calculated from the company’s listings. That was just slightly up from $2,498 in June 2025. In the broader region, rents remained flat year over year. Real estate website Zillow, which calculates rents based on its own listings and tends to skew toward higher-end buildings, estimated rents in Boston climbed 2.9 percent from June 2025 to June 2026, and 2.6 percent in the Greater Boston metropolitan area. That is in keeping with the longstanding trend around here: Rents have been on a steady upward march for decades, with the exception of the pandemic years, when they fell briefly before the rental market caught fire. But cracks have begun to appear lately in the region’s economy. The local biotech industry is faltering, and so are the universities that prop up much of what makes the region tick. Elevated inflation and runaway living costs have put a damper on things, too. Some have speculated that a weakened local economy could help nudge rents down. And, indeed, that has happened in some other markets, including some of Boston’s high-cost peer cities. In Los Angeles, for instance, overall rents were down 1.4 percent through July, according to Apartment List. In Washington, D.C., and Seattle, they were down 2.7 percent. And rents dipped 0.6 percent in San Diego. The other dynamic driving rents downward elsewhere: a surge in housing production. Many places saw big upticks in building permits for new multifamily housing in 2021 and 2022, projects that have finished construction and opened in the last year or so. That has helped drive up inventory in many places that have long had significant housing shortages. There may be no bigger example of that than Austin, Texas. The city added roughly 120,000 new units between 2015 and 2024, and rents there have been dropping steadily, down nearly 8 percent between July 2023 and July 2024, according to Apartment List, and 3.8 percent in the last year. To be sure, Greater Boston saw a boost in construction too; state officials have said Massachusetts added 34,500 homes in 2025, a huge increase from the annual average. That helps, but not enough to bring rents down. Other places have built more, and Greater Boston faces a bigger shortage. “Boston has seen a lot more units coming online relative to its own historical benchmark,” said Chris Salviati, chief economist at Apartment List. “But relative to the Austins and Phoenixes of the world, where you’ve seen meaningful reductions in the cost of rent, it’s nowhere near that level.” It’s hard to argue that rents going up is a good thing, said Salviati. It is a symptom of the city’s extreme shortage of homes, and it makes living here extremely difficult for renters, especially low- and middle-income families. But it does reflect the strength of Boston’s economy. Even with some signs that the rental market has weakened slightly in some student neighborhoods such as Brighton and Brookline, overall demand to live in Boston is still high. Boston is in a select group of expensive cities — including New York City and San Francisco — with alluring local industries and universities where demand to live is so strong and homes so few that housing costs continue to rise regardless of local and national economic swings. In New York, rents were up 3.4 percent year over year in July. And in San Francisco, bolstered by an AI boom, they’ve soared 23 percent in the last year above levels that were already the highest of any big city in the country. It would take a sustained period of significantly increased housing production, perhaps coupled with a worsening downturn, for rents here to fall, said Orphe Divounguy, a senior economist at Zillow. That does not appear to be in cards right now. Permits for new homes have fallen steeply since 2022 — 2023 and 2024 were the slowest years for new construction in Boston since the Great Recession — meaning few new apartments will come online over the next few years. “The fact remains that there is a massive housing deficit in the Boston area that is ultimately driving up rents,” said Divounguy. “That shortage built up over many many years of underbuilding, and it is going to take sustained effort to build out of it and bring costs down.” Andrew Brinker can be reached at andrew.brinker@globe.com. Follow him @andrewnbrinker.

title: The Buc-ee’s Marketing Lesson Rory Sutherland Says Every Founder Should Learn From
text: The Buc-ee’s Marketing Lesson Rory Sutherland Says Every Founder Should Learn From. When it comes to marketing a business, founders sometimes focus on the wrong things, says Rory Sutherland, vice chairman of the Ogilvy & Mather group of companies. The advertising expert, who has given multiple TED talks and written several books on the marketing industry, is the co-founder of a behavioral science practice at Ogilvy that applies psychological insights to solve business challenges. Successfully marketing your business ultimately comes down to a handful of factors, says Sutherland, who was a recent guest on the My First Million podcast. He offered these nuggets of advice for founders trying to identify the best way to market their company, including a helpful lesson from Buc-ee's. Eliminate spec speak Sutherland says founders too often communicate a product or service's benefit by focusing on technical specifications rather than the outcomes customers will experience. The nuts and bolts don't matter, he says. The results do. Sutherland pointed to James Watt, who invented the term "horsepower" rather than focusing on the details of the steam engine. "An invention isn't an innovation until it changes behavior," he said. "The only real measure of the effect you're having on innovation is the extent to which you change behavior." Reverse benchmarking Competing on a feature-by-feature basis with a competitor is a losing game, says Sutherland. It makes it hard to stand out and the bar is constantly being moved. Instead, he says, founders should improve one thing that their competitors neglect. He calls this reverse benchmarking. Trillions of dollars each year are invested chasing metrics that customers often don't notice or care about. But focusing on something small can have huge returns. He pointed, as an example, to the gas station convenience chain Buc-ee's, which became known for having remarkably clean bathrooms. "[Take] something that's bad about the category [and do] it spectacularly," he said. "That's what Buc-ee's did. They basically started with an insight around women's restrooms. You could have just had averagely clean women's restrooms. You would have benchmark. No, no, no! They're like the bloody Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, right?" He added: "Look at all the metrics that everybody cares about in the category, find a metric that's been completely and ridiculously neglected, and double down on that thing now." Prioritize friction removal over bigger, faster, better Removing a tiny friction point can be more valuable than a major engineering breakthrough, Sutherland says, adding that these small touches can create disproportionate value. He mentioned how getting a rental car at the airport could be dramatically improved without any tech advances, as an example. Instead of having to wait at a car rental desk, which is a frustrating experience then wander around a parking lot looking for your vehicle, he said rental car companies that met customers at the arrival gate and walked you to the car (and perhaps have the air conditioning turned on in advance) could stand out in a market where the big players are largely interchangeable. For the most part, Sutherland said, customers don't want additional capability. They want to cut their anxiety. Compete on psychology, not price On a similar theme, while competing on price has its advantages (and pitfalls), the real battle to win, said Sutherland, is one that results in the customer feeling better. Emotions will always triumph over economics. He pointed to Uber as the best example of this. The company, he said, improved waiting for a ride, removing the uncertainty from the process and made payment a much more streamlined process. The process of getting from point A to point B is the same as a taxi, though. "The economists and what the Harvard Business Review would say is that they achieved [success] through lower prices," said Sutherland. "I don't think they did. I don't think Uber is reliably cheaper, necessarily. I think they achieved it through better psychology." Embrace uncertainty One of the biggest advantages that entrepreneurs have, said Sutherland, is they are able to make intuitive bets. That's something a large corporation can't do. If you're able to be comfortable in an uncertain environment, you can ignore the status quo and focus on innovation. Put another way, entrepreneurs have more freedom to take big swings. The data large corporations study is past-focused, so decision making has a status-quo bias. Founders can look past that. "The way that businesses are structured as you push responsibility and accountability further and further down the organization, they become more and more risk-averse and they become more and more uncertainty adverse," he said. Nimble entrepreneurs, on the other hand, are able to adapt, reinvent and reposition their businesses in pursuit of breakthroughs, even when there’s a risk in doing so.

title: Dallas says it’s redefining government with new $5.6 billion budget proposal
text: Dallas says it’s redefining government with new $5.6 billion budget proposal. Dallas’ largest ever proposed budget relies on job cuts, privatizing services and reducing hours at libraries to offset the rising cost of the police and fire departments. The city’s $5.6 billion budget proposal would close a projected $51 million shortfall by eliminating 296 positions from payroll and reducing hours and programs at some city facilities. The job cuts and reorganization alone are expected to save the city $17.3 million. City Manager Kimberly Bizor Tolbert said the current budget is not a “one-time fix.” Financial forecasts and technology are evolving quickly, forcing the city to adapt its services, she said. Growing pension payments and rising costs are forcing the city to consider privatizing services, lowering its minimum hourly pay for some custodial or temporary service workers and eliminating the co-pay program offered as part of employees’ healthcare benefits. The budget proposal calls for a modest tax rate decrease but also includes some increases to fees for certain city services. And, the city could withdraw roughly $719,000 in stipends and management payments, affecting partners like the Trinity River Audubon Center, Cedar Ridge Preserve, the Dallas Arboretum and the Dallas Zoo. The City Council will begin discussing the proposed budget Tuesday and will vote on a final plan Sept. 16. Some council members have shown early support for Tolbert’s proposal, saying they’re pleased no libraries or recreation centers would be closed, though they acknowledge government spending has grown. The financial pressure is not an isolated issue. Austin, Houston and San Antonio are also short tens of millions of dollars and put the onus of budgetary issues on wage, pension and public safety costs. Council member Paula Blackmon said people are feeling uneasy about the economy. “We're not exempt from those prices going up either,” she said. Private sector services City government is evolving and Tolbert said the city was prioritizing services such as infrastructure and public safety that ranked high in the recent community survey. The city’s budget proposal calls for more funding for the fire and police departments, and less for libraries as the city seeks to privatize or outsource services. Library programs such as adult GED learning classes and citizenship classes would be turned over to private partners. And city staffers are looking for private operators for the Cedar Crest Golf Course and Southern Skates Roller Rink. “Instead of looking at who's delivering that service, look at it as — is the service going to be interrupted?” Blackmon said. The proposed budget also slashed other programs that were deemed to not be part of the city’s core services. The municipal court’s underutilized Public Inebriated Sobering Diversion Program was cut. The Arts and Culture department lost 12 positions, including one that was transferred to convention services and three cuts in the public arts program. The housing and community empowerment department’s budget was reduced. The IT department’s budget went down by $8 million. The city saved another $16.22 million in future replacement costs by removing 164 underutilized vehicles. Though Dallas plans to keep all 29 library branches open next fiscal year, the budget proposal eliminates 72 library positions and restructures services around five flagship locations with extended hours and programming. “No one wants to see employees lose their jobs, and I regret that those reductions were necessary,” council member Kathy Stewart said. Taxpayer impact The tax rate might have seen a slight decline, but some fees could increase. The city’s proposal cuts the property tax rate by 0.10 cents per $100 of assessed value, a move that will save the median homeowner $62 next year. The reduction only impacts the account used to pay off the debt, and would result in $2.3 million in foregone revenue. The rate the city relies on for operating dollars remains unchanged in the draft budget. But true savings for taxpayers are uneven, partly due to different fee rates households will incur based on whether they have curbside or alleyway trash pickup. If you’re among the 64% that has curbside trash pickup, you may save about $19 next year. If you have an alley pick up, you’re going to pay a premium — $41 more. Starting February next year, the curbside collection fee would decrease by about $2 to $37.76 and alley service will go up to $45.22. Stormwater, ambulance, fire inspection and permitting fees went up substantially to help pay for department operations and infrastructure projects. Council member Lorie Blair said residents wanted tax relief. “You can't provide more with less,” she said. Budget winners Every department was asked to prune their expenses, but some fared better than the others. Funding for the police and fire department grew at 6.9%, outpacing the general fund’s 4.1% growth. Public safety costs typically rise with every budget cycle and come largely from pension payments, overtime laws and compensation. To get out of that bind, the draft recommends asking voters to approve $500 million in pension obligation bonds, with the hope that investments will get a higher rate of return. Experts say the measure should be a last resort. The city’s transportation department funding also grew, with more investments in pavement markings and bridge maintenance. Tolbert’s proposal adds $142.8 million in funding to repair and maintain 800 lane miles, a jump from 759 miles. The plan increases funding for deferred maintenance at city-owned facilities, continued funding for the bike plan and will add 50 extra traffic signals for safer roads. The proposed budget increased the parks and recreation budget by about $2 million to $119.3 million. But the extra funding also included cutting 30 positions to preserve recreation centers, pools, park maintenance and safety operations. Park Board member JR Huerta said people value parks more than ever now and if council members try to take money away from them, people are going to be upset. A park is “the simplest thing you can give to a resident,” Huerta said. “You can always give them a nice park.”

title: After closing stores, retailers make a risky cash trade
text: After closing stores, retailers make a risky cash trade. Anyone watching late-night television has heard those ads that urge people to sell the rights to a structured settlement won in a lawsuit to get cash now. "If you agree to take your award or settlement as a structured settlement, instead of receiving one large amount from the plaintiff, you will receive periodic payments over the course of a fixed number of years," according to Nolo.com . The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) explains why selling your settlement for quick cash can often be a very bad idea. "When you sign over some — or all — of your structured settlement payments to a company in exchange for a lump sum of money, it’s called 'factoring.' But you won’t get all the money you would’ve collected over time — and it might leave you without a way to pay your bills," the FC warned. It's a practice dangerous enough to consumers that "Last Week Tonight" host John Oliver did a segment on it, warning people to "run, don't walk, run away" from factoring companies. Now, two struggling mall retailers, American Eagle Outfitters and The Children's Place, have sold the rights to their federal tariff refunds for pennies on the dollar. The transactions differ in important ways. Structured settlements are designed to provide long-term income for individuals, while tariff refund sales are corporate financing decisions. The similarity is that both involve accepting less money today in exchange for giving up a larger future payment. American Eagle Outfitters has closed stores Both American Eagle Outfitters and The Children's Place have closed stores as part of a broader restructuring plan. "American Eagle Outfitters has closed three stores in Pennsylvania as part of its restructuring plan to close 35 locations nationwide," TheStreet's Kirk O'Neil reported in January. The chain also made additional cuts beyond its store closures. American Eagle will discontinue third-party logistics services over the next several months and will close operations at its Boston and Dallas fulfillment centers in the first half of 2026. The company had previously announced that its La Palma, Calif., fulfillment center would close this year, but its Atlanta fulfillment center will continue to provide distribution services for American Eagle brands. Turnaround efforts have generally shown progress, according to the company's first-quarter earnings release . Total net revenue of $1.2 billion increased 10% to last year. Total comparable sales increased 8%. Aerie comparable sales grew 25%. American Eagle comparable sales decreased 2%. Gross profit of $456 million rose 41% from $322 million last year. American Eagle has a manageable debt load, with cash and cash equivalents at about $103.3 million as of May 2, 2026. The chain also has a revolving credit facility of up to $700 million with $85 million outstanding. The Children's Place closed stores, too The Children's Place began the process of closing stores in 2020. "Executives said 300 stores will permanently close in the next 20 months: about 100 by the end of the second quarter for a total of 200 closures this year, and another 100 set to close in 2021," reported Retail Dive . The chain has continued to selectively close locations since that initial 300, but its recent financial results show less progress than American Eagle's turnaround, according to the chain's first-quarter earnings release . Net sales decreased $26.9 million, or 11.1%, to $215.2 million in the three months ended May 2, 2026, compared to $242.1 million in the three months ended May 3, 2025. The decrease in net sales was driven by a decrease in direct-to-consumer (DTC) sales of 10.2% due to lower traffic compared to the prior year period. Gross profit decreased $17.4 million to $53.4 million in the three months ended May 2, 2026, compared to $70.8 million in the three months ended May 3, 2025. Operating loss was $42.2 million in the three months ended May 2, 2026, compared to a loss of $24.1 million in the three months ended May 3, 2025. Unlike American Eagle, which still has a sizable liquidity cushion, The Children's Place is operating with a much tighter financial position. The company ended the first quarter with $4.8 million in cash and $82.8 million in total liquidity, including available borrowing capacity, while carrying $150 million in revolver borrowings. It also burned $53.8 million in operating cash during the quarter. In response to the results, CEO Muhammad Umair shared that the company has sold the rights to its tariff refunds. More Retail: Dollar General copies Costco’s playbook with a discount twist Pepsi and Coca-Cola bet big on soda Americans say they want Iconic supermarket chain closes more stores and facilities "While keeping our prices stable has narrowed our profit margins, further compounded by product cost headwinds from higher tariffs, we have filed for tariff refund claims amounting to approximately $40 million, which we expect to partially offset margin dilution during this fiscal year, and of which $5.5 million has already been received to date," he said. The company, he noted, gave up some of its future payment in order to get its cash now. "Consistent with prior disclosures, we have monetized most of these claims at a discounted rate, by selling the future receipt of these funds to a purchaser," he added. American Eagle Outfitters has progressed with its turnaround plan. Shutterstock American Eagle Outfitters also sold its refunds American Eagle Outfitters Michael A. Mathias, who just transitioned from CFO to strategic advisor for the brand, discussed tariff refunds during the chain's first-quarter earnings call . "We have applied for roughly $190 million in tariff refunds and anticipate a $140 million net cash benefit," he said. The company, he explained, did sell the rights to some of its refunds. "We at the beginning of the year, we sold about $70 million worth of claims for roughly a $20 million net number. So our net number on the $190 million total filings will be around, should be $140 million if we do get it all back. And, again, we are a little over $100 million back so far, which our portion of that net is around $70 million," he added. Selling refunds comes with a risk American Eagle Outfitters and The Children's Place are taking less cash overall to get their money faster. “For the seller, a lot of the risk is purely the economics of that transaction because of the uncertainty on exactly when an importer will receive their tariff refund,” BDO Managing Principal David Wong told Retail Dive . “That’s been the biggest risk. Do I want to take a discount on the amount that could be refunded to me and get upfront cash today, and how does that compare with the full amount plus interest if I got that amount at a later date?” American Eagle and The Children's Place are not alone in selling their refund rights. With refunds rolling out in phases, some businesses in need of cash are growing impatient, Neil Seiden, managing director at business loan advisory firm Asset Enhancement Solutions, told The Wall Street Journal . “What we’re seeing now is an increase in folks looking to sell the claims,” he said, noting that inquiries have jumped by at least 50% since early June. Academy Sports and GoPro also sold rights to at least a portion of their refunds, according to the The Journal. Those companies sold their rights before the Supreme Court decision that paved the way for the actual refund payments to be made. When a company sold, and at what rate, makes it clear whether a company made the right choice, according to Gregory Husisian, a partner at law firm Foley & Lardner . “There is still a major category of refunds where both the timing and whether you will get it is uncertain,” he said. “If you’re getting something pretty close to a full recovery and you’re getting it quicker, that combination might be enough.” American Eagle Outfitters sold $68.9 million of the retailer’s refund claims for $18.6 million in cash, while The Children's Place sold $38.2 million of its refund claims at a total purchase price of about $25.7 million, according to Retail Dive. title: Walt Disney has permission to build a new Florida theme park
text: Walt Disney has permission to build a new Florida theme park. Walt Disney has not opened a new full-size theme park at Florida's Disney World since adding Animal Kingdom in 1998. You could even argue that DAK, as it's known to fans, wasn't even a traditional full-day park until it opened the "Pandora: The World of Avatar" land in 2017. The company has not simply sat back on its heels since 1998, though. It has significantly expanded Disney's Hollywood Studios by adding Star Wars and Pixar-themed lands as well as numerous rides, and by overhauling an entire section of Magic Kingdom. It has not, however, made any moves to build a fifth theme park on the property, even after rival Universal Studios opened its third full-size theme park, Epic Universe, in May, 2025 as part of an effort to give visitors more reasons to spend their entire vacation on-property. Walt Disney executives have even openly talked about expanding their four existing Disney World parks rather than opening another. But while the company has not shared plans for a fifth gate, it did secure permission from the Florida board that governs its property to build one. Disney World has steadily added and revamped its parks At the time of Epic Universe's opening, speculation ran high that Walt Disney would build a fifth Florida theme park, and some experts even saw it as inevitable. “Disney and Universal are in the greatest boxing match they’ve ever been in at this point in time, and it’s a slug fest,” Dennis Speigel, owner and founder of consulting firm International Theme Park Services, told Disney Tourist Blog . “I believe that within 12 to 16 months, Disney will announce its fifth gate theme park, because it’s necessary.” And although we're still a few months away from that deadline, the company has not done or said anything to suggest it will meet that timeline. In fact, Disney executives have actively discussed expanding the existing parks. Disney's CFO spoke about adding new lands and attractions to the company's parks during May's MoffettNathanson's Media, Internet & Communications Conference . "Without expansion, we don’t necessarily have the ability to grow attendance massively because it’s already filled up. Now we could jam more people into the park, but then the guest experience declines, and that’s actually bad for the brand. So you don’t want us to do that, and we don’t think it’s a good idea either," he said. He also shared that new attractions help the company keep ticket prices high. "When you put in a big new attraction, you actually see a surge in demand for it as well. So we tend to fill those things up really, really quickly without having to discount," he added. "And in fact, it actually offers some ability to charge more because essentially, you're offering something new that wasn't there before." Tabitha Heath, a travel agent with Postcard Travel Planning who serves as the company's Disney expert, thinks it's more important for the theme park giant to keep evolving rather than adding a new park. "With the new expansions and theme plans at Disney World, they will excite new customers and old ones, too," she told TheStreet. "A lot of the new changes across all the parks will encompass multiple generations and bring back some of the old rides and themes." Disney World expansions since Animal Kingdom opened (1998) While Disney hasn't built a fifth gate, it has steadily expanded its existing parks with new lands and attractions over the past 27 years. Asia (Animal Kingdom), 1999: New land added with "Kali River Rapids" and "Maharajah Jungle Trek." "Expedition Everest" (Animal Kingdom), 2006: Major roller coaster added to the Asia section. New Fantasyland (Magic Kingdom), 2012: Largest expansion in Magic Kingdom history, adding areas themed around "Beauty and the Beast," "The Little Mermaid," and more. "Seven Dwarfs Mine Train" (Magic Kingdom), 2014: Family coaster added as part of New Fantasyland. Pandora: The World of Avatar (Animal Kingdom), 2017: New land featuring "Avatar Flight of Passage" and "Na’vi River Journey." Toy Story Land (Hollywood Studios), 2018: Pixar-themed land featuring "Slinky Dog Dash," "Toy Story Midway Mania," and "Alien Swirling Saucers." Star Wars: Galaxy’s Edge (Hollywood Studios), 2019: New Star Wars land featuring "Millennium Falcon: Smugglers Run" and "Rise of the Resistance." "Mickey & Minnie’s Runaway Railway" (Hollywood Studios), 2020: New attraction replacing "The Great Movie Ride." "Remy’s Ratatouille Adventure" (EPCOT), 2021: New attraction added to the France pavilion. "Guardians of the Galaxy: Cosmic Rewind" (EPCOT), 2022: Epcot’s first roller coaster. "TRON Lightcycle / Run" (Magic Kingdom), 2023: New Tomorrowland roller coaster. "Journey of Water, Inspired by Moana" (EPCOT), 2023: Interactive water attraction added during Epcot’s transformation. "Tiana’s Bayou Adventure" (Magic Kingdom), 2024: Replaced "Splash Mountain" with a Princess and the Frog-themed attraction. "Zootopia: Better Zoogether!" (Animal Kingdom), 2025: New 4D show replacing the former "It’s Tough to Be a Bug" experience. Sources: All items sourced from the Disney World website Disney World clears way for 5th theme park Disney World used to govern itself under the former Reedy Creek Improvement District, which is now known as the Central Florida Tourism Oversight District (CFTOD). Instead of Walt Disney controlling the district where its parks sit, it's now governed by the CFTOD, which is appointed by Governor Ron DeSantis , who has been a vocal Disney critic . More Travel: Disney World shuts down part of legendary resort Popular Disney World ride shut down with no explanation Tourists stranded as travel agency files bankruptcy, cancels trips Still, after multiple lawsuits were dropped by both sides, the CFTOD and Walt Disney have, at least to outward appearances, worked together on the future of the 43-square-mile Disney World property. That massive area consists of four theme parks (Magic Kingdom, Epcot, Disney's Hollywood Studios, and Disney's Animal Kingdom), two water parks (Disney's Typhoon Lagoon and Disney's Blizzard Beach), a dining/shopping complex (Disney Springs), and more than 20 resort hotels, among other attractions. The CFTOD marks unbuilt land inside the property as "suitable," "marginally suitable," "marginally unsuitable," or "unsuitable" for development. A "suitable" ranking does not mean that Disney will build something on the site; it just means that it could. The CFTOD compiled a 406-page document entitled Comprehensive Plan 2045 in an effort to "provide the basis for future decisions regarding land use, development, conservation, and infrastructure" in September 2025. While the plan does not authorize construction, it establishes where future development could legally occur. An update to that plan was released in July, containing language that clears the way for a fifth gate at Disney World, while indicating that the project not underway. "Although Table 2-1 (Maximum Development 2025- 2045) allows for development of one major and two minor theme parks there are no plans under review. Approximately 850 acres would be required for these uses," Plan 2045 shared. "Star Wars: Galaxy's Edge" was a major expansion to Disney's Hollywood Studios. Daniel Kline&solTravelHost DIsney World has big expansion plans New Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro openly talked about expanding Disney World's existing parks for years in his previous role as Parks Chairman. He did address those plans during the company's third-quarter earnings call . "As always, we're being disciplined in our capital allocation with a focus on expanding our capacity around the world and driving incremental demand. The pipeline includes major attractions at every site, including Villains Land in Orlando and the Avengers Campus expansion in Anaheim, amongst others in the U.S. and our previously announced cruise ship expansion," he said. As a Disney World and Universal Studios Orlando passholder who has covered the industry for decades , I actually prefer this approach. Disney's parks can get very crowded, and any added attractions, as long as they continue to cap attendance, should help deliver a better experience. Epic Universe does make Universal Studios a property that now takes more than two days to completely experience, but Disney World still has a massive advantage with each park in the complex deserving at least one full day. I have been able to do most of the rides at Universal Studios and Island of Adventure in one long day, but a day and a half is more realistic. Add in a day for Epic Universe, and Universal Studios Orlando is still a long weekend park, while Disney World can fill up a weeklong vacation. That will only improve for Disney World as it keeps rolling out new attractions.
